name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election season is done. Holiday season is approaching. And lawmakers still have dozens of big decisions to make.
description: It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session.
text:
THERE’S NO PLACE like the State House for the holidays.
It’s easy to forget amid all the hubbub of a national blue wave and a nine-question state ballot, but with the election now past, the Legislature has a long list of business left to accomplish in the eight holiday-punctuated weeks remaining before the 2025-2026 term draws to a close.
“Long” might actually be an understatement. There are 12 House-Senate negotiating panels still working to finalize compromise bills, plus a late-moving spending proposal needed to close the state’s financial books. But because legislative leaders prefer to cram multiple topics into each omnibus package, the number of discrete policy decisions still in play reaches into the dozens.
By our count, there are more than 40 significant policy choices the Democrats who control Beacon Hill need to make before the final gavel rings out on January 5, 2027, ranging from whether to upzone the entire state for duplex development to whether to ban the sale of dogs, cats, and rabbits in pet stores. Any bill left unfinished by the term’s end will expire, and lawmakers will need to start the process from scratch after they’re sworn in for the 2027-2028 session.
Our tally may be exhausting, but it is not exhaustive. We did not include every one of the discrepancies in spending between House and Senate legislation, which are more granular.
It’s a lot to track, even for professional Beacon Hill-watchers.
Because almost everything is now in the hands of conference committees, the actual policy decisions will essentially be made behind closed doors by only a handful of Democrats. Each panel is working to iron out differences between the underlying House and Senate versions of a bill; once its members reach agreement, the rest of the Legislature will only get a chance to vote up or down on the final accord — usually with no more than a day or two’s notice on the actual substance — without making any further changes.
House Speaker Ron Mariano said Friday that the negotiating teams are ” making progress and working hard.”
“It’s important to understand that these are complex policy decisions that take time, and often many conversations and meetings to resolve,” Mariano said in a statement to CommonWealth Beacon. Stretching the timeline, he added, gives lawmakers “more time to work diligently to reach the best possible policy outcomes — understanding that the content of the final product is far more important than reaching an agreement quickly solely for the sake of doing so.”
It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session. For decades, lawmakers set themselves an earlier deadline, writing into their internal rules that no formal sessions can take place after July 31 in the second year of the term. Roll call votes can only happen in a formal session, so the rule effectively meant the only lawmaking that could occur after the cutoff date needed to be uncontroversial enough to win unanimous support.
Prior generations of lawmakers created the deadline almost immediately after a stinging controversy about lame-duck session shenanigans. Weeks after the 1994 election, with only a bit more than a month left in the legislative term, Republican Gov. Bill Weld suddenly filed legislation authorizing a 55 percent pay raise for lawmakers even though, as CommonWealth’s Dave Denison put it, he was previously “on record as being cool to the idea.” The Legislature quickly approved the measure, and days later, they also advanced a tax cut bill that had been quietly amended to include a capital gains tax cut — a Weld priority that had long failed to gain traction.
After drawing intense criticism for what struck many as a quid pro quo exchange, lawmakers the following year codified a new rule: Formal sessions, and therefore major business of any kind, must end by July 31 in the term’s second year. Republican Rep. David Peters of Charlton, who self-identified as “one of the loudest critics of the system,” at the time called the new deadline “one of the most significant reforms I’ve seen since I’ve been in the building,” according to a 1995 State House News Service report.
Three decades later, the current crop of legislative leaders decided the rule was worth tweaking after a pair of especially chaotic sprints to the finish line. In both 2022 and 2024, the House and Senate headed into July 31 with several major bills stuck in conference committee. Still hoping to strike deals, lawmakers kept the sessions going well past sunrise on August 1, then adjourned with some matters still unresolved.
This term, lawmakers agreed to a different approach. The Legislature’s new rules still require major bills to get an initial round of approval in both the House and Senate by July 31, but as long as conference committee negotiations started by that date, lawmakers can reconvene in a formal session any time before the term ends to greenlight a final compromise version.
Lawmakers sent 12 different matters into conference committees by the deadline this term. None produced any agreements by Election Day, leaving essentially the entire pile of business that was unfinished on August 1 to be decided in lame-duck sessions — including a potential rewrite of a public records ballot question voters just approved in a landslide.
“The whole point behind the July 31 extension for conferences was to take the pressure off the last couple of weeks and say, ‘We’re close here, if we meet a few more times on this, we can wrap this up before the end,’” Mariano said in the summer.
It’s safe to say the pressure is back on.

text:
A voter fills out a ballot at the Portland Expo in Maine’s June 9, 2026, primary election. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)I hope this column will rescue the ballot of someone you know from being discarded.
You can help.
The 2026 election has not ended.  There are 61 counties in North Carolina where voters with ballots in limbo could decide who wins or loses. The close contests include three Congressional races, several contests for seats in the General Assembly, and more than a dozen local elections, from school board to district attorney.
NC elections board moves to make it easier to toss voters’ ballots

More than 35,000 provisional ballots are still being evaluated by local election officials to see if the person qualifies to vote. Maybe their name didn’t show up on the registration rolls for one reason or another, so they had to cast a provisional ballot. Or they didn’t have an approved photo ID to show the poll worker.
These voters have until noon Tuesday to contact their county board of elections and provide additional information or confirm the official’s research that they are qualified to vote.
Another 700 or so voters who submitted a ballot by mail also need to take immediate action before Tuesday at noon. Some glitch – perhaps an unsealed envelop or missing identity information – is holding up the final decision on whether their ballot will count.
Some of these voters have been contacted by strangers affiliated with a partisan or nonpartisan group. But they may not trust that messenger or may not think it’s worth the time to fix something that shouldn’t be a ballot-counting barrier anyway.
That’s where you come in. Search this list of affected voters in your county. If you know someone on it, please be a trusted messenger and urge them to take action.  It may not be clear what needs fixing – the key is they should immediately contact their county board of elections and learn what is needed. Right away.
One more group of about 250 voters are also on the searchable list.  They used “same-day registration” to register and vote during early voting.  But a verification mailing to them bounced back, so the board of elections may disqualify their ballot – unless they take action by Thursday at noon.
Please go to the names on the list in your county and look for people you know.  There are still undecided contests from Congressional seats to the local courthouse and school board.  Let your friend know that her or his ballot can still count — and could decide who wins and who loses an important election.

name: VTDigger
title: My teeth could kill me
description:
I’ve survived avalanches and earthquakes, but a lack of dental care could be what finally does me in.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  My teeth could kill me.
text:
Dear Editor,
I’ve experienced avalanches, tornadoes, earthquakes, high-voltage shocks and aggressive toxins. And always gotten through. Usually shaken but escaping being stirred into nothingness. Ribs, arms, fingers, legs, back, neck — I’ve broken them all. And while not fun, none of them were dead ends. The hassle and patience of healing was always just a hiccup in my adventures. 
Twenty-five years ago, while training for an extreme skiing competition in Crested Butte, Colorado, I broke my back and neck. “Just” hairline fractures, though my brain was knocked around a bit. As I was getting carted off to the hospital, all I could think was, “At least I didn’t blow a knee,” a common career-ender for alpine professionals. Back then, I was not thinking, “At least I didn’t break a tooth.”
I should have been. My body withstood remarkable abuse for decades. But my teeth are possibly what will kill me. 
Bad teeth are not just a cosmetic issue. An infection could give me mortal sepsis. And my only access to dental care is the emergency room. 
Modern health coverage considers teeth essentially disconnected from the rest of the body. And here is how extreme it has gotten: A concussion triggered seizures that resulted in falls that broke teeth. Many tens of thousands of dollars have been spent to fix up my entire body — except the teeth I broke.
I cannot get dental coverage, or come close to being able to afford it out of pocket. I’ve looked carefully for a solution — from free clinics and dental school programs to Medicare and private insurance — but my only options are luck, care, home remedies and the emergency room. If an infection starts to push me into mortal danger? Then health insurance will, hopefully, save my life. But all this will do is treat the symptoms and reset the clock for a new emergency. Such duct-taping of underlying problems is costing us all a lot of money. Much more than if we simply recognized that teeth, like bones, are simply part of our body.

READ MORE

You could be in full-body traction, perhaps from doing something moronic like driving drunk, or tumbling down an avalanche chute. But having bad teeth, even from an accident outside your control? That will create more social barriers and earn more scorn than a body cast. And I’ve been brainwashed by our culture just as much as anyone else: The shame of showing my mouth in public outweighs the pain of simply being alone. 
I hope that a wave of rationality is coming and that we build a structure where we can thrive and help each other stay healthy. A framework of compassion over profit. 
Meanwhile, I count myself lucky. Unlike others in an even worse position, I have food, water and warmth. I also have Tylenol, tooth drops, good books and hope. I know that problems with my teeth are minuscule compared with the health brutality many people are experiencing. I still believe that we, America, are going to reprioritize things and figure these issues out together.
Todd Murchison
Brattleboro, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  My teeth could kill me.

title: Commentary: So who’s the Nevada Republican leader now? Root?
description: If there’s one person who may be even more responsible for the Republicans’ historic-folkloric loss in Nevada’s second congressional district than Trump, it would be conspiracy marketer and decorative state whackadoodle Wayne Allyn Root.  Trump had to get his Nevada congressional endorsement intel, such as it was, from somewhere. text:
If there are Nevada Republicans who understand the need to reject Trump and Trumpism, now would be an opportune time for them to step up and say so. Better late than never.(Image from a flyer for the Clark County Republican Party Lincoln Day Dinner in March 2026)
If there’s one person who may be even more responsible for the Republicans’ historic-folkloric loss in Nevada’s second congressional district than Trump, it would be conspiracy marketer and decorative state whackadoodle Wayne Allyn Root. 


Trump had to get his Nevada congressional endorsement intel, such as it was, from somewhere. At least in the CD2 primary, Trump obviously wasn’t taking cues from Camp Lombardo. The governor was backing someone other than the quack Trump’s endorsement propelled into the general election.


The Nevada person who was most likely instrumental in getting Trump to back the quack would have been Root, a fixture in the MAGA media universe, an occasional warm-up act at Trump’s Nevada rallies over the years, and a very early and loud supporter of the extremely low-quality candidate who would become the first Republican in history to lose CD2. 


This week, for a couple days after what Ron DeSantis described as an “extinction-level event” for Republicans, it looked like Trump might hole up in his happy place and concentrate on redecorating for the remainder of the most disgusting presidency in U.S. history. 


Those hopes were dashed Friday when Trump announced he was turning to the neo-Nazi Nosferatu doppelganger, Stephen Miller, to be his new chief of staff. The fresh consensus is that a Miller-guided Trump will lean in to his underlying instincts and double down on divisiveness, destruction, lawlessness, and senseless chaos.


Root is tickled pink.


“Susie Wiles out- BRAVO!” Root posted on X Friday after the Miller news dropped. “Spend next 2 months left in 2026 confirming 100 GOP judges, nuking filibuster to pass entire Trump agenda, and CHALLENGE THE ELECTION. Time now for my “NEED USA”- National Emergency for Elections Declaration. It was rigged & stolen.”


What’s left of congressional Republicans are unlikely to have much appetite for Root’s prescriptions. Some are openly expressing disgust at Trump naming Miller chief of staff.


For years, Democratic pollyanas have been predicting the MAGA fever will break, and Republicans will rejoin the reality-based community. Maybe it’ll really happen this time.


But then, it also looked like that was going to happen on January 7, 2021.


There’s currently a Republican vacuum in Nevada, in leadership, ideology, and purpose.


Yes, Root’s a preposterous figure. 


He’s also a preposterous figure who was sought out by the Clark County Republican Party in March of this year to emcee its Lincoln Day Dinner. The event’s featured speakers were Lombardo and Nevada Republican Party chair and proud 2020 fake elector Michael McDonald. Lombardo hailed Root as an “awesome spokesperson” for Republicans.


And as of Wednesday morning, Root is a preposterous figure who might be the most nationally prominent Republican in Nevada.


Nevada Democrats are currently and understandably celebrating because they won All The Things. 


Spoiler: Republicans are going to win some elections in Nevada again.


What kind of Republicans will they be? A MAGA garbage fire and brimstone revival led by the screeching, shrieking likes of Root, McDonald, and Michele Fiore? 


Or are there any serious, sensible Nevadans, i.e., Republicans who Root refers to as RINOs, willing to denounce Trump’s lawlessness, corruption, malevolence, and incompetence?


Addled as he is, Trump remains wracked by demons and obsessed with himself, images of unlimited autocratic power dancing in his head.


If there are Nevada Republicans who understand the need to reject Trump and Trumpism (and Miller), now would be an opportune time for them to step up and say so. Better late than never.


Unless they don’t mind risking the chance that the political opposition to Democrats in Nevada will be shaped not by facts and public policy priorities, but by the noxious and polarizing fanaticism of people like McDonald and Root.

name: VTDigger
title: Setting the goal: more households with workers
description:
Next Gen Brattleboro launches with a four-organization alliance, a case for growth, and a $1 million match for a new leadership fund.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Setting the goal: more households with workers.
text:
Kate Trzaskos, executive director of the Downtown Brattleboro Alliance, center, listens to Brattleboro Regional Chamber of Commerce executive director Rachel Shields Ebersole. Photo by Randolph T. Holhut/The Commons

This story by Virginia Ray was first published in The Commons on Nov. 4, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — When State Treasurer Mike Pieciak asked his father what he earned after moving to Brattleboro in 1970, the answer was $10,000 — about $80,000 in today’s dollars. On that salary, his father, the family’s only wage earner, supported a child and owned a home.
“To think about what family could have one spouse working, have a child, and own a home on an $80,000 salary — it doesn’t feel realistic,” Pieciak told a packed Latchis Theatre on Oct. 28. “What do we do to solve that challenge?”
That question framed the public launch of Next Gen Brattleboro, an alliance of the town, the Brattleboro Development Credit Corporation, the Downtown Brattleboro Alliance, and the Brattleboro Regional Chamber of Commerce.
Its goal, which organizers call “802 by 2032,” is to bring 802 new working-age households to town in the next six years.
The evening ended with news from the Vermont Community Foundation: a $1 million matching challenge to launch a new Greater Brattleboro Leadership Fund.
Pieciak, who grew up in Brattleboro, said communities that aren’t intentional about affordability “are going to be left behind. And oftentimes, unfortunately, those communities are our small towns and our rural neighbors.”
“The fact that Brattleboro is being intentional about that question is a huge step in the right direction,” he said.
‘A north star for our town’
Emcee Emma Spett opened by listing the questions she said every small town in Vermont is asking: “Who will run our businesses? How are we going to fill our schools and keep our downtowns vibrant and busy? How can we afford to live here and stay here?”
Spett and her fiancé, Andrew Baldracchi, moved from Burlington to Jamaica about two years ago to open River & Rye, a restaurant and inn. Spett is also a program manager at the University of Vermont’s Leahy Institute for Rural Partnerships.
She said she still thinks Brattleboro “is the coolest place on the planet.”
Brattleboro Town Manager John Potter described Next Gen Brattleboro as three things: an alliance of the organizations on stage; a movement built on four pillars (affordability, advancement, vitality, and belonging); and, as “a north star for our town,” the 802-by-2032 goal of attracting younger people and working-age families.
“As a forester, I’d be remiss to not remind everybody that the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago,” Potter said. “The second best is today.”
For the town, he said, the payoff is affordability. A larger tax base would help pay for services that residents and visitors value.
Growth brings its own costs, Potter acknowledged, “but I think we have the economies of scale in this town, with a full-service town, that will ultimately be better for the whole community.”
BDCC Executive Director Adam Grinold called the target aspirational but concrete: “802 new working-age households,” he said, adding that each includes someone who needs a job, “and behind that job is an employer who needs a person.”
About 15 years ago, Grinold said, BDCC and its regional partners began studying the region’s demographics. They found an aging workforce and a shrinking population and set two goals in response: lower the median age, and raise wages.
“If we don’t move the needle on those numbers, the employers that are here will run out of people before they run out of ideas, and the employers not yet here [will] never come,” he said.
BDCC concentrates on attracting manufacturing and health care, which pay more than the average job in Windham County, Grinold said. That means helping manufacturers such as G.S. Precision and Fulflex stay and expand, and supporting workforce training at the Brattleboro Retreat and Brattleboro Memorial Hospital.
But a job alone won’t keep a young family here, he said.
“We need to be able to have childcare. We need workforce training. We need healthcare. If we don’t have those things, those folks leave,“ Grinold said. “And not one of our organizations can do all of those things for everyone.”
‘Everyone’s downtown’
Kate Trzaskos, executive director of the Downtown Brattleboro Alliance, said Main Street is where the region checks its pulse.
“Brattleboro is everyone’s downtown,” she said. “If you live in Vernon or Dummerston or Jamaica and you say, ‘I am going downtown,’ we all know where you are talking about.”
When downtown is thriving, with crowds out for First Fridays, that energy ripples across the region, Trzaskos said.
“And the reverse is also true. When we feel like somebody else is closing their business, I think you feel that across the community.”
The alliance is launching a program called Vacant to Vibrant to fill empty storefronts for the holiday season. More than 40 applicants have proposed projects, she said, an effort made possible by working with the town, the landlords, and other partners.
“We need to be doing more of that. We don’t need to change Brattleboro,” Trzaskos said. “We just need to take what’s great about it and just turn the dial up.”
Rachel Shields Ebersole, six months into her job as executive director of the Brattleboro Regional Chamber of Commerce, said the alliance itself is news. The four organizations have long worked well together, she said, but “it took a lot to get us all in the same room regularly and agreeing on: How are we going to work together? What is it going to look like?”
“No business owner is just a business owner,” she said. “They’re a partner, they’re a parent, they’re a resident.”
She told of a young family who found Brattleboro online and stopped by the chamber office while visiting to ask what it was like to do business here.
She introduced them to someone in their field, connected them to BDCC, which is participating in the state GROW (Grants for Relocation Outreach Work) program for new and returning Vermonters. And, because they had a child the same age as hers, Shields Ebersole pitched them on her children’s school and explained how Vermont’s childcare credits work.
A few months later, the family walked into her office and announced they had moved.
“So, check that one off,” Shields Ebersole said, noting the goal is now officially “801 households.”
Asked to name Brattleboro’s superpower, Shields Ebersole pointed to “people who make stuff happen.”
Trzaskos said it is “a place where you can be the fullest expression of yourself” — plus a bit of local lore about a crystal beneath the town.
Grinold said it is “the realistic kind of optimism.”
Potter offered a hot take. “The drama. I’ve worked in other towns where there’s, like, apathy,” he said. “And I think drama is the opposite of apathy.”
‘Data is not destiny’
Kevin Chu, executive director of the Vermont Futures Project, put Brattleboro’s goal in a statewide context.
The son of immigrants who came to Vermont from southeastern China in 1986, Chu said he worries that the opportunity his parents found here “might not be as likely today as it was 20, 30, 40 years ago.”
The nonpartisan group’s Vermont Economic Action Plan, released in January 2025 after conversations with more than 5,000 Vermonters in all 14 counties, looks at workforce shortages, the housing crisis, and strains on healthcare, education, and childcare and traces these problems to two root causes: demographics and housing scarcity.
In 2000, Chu said, Vermont had about 226,000 residents ages 25 to 49 and about 77,000 who were 65 or older. Today about 30,000 fewer people are in the younger group, while the 65-and-older population has nearly doubled.
That shift has “massive implications for our workforce, for our economy, for healthcare, for our tax burden,” he said.
In 2025, Vermont averaged 14,000 to 15,000 job openings a month against 7,000 to 8,000 job seekers, Chu said. “So if everyone in Vermont who was looking for a job found a Vermont-based job, we’d still have thousands of jobs to fill.”
The Vermont Department of Labor projects about 17,000 workforce exits a year through 2034, Chu said. Only about 5,000 high school seniors live in the state.
“Even if we retain 100% of those students, it doesn’t close that gap,” he said, adding some in-migration is necessary.
That gap analysis underlies the Vermont Economic Action Plan’s population target of 802,000 Vermonters by 2035. The area-code number is good marketing, Chu acknowledged, “but it’s actually informed by that workforce gap analysis.”
Brattleboro grew by about 79 people from 2010 to 2024, he said, while its median age rose. The town has fewer working-age residents relative to children and seniors than the state as a whole.
“Data is a good starting point for understanding where we are and how we got here, but it doesn’t dictate where we have to go,” Chu said. “Data is not destiny. We’re choosing what the destiny is for Brattleboro.”
‘Yes is the answer’
Any talk of growth has to include housing, Chu said. More than 40% of Brattleboro’s homes were built before 1940, compared to more than 20% statewide, and construction has dropped sharply since the 1970s.
Average household size has also shrunk from about 3.21 people in 1970 to 2.18 statewide and about 2.12 in Brattleboro.
Even if Vermont’s population had not changed since 1970, Chu said, the state still would have needed about 65,000 new homes just to keep up with that trend of smaller households.
He got a laugh with a pair of slides.
“One of these things is accused of attracting crime, lowering property value, and changing the character of places, and it’s actually illegal in many communities,” Chu said of housing. “And the other one is cannabis.”
In some places, he said, it may be easier to open a dispensary than to build housing.
“We have to shift the default so that ‘yes’ is the answer when new housing gets proposed,” he said.
The demand is already here, Chu argued. About 10,000 people work in Brattleboro, and 71.6% of them — more than 7,000 people — live somewhere else, according to the Census Bureau’s OnTheMap commuting data.
“You would only have to capture a small portion of that to reach that 802 goal by 2032,” he said.
Public opinion is moving his way, Chu said. In the Vermonter Poll, conducted with the University of Vermont, more than 80% of respondents last year ranked keeping Vermont’s population growth and density low as the least important of three priorities; affordability ranked first. A majority now supports growing the population to strengthen the workforce, the poll found.
Support for new housing softens closer to home — statewide, then in respondents’ towns, then in their neighborhoods — but “there are more people that say yes than no at every single scale,” he said.
The alternative, which Chu called the “scarcity pathway,” means hard conversations about losing hospital services and consolidating schools. A community defined only by what it says ‘no’ to is in what he called “economic stick season.”
He likened the roughly 2% annual growth he said it would take to get there to building strong bones.
“You can’t just chug a gallon of milk once in a while and hope you have strong bones,” Chu said. “You have to drink your milk every single day.”
Why bet on Brattleboro?
A second panel brought up business owners, artists, and educators who have already made their bet on the town.
“If we want 802 more households to make the same bet, we need to know what makes it easy and what gets in the way,” Spett said.
Jessica Daley Kull, co-owner of the Vermont Country Deli, moved back from the West with her husband, Mike, in 2014 after her parents asked them to join the family business.
The couple wanted to start a family near relatives, she said, and found unusually strong support here: close collaboration among midwives, doctors and the birthing center, and easy access to lactation consulting and children’s services such as occupational and speech therapy through the Winston Prouty Center.
About two years ago, when her parents retired, the couple bought the business.
“We’re kind of the gateway to Vermont,” she said, noting the deli as the first stop for many visitors and their last on the way home.
“A lot of small towns have the problems that we have here,” she said, “but I think what makes Brattleboro unique is the way we’re going about solving them.”
Will Kasso Condry and Jennifer Herrera Condry, cofounders of Brandon-based Juniper Creative Arts, a family collective of educators, community muralists, and healing arts practitioners, run Sucka Punch, an annual three-day graffiti jam that brings artists, MCs, DJs, and breakdancers from around the country to town.
“It’s gritty. It’s urban. It’s just enough urban for us to do what we do, and we can experiment in ways that we wouldn’t be able to anywhere else in the state,” Kasso Condry said of Brattleboro.
So many children turned out for the first jam that the pair expanded youth programming this year.
“Hip-hop culture is the only internationally recognized culture that was started by youth,” Kasso Condry said. “It’s important for us to give it right back.”
Herrera Condry credited the town for embracing the event, along with a property owner who invests in hosting it on his buildings, a museum partner (Brattleboro Museum & Art Center), and the Downtown Brattleboro Alliance, which provides volunteers and helps them navigate “town politics and things like that.”
The goal, she said, is to “not create anything new, but build on what’s already working.”
Gabriel Erde-Cohen, founder of We Clean Heat Pumps and the BRCC’s Entrepreneur of the Year, started the business as a side job cleaning units for Saxtons River Solar Electric, the solar and heat pump installation company his wife and father-in-law founded. They asked him for three years running before he finally agreed.
“I said, ‘No, that sounds terrible,’” he said, but that was before he ended up falling in love with the work and connecting with Green Mountain Power’s heat pump lease program, which helped the business grow.
Based in Brattleboro for eight years, We Clean Heat Pumps now operates in 13 states and performs more than 10,000 cleanings a year.
“The goal is to expand with those Vermont values,” he said. One of those values: paying employees a living wage.
Dory Hamm, a Dummerston native who returned after spending most of his 20s away, is a founder and curator of the Museum of Things Tiny and Found.
In its first six months, the museum has drawn 7,500 visitors, brought in $20,000 through its weekend model, and employed 19 people between the museum and its festival. It also keeps about eight gig workers busy.
Great projects start with an obsession, he said: “Lean into what you love, and then find the people that want to help you.”
Christy Betit, who runs BDCC’s Pipelines and Pathways career education program in schools across Windham County, works with more than 1,000 students a year and connects them with 150 to 200 local professionals through events such as the Reality Fair and career fairs.
In every classroom, students are asked to line up along an imaginary line from “I want to live in Vermont for the rest of my life” to “I want to get as far away from Vermont as humanly possible.”
Most land in the middle or at the stay end, Betit said: “They love it here. They want to stay here.”
The program’s job is to make sure students leave school with a plan, “so that they’re not pushed out of the nest after high school,” Betit said. “So they want to stay here. Let’s give them some housing.”
Also during the evening, students from the University of Massachusetts Amherst’s business and landscape architecture programs described semester-long studio projects envisioning Brattleboro sites.
Their final presentations are set for Dec. 9 at High Street & Green, 22 High St., in the former First Proof Press space near the building’s High Street entrance at a time to be announced.
And in a live audience poll asking what Brattleboro should look like in 2032, the most common answer was “vibrant.”
A $1 million challenge
The night’s biggest news came last.
Elizabeth Catlin, a Vermont Community Foundation board member who has lived in Dummerston for more than 30 years, said she moved here at age 32 to raise a family and has “kind of live[d] the Next Gen Brattleboro dream.”
She said she has often heard that southern Vermont gets forgotten in favor of the north, but through her work on the foundation’s board, she can assert that “that is not true.”
Dan Smith, the foundation’s CEO for the past 10 years, said he had spent the evening scribbling on his program to get the message right, because it was not one he had been in a position to deliver in his decade of work in that role.
The foundation is partnering with Next Gen Brattleboro to create the Greater Brattleboro Leadership Fund, an enduring fund to support organizations in Brattleboro and surrounding communities.
On his drive to the event, Smith said he got a call from Elizabeth Marks, the foundation’s senior philanthropic advisor for southern Vermont: A $1 million matching challenge had been secured to launch it.
Smith did not name the donors.
“This is not about the VCF,” he said. “This is about some folks who saw what you all are doing and believed in it so much that they were willing to make those commitments.”
The match, he said, is “an invitation to others to help grow this into something that endures for this region and for this town and for all of your neighbors.”
“This is what it looks like for communities to thrive,” Smith continued. “This is what it looks like to have leadership that’s local, that is focused on shifting the conditions that hold our challenges in place and bring in new resources and new people to town.”
‘It will not happen’ without intention
Pieciak closed the evening where he started: with intention.
Brattleboro has strengths “that can’t be manufactured,” he said, “things that cannot be bought: that deep sense of community, that deep commitment to place, and that deep commitment to each other.”
But it is up to residents, too, Pieciak added.
“If we are not intentional about making this vision become a reality, it will not happen,” he said.
He then asked the audience to stand and clap “if you’re going to keep standing up for your neighbors” and get involved.
They did.

name: VTDigger
title: Report finds Vermont is experiencing unprecedented weather extremes
description:
Municipalities and the outdoor recreation industry are trying to prepare for an uncertain future, but there’s only so much they can do.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Report finds Vermont is experiencing unprecedented weather extremes.
text:
A snowmaking gun operates at the Mad River Glen ski area in Fayston in Jan. 2023.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
This is the first of two stories on the findings in a new climate assessment. The second story will look at adaptation strategies that the report says could reduce climate risks. 
Ski areas have a lot of priorities to balance when it comes to making snow in a changing climate.
The majority of snowmaking machines at Vermont’s ski areas are several times more energy-efficient than older models, which is helpful as resorts are increasingly reliant on snowmaking, said Molly Maher, president of Ski Vermont, a trade association.
But, she said, when Vermont winters are increasingly experiencing “roller coaster temperatures” and more melting, snowmakers have to be put to work more often. Starting up a snowmaking system takes a lot of time and work — which means money and even more energy. 
“We get snow, then it warms up, and we lose the snow, and then we have to make more snow,” she said. “That, that we don’t like to see.”
Maher’s comments mirrored the findings of the most recent Vermont Climate Assessment, released late last month by the University of Vermont’s Gund Institute. The report is an unflinching look at what Vermont is currently facing year-round in a changing climate, and what residents can expect in the future. It’s the third statewide assessment; the first two were published in 2014 and 2021.
Vermont winters, the latest report says, are seeing inconsistent freeze-thaw cycles, decreased snowpack and more precipitation in the form of rain. 
Those conditions have resulted in a shorter winter sports season and an increased reliance on snowmaking, according to the report.
Last year was a great year for snow, but Maher said ski areas are waiting to see what this year brings, even if it’s shorter periods of freezing temperatures.
“They’re just trying to be as efficient as possible so that they can take advantage of shorter windows if they have to do that,” Maher said. As cold snaps become shorter and more unpredictable, she said, ski areas are adapting with snowmaking systems that can be turned on and off quickly.
She’s also seen changes in more than just temperature volatility: High winds are shutting down ski lifts more often, and recent flooding has caused infrastructure damage at some ski areas. For example, the ski town of Ludlow was hit hard by flash flooding in 2023.
Beyond the winter season, the state is experiencing unprecedented weather extremes, and its climate is getting warmer, wetter and more variable, according to the Gund Institute study.
Average annual temperatures have increased in Vermont by 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit since 1900. The report also found that southeastern Vermont has warmed over a degree more than the rest of the state.

Read The Coming Storm series in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS)

And winters have warmed the most, by 4.6 degrees Fahrenheit since 1900.
The report looked into how climate indicators are changing over time, showing that in many cases the pace of change is increasing.
Average annual snowfall decreased by 4.9 inches per decade over the last 65 years. But that decline is accelerating: Annual snowfall decreased by 8.4 inches per decade in the last 35 years.
The report cites aging infrastructure as a major risk to communities in a changing climate. That is already top of mind for many local municipalities, according to Ted Brady, executive director of the Vermont League of Cities and Towns.
He said an increase in severe weather events has resulted in higher costs for maintaining roads and municipal infrastructure like water and wastewater systems. And he sees municipalities facing more disasters than ever before.
“They’re kind of becoming experts in disaster funding,” he said. “They’re becoming experts in resiliency. Those towns that haven’t been impacted by severe weather events know that they’re not far away from being impacted by a severe weather event.”
And because municipalities are investing so much of their capacity toward climate-related disasters, they’re not able to put that capacity elsewhere.
“If your town manager or your selectboard chair … is spending all their time negotiating with FEMA over reimbursements for your fire station, you’re not spending time worrying about what the future of your library looks like,” he said, describing it as a missed opportunity.
So much of the energy of local governments is going toward repairing or updating infrastructure, and he said it shows up in every conversation in towns across the state.
He said he’s seen an increased interest and participation in conservation and energy committees in local governments.
The authors of the assessment say action is required now to adapt to future climate risks. They call for “coordinated planning and investment in natural, physical, financial, and social infrastructure.”
Brady said Vermont and its governmental bodies have done a good job building systems to try to help local governments, and that it’s ahead of the curve in many ways. But he said the system needs money to make real change on the ground.
“Our municipalities have so many infrastructure needs: water, wastewater, stormwater, paving roads, redoing bridges, redoing culverts. … There’s not enough money from the state trickling to the towns to help them overcome these challenges,” he said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Medicaid expansion supporter hopes lawmakers ‘move on’ after latest ballot fight
description: After South Dakota voters rejected a ballot question Tuesday that could have triggered a repeal of the state’s Medicaid expansion mandate, some people who worked to defeat the measure said lawmakers should listen to voters and stop tinkering with the program. Some lawmakers, meanwhile, remain concerned about the program’s effects on the state budget. The […]
text:
An economic assistance application for the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/110526-Amendment-I-Follow-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
After South Dakota voters rejected a ballot question Tuesday that could have triggered a repeal of the state’s Medicaid expansion mandate, some people who worked to defeat the measure said lawmakers should listen to voters and stop tinkering with the program.
Some lawmakers, meanwhile, remain concerned about the program’s effects on the state budget.
The state’s Republican-dominated Legislature sent Amendment I to the ballot, where it failed with 56% of the votes against it and 44% in favor.
Medicaid is a joint federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes. In South Dakota, it traditionally covered specific low-income groups such as children, elderly people and disabled people. In 2022, South Dakota voters approved expanding Medicaid eligibility to low-income adults with the federal government paying for 90% of the program and the state paying the remaining 10%. Amendment I would have repealed the expansion requirement if the federal government reduced its funding share.
Opponents of the amendment said voters have been clear on Medicaid expansion.
“I think it shows that a majority of South Dakotans supported Medicaid expansion in the past and still do, and just don’t want to mess with it,” said Tim Rave, a Republican former legislator who’s now president and CEO of the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations.
1,213 South Dakotans could lose Medicaid as federal work requirements take effect, department says

Rave said he isn’t sure if state lawmakers will ask voters again to consider changes to the program. In 2024, voters approved an amendment from lawmakers that authorized work requirements for Medicaid expansion recipients, predating a work requirement included in federal legislation approved the next year. Rave said his focus now will be on the state’s revenues and how they could impact healthcare funding.
Deb Fischer-Clemens, president of the South Dakota Nurses Association and a Democratic former legislator, led the opposition group No on I. She’s “hopeful that the message is clear and that we aren’t going to have to deal with this again.”
“I just hope that they move on,” she said of lawmakers. “Other than that, we’ll be watching. We will be watching and paying attention and listening.”
Her attention turns now to “the big picture,” she said, addressing Medicaid changes such as work requirements that came with President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The state Department of Social Services has estimated 1,213 people on expanded Medicaid, about 4% of the group, could be disenrolled after federal work requirements are implemented next year.
Rep. Will Mortenson, R-Fort Pierre, sponsored the resolution that sent Amendment I to the ballot. He said Tuesday that South Dakota’s schools and nursing homes, and the state’s balanced budget, could be imperiled if the state has to shoulder a bigger share of expanded Medicaid costs in the future.
“I hope the Legislature keeps an eye on this issue going forward,” said Mortenson, who did not seek reelection this year.

Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, speaks in the state Senate at the Capitol in Pierre on Feb. 11, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)

Lawmakers estimated last year that if the federal government reduces its support to 70%, the state would be on the hook for about $72 million to sustain the expansion. That worries state Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, who won her bid for reelection Tuesday and sits on the state’s budget committee. She said “something has to be done” about the potential budget constraints that would come with reduced federal funding, but she isn’t sure if lawmakers will address the program again in the near future.
Voters on Tuesday also rejected Amendment L, another lawmaker-proposed amendment that would have raised the threshold for voter approval of state constitutional amendments from a simple majority to 60%. Voters put Medicaid expansion in the state constitution with 56% percent support in 2022, after Republican lawmakers refused to approve the expansion legislatively.
Some lawmakers said a higher threshold for voter approval of constitutional amendments would protect the constitution from policies that don’t belong in it, while preserving it for fundamental elements like the structure and function of government.
It was the third time in recent elections that voters have denied attempts by lawmakers to raise the bar for certain types of ballot questions.
In 2018, voters defeated Constitutional Amendment X, which would have raised the threshold for constitutional amendments to 55%. Constitutional Amendment C failed in 2022. It would have required 60% voter support for ballot questions that increase taxes and fees, or require the state to spend $10 million or more in a measure’s first five years of implementation.
Reynold Nesiba, a Democratic former legislator from Sioux Falls who has worked on previous ballot questions, said Amendment L represented the Republican Party in South Dakota “whittling away at direct democracy” and engaging in “sour grapes” against approved amendments like Medicaid expansion.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Vermont wants a farm show’: Long-running agricultural event returns in April
description:
The Vermont Farm Show was canceled beginning in 2021, but it’s restarting in the spring with a new vision.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Vermont wants a farm show’: Long-running agricultural event returns in April.
text:
Samual Jones, 3, of Milton, looks at Alison the cow with his dad Greg Jones, as Louie Terwilliter from Vermont Technical College looks on at the Vermont Farm Show. Photo by Bob LoCicero/VTDigger

The Vermont Farm Show, a historic meeting place for farmers since the 1930s, is set to return next spring with the first show in seven years taking place April 16-17 at the Champlain Valley Exposition in Essex Junction.
The show, which attracted farmers and vendors from Vermont, New Hampshire, New York and elsewhere, stopped in 2021 in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic. Originally geared toward dairy farmers and maple producers, it used to be a trade show and a place for agriculture and labor associations to meet.
Now, the show’s new organizers want to expand the focus to include education and engagement for the wider community connected to agriculture, not just farmers themselves.
“The re-envisioned event will bring together farmers, producers, industry, and the public for an experience that honors tradition while embracing innovation,” the Vermont Farm Show Foundation wrote in a press release. “This truly marks a new chapter for the Farm Show.”
The foundation, a nonprofit that has taken over as organizer of the show, says its goal is to preserve the legacy of the event and build agricultural knowledge and community for farmers and nonfarmers alike.
Kim Stinson, the foundation’s director, said that in the years the farm show wasn’t running, it was going through significant changes.
In 2024, the Vermont Farm Show’s board of trustees set in motion an engagement process that asked the public, the industry and farmers across the state what they needed and wanted from a reimagined farm show. In the years following, the show changed its tax status and was granted 501(c)3 nonprofit status this year.
“It was determined that yes, Vermont wants a farm show. This is important,” Stinson said. “Our agriculture is a cornerstone of our state’s identity, so here we are.”
The farm show was also a cornerstone of agriculture in Vermont and grew over time to accommodate the changing industry in the state. The show outgrew its original home in Barre and moved to the Champlain Valley Expo in 2012, where even more space was filled with exhibitions. The nonprofit foundation credits the diversifying agricultural sector at the time for the show’s expansion.
The show was one of the “most important gatherings” of the year, said Amanda Ryan, director of operations with the Vermont Farm Bureau.
Ryan said the Farm Bureau is pleased that the show is back on. The bureau has exhibited at the farm show in the past and plans to participate in 2027. 
Lindsey Brand, marketing and communications director for Northeast Organic Farming Association of Vermont, said many of the association’s members are excited the show is coming back and that NOFA-VT staff and members will be in attendance in the spring.
Ryan said the farm community was suffering the loss of the show, and she’s “curious what the reboot looks like.”
According to Stinson, the reboot will include more interactive elements, including hands-on exhibits, workshops and panels. She said there will be products to sample and buy, equipment demonstrations, and perhaps an outdoor component, since the show will be held in the spring.
Traditionally, the show was held in January. Stinson said the board hopes, based on feedback during the engagement process, that hosting it a little later in the year may help people traveling from farther afield to avoid potentially harsh winter weather. And she said the longer spring days help, too.
While the original farm show was an annual multiday event, the foundation is looking beyond the show to try to meet the needs of the agricultural community in different ways.
“Instead of just having an annual show once a year, we’re really looking at the year-round aspect of, what can the Vermont Farm Show Foundation do to support agriculture year-round?” Stinson said.
She also pointed to the much broader network of Vermonters connected to the farming community, like mechanics, electricians and grocery workers. She hopes the upcoming show strengthens and celebrates that network.
“There’s so much connection in every aspect of the Vermont economy that connects back to agriculture,” she said. “It almost looks like a giant food web. Like, how are we all interconnected?”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Auditor raises eyebrows after signing tax deeds for a friend
description: Two state lawmakers are raising questions after the state auditor appears to have stepped to fix a deed issue for a friend.
text:
A West Virginia Watch investigation found West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt’s signature on tax deeds, a move outside of state law governing the sale of delinquent tax properties. (Photo illustration by Amelia Ferrell Knisely)Two state lawmakers are raising questions after the state auditor appears to have stepped to fix a deed issue for a friend.  
The West Virginia state auditor is the state’s bookkeeper and responsible for rooting out fraud, waste and graft within both state and local governments. And in recent years, the auditor has been placed in charge of handling the sale of properties with delinquent taxes. 
But several property transactions in Kanawha and Boone counties show Auditor Mark Hunt may have stepped outside the bounds of the law to sell properties to a Charleston-based attorney who has amassed a land empire throughout the state. 
And records show that same attorney also worked for the Auditor’s Office.
West Virginia Watch, responding to news tips, searched land databases and visited a county clerk’s office to look for deeds with Hunt’s signature. It found that Hunt, a former state senator elected to the office in 2024, personally signed nine tax deeds between March and June 2025.  
State law governing the sale of delinquent tax properties, meaning properties lost because the owner didn’t pay their taxes, states that the deputy land commissioner – not the auditor – is supposed to sign those deeds. 
Hunt said when he came into the office in 2025, the land division that handles the deeds was in disarray, with files upon files of deeds in boxes. When Hunt’s office received a phone call from Robert L. Johns, a bankruptcy attorney, asking about deeds that had not yet been signed, the auditor said he became concerned that the office would be sued if the problem wasn’t fixed. 
A spokesperson for the prior Auditor, now Attorney General JB McCuskey, declined to comment about the state of the office. 
“This is our fault,” Hunt said. “So seeing inequity, I made a decision that I believe the 500,000 people who voted for me gave me that to make a judgment call. I made a judgment call to issue the deeds. 
“There’s no nefarious things here,” Hunt added “Frankly, it’s something I forgot even happened until this tempest in a teapot has come up in the last couple weeks.” 
But state code already addresses what should happen when the Auditor’s Office fails to provide the deed in a timely fashion. The person who bought it must take the deputy land commissioner to court. 
Records show two of the nine deeds were signed beyond a deadline mandated by state law, which Hunt said was due to the disorganized state of the office. 
Sen. Ryan Weld, R-Brooke, speaks on the Senate floor on Feb. 27, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Sen. Ryan Weld, R-Brooke, is an attorney who deals with property rights and has lent a hand in rewriting how the state responds to owners who don’t pay their taxes. 
“It clearly states that deeds for people who purchase properties at these tax sales are issued and signed by the deputy commissioner,” Weld said. 
When a West Virginia landowner fails to pay property taxes, the county can seize the property for back taxes. Prior to changes in 2022, this was handled by the local sheriff. Now, the state auditor’s office handles the sale. An outside party can bid to buy the deed, at which point they have to notify the current owner. If the current owner doesn’t pay up on their taxes or respond, the outside party can then buy the deed to the property outright. 
Hunt’s cursive signature on the documents and the issuance of deeds to someone employed in the auditor’s office is extremely troubling to Weld. 
“On its face, it looks as if it’s intentional. And so you have to ask the question: Why?” Weld said.
Hunt defended his signature on the deeds. 
“The deputy commissioner works under and through me and through my authority,” Hunt said. “It would be foolish to think that the commissioner’s boss couldn’t sign the same deed, or any other matter in the office … I can sign whatever I need to sign to make the office work.” 
Hunt also pointed to a different piece of state code to support the practice he said he only did for Johns.  
Seventeen thousand deeds come through the auditor’s office a year, he said. 
Hunt, a lawyer by trade, added that “common law” protects his right to sign the deeds regardless of what the state code says. None of the allegations are criminal, he said.
“If someone would have a problem with me signing that deed instead of the deputy commissioner, someone has the right to go to circuit court and have it set aside,” Hunt said. 
Weld said this isn’t a paperwork issue – peoples’ homes are at stake. 
“You always have to be extremely cautious when you’re crafting legislation or statutes that affect people’s property rights and their ownership in it, and so that’s why we (lawmakers) went the painstaking lengths when we revised all of this several years ago to ensure that we were taking into account those rights,” Weld said. “You don’t want to see someone lose their property or lose their house simply because they didn’t pay their taxes.”
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha (Photo by Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, is the president of Empower Oversight, a nonprofit law firm that specializes in whistleblower cases and investigating government corruption. He said the deeds and Hunt’s explanation are concerning. 
“The law isn’t a buffet a public official can pick and choose from at will. The code here explicitly limits when the Auditor’s office can issue a deed,” he said. “If they make a mistake and should have issued a deed earlier, the remedy for that is to apply to a judge for execution of the deed, as state code requires.” 
Mark Hunt has served as West Virginia State Auditor since January 2025. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely for West Virginia Watch)
Hunt signed deeds for employee in auditor’s office
The nine deeds signed by Hunt went to MAPA LLC, a landholding company incorporated under Patricia Johns, the wife of Robert Johns. 
Both Johnses are listed as incorporators of a number of limited liability companies that hold hundreds of parcels of land throughout the state, with a total appraised value of $38 million. 
“I’ve known Bob for many years. He’s been a friend for years,” Hunt said, calling him an expert in the land process. Johns typically buys “scrub land,” like hillsides or creek beds that residents lost due to back taxes, Hunt explained.
“Over the years, he has bought a lot of land, and he pays a lot of taxes to the state of West Virginia because this is what the selling of this delinquent land’s about,” he said. 
Johns did not respond to multiple email interview requests for this story.
During the 2024 election, Patricia Johns donated $1,000 to Hunt’s campaign, as she did in his 2022 run for state Senate. 
The West Virginia State Checkbook, an online repository of how state finances are spent, shows Robert Johns worked at the auditor’s office in 2025, the latest calendar year available, and was paid a little more than $14,000. 
Hunt said he brought Johns into the auditor’s office to deal with McDowell County’s potential insolvency in 2024. Johns, a U.S. bankruptcy trustee, worked as the receiver for McDowell County to sort through the impoverished county’s financial issues. 
“We kept him on the payroll because there’s other towns that have become insolvent and have lost their charters, and that’s just a function that we provide,” Hunt said. “We got Bob as kind of a deal.”
Johns also works for the auditor’s office as a consultant on land issues, Hunt said.
Records show MAPA was buying delinquent property through July 2026.
Leavitt called the transfers, and the relationship between Johns and Hunt “cronyism.” 
“Mark Hunt’s claims that he had to correct a mistake made before he arrived don’t match up with evidence that he continued illegally approving deeds months into his tenure,” Leavitt said. 
Hunt said he wasn’t cutting a friend a break. He said there are six people, including Johns, buying 90% of the delinquent land throughout the state. The fact that he intervened to correct issues with Johns’ property isn’t unusual. 
“I don’t care if it’s Bob Johns, Bob Smith, Tom Johns, Tom Smith,” Hunt said. “If they had the same issue, I would have done the same thing.”
This isn’t the first time Hunt’s office has come under scrutiny. 
Earlier this year, journalist Kyle Vass reported Hunt hired state Sen. Jay Taylor, R-Taylor, on a contract basis to work at the Auditor’s Office, after being told by  Attorney General JB McCuskey that full time state government work by a sitting lawmaker was barred by the state constitution. 
Taylor said he was unaware there was an issue and was told by Hunt that everything was fine. 
In late October, Brad McElhinny of Metro News reported that the Auditor’s Office was served a federal grand jury subpoena. 
“Those federal subpoenas contained a clause that we’re not supposed to talk about the contents of,” Hunt said. “I don’t know what they’re doing, but I will tell you that no one’s even talked to me.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: DeSoto County, a Republican stronghold, key to Scott Colom’s midterm election performance
description: President Donald Trump embraces Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
If Democrat Scott Colom ultimately wins Mississippi’s closely contested U.S. Senate race, upsetting Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, he needs to send a special thank you to the Memphis suburb of DeSoto County.
Surprisingly, it appears Colom will win DeSoto County, long viewed as one of the state’s Republican strongholds. But more important than the DeSoto victory for Colom is the vote totals in the county.
In the 2024 presidential election, Republican Donald Trump garnered 48,064 votes in DeSoto County to 29,023 for Democrat Kamala Harris.
When all the votes from Tuesday’s election are finally counted in the coming days, Colom will ultimately match Harris’ vote total in DeSoto County or fall just short of it. By the same token, Hyde-Smith garnered fewer than 25,000 votes in DeSoto County, significantly underperforming Trump. The last time she was on the ballot, in the presidential election year of 2020, Hyde-Smith performed as well as Trump in DeSoto County, winning more than 40,000 votes.
Put simply, if she had performed as well this year as she did in 2020 in that one county – DeSoto – she would not be staring at a potential history-making upset.
If he does win, Colom would be the first Democrat in Mississippi to win a U.S. Senate race since 1982 and the first challenger to upset an incumbent Mississippi senator since, gulp, 1942.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
A long-running joke is the political prognosticator proclaiming to a spellbound audience that the outcome of the election would depend on turnout. All election outcomes depend on turnout.
But Tuesday’s Senate election in Mississippi really, no really, depended on turnout, and Scott Colom and his team should be credited for a campaign that turned out his voters for what could be one of the most improbable victories in the history of not only the state but the nation. Hyde-Smith was not able to turn out her voters at the same level.
It is no secret that midterm election turnout is generally much less than the turnout in presidential elections. The turnout for this year’s midterm in Mississippi is most likely record-breaking, nearing 1 million votes, but still more than 200,000 short of the turnout in the 2024 presidential election and more than 300,000 short of the total in the 2020 election.
The midterm turnout will be about 100,000 more than the 2023 Mississippi gubernatorial election in which incumbent Republican Tate Reeves beat Democrat Brandon Presley by about 25,000 votes.
DeSoto County provides the example of how Colom was able to exceed Presley’s performance. Colom got nearly 15,000 more votes than Presley in the county.
DeSoto is not the only reason for Colom’s stunningly strong performance, but it is the biggest factor.
And it should be noted that DeSoto County has long been a bit of an enigma when it comes to Mississippi electioneering.
DeSoto for years has been the fastest or one of the fastest-growing Mississippi counties, thanks in large part to Memphis transplants. While the county grew to one of the state’s largest, it also was home to a large number of low-propensity voters. The Tennessee transplants did not appear to take much of an interest in Mississippi elections.
In 1999, Ronnie Musgrove, Mississippi’s last Democratic governor, barely lost to Republican Mike Parker in DeSoto County by a vote of 9,301 to 9,144. But in 2003, Musgrove’s Republican challenger, Haley Barbour, recognized the potential of DeSoto County and spent an inordinate amount of time campaigning in the Memphis suburb. Then-President George W. Bush campaigned for Barbour in DeSoto County. Barbour’s work led to him defeating Musgrove in DeSoto by 18,689 votes to 8,876 votes.
With that performance, DeSoto was birthed as one of the state’s  Republican strongholds.
Trump captured more than 60% of the votes in DeSoto County in each of his three presidential campaigns and a high of 48,064 votes in 2024. Remember, Hyde-Smith won fewer than 25,000 votes there last week.
Outside of presidential elections, though, DeSoto countians still appear to have only a lukewarm interest in Mississippi elections and politicians.
That is most likely why Trump came to DeSoto in 2018 during Hyde-Smith’s initial Senate campaign to stump for her.
This year, Trump opted to go to Corinth in northeast Mississippi instead of DeSoto County on the northwest side of the  state to campaign for Hyde-Smith.
Perhaps that decision was the wrong one. Or perhaps, Trump’s policies are unpopular even in what is believed to be a Republican stronghold like DeSoto County.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont’s Sen. Bernie Sanders poised to get back powerful committee chair in new Congress
description:
He wants the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee to “be very aggressive about moving toward ‘Medicare for All’” and restore the healthcare subsidies Congress allowed to lapse last year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont’s Sen. Bernie Sanders poised to get back powerful committee chair in new Congress.
text:
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, speaks during a press conference with U.S. Senator Peter Welch, D-Vermont, at the Statehouse in Montpelier in February 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
After Tuesday’s election swept Democrats into control of both houses of Congress, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said he intends to get back the powerful post he held two years ago: chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.
He’ll use that post, he said in an interview, to try to rescind provisions in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act that are slated to push millions of people off Medicaid and to restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that helped many people afford health insurance before Congress allowed the subsidies to lapse last year. 
Sanders also wants the committee to “be very aggressive about moving toward ‘Medicare for All,’” he said Thursday. “We’re going to move to do what every other major country does: guarantee healthcare to all people as a human right.”
Sanders’ post would likely be the most high-profile example of the expanded power the three members of Vermont’s congressional delegation will enjoy when a new Congress is seated in January. As of Friday afternoon, Democrats — with whom Sanders caucuses — were projected to control at least 54 seats in the Senate and 253 in the House, according to The Associated Press, though some races still hadn’t been called. The election has been widely viewed as a rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party. 
Sanders said he also wants to advance legislation called the PRO Act that would make it easier for workers to join a union and bargain collectively with their employer. The bill passed the House in 2020 and again in 2021 but has repeatedly stalled in the Senate. 
He wants to pass a bill that would raise the federal minimum wage to $20 per hour, from the current $7.25, he said, as well as legislation that would raise taxes on billionaires to fund low- or no-cost early childhood education and daycare for families nationwide.  
Sanders had two major takeaways from the election: There is “growing revulsion and disgust with the behavior and the policies of the Trump administration,” he said, while people are also deeply worried about how to afford necessities like food and gas. Those rising costs are tied to Trump’s war in Iran, which Sanders said the new Congress needs to end along with “U.S. military aid to the extremist government in Israel.” 
The new Democratic-controlled Congress will need to be good, he said, at “walking and chewing bubblegum at the same time.” 
“Trump’s illegal and unconstitutional actions cannot be ignored. He has got to be held accountable. Period,” Sanders said. “But, on the other hand, if that’s all that we do, and we ignore the pain and anxiety that working families are experiencing all over this country, we will be a failed Congress. So, I think we have to do both.” 
That’s a sentiment shared by Vermont’s two other members of Congress. 
U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt., said she plans to push for legislation that builds on the bipartisan housing law Congress enacted earlier this year without Trump’s signature. It included provisions to streamline projects’ environmental reviews, remove restrictions on manufactured home construction, boost access to small-dollar mortgages and limit the number of homes a private equity firm can own. Balint wants to see additional housing reforms designed for rural communities, like many in Vermont, she said. 
Congress also needs to prioritize taking on corporate consolidation across a wide array of industries, she said, including fertilizer production, grocery stores, ticketing platforms and even fire truck manufacturing. 
Balint mentioned the Iran war too and thinks “step one” to ending the conflict is removing Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth from office. Impeachment proceedings start in the House; Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said he’ll again introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as Monday, unless the secretary resigns first. 
“I keep telling people, it’s a target-rich environment. We have to be disciplined,” Balint said.
Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., told VTDigger’s Vermont Conversation podcast last week that although Democrats are right to celebrate their sweeping gains in Congress, the vote “was not a big embrace of Democrats.” Instead, Welch said, “what Democrats have been given by the American people is an opportunity to earn their trust.”
Top priorities for the new Congress should be repealing Trump’s tariffs on goods from Canada and many other countries around the world, he said, as well as taking whatever steps it can to curb the president’s immigration enforcement tactics, which he called violent and cruel. 
Democrats should focus on governing rather than political retribution, Welch told podcast host David Goodman.   
“There will be corruption investigations,” Welch said. But accountability should be “about making life better for everyday people, not a focus on corruption that is about vengeance and payback.”
Olivia Gieger contributed reporting.
