name: Mississippi Today
title: Secretary of state ignored demands to reinstate voters inactivated by unverified Experian data days before midterms: ‘Harm is falling on eligible voters’
description: Secretary of State Michael Watson speaks to the media during the Neshoba County Fair in Philadelphia, Miss., Thursday, Aug. 1, 2024.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
In the days before the midterms Tuesday, a coalition of the nation’s leading civil rights groups warned Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson he needed to reinstate any voters inactivated by his office’s deployment of unverified credit bureau data by Election Day. He never responded.
In the wake of that decision, an unknown number of eligible voters arrived at the polls Tuesday, only to find what has happened in nearly every federal election since Mississippi’s first experiments with Experian’s information two years ago: Properly registered voters had been mistakenly inactivated after the secretary of state provided local election officials with inaccurate address lists pulled from commercial data.
The letter the coalition sent Watson, obtained by Mississippi Today, warned the state’s top elections official that known errors in the data could threaten to disrupt voting in the midterms.
Elections experts say the errors now open up more room for uncertainty in ruby-red Mississippi’s razor-thin U.S. Senate race, as Democratic candidate Scott Colom’s narrow lead threatens to unseat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in what would be an historic upset. Local election officials are steeling themselves for more days of counting thousands of affidavit ballots, which include votes cast by inactive registrants, after a surge in inactivations left over 230,000 voters statewide inactive by Election Day.



County election officials said many wrongful inactivations trace to Watson’s $50,000 deal with Experian in 2024 to supply the company’s unverified address data to all 82 counties. From there, election commissioners would use the information to identify and inactivate voters who may have moved. It marked the first time that the state turned to anything other than government data, primarily records from the U.S. Postal Service, to accomplish the routine task of cleaning the voter rolls.
When the secretary of state’s office began sending out address lists from the data to every county last year, Watson’s office announced the deal would “strengthen the integrity of elections.” But Mississippi Today uncovered in March that errors in Experian’s data went unverified at every stage of the voter-roll maintenance process, resulting in properly registered voters discovering they had been mistakenly inactivated.
To prevent these issues from arising during the midterms, the coalition of national and state civil rights groups — including the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, ACLU of Mississippi and the Southern Poverty Law Center — sent a list of demands to Watson and Laura Henderson-Courtney, senior attorney of the secretary of state’s elections division, four days before the midterms. Their top demand was that the secretary of state’s office “protect” voters by reinstating by Election Day anyone inactivated based on Experian’s data.
“Mississippi voters did everything the law asked of them,” the coalition wrote to Watson, who is currently running for lieutenant governor. “We urge your office to do the same, and to restore them to the rolls before they go to the polls Tuesday.”
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party at the Ice House in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The groups also urged the secretary of state’s office to preserve inactive voters’ access to the ballot box by giving the poll managers and local officials responsible for conducting the midterm elections written instructions to ensure inactive voters were provided with affidavit ballots, as state law requires. 
“The voters on this list did nothing wrong,” the letter stated. “Restoring them to active status does not weaken list integrity.”
The secretary of state’s office did not respond to any of the groups’ demands, according to records obtained by Mississippi Today. Neither Watson nor his office agreed to an interview with the news organization, but Assistant Secretary of State Liz Jonson acknowledged that the office received the coalition’s letter.
“The ACLU, nor any other third party, have the authority to dictate applicable state and federal laws regarding elections in Mississippi,” Jonson wrote in an email. “Per state law, the Statewide Election Management System (SEMS) is currently in a blackout period thus no systemic voter roll maintenance is allowed.”
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, left, with her daughter Anna-Michael Smith and husband Mike Smith, speaks to supporters during her watch party held at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
While Mississippi law bars officials from inactivating or purging voters 90 days before a federal election, it places no such restrictions on correcting voters to active status.
Voter records and local election officials have both confirmed that errors followed the secretary of state’s decision to introduce Experian’s data, but on Friday, Watson stopped short of acknowledging the known errors as anything more than a possibility in an interview with the Magnolia Tribune. 
“The state did move to commercial data for voter roll maintenance, and I’ve seen some folks saying it was bad data,” Watson said. “Was some of the data off? Perhaps.”
After months of warning signs, problems mount on Election Day
By the afternoon of Election Day, problems quickly emerged: Voters discovered their names were missing from poll books, election hotlines sounded off with questions from inactive voters, and the local officials running the polls said they were overwhelmed with the influx.
Amid the chaos, Watson took to Facebook to respond to concerns posted by a Lee County election commissioner.


Four hours after the polls had opened, Election Commissioner Jamie Gunnells, who oversees the Tupelo area, was seeing so many voters learn they were inactive that he posted a warning on Facebook alerting anyone else coming out to vote about the situation. 
He told constituents there was a “major disruption” at the polls due to what he called the “Experian fiasco:” A set of “old” address data that the secretary of state provided earlier this year for voter-roll maintenance had made “many” voters inactive.
Gunnells told Mississippi Today he felt he needed to get the information out before more inactive voters were blindsided at the polls. As he cycled among the three polling places in his district, his 13-hour Election Day shift was filled with confusion, anger and fear from voters who were surprised to find they were inactive. 
He said some voters were so frustrated about the issue that they left the polls without casting an affidavit ballot.
In response to Gunnells’ Facebook post, Watson stated that the responsibility for errors in the data fell on election commissioners like him.
“Ultimately, no matter what data is sent to the election commissioners, you should understand your job is to verify the information before acting upon it,” Watson replied. “That said, our goal is to send you the best information available, and we did so.”
Voters fill out their ballots at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Jackson during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Mississippi is a bottom-up state for elections, meaning the actual work of cleaning voter rolls and marking voters as inactive falls to county election commissioners. Under state law, however, the secretary of state is legally responsible for training these county officials to do that job.
Gunnells and other election commissioners said the secretary of state never cautioned them beforehand that they should check the list of addresses pulled from Experian’s data for errors, leaving them to discover the mistakes after voters had already been inactivated.
When Watson’s office announced its partnership with Experian, the office wrote that the deal would “bring a new level of reliable data” to the voter rolls. But records released by the secretary of state’s office show that in the contract for the deal, Watson’s office signed off on Experian’s disclaimers that the company couldn’t guarantee the “accuracy or reliability” of its data.
“He started pointing figures at us: ‘We should have verified the data that they sent to us,’” Gunnells said. “I mean, how are we gonna verify it?”
Even more voters mistakenly inactivated
The issues that emerged during the midterms came as no surprise to voters like Thomas Minor and Heather Williams, who discovered in the primaries that they had been mistakenly inactivated. Address lists the secretary of state pulled from Experian’s data incorrectly flagged they had moved.
The list placed Williams at an address she hadn’t lived at in years. Minor had lived in Itawamba County his whole life, but the list said he resided 160 miles away, in a Delta town he had never stepped foot in.
Thomas Minor, photographed March 18, 2026, at his local polling place in Fulton, discovered during the March 10 primaries that his name was missing from the poll book. County election officials had mistakenly inactivated him after the secretary of state provided them with incorrect address information sourced from Experian’s data. Credit: Madeline Nguyen/Mississippi Today
In the voting-rights coalition’s letter to Watson last week, the groups outlined both voters’ cases as proof of the known errors tied to the secretary of state’s decision to introduce Experian’s data. 
“He could have rectified some of this stuff and made the process a lot easier,” Minor said. “They should have learned their lesson back then.
“It makes me think he doesn’t care about the voting process.”
Harya Tarekegn, the director of advocacy and policy for an organization in the coalition, the Mississippi Center for Justice, said in a press conference Friday that she believes many affidavit ballots in the midterms were cast by voters who were inactivated based on Experian’s data.
One of them was Starkville resident Kailyn Lott. Eight months after what happened to Minor, Lott said she encountered a strikingly similar situation when she showed up to vote for the midterms Tuesday. She learned that she was marked inactive when she came to vote at the same fire station where she voted in her first election, the 2024 presidential contest.
When she got to the polling place, she discovered her name was missing from the poll book. She was inactive.
As she waited in line for an affidavit ballot, she said she saw more and more people encounter the same issue. At the front of the line, she discovered what caused the problem in her case: Her voter registration listed her address as her parents’ house in Pontotoc County, which she said is linked to an old credit card she opened as a kid.
Harya Tarekegn, director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, speaks during a voting rights rally at the Capitol in Jackson on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Voter records from the secretary of state’s office show county election officials originally inactivated Lott last year due to address conflicts, a month after Watson’s office provided them with a list of addresses pulled from Experian’s data.
Despite the confusion, Lott was adamant about her right to vote. She showed poll workers her voter ID card and ultimately cast an affidavit ballot. But she’s worried others weren’t so lucky.
“When people hear stuff like this, it definitely deters them from voting because it just further instills in their mind that it doesn’t matter if they go and vote,” Lott said. 
Minor said in his case, his inactive status ultimately kept him from casting a ballot during the primaries — marking the first time he’s missed an election in 12 years. While poll workers provided him with a ballot envelope, he said they failed to give him the affidavit ballot itself for him to fill out his vote. 
It was his first time going through the process, and in his confusion and rush to get to his job at north Mississippi’s Toyota car plant, he thought he had done everything he needed to vote.
It wasn’t until after he left the polls that he realized he never filled out a ballot.


Watson posted on social media Friday that the affidavit process exists as a “safety net” to correct “errors” made by election commissioners and preserve inactive voters’ right to the ballot box. 
“We have implemented every available resource to ensure our elections are secure, and to ensure we do not have dead people, illegal aliens, people with false addresses, or nonresidents voting in our elections,” Watson stated. “It may take voters a little longer for final results to come in, but it will result in more accurate voter rolls which will speed up the process in the future and decrease opportunities for voter fraud in MS.”
But to voting rights advocates, Minor’s experience is a testament to how inactivation can threaten eligible voters’ right to the ballot box, especially when they’re not aware of the affidavit process.
“The State cannot walk away from an unreliable data source while leaving in place every inactivation that source produced,” the voting rights groups stated in their letter last week.
Consequences beyond the midterms
Under state law, any voters inactivated by the data are now on the path to have their voter registrations purged if they don’t correct their status with their county’s circuit clerk or vote within two federal general elections — a period of about two to three years. Once a voter is purged, they need to reregister before their ballot will count again.
Now that the midterm elections have passed, the door has opened up for election commissioners to begin purging some of the first voters who were inactivated based on Experian’s data. These voters were marked inactive in early 2024 in Lafayette County, where the secretary of state first experimented with using Experian’s data to clean the voter rolls.
Watson called the pilot a “success,” and it cleared the way for his office to expand the use of Experian’s data to all voters on the state’s rolls.
Affidavit and absentee ballots are being processed by election officials, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
But Mississippi Today found errors emerged from the data during those early tests, resulting in the inactivation of properly registered voters. One was Jordan Jones Higginbotham, an Ole Miss student who discovered she was inactive before the 2024 primaries after an address list that the secretary of state drew from Experian’s data incorrectly placed her in Madison County.
Any Lafayette County voters in this experiment who were inactivated before the 2024 presidential election and who have not voted since then are now on the board to be purged. The voting-rights groups demanded Watson to agree by next Friday to halt any purges of voters who were inactivated based on Experian’s data and to stop using any unverified address data from a commercial broker on the voter rolls.
Jonson wrote that the secretary of state’s office would respond to the coalition’s letter in “keeping with our standard operating procedure.” She did not answer questions from Mississippi Today about whether the office would act on the groups’ demands.
But as the country turns its eyes to Mississippi’s Senate race and the candidates’ campaigns gear up for a legal battle over the vote count, the coalition remains hopeful for change.
“One of the unintended benefits of all of this chaos is that it shines a light on how antiquated election administration is in Mississippi,” said Amir Badat, the Mississippi voting rights attorney with Fair Fight Action who represented the groups in the letter. “That’s going to be critical for us to be able to advocate for improvements to the system.”
A motorist traveling near Freedom Corner at Medgar Evers Boulevard and Martin Luther King Jr. Drive encourages the public to get out and vote during midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Last week, the secretary of state’s office said it has stopped providing Experian’s data for voter roll maintenance, although the office did not respond to questions from Mississippi Today about exactly when or why the partnership ended.
The secretary of state’s office wrote in a statement to WAPT that it had switched to IDI Data, a smaller company that brokers information drawn from a variety of sources — including the major credit bureaus and government records — to help customers track people down.
On Election Day, Watson posted on Facebook that his office had a “new vendor with more features and info than the last.” But voting rights groups remain unconvinced that errors will no longer emerge just because the secretary of state’s deal with Experian has ended.
“That decision speaks for itself,” the coalition wrote to Watson last week. “If Experian’s data is not reliable enough to use going forward, it was never reliable enough to strip Mississippians of active status and subject them to potential removal.”
You can check your voter registration status and track your affidavit ballot on the secretary of state’s website at yallvote.ms.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Outside review details discrimination complaint against a Utah Democrat
description: The Utah Senate released a discrimination inquiry that colleagues are pointing to as they urge Sen. Kathleen Riebe, a Democrat, to resign.
text:
Senate Minority Caucus Manager Kathleen Riebe, D-Salt Lake City, listens during a press conference with Democratic senators at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 21, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Utah Senate released findings of a harassment and discrimination inquiry Friday that the chamber’s Democrats are pointing to as they call on Sen. Kathleen Riebe to resign. 
Among the most notable findings: the attorney who investigated a legislative employee’s September complaint against Riebe, a Democrat from Cottonwood Heights, reported that the senator acknowledged telling staffers that she did not want gay interns “who were coming out of the closet.” 
The report, released Friday, outlines the alleged admission and wide-ranging charges of bias based on sexual orientation, race and religion against Riebe, who has served for seven years in the Legislature. 
The inquiry found it’s more likely than not that the way Riebe treated the staffer was motivated at least in part by race, national origin or ethnicity, and that she violated the Legislature’s internal antidiscrimination policy. The review does not name the staffer or her job title. It identifies her as an immigrant who is not white. 
The 19-page report — obtained by Utah News Dispatch through a public record request — was redacted throughout to conceal most names, along with roughly a dozen paragraphs. In one instance, a full section is blocked. The obscured portions render some of the allegations and findings unclear.  
Sen. Kathleen Riebe, D-Cottonwood Heights, is pictured on the first day of the legislative session at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Also on Friday, the Senate made public a letter from Senate President Stuart Adams detailing the four corrective actions imposed on Riebe in connection with the review, but each is blacked out. 
The public release of the documents comes two days after the senator said broadly she disputes the allegations and would not step down. Fellow Democratic senators, citing the results of the inquiry, have called on her to resign. 
They announced less than an hour before polls closed on Election Day that they had voted to remove Riebe from their caucus. The news cast a shadow on an otherwise celebratory night for Utah Democrats, who will send a candidate to the U.S. House for the first time in six years and flipped more state legislative seats than anticipated in what supporters are cheering as a “blue tsunami.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Riebe did not directly respond to the allegations against her, including “a sustained course of disparaging, intimidating, and belittling treatment.”
She said in a Friday evening prepared statement that she is listening to the concerns and will continue to do so as she remains in office. 
“I care about the people I work with,” Riebe said. “I want every person who works in the Utah Senate to feel respected and valued. When people raise concerns, I owe them my attention and my effort to get better. I give them both.”
She said she’s spent her career fighting for underrepresented groups and pledged to keep doing that. 
“I will keep learning,” Riebe said. “And I will keep working for the people of Senate District 15 and for every Utahn who has ever felt unheard.”
Additionally, the employee reported Riebe has said “it is not fair to invest money for people here illegally” and questioned the immigration status of some people. She also alleged the senator questioned in a meeting why Utah’s dual-immersion programs would teach a specific language — the employee’s first language, which was redacted — and asking who “even speaks” it.
The employee said Riebe’s complaints about other senators were mostly directed to women of color.   
Sen. Riebe resists calls to resign over harassment, discrimination allegation

Another witness reported Riebe “blamed the presidential election on the trans and LGBTQAI+ community, saying words to the effect of ‘what these people have done to the party,’ and that ‘immigrant issues’ and ‘queer issues’ cost the Democratic Party the election.” The same witness said Riebe favors white people who are not “Mormon,” a term for members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, or LGBTQ+. 
In an interview with the investigating attorney, Paul Smith of Parsons Behle & Latimer, Riebe said she would never take money away from immigrants and denied blaming the 2024 presidential election on the LGBTQ+ community or immigrants. 
A description of the employee’s complaint states it relays how Riebe called her “fat” and “huge” while she was pregnant and asked how she affords her clothes. 
In the investigation, Riebe denied asking how the employee could afford her clothes, but said the employee has an “amazing wardrobe” and recalled seeing her footwear one time and asking, “you have $2,000 pair of shoes?” 
Riebe said she didn’t say anything else on the topic and denied making comments about the staffer’s body during her pregnancy.
People arrive to work at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on the first day of the legislative session, Tuesday, Jan. 20, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
A week after the legislative employee filed a complaint, Riebe lodged her own complaint, the report states, alleging the employee’s account of harassment and discrimination was actually retaliation. 
During the inquiry, Riebe said the staffer “engaged in impermissible partisan activity” by working on another senator’s campaign, and alleged the employee’s close relationship with that senator “created a detrimental ‘allegiance,’” the investigator wrote. 
Riebe had told someone that she’d received a screenshot image showing the employee was running another senator’s campaign, the report states, and believed the employee’s subsequent report was retribution. The staffer explained she had not accepted an offer for a position with the campaign, while witnesses said they told Riebe no formal campaign had been established. 
Riebe, an educator, was first elected to the state Senate in 2018 after serving on the Utah State Board of Education. Earlier this year, she ran to represent Utah’s newly drawn 1st Congressional District before dropping out to endorse Ben McAdams. Her current Senate term runs through Jan. 1, 2029.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: New outbreak of mpox in Anchorage prompts advisory from state health officials
description: A rare viral disease has emerged in an outbreak in Alaska’s largest city that appears to be expanding, state health officials report. There are now four new cases in Anchorage of mpox, a viral disease formerly called monkeypox that is spread through close contact and can be fatal. None of the patients reported traveling outside […]
text:
A colorized electron micrograph image shows mpox virus particles, in red and yellow, found within infected cells, colored blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for differences in shape. The image also features virus factories, shown in brown, where viruses replicate, mature and assemble. (Image provided by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/National Institutes of Health)A rare viral disease has emerged in an outbreak in Alaska’s largest city that appears to be expanding, state health officials report.
There are now four new cases in Anchorage of mpox, a viral disease formerly called monkeypox that is spread through close contact and can be fatal.
None of the patients reported traveling outside the state in month-long period before becoming infected.
It is the highest number of annual mpox cases in Alaska since 2022, when five cases were diagnosed in the state amid a global outbreak. Between 2023 and 2025, there were only two Alaska cases.
Three of the Anchorage cases emerged in October and were reported last week through a state Department of Health alert intended to raise awareness in the public and among healthcare providers. The fourth case was reported to state officials on Thursday, said Dr. Joe McLaughlin, Alaska’s state epidemiologist.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The four Anchorage cases are among men who reported no travel outside of Alaska in the past 30 days, Mclaughlin said. That is a contrast with the previous Alaska cases, all of which were among people who had recent travel experiences. Up to now, travel had been implicated in the spread of mpox in Alaska.
Officials are currently trying to track the source of infection, said McLaughlin and Dr. Randi Rollins, a U.S. Centers for Disease Control epidemiologist working with the Alaska Department of Health.
The lack of reported out-of-state travel “does not necessarily establish that the monkeypox virus is circulating here in Alaska,” Rollins said. “They may have had exposure to somebody who traveled to Alaska, and they may be the end of that transmission line at this point. We don’t know.”
Mpox is characterized by lesions that appear on various parts of the body.
It usually takes three to 17 days after infection for symptoms to emerge, Rollins said, and in the first phase, the symptoms are flu-like: “fever, chills, fatigue, headache, sore muscles, and even swollen lymph nodes.” The lesions develop in the second phase, with bumps that are firm to the touch or sometimes tender, she said.
Some people skip the early symptoms and do not have any signs of infection until the rash phase develops, she said.
The sickness lasts a few weeks, and patients are considered to have recovered when all the lesions are gone. Until that last lesion is completely healed, “the person is still infectious and can transmit monkeypox, and that can typically take two to four weeks,” she said.
McLaughlin said the Alaska patients are isolating and recovering. Two of the reported cases were among men who are partners, but it is unknown whether there are any additional links between any of the patients, he said.
Increase in cases nationally
The new outbreak of mpox in Anchorage fits a national pattern. After a lull that followed the 2022-23 global outbreak, cases are on the rise again in the United States. An uptick in infections started in March, the CDC reported.
The virus circulating now is genetically different from the variety behind the global outbreak in 2022, which is called clade II.
The currently circulating virus is called clade I. In Central Africa, the clade I variation had been more deadly than the clade II variation. But the current variation of the clade I virus appears to be not particularly deadly, according to health officials.
Spread of the virus happens through close contact, including but not limited to sexual contact.
 

A vial containing the mpox vaccine is seen on July 23, 2022, in London, England. This type of vaccine, called JYNNEOS or Imvanex, is available in Alaska for anyone considered to be at elevated risk, including people who have been in contact with infected individuals. (Photo by Hollie Adams/Getty Images)
 

	Alaska health officials are encouraging anyone considered to be at risk of infection to get vaccinated.
The JYNNEOS vaccine, approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2019, guards against both clades of mpox, as well as smallpox, a disease that historically killed much of the world’s population but is now considered to have been eradicated.
The vaccine, which is administered in two doses, is available through the Anchorage Health Department and other health providers.
It is recommended for certain groups of people considered to be at higher risk for infections. Those include men who have sex with other men, anyone with exposure to another person suspected of having mpox, people who are traveling to parts of the world with mpox outbreaks and medical workers, such as those employed in labs or healthcare facilities, whose jobs put them at risk of being exposed to this and other pathogens.
The vaccine is effective even for people already infected with the virus, reducing risks even for those who might develop the disease, Rollins said.
For anyone who has been exposed, “it’s recommended that you get that vaccine within 4 days of exposure,” she said. While that time window is ideal, “you can get it up to about 14 days and still see effectiveness at reducing disease severity,” she said.
State immunization records show that since 2022, 851 people in Alaska have received a first dose of the JYNNEOS vaccine and 604 receiving a second dose, Rollins said.
New borealpox cases reported
While healthcare providers are being advised to watch for the resurgence of mpox, there is news about a rarer type of pox disease: borealpox.
Two cases of borealpox, formerly known as Alaskapox, have been diagnosed this year, Rollins and McLaughlin said.
That brings the world’s total number of diagnosed borealpox cases to nine.
The disease, related to mpox, smallpox and other poxes, was first identified in 2015 in Fairbanks. The first six cases were found in Fairbanks and were considered to be mild. Like other pox diseases, they were characterized by skin lesions and some flu-like symptoms.
However, in January of 2024, a Kenai Peninsula man died from borealpox after being infected by what scientists discovered was a genetically different strain of the virus. The patient was in his 60s and had an immune system weakened by treatment for cancer.
This year’s two borealpox cases, like the previous Fairbanks-area cases, were mild, Rollins said.
“It was the lesion that came to the attention of both patients, and they sought treatment for the lesion,” she said. “One patient did experience respiratory illness, fever, muscle aches, joint aches.”
Scientists say borealpox circulates among small mammals. So far, red-backed voles, which are plentiful across most of Alaska, have been identified as a major reservoir. Investigation of cases so far has focused on household pets that appear to have encountered infected voles or other small mammals.
Unlike the case with mpox, there is no vaccine for borealpox. But some scientists are working on developing one, and some are investigating the effectiveness of certain antiviral medicines to treat infections.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Serving those who served: Why civil legal aid matters
description: Veterans have been in the spotlight as Americans across the country have celebrated our nation’s 250th birthday. And rightly so — the rights and freedoms that we enjoy are secured by the courage and sacrifice of our veterans. But while veterans took an oath to defend our rights, their own rights sometimes go undefended in […]
text:
Soldiers from Ft. Lee, Virginia help mark Veterans Day ceremonies at the World War II Memorial November 11, 2011 in Washington, DC. Veterans Day in the United States honors those who have served in the nation's military and also coincides with the anniversary of the conclusion of hostilities on the western front in World War I.  (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)Veterans have been in the spotlight as Americans across the country have celebrated our nation’s 250th birthday. And rightly so — the rights and freedoms that we enjoy are secured by the courage and sacrifice of our veterans. But while veterans took an oath to defend our rights, their own rights sometimes go undefended in our legal system when they face critical civil legal issues such as eviction, consumer matters and access to earned benefits.
For example, an Alaska veteran who served in the Army and lived with severe disabilities could not access VA healthcare because of his discharge status. After years of unsuccessful efforts to correct this error, he sought help from Alaska Legal Services Corporation. With free legal support from an ALSC attorney, he submitted a final application before a critical deadline and was approved. As a result, he can now access the healthcare he needs, a change that has been truly lifesaving.
Stories like his are not uncommon. Alaska has the highest number of veterans per capita in the nation, and many face legal problems that impact their quality of life. A study by the Legal Services Corporation found that over three-quarters of veteran households nationwide experience at least one civil legal problem each year and only 8% get the help they need to solve those problems. According to the VA’s annual CHALENG survey, legal issues are among the most persistent challenges facing homeless veterans. In fact, seven of the top-ten unmet needs reported by veterans in 2025 were legal matters, including family law, child support and debt issues.
When veterans do not get help with their legal problems, they face a cascade of social and financial consequences. In that Alaska veteran’s case, his incorrect discharge status and ineligibility for VA benefits limited his access to medical care, worsening his health and hindering his ability to work. Such consequences extend far beyond the individual household and ripple throughout our communities.
There are two major challenges with getting legal help. First, veterans must recognize that the challenges they face have legal solutions. Many people mistakenly believe lawyers are only necessary or helpful when someone has done something wrong. But civil legal aid exists to help people find solutions to a variety of challenges including unsafe housing conditions, access to veterans’ benefits and even military discharge upgrades. Second, after recognizing the need for legal assistance, there is the challenge of finding qualified, affordable help. In Alaska, we have legal deserts — places with no lawyers, courthouses or other legal infrastructure. For low-income veterans, Alaska Legal Services Corporation is the only statewide provider of free, comprehensive civil legal help. Because of limited funding, ALSC has historically had to turn people away: for every individual served, another goes unserved. 
There is good news: In Alaska, our state, tribal and local government and private foundation partners increasingly recognize the importance of civil legal aid for veterans, and all Alaskans. National philanthropic partners have also recognized legal aid’s lasting impact. The Bob Woodruff Foundation is one such philanthropic funder. BWF ensures that our nation’s veterans, service members, their families and their caregivers — those who stood for us — have stable and successful futures. BWF has invested more than $7.5 million in civil legal aid organizations nationwide. In 2023, BWF began funding a full-time ALSC attorney dedicated to helping veterans across the state. Now in its third year, this partnership has provided legal help to more than 125 Alaska veteran households. 
The success of the BWF-ALSC partnership demonstrates what is possible when legal aid is adequately funded, making threats to other critical funding sources all the more concerning. Legal Services Corporation — the largest funder of civil legal aid in the country — faces proposed elimination and significant cuts under the current federal budget process. If LSC were eliminated, ALSC estimates it would assist 13,000 fewer Alaskans, including hundreds of our veterans. In the last federal fiscal year, LSC avoided elimination and major cuts with a strong show of bipartisan support, including from Alaska’s congressional delegation. 
Alaska’s veteran families deserve a holistic approach to solving problems they face. They should know that help is available, that legal solutions exist and that they do not have to face these challenges alone. If you know a veteran in need of legal help, reach out to ALSC at 888-478-2572. If you want to volunteer to help veterans with their legal problems, you can sign up at https://www.alsc-law.org/volunteer/.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Big win, big loss for Democrats in Montana
description: In the “blue wave” that washed over the country this week, liberals in Montana notched both an historic win and a conspicuous loss. Montanans will send Democrat Sam Forstag to Congress, and supporters of his victory in the western district danced at the Florence building in Missoula in the wee hours Wednesday. It’s the first […]
text:
Independent U.S. Senate candidate Seth Bodnar, left, talks with supporters downtown Missoula on election night 2026. (Keila Szpaller/Daily Montanan)In the “blue wave” that washed over the country this week, liberals in Montana notched both an historic win and a conspicuous loss.
Montanans will send Democrat Sam Forstag to Congress, and supporters of his victory in the western district danced at the Florence building in Missoula in the wee hours Wednesday.
It’s the first time in 32 years a Democrat was elected to represent the Treasure State in the U.S. House.
But a clash on the left that helped Republican Kurt Alme claim victory in the U.S. Senate race showed little sign of a resolution this week.
Voters in states arguably redder than Montana will send Democrats to the U.S. Senate.
Texas hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988 but James Talarico fended off a Republican backed by Elon Musk’s millions. Kansas elected a Democrat for the Senate for the first time since 1932.
In the Treasure State, the left split on strategy and endorsements, and so split the vote — as predicted.
Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead earned just 12% of the vote. The independent, Seth Bodnar, earned 38%.
Bodnar’s supporters tried to push Bankhead out of the race after the primary, and Thursday, the blame game continued.
Montana Democratic Party executive director Emily Marburger described the “independent experiment” as a failure.
On the other side, Nancy Keenan, a Bodnar supporter and former director of the Montana Democratic Party, described Bankhead as a “spoiler” who “refused to withdraw.”
Kal Munis, a political scientist at Montana State University, said the loss is leaving anger and frustration in its wake.
“There’s a huge missed opportunity that’s going to be settling in on people today and over the coming weeks,” Munis said Wednesday. “And someone has to be the scapegoat.”
Political analyst Lee Banville, with the University of Montana, said 2026 is being called a “once-in-a-generation” election, but on the left, the Senate camps “chose to fight themselves” rather than the Republican.
“They’re spending so much time blaming each other that they’re not actually talking about, well, what should we do next?” Banville said.
Dueling strategies
Munis said the loss doesn’t fall on Bankhead, although she was “a C-tier candidate.”
He said people who are part of the “old guard Democratic establishment” devised a plan to run an independent in red Montana and failed to execute.
In 2024, Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Tester lost his reelection bid in a defeat that left Montana with an all-Republican Congressional delegation.
Tester, who had won three Senate campaigns, described the party as “poison,” and some Democrats worried he was right. Wednesday, Tester called 2026 a “missed opportunity” and said people can “blame whoever they want.”
But Munis said the old guard chose a Democrat to run as an independent to try to fool the voters, though Bodnar insists he’s an independent.
Munis said the tactic was an attempt to “pull the wool over people’s eyes.”
Then his supporters failed to close down the Democratic lane, he said. He said even having Tester himself — or a high-profile surrogate — run in the primary to win and drop out would have done the trick.
Bankhead, a newcomer, won the primary.
Like Bodnar, she’d been in Montana less than a decade and hadn’t run for office before, but unlike him, she didn’t have a high profile or political connections. Bodnar served as president of the University of Montana for eight years until January 2026.
Banville said Bankhead was not successful at raising money, especially compared to Bodnar, and she struggled to rally a base.
They both lost.
Democrat and former U.S. Sen. Max Baucus told “This American Life” that some Montanans directed funding to Bankhead in the primary thinking she would withdraw. He called it a “mistake.”
Munis said Bankhead is “a small fish” who is easy to blame. But he said the idea she would abandon her primary win doesn’t account for the ego of any politician, especially one pledging to fix a problem and earning a win.
“That should have never been left to chance,” Munis said.
‘Humble charisma’
Munis said the electoral environment was right for a Democrat, and dissatisfaction with Republican U.S. President Donald Trump buoyed Forstag to his U.S. House win.
Forstag also brought unique strengths, he said. Munis said he has good instincts, and he or someone in his campaign understands “the power of the ground game.”
Forstag is also young and hip — Munis, a faculty member, said he sees college students much more excited about the 32-year-old than they would have been for older Democrats who sought Congressional bids.
Forstag somehow escaped the pall of the socialist mantle opponent and Republican Aaron Flint tried to place on him — Munis said he stayed focused on wages and affordability.
Bill Lombardi, who helped launch Tester’s first U.S. Senate campaign and worked for Baucus, said he hadn’t seen as much energy for a candidate in 30 years.
“He (Forstag) had a humble charisma that people latched onto,” Lombardi said.
On the Senate side, the big money didn’t flow to Bankhead, and Lombardi said Bodnar’s supporters tried to paint her as a bad candidate — Banville said she remained largely unscrutinized, and he saw no evidence she would have been successful.
But had money flowed to a Democrat, Munis said, it would have helped float all boats because historically, the Senate candidate would work with other Democratic candidates and the Montana Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee.
“All that money that Bodnar brought in? It didn’t help anyone. It didn’t help anyone but himself,” Munis said.
‘Missed the blue tsunami’
In an email after the election, Marburger, director of the Montana Democratic Party, said this state’s U.S. Senate race “could have been part of the blue wave” too.
She pointed to the “independent experiment” as the problem.
“States that attempted to run independents like Nebraska and South Dakota by and large missed the blue tsunami,” Marburger said.
A spokesperson said she didn’t know the reason the party was unable to convince Bodnar to run as a Democrat.
Marburger also touted Forstag’s win as one “for working people.”
Banville said the messages from Forstag and Bodnar sounded similar, and Bodnar proved he could raise money, and he overperformed.
Bodnar earned nearly as great a share of the vote as the independent in South Dakota, who did not have a Democrat or Libertarian in the race. In Montana, he cut into support for the Republican, who won with just 48%.
In her analysis of the election, Keenan said Bodnar’s race helped other candidates, too.
“Bodnar ran a competitive race that forced the GOP to expend resources in Montana (including millions to prop up Alani Bankhead) — resources that thankfully were not redirected to the western Congressional district or Supreme Court races,” Keenan wrote.
Republican U.S. Sen. Steve Daines was expected to run for re-election but tapped Alme at the last minute.
In an email to the Daily Montanan, Keenan said Democrats are a minority in Montana, they need strong candidates who align with their values, and Bankhead could have helped a candidate who “had a real shot at winning.”
Keenan said 42% of Montanans identify as independents.
“The real blown opportunity for democratic values this cycle was the failure to be responsive to the Montanans who are increasingly identifying themselves as politically independent,” Keenan said.
If Montanans on the left want to win in the future, Banville said they need to stop fighting what looks like a “weird sort of civil war.”
He said they can choose to keep running statewide candidates who might be Democrats as independents, or they can create a party that’s more welcoming to an independent voice — and stick with the two-party system.
“Republicans never really had to break a sweat,” Banville said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey move puts abortion law into effect early, relaxing restrictions and teeing up fierce 2028 ballot fight
description: In the letter announcing the preamble, Healey said the state’s exemptions to its previous restrictions on later abortions have proven “too narrow to account for the full spectrum of high-risk pregnancy complications that can arise later in pregnancy.”
text:
THIS MAY FEEL FAMILIAR.
Opponents of a recently passed law gathered enough signatures to freeze the law in its tracks until voters can weigh in at the ballot box, but the governor has signed an emergency preamble forcing the law into effect immediately.  
Hot on the heels of Bay State voters turning away an effort to repeal a sweeping gun control law, they’ll almost certainly face a similar conundrum on abortion in 2028. 
A coalition of anti-abortion groups announced in the last week of October that they had gathered nearly 100,000 signatures to repeal Chapter 188 of the Acts of 2026, which eliminates previous restrictions on abortions beyond 24 weeks of pregnancy, leaving the decision to the “professional judgment” of the physician. 
The changes were signed into law by Gov. Maura Healey in August, and set to take effect this Sunday. Healey at the time said this took government out of an “incredibly rare” and personal decision. State health officials report that in 2024, the last year of available data, 99 of the state’s 49,450 abortions took place at 24 weeks of pregnancy or later. 
Anti-abortion activists and some religious leaders immediately decried the law, and Catholic Church leaders in Massachusetts released a letter condemning the permissiveness of the new legislation.  
The Compassionate Care Coalition, backed by Massachusetts Citizens for Life, says it delivered around 113,000 signatures to the secretary of state’s office, surpassing the 49,716 required to suspend the law until it can be decided by repeal referendum on the 2028 ballot. 
“The people of Massachusetts did not ask for abortion through all nine months, and in a matter of weeks they made that clear,” said Sam Miele, chair of the Compassionate Care Coalition and director of Massachusetts Family Action, in a statement on October 29. Now, he said, “voters will have the final say.” 
Until they do, thanks to the emergency preamble, the law will be in effect and cannot be suspended.  
In the letter announcing the preamble, Healey said the state’s exemptions to its previous restrictions on later abortions — limited to situations imperiling the patient’s life or health, or lethal or grave fetal diagnosis — have proven “too narrow to account for the full spectrum of high-risk pregnancy complications that can arise later in pregnancy.” 
Healey has long touted the state’s abortion laws as a point of pride. 
The state “is home to some of the best hospitals in the world, and our laws contain some of the strongest abortion protections in the country,” Healey wrote. Yet, she said, some patients have had to leave Massachusetts to get abortions after the 24th week, facing significant out-of-pocket costs, or forego the care entirely, 
In a Substack post, she recounted the story of an expecting mother who found out about fatal fetal defects at 31 weeks, and needed to travel out of her home state alone to get an abortion in Washington, D.C. “That is unacceptable,” Healey wrote. 
Healey similarly attached an emergency preamble to a sprawling 2024 gun law updating and expanding the state’s restrictions, after opponents gathered enough signatures to suspend it until voters could consider a ballot referendum on whether to keep it. Just over two thirds of voters decided to preserve the law on Tuesday, rejecting the repeal effort. 
Whether the abortion law repeal will make it to the ballot depends on whether the secretary of state’s office certifies enough signatures. A spokesperson for the office said Thursday that staff was prepared, once the 5 p.m. Friday deadline for signature submissions passed, to begin the process of reviewing each sheet for disqualifying marks and tallying the signatures by county. The process typically takes 1 to 2 weeks, depending on the number of petition sheets filed. 
The repeal campaign savaged the emergency preamble on Friday afternoon. 
“Governor Healey’s preamble reflects an utter disregard for the men and women she was elected to represent,” wrote Myrna Maloney Flynn, president of Massachusetts Citizens for Life and vice chair of the Compassionate Care Coalition. “In a matter of a few weeks, more than 113,000 of her constituents went out of their way to oppose a highly controversial, deeply consequential, law that blindsided legislators and voters alike. Healey ignored their questions and concerns on August 10, and she has once again prevented any dialogue.” 
Massachusetts has scrambled to adapt to the changing legal status of abortion around the country in recent years, particularly after the US Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade in 2022. 
The previous year, Massachusetts lawmakers overrode Republican then-Gov. Charlie Baker’s veto of part of the ROE Act, which updated the state’s abortion laws and included a provision allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to seek abortion care in consultation with their health care provider. 
But in June 2022, on the day of the Supreme Court’s decision, Baker issued an executive order prohibiting executive branch cooperation with out-of-state investigations targeting lawful abortions in Massachusetts. His move was later codified and expanded upon by the Legislature. 
That law prevents cooperation with other states looking to discipline Bay State providers, limits the release of sensitive data, allows prescription labels to display a practice name instead of an individual physician’s name, and codifies a state requirement for abortion care to be provided in emergencies when medically necessary. Today, it is being challenged a coalition of Republican state attorneys general, in a challenge that may be taken up by the US Supreme Court.  
Healey moved to stockpile the abortion drug mifepristone in 2023, worried about restrictions on telehealth and abortion care provided via mail. The nation’s high court ruled earlier this year that the medication could remain accessible by mail. 
In her letter, Healey said “any further delay in implementing the Act would prolong uncertainty for patients, families, physicians and health care institutions, and risk further harm to the health and safety of women in Massachusetts.” 
Abortion access groups and doctors cheered the governor’s emergency preamble decision. 
Rebecca Brendel, president of the Massachusetts Medical Society, said the move “protects the physician-patient relationship.” Physicians, she said, must make complex, individualized treatment recommendations “based on scientific evidence, established standards of care, and circumstances unique to our patients. Decisions regarding abortion care later in pregnancy should be no different.”  
Lawmakers recognized that at no point in a pregnancy is a politician more fit than a doctor to make those evaluations, said Sheila Ramirez, executive director of the Planned Parenthood Advocacy Fund of Massachusetts, in a statement.  
“Voters will get the chance to affirm this at the ballot in 2028,” Ramirez said, “but in the meantime, we are grateful Governor Healey is making sure patients facing unexpected, devastating circumstances later in pregnancy can get the care they need in their own state.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Lawyers, advocates hover as Mississippi election officials count final Colom, Hyde-Smith votes
description: Harya Tarekegn, director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, speaks during a voting rights rally at the Capitol in Jackson on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Warring lawyers and advocates swarmed election offices across Mississippi on Friday to continue watching poll workers count outstanding ballots in the state’s U.S. Senate race.  
With all but one other U.S. Senate race across America already decided, the nation has fixed its attention on the Magnolia State nail-biter between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom. Local election officials continued processing thousands of outstanding absentee and affidavit ballots.
The narrow margin between Hyde-Smith and Colom has already shocked many across the nation, but it remained too close to call on Friday. Colom led by nearly 2,500 votes with nearly 1 million votes cast.
READ MORE: 2026 Mississippi election results
At a press conference in front of the state Capitol in Jackson on Friday, a coalition of voting rights organizations called for transparency in the counting of remaining ballots, but urged the public not to disrupt the process.  
Harya Tarekegn, the director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, said there were about 20,000 affidavit ballots —​​ called “provisional ballots” in many other states — cast in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race. 
Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Tarekegn told Mississippi Today there were about 2,100 affidavit ballots in north Mississippi’s DeSoto County, a traditional Republican stronghold where Colom currently leads by six percentage points, an illustration of Colom’s massive inroads in areas dominated by the GOP.
“What are Republican areas? DeSoto County, they said that was a Republican area. We won,” Colom said. 
Tarekegn also said on Friday there were 1,667 affidavit ballots left in Rankin County, where Hyde-Smith leads, and 1,931 in Madison County, another often Republican-voting county where Colom holds a narrow lead. 
But Hinds County, the state’s most populous area and a Democratic stronghold, is “the big enchilada,” Colom’s supporters note. Election officials told Mississippi Today they expected the counting of affidavits to continue through the weekend ahead of a Nov. 13 deadline.
Media, allies and observers from both campaigns flocked to the Hinds County Election Commission’s downtown Jackson office on Friday, filming commissioners as they processed ballots by hand.
Ray Chambers, attorney for the Hinds County Election Commission, didn’t want to speculate on a timeline beyond noting the deadline.  
“I predict they’ll be done in time,” Chambers said.  
In the north Jackson suburb of Madison, the Madison County Election Commission posted a sign saying the commission started processing affidavit ballots a day after the election. But commissions across the state are not following a unified schedule. Instead, a patchwork of meetings across the state sent representatives of both candidates scrambling to observe the counting of the ballots that will decide the Mississippi Senate race. 
Mississippi has a “bottom-up” system of election administration, where 82 county circuit clerks and election commissions are responsible for processing their own affidavit and absentee ballots. 
Harya Tarekegn, director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, speaks during a voting rights rally at the Capitol in Jackson on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
They are required to process the ballots and transmit the results to Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office by Nov. 13. 
Tarekegn said the election commission meetings are open to the public, but the public should not disrupt or publicly challenge decisions made by election officials. 
She also said voters who cast affidavit ballots only need to return to their local circuit clerk’s offices if they experienced voter ID issues at their polling place so that they can present a valid ID. 
The campaigns for Hyde-Smith and Colom have both said they believe they have a path to win the election.  
Hyde-Smith said on Friday that her campaign is not backing down and that the election was not over. She has not made any public appearance or scheduled a press conference since Tuesday’s election. One of her few public statements since the election was published in a social media post written in the third person.  
Touring a Black-owned bookstore on Jackson’s historic Farish Street, Colom on Friday stopped short of calling on her to concede the race, but he said she needs to answer questions from the public and the media as she continued trailing in the election results. 
“She’s still our senator,” Colom said. “Where is she? Why is she not doing any interviews? Why can’t she explain what her pathway to success is?” 
Upbeat and optimistic on Friday, Colom outlined what his early legislative priorities would be in Congress and, promoting Marshall’s Bookstore, told reporters about his affinity for the works of authors Leo Tolstoy and Robert Caro.  
A possible legal fight over the count also continued brewing Friday, a day after the fundraising arm of the Senate Republicans demanded election officials around the state separate and preserve affidavit ballots. 
In response, the Colom campaign sent a letter claiming the Republican group’s request was illegal and violated voters’ right to privacy. Once affidavit votes are accepted and counted, they are supposed to be treated like other ballots, and not have anyone’s name attached. State and federal courts have upheld voters’ right to privacy and secret ballots.

Born: 04/08/1953
Edinburgh, Scotland

Lebanon, NH
Details of service:

In Loving Memory of Susan Newell (nee Donaldson).
In the early morning hours of September 11th, 2026, Susan, a native of Edinburgh, Scotland, passed away peacefully after a life that carried her from Scotland to the United States nearly 48 years ago. A graduate of the Edinburgh School of Nursing, she was a Registered Nurse and Certified Midwife.
Fiercely proud of her Scottish roots, she carried Scotland with her wherever she went, finding particular joy in the friendship, music, traditions and camaraderie of the Highland Games throughout Vermont and New England. Her Scottish spirit was unmistakably her own — strong, spirited, independent and deeply proud.
She is survived by her beloved son, Cooper; her brother, Rod, and sister-in-law, Philippa; two nephews; and her great-niece and great-nephew in England.
Susan will be deeply missed. She leaves behind not only the people who loved her, but the warmth, generosity, laughter, and unmistakable spirit that made her uniquely Susan.

title: Oil hunt in Arctic refuge is on hold until at least mid-January, Alaska developer says
description: In a court filing Thursday, officials with the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority said their plans to explore for oil in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge are on hold until at least mid-January as they wait for permission from the federal government. The refuge, located to the east of Prudhoe […]
text:
Fall colors are seen on Aug. 24, 2015, along the Canning River on the western edge of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. (Photo by Katrina Liebich/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)In a court filing Thursday, officials with the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority said their plans to explore for oil in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge are on hold until at least mid-January as they wait for permission from the federal government.
The refuge, located to the east of Prudhoe Bay, is believed to contain vast oil and gas deposits but has been off-limits to development for decades. A bill passed during the first Trump administration mandated an oil and gas lease sale, but work has been paused amid legal challenges.
Congress approved additional lease sales last year as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act proposed by Trump.
AIDEA’s current exploration plan involves using above-ground vehicles to seismically survey for oil and gas without drilling.
“Based upon communications with the contractor handling the geophysical exploration permit submission, it is the undersigned’s understanding that, as of November 2, 2026, a decision on AIDEA’s application to conduct seismic activity is not anticipated until mid-January 2027,” wrote attorneys for AIDEA, a state-owned corporation that owns oil leases in the refuge.
Thursday’s filing came after oral arguments last month over the legality of the federally authorized plan to drill within the refuge. Democratic states, environmental and tribal organizations have been fighting to overturn the plan, which includes lease sales in 2021 and 2026.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason, overseeing the legal case, asked for a status update after hearing oral arguments.
Thursay’s filing contained that update and could determine whether Gleason renders a verdict on the lawsuit.
Attorneys for AIDEA said that even though it is waiting for federal permission, its contractor is already getting equipment ready.
“Staging and preliminary work outside ANWR has already begun and will ramp up further at the end of November,” said attorneys for the state-owned corporation.
They implied that a ruling this month would be beneficial.
“AIDEA will incur significant financial impact if it is forced to terminate its seismic program after November 29, 2026,” they said.

name: WyoFile
title: Republicans swept Wyoming, but voters here swung left compared to 2024
description:
Republican candidates for federal office enjoyed smaller margins-of-victory in the midterms compared to the last presidential election. Wyoming’s delegation will lose influence with the flip of the House and Senate. 
The post Republicans swept Wyoming, but voters here swung left compared to 2024 appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Although the blue wave that delivered one of the largest midterm election landslides in decades largely spared Wyoming, Republican candidates for federal office have lost voters and leverage, new data shows.
Wyoming voters swung more Democratic in Tuesday’s general election when casting ballots for federal office compared to 2024. That’s according to an analysis of election data by the New York Times, which also breaks down how different voter groups in Wyoming shifted from two years ago. 
It showed that across multiple demographics, from age to race, Wyoming swung to the left in 2026. That was especially the case for younger and nonwhite voters.
Ryan Williamson, an associate professor in political science at the University of Wyoming, says the analysis’ top line holds up. But its dissection of voter groups should be considered with caveats. 
“Wyoming didn’t see Republicans lose in the same way that other states saw Republicans lose,” Williamson told WyoFile. “Despite that, we still saw Wyoming swing about 15 points towards the Democrats relative to Trump’s 2024 margin, which is approximately the national swing.”

Republican primary candidates for U.S. House of Representatives David Giralt, Chuck Gray and Reid Rasner participate in a forum on Thursday, July 23, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

Put another way, Wyoming voters gave Republican candidates for federal office smaller margins-of-victory than they did two years ago. 
Republican nominee Chuck Gray, for example, won the race for U.S. House on Tuesday by 25 points against Democratic nominee Lisa Kinney. Two years ago, Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman won that same race by more than 47 points against Democrat Kyle Cameron. Hageman, who ran and won the race for U.S. Senate this year, also enjoyed a smaller margin of victory compared to 2024, beating Democrat James Byrd by about 30 points. In 2022, Hageman beat Democrat Lynnette Grey Bull by about 45 points. 
So while election outcomes in Wyoming didn’t result in any Democratic victories for federal office, a shift from two years ago is clear. 
The biggest change, according to the New York Times’ analysis, was among young voters, specifically between the ages of 18 and 29. Young Wyomingites swung 26 points for the Democrat in the Senate race and 39 points toward the Democrat in the House race. 
However, Williamson said not to read too much into the subgroup analysis for a number of reasons including the small sample size. 
The New York Times relied on “extensive, detailed data,” according to its methodology description, including voter interviews and files, precinct results, and turnout data, and says its analysis will be updated as more data becomes available. But out of the 25,236 voters it interviewed for its survey, only six were Wyoming voters. Plus, it has yet to incorporate precinct-level data. 

Republican U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman talks during a forum for U.S. Senate candidates hosted by the League of Women Voters of Wyoming on Wednesday, July 8, 2026, at Casper College. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)

“I wouldn’t say outright ignore the breakdowns by subgroup, but just acknowledge that they’re based on you know a very, very small sample size and a lot of the results are necessarily just going to be an artifact of the national trend being applied to the Wyoming data.”
Williamson pointed to analysis of the House race broken down by gender. 
“For example, it says men swung 17 points and women swung 11 points,” he said. “That matches the Times’ national numbers almost exactly at 18 points for men and 13 points for women, so that’s mostly just the aggregate model applied to Wyoming data, and so we won’t know until we have more data or just additional time to investigate this sooner.”
The main thing that interests Williamson about this election isn’t so much the results, but their impact on Wyoming’s incoming federal delegation. All three “were in relatively influential positions, or at least in much more influential positions than they are now,” he said. 
Sen. John Barrasso has served as the second-ranking Senate Republican since 2025 when he became majority whip. The job of minority whip is a very different one. 
“Instead of enacting change, it’s just going to be about trying to preserve the status quo, and that may be difficult given how large the Democratic victory was,” Williamson said. 

President Donald Trump speaks with reporters as Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., from left, Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., listen on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, June 24, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

Hageman will be joining Barrasso in the upper chamber, but as a junior senator from the smallest state, she’s less likely to “have as much opportunities for the kind of prime committee positions” she had in the House, Williamson said. 
Hageman currently chairs the House Committee on Natural Resources’ Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife and Fisheries, and serves on three other subcommittees. Her new committee assignments in the Senate will be decided before Congress convenes in January.
As secretary of state for the last four years, Gray has served as Wyoming’s second most powerful elected official. Things will be much different for him in 2027. 
“Being a freshman member of the House of Representatives comes with remarkably little influence when you’re in the minority because the House is a purely majoritarian body,” Williamson said. 
And given the size of the incoming Democratic majority, the speaker will have “35 to 40 votes to spare” before they will “have to start thinking about making concessions to the minority,” he said. 
While the election may be over, Williamson said a lot of unknowns remain. 
“This is a historically large shift, and what exactly it means is kind of still up in the air,” he said.
Williamson alongside Andrew Garner, professor of political science at UW and Jim King, professor emeritus, will discuss 2026 outcomes and present their key findings from the 2026 Wyoming Election Year Survey at 5:30 p.m. Monday in the Wyoming Union Yellowstone Ballroom on Laramie’s Campus.
The post Republicans swept Wyoming, but voters here swung left compared to 2024 appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal judge sets hearing to determine fate of Mississippi Olivia Y. foster care lawsuit
description: Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders, right, speaks in Jackson at a Joint Legislative Budget Committee meeting on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Lawyers for Mississippi’s foster care system and attorneys representing the children who’ve lived inside it will each have 40 minutes to argue early next year if  the state’s child welfare system still needs continued federal safety oversight. 
The hearing, scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Jan. 25 in Jackson, signals the next iteration of the Olivia Y. v. Barbour federal lawsuit — a decades-old case in which lawyers alleged that Mississippi children, like then-three-year-old Olivia Y., were unconstitutionally endangered in the state’s foster care system. 
In 2008, attorneys for both sides agreed to court-mandated monitoring of Mississippi’s child welfare system. Monitoring requirements have changed since then, but versions of the oversight have remained. Reports from the monitors have consistently found dangerous conditions in the system. 
In May, lawyers for Gov. Tate Reeves and Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders filed a motion to end this court oversight. They wrote that the state had taken the necessary steps to guarantee foster children’s rights to reasonably safe living arrangements “now and in the future.”
That statement was scrutinized in July, when the court monitoring group Public Catalyst published its 2025 report of conditions within Mississippi’s child welfare agency. The group found that the department had met just 22 of 107 applicable safety measures. Failed measures included the rate of foster child abuse within the system and social workers placing children in unlicensed homes, like hotel rooms.
Sanders and Marcia Lowry, the lead plaintiff lawyer representing Mississippi foster children, have each publicly defended their positions since. Sanders, at an October legislative budget hearing, said meeting all the measurements of the federal monitoring is unrealistic. Lowry told Mississippi Today in September that lawyers for the state Child Protection Services Department had already agreed to meet them.
Now, each party will make their case in early 2027 to U.S. Chief District Judge Halil S. Ozerden, who’s overseen the lawsuit since 2020.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Secretary of State launches audit into uncounted Johnson County absentee ballots
description: State and local offices have launched an audit into more than 2,000 midterm election ballots left uncounted in Johnson County, though race outcomes are not expected to change. According to a Friday afternoon joint statement from Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate and Johnson County Auditor Julie Persons, an official in the Johnson County Auditor’s […]
text:
Johnson County election officials identified more than 2,000 uncounted absentee ballots from the midterm elections.  (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)State and local offices have launched an audit into more than 2,000 midterm election ballots left uncounted in Johnson County, though race outcomes are not expected to change.
According to a Friday afternoon joint statement from Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate and Johnson County Auditor Julie Persons, an official in the Johnson County Auditor’s Office on Thursday identified about 2,017 absentee ballots that were not included in unofficial results from Tuesday’s local, state and federal elections.
The audit, which was set to begin “immediately” on Friday and wrap up by Nov. 9, will focus on the county’s Absentee and Special Voters Precinct. Based on current unofficial results, race outcomes are not expected to change, the joint statement said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This is why we employ a layered approach to election security, and scenarios like this prove that our checks and balances work,” the joint statement stated. “This is also why we continue to remind Iowans that all results reported on Election Night are unofficial.”
Each Iowa county’s Absentee and Special Voters Precinct is still counting ballots cast through programs allowing survivors of domestic violence and similar issues and overseas Americans to vote, according to the joint statement, and election results will not become official until “county and statewide canvasses have been completed.”
Johnson County is part of Iowa’s 1st Congressional District, where Democrat candidate Christina Bohannan was called by the Associated Press to have beaten Republican incumbent Mariannette Miller-Meeks with 54% of the vote — nearly 32,000 votes. None of the unofficial results for statewide office were within 2,017 votes.
The only contested legislative race within that margin was in House District 91, where Republican Judd Lawler was leading Democrat Mark Divitt by 940 votes in Johnson County. In House District 92, which is split between Johnson and Washington counties, incumbent Republican Rep. Heather Hora was leading Democrat Brittany Erickson by 2,020 votes.
Iowa broke a turnout record in the midterm election, with Pate telling reporters Wednesday that the more than 1.38 million votes cast in the 2026 midterms surpassed the previous record of nearly 1.33 million set in 2018.
“We will continue to monitor the situation and work closely together as the audit is completed,” the joint statement said. “We are confident in Iowa’s layered approach to election security and the safeguards in place that keep Iowa elections safe and secure.”
