title: Promising growth, Utah-based investor leads board takeover at Ethan Allen
description:
“I’m not a private equity firm,” said Doug Bergeron, who holds a roughly 5% stake in the company. “We're completely committed to the state of Vermont.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Promising growth, Utah-based investor leads board takeover at Ethan Allen.
text:
The Ethan Allen factory pictured in Orleans. Photo by Fred Thys/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Three of Ethan Allen’s five board members were ousted on Wednesday in a shareholder vote, marking a successful takeover led by Utah-based investor and former Verifone CEO Doug Bergeron. 
Ethan Allen, a furniture and interior design company, was founded in Vermont in 1932, and has long been an “anchor employer” in the state’s Northeast Kingdom, according to Commerce and Community Development Secretary Tayt Brooks. Today, the company operates manufacturing operations across the U.S., Mexico and Honduras with more than 300 Vermonters employed at facilities in Orleans and Beecher Falls.
Bergeron won a similar proxy contest at the retail tech firm Canteloupe in 2020, and is the founding CEO of DGB Investment.
He said in an interview Friday that Ethan Allen has not kept pace with competitors in terms of growth, but can reverse course financially by modernizing its approach to sales and marketing, among other changes. When Bergeron was told there was no place for him on the board, he decided to take matters into his own hands, he said.
“The existing management team loves (the company), but they don’t know how to love it in a modern way,” he said.
Longtime CEO and board president of Ethan Allen, Farooq Kathwari, was among those voted off the board this week. The company had announced in September that it would seek a new CEO.
The company’s outgoing leadership declined to comment on the change beyond a brief statement Wednesday announcing the contest’s preliminary results. An earnings call scheduled for Monday, Nov. 9, was subsequently cancelled, though the company still plans to release its quarterly financial reports that day. 
Bergeron’s priorities for changing course at the company, he said, primarily lie in the customer-facing side of the business. 
The business’ U.S. manufacturing facilities, including those in Vermont, Bergeron added, are at an increasing advantage as tariffs make international sourcing more complex and expensive. And having producers close at hand, both to implement new designs and access customers more directly, is helpful too, he said.
“I’m not a private equity firm,” said Bergeron, who holds a roughly 5% stake in the company. “We’re completely committed to the state of Vermont.”
Bergeron plans to visit the state next week, he said, when he will see both Northeast Kingdom facilities and speak with workers there. The message, he said, will be one of confidence — he foresees increased capacity and a growing workforce in the region over time.
“There will be nothing but growth here,” Bergeron said he’ll tell employees. “You can’t cut your way to prosperity.”
Brooks, who has been following the company’s leadership change closely, said in an interview Friday that those goals were “encouraging to hear.” He also hopes to speak with Bergeron during his trip to Vermont next week to discuss the company’s continued presence in Vermont in more detail, he said.
Local business leaders responded with cautious hope.
“I think whenever you know you’re an employee and you see upheaval, you know that’s cause to be nervous,” said Cathy Davis, President and CEO of the Lake Champlain Chamber of Commerce.
But the new leadership’s focus on digital retail as they look to transform the company could be positive for its Vermont manufacturing workers, she said. Ethan Allen also operates one retail store in Chittenden County.
“I would say I would be cautiously optimistic that these changes would result in, you know, a greater focus on sales, and recognizing that the facilities in Vermont are a valuable asset to the company,” Davis said.
Loralee Tester, who leads the Northeast Kingdom Chamber of Commerce, reiterated the company’s importance to the region, particularly given the area’s rural character. Even though the business’ Vermont workforce is a fraction of what it once was — Ethan Allen boasted 1,200 staff across the state in the early 2000s before a series of layoffs and offshoring — its economic power is felt keenly in those small northern communities.
Kathwari said in 2021 that a “shortage of labor and the escalation of manufacturing costs” had driven those changes. It’s a common story — and a common set of challenges — for such companies, Tayt said.
The wellbeing of companies like Ethan Allen are crucial to the region, and the state at large, Tester said.
“Our manufacturers are really the lifeblood that keeps things ticking in a lot of ways,” she said. “The people who work there and run those facilities are just — it’s so important to the economy here.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa House speaker says no special session before new governor takes office
description: Iowa House Speaker Pat Grassley said Friday he does not believe a special legislative session will be called before Gov.-elect Rob Sand takes office in January. Though Republicans maintained majority control over both chambers of the Iowa Legislature in the 2026 election, state lawmakers will no longer be working with a Republican governor. Sand, a […]
text:
Iowa House Speaker Pat Grassley answered questions from reporters in the Iowa House chambers Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa House Speaker Pat Grassley said Friday he does not believe a special legislative session will be called before Gov.-elect Rob Sand takes office in January.
Though Republicans maintained majority control over both chambers of the Iowa Legislature in the 2026 election, state lawmakers will no longer be working with a Republican governor. Sand, a Democrat, will take over when Gov. Kim Reynolds ends her term. In addition to losing the governorship, Republican majorities shrunk in both legislative chambers.
Some Democrats and observers have questioned whether Republicans would use the final two months before Sand takes office to restrict gubernatorial powers by calling a special session. But Grassley told reporters Friday, “I would say at this point in time, that’s not on the table.”
State legislatures in Michigan, Wisconsin and North Carolina have used so-called lame duck sessions to restrict future elected officials’ powers after the majority party’s candidate lost an election.
Sand said during a taping of “Iowa Press” earlier Friday that he hoped lawmakers would not restrict his power in an effort to respect voters’ choice in the 2026 election.
“To come in now after the fact and change the meaning of what those voters said, that’s not public service. That’s politics,” Sand said.  “I don’t think that they’ll do that because I would hope and trust that they’re public servants.”
There were several measures making changes to gubernatorial powers discussed during the 2026 session. Reynolds signed into law a ban on future governors’ ability to restrict private businesses’ operations and order places of worship to close during disasters and public health emergencies. These were actions Reynolds, as well as many governors throughout the country, took during the COVID-19 pandemic. The law also requires governors to get legislative approval for election law and regulation changes.
Another proposal discussed during the session would have created “continuing appropriations” in the state. Senate File 2388, introduced by Senate Republicans, proposed having state government funding continue based on the budget approved during the preceding year if the governor does not approve a budget by July 1, the start of the fiscal year. Democratic lawmakers heavily criticized the proposal as a “power grab” that would allow GOP majorities to refuse to negotiate with a Democratic governor — and House Republicans eventually shot the legislation down.
Though he said lawmakers would not return to Des Moines for a special session before January, Grassley also alluded to likely future conflicts between GOP lawmakers and the Democratic governor.
“If there are some issues that the governor-elect wants to propose that we can have a conversation about that are reasonable and responsible for Iowans, we’ll engage in that,” Grassley said. “But at the same time … we’re not going to be afraid to draw the line if there’s things that we think go too far or start to compromise our principles.”
Sand said his hope was to find compromises with state lawmakers, saying there was a reason why he was elected in 2026 while the Iowa Legislature stayed in Republican control.
“There are going to be 55 Republican legislators in the Iowa House next year, 21 of them will be in districts that also picked me as governor,” Sand said. “Iowans want us to work together. This is one of those things that is just, like, an abundantly clear message. You want to talk about messages from the campaign? That level of ticket crossing for different parties is a pretty clear message to me. They want balance.”
Grassley will maintain his position as House Speaker in 2027 as the GOP House lawmakers reelected him to the leadership position Friday. House Majority Leader Bobby Kaufmann will also continue to serve in his role, as will Rep. John Wills, R-Spirit Lake, as speaker pro tempore and Rep. Henry Stone, R-Forest City, as majority whip. Senate Majority Leader Mike Klimesh and Senate President Amy Sinclair will also continue to serve as leaders in the upcoming session, according to a news release from Senate Republicans.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico immigrant groups urge Legislature to crack down on local police ‘handoffs’ to ICE agents
description: New Mexico immigrant advocates on Friday released emails and other evidence they say show that some local law enforcement agencies have widespread practices of referring arrestees and detainees to federal immigration agents for deportation.
text:
Teague González, executive director of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, speaks Nov. 6, 2026, to an interim legislative committee about the organization’s push for a state law cracking down on local law enforcement coordination with federal immigration agents. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico immigrant advocates on Friday released emails and other evidence they say show that some local law enforcement agencies have widespread practices of referring arrestees and detainees to federal immigration agents for deportation. 
In a news conference held at the state Capitol, the advocates said the practice undermines state laws aimed at prohibiting local resources from aiding President Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, and they urged lawmakers to pass legislation during the upcoming session starting in January that cracks down on the practice.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Since January 2025, according to the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, at least 242 detainees at New Mexico’s immigrant detention facilities arrived there through some form of assistance from local police or sheriffs’ deputies. 
Teague González, the law center’s executive director, told lawmakers during a presentation Friday that local law enforcement agencies conduct “handoffs” of local arrestees to ICE in a variety of ways, including by taking them to parking lots where federal agents are waiting or driving them directly to local U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement offices. 
One such detainee, Brando Chavez Martinez, was riding in a car southbound on Interstate 25 with two friends on the way to a family wedding on May 22, 2026, when Sandoval County Sheriff’s Office deputies pulled over the vehicle, according to the law center. Even though Chavez Martinez had no criminal history, the deputies transferred him to ICE agents, who took him to the Torrance County Detention Facility in Estancia. 
Lt. John Castañeda, a spokesperson for the sheriff’s office, told Source NM on Friday he had no immediate additional details about the case advocates outlined, but he said the sheriff’s office does not have a policy prohibiting its deputies from coordinating with federal agents. 
According to advocates, more than two dozen local policies exist statewide that ban, in some form, the use of public resources for federal civil immigration enforcement, but no uniform policy exists. 
New Mexico Corrections head says settlement likely in suit over sending people on probation to ICE

In Albuquerque, for example, police and jail officials are prohibited from coordinating with ICE, but that’s not the case in nextdoor Sandoval County, where Castañeda told Source NM the county has “no specific policy that says we’re not going to help ICE.”
The Legislature earlier this year passed House Bill 9, which prohibits counties from using their local jails for immigrant detention, but that bill is currently tied up in litigation between the U.S. Department of Justice and the state. 
During the 2025 session, lawmakers approved the Nondisclosure of Personal Information Act, which prohibits all state employees from passing personal information, including immigration status, to federal immigration authorities. 
The law center and other groups including Somos Un Pueblo Unido and Contigo Immigrant Justice filed public records requests in September of all 33 New Mexico counties and 13 cities and towns to share “all communications” they’ve exchanged with ICE and other federal immigration entities. 
Supporters of a bill cracking down on local police coordination with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement applaud Nov. 6, 2026, during a news conference in the Roundhouse rotunda. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Of those 48 jurisdictions, 13 produced responsive documents; 12 said no documents exist; eight requested more time and 16 did not respond in potential violation of the Inspection of Public Records Act, according to the law center.
Documents from 10 of the counties showed “some level of communication and/or collaboration” with federal immigration enforcement agencies, according to the law center.
Eddy and Lea counties in southeast New Mexico were among them, according to documents the groups obtained via public records requests. Both counties engage in regular communication with ICE officials, including county jail staff providing them with a “nearly daily list of foreign-born individuals” who are brought to their local jails before they go before a judge and regardless of their reason for arrest, according to the law center.
Officials from both counties did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Friday.
Two state lawmakers — Sen. Antoinette Sedillo Lopez (D-Albuquerque) and Rep. Cristina Parajón (D-Albuquerque) — said Friday they will carry legislation into the 60-day session beginning Jan. 19 that aims to crack down on the practice of local law enforcement referrals to ICE. 
Previous legislative efforts, beginning in 2005, at prohibiting local resources from being used for federal civil immigration enforcement have failed, but Parajón told Source NM on Friday that she is optimistic the Legislature in 2027 will pass the bill.
“We’re still in the drafting phase, but we are dedicated to doing it,” she said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Effort to recall Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry fails
description: The effort to get Gov. Jeff Landry recalled from office has officially failed, the Louisiana Secretary of State's office announced on Thursday. The lead organizer of recall effort said she did not turn in the required signatures before the Nov. 2 deadline
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry, left, and Attorney General Liz Murrill, right, pictured at a press conference on July 22, 2026. An effort to get Landry recalled from office officially failed Thursday after the organizer didn't submit the required signatures to call an election, which would have needed 500,000 people to sign. (Photo by Piper Hutchinson/Louisiana Illuminator)The effort to get Gov. Jeff Landry recalled from office has officially failed, the Louisiana Secretary of State’s office announced on Thursday. The lead organizer of recall effort said she did not turn in the required signatures before the Nov. 2 deadline 
Marian Gbaiwon, who oversaw the recall, said in a video posted to Facebook on Thursday night that she did not turn in any signatures to registrars of voters because they hadn’t met the number needed and did not want the signatures to become public record. 
“Why would we submit them and subject people unnecessarily to unnecessary scrutiny?” she said in the video. 
To recall a statewide elected official, a petition needs to get at least 20% of active registered voters statewide to hand-sign their names to a petition. When the petition to recall Landry was filed on May 4, Louisiana had just over 2.5 million voters, meaning around 500,000 people would have needed to sign their names to the petition in order to call an election. 
The effort to circulate the recall petition led by Gbaiwon and the organization Louisiana Deserves Better began to crumble over the summer when dozens of volunteers and collaborators left the effort amidst allegations of mismanagement. Volunteers said Gbaiwon failed to be transparent on how donations were spent and did not provide any accounting of the number of signatures collected.
Landry responded to the recall efforts’ failure on social media Thursday, saying the failure as well as Louisiana’s election of a Republican to the U.S. Senate stood out as a “bright spot” for conservatives amidst national losses to Democratic candidates in the midterm elections. 
“Despite widespread media coverage seemingly cheering on the recall effort, no registrar in any Louisiana parish has reported receiving signatures by the November 2 deadline,” he said in a post on X. “Our voters made clear they want conservative leadership, common-sense solutions, and greater opportunities.”
Signatures on a statewide recall petition are reported to the registrar of voters in each of the Louisiana parishes to be certified. Usually, certified reported signatures would then be sent to the Governor to issue a call for an election, but because the Governor was the subject of the recall petition, signatures from each parish would have been sent to the Secretary of State’s office. 
Another effort to recall Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill began around the same time efforts to recall Landry did. Officially filed with the Secretary of State’s office on May 13, the petition is still active, needing a similar 500,000 signatures to call an election. The deadline to collect these signatures is Monday. 
Murrill’s office did not respond to calls and text messages requesting comment on the recall. 
No statewide elected official in Louisiana has been recalled in the past sixty years. Some efforts to recall elected officials in towns and smaller municipalities have been successful in the past. In those cases, the number of signatures needed was far fewer than it would be for a statewide elected official.
In total, 76 recall elections have successfully removed an official from office in Louisiana since 1966, when the Secretary of State’s office began keeping records on recall elections. Most officials were mayors, school board members or city council members. 
Efforts in recent years to recall elected officials in areas with a larger voter base have failed to get the minimum required signatures, including attempts to oust former New Orleans’ mayor LaToya Cantrell. Only 27,243 of the over 67,000 signatures were found to be valid on the petition, the majority disqualified for reasons such as repeat signatures, profanity, fake names or mislabeled pages. 
Another 2017 attempt to remove Jefferson Parish President Mike Yenni from office came up short of the 90,000 signatures needed to require an election, despite Yenni admitting to sending “improper text messages to a young man” who was 17 years old at the time.
An effort in 2024 to remove St. Tammany’s coroner, Christopher Tape, after other elected officials in the parish expressed their concerns over Tape’s history of sexual abuse allegations failed to get the minimum number of signatures. 
Tape was accused of forcing himself on a girl who was under the age of 12 and indicted on six charges in August 2002. The case against Tape was dismissed in February 2003 after nine months of delay in his trial led the court to find a violation of his right to a speedy trial.

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington City Council president launches bid for mayor
description:
Democrat Ben Traverse said the success of the city depends on lifting everyone up. “Because the truth is, we’re all in this together.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington City Council president launches bid for mayor.
text:
Democrat Ben Traverse, Ward 5 representative and president of the Burlington City Council, announced his bid to run for mayor at a press conference in Battery Park on Nov. 6. 2026, flanked by supporters of his campaign. Photo by Auditi Guha/VTDigger.

BURLINGTON — City Council President Ben Traverse is running for mayor, potentially setting up a contest with the incumbent, Progressive Emma Mulvaney-Stanak.
The mayor said Friday, in a statement via her political director, that she will make an announcement about her reelection plans in the next few days. 
Traverse, a Democrat, launched his campaign Friday, vowing to work collectively across the political aisle and with neighbors and businesses “because we all have a stake in Burlington’s future.”
“I’m here today because I love Burlington, because I believe deeply in this city’s future, and because I believe if we work together, our best days are still ahead of us,” Traverse, 42, said to applause at the Battery Park pavilion where dozens of people gathered, many of them carrying signs in support of his campaign.
Traverse first won the Ward 5 seat representing the South End neighborhood in 2022 and has been reelected twice. He became the council president in April 2024 when Mulvaney-Stanak won the election to become the first woman to hold the city’s top job.
Traverse has often clashed with the Progressive mayor, most recently on a proposed public safety resolution called Burlington Forward. The proposal, introduced by Traverse and other council Democrats, was tabled until Dec. 7 after heated debate. It aims to expand police presence downtown and support both businesses and those who threaten or break the law in a compassionate way. 
The mayor and the Progressives on the council called it “Burlington Backwards,” criticizing its approach toward drug use and homelessness downtown, and said it wouldn’t do enough for the problems facing Burlington.
After a recent deadlock, a new ad-hoc committee was formed to rework the proposal. It includes the mayor, Traverse and other Democrats and Progressives.
Vermont’s most populous city has faced significant challenges in recent years, including homelessness, public drug use, theft and continued staffing issues at the police department. Some businesses have said they struggle to survive downtown.
Traverse on Friday criticized the mayor as having failed to address these issues adequately and said he couldn’t name any initiatives that have moved forward recently.
“Burlington is stuck at the moment,” he said to reporters after the press conference. “And yes, it has been a growing level of frustration.”
Mulvaney-Stanak recently appointed a new police chief, although Traverse said that move came too late given that the last police chief left two years ago. He also called her plan to open an overdose prevention center downtown a failure, but did not go into specifics.
Traverse declined to say whether he will support the police chief appointment at Monday’s meeting. He did say police staffing would be one of his priorities as mayor and that he would like the number of police officers in the city to be closer to 90 than the current 54.
The mayor and her political director did not respond to questions beyond a brief statement.
Traverse vowed to practice an inclusive style of leadership if elected.
“Too often in Burlington, we are divided by those who use wedges for political gain,” he said at the press conference. “Ward against ward, homeowners against renters, business owners against workers, our police officers against the communities they serve — as though one person’s success has to come at the expense of another’s. I reject that kind of politics and believe the success of our community depends on lifting everyone up. Because the truth is, we’re all in this together.”
Traverse is a labor lawyer for the University of Vermont Health Network. He previously worked in the labor and employment division of the New York City Law Department and has clerked in Vermont courts. 
Prior to being on the City Council, Traverse was chair of the Burlington’s parks and recreation commission. He also served on the Housing Board of Review and the Ward 5 Neighborhood Planning Assembly, according to his campaign website. 
Supporters who attended the campaign launch included Ranjit “Buddy” Singh, a Democratic South District city councilor. Singh credited Traverse with leadership on the council, from working to present creative solutions around housing to his commitment to the South End Innovation District.
The mayoral election will take place on Town Meeting Day in March.

title: Judge orders Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to detainment of D.C. woman
description: A Washington D.C. Superior Court judge has ordered the Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to an incident in May in which guards members detained a woman outside her home.   D.C. resident Anna King filed a separate $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard in July for injuries and distress she said she […]
text:
A video shows Idaho National Guard members approach Washington D.C. resident Anna King at her home in May. King has filed a $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard. The U.S. Attorney's Office charged King with assault. (Screenshot from video)  A Washington D.C. Superior Court judge has ordered the Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to an incident in May in which guards members detained a woman outside her home.  
D.C. resident Anna King filed a separate $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard in July for injuries and distress she said she experienced when she was detained on May 8. Members of the Gem State’s National Guard have been in the nation’s Capital since February as part of a Joint Task Force, although there was no public announcement of the deployment until after King filed her claim, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Under the direction of D.C. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro at a hearing Thursday, the Idaho National Guard, D.C. National Guard and U.S. Department of Defense will have to produce, or explain why they can’t produce, documents related to the detainment of King. 
King wrote in her tort claim against the Idaho National Guard that the troops did not explain why they were detaining her or provide a warrant when they approached her that evening.
A video of the incident shows three men in National Guard uniforms approaching King, who had been sitting on a bench outside her apartment.
King told the guards members not to touch her. She walked toward the steps to go back into her apartment, but the troops blocked her, the video showed. Two of them pinned her against the ground and secured her wrists behind her back. 
The U.S. government charged King with two counts of misdemeanor assault on a police officer on May 9. In August, the U.S. Attorney’s Office added three more charges of simple assault. The charges stem from alleged assaults on May 6. 
King pleaded not guilty and asked for a trial. 
King’s attorney, Jeffrey Nestler, said the Idaho National Guard provided one document, but the legal team felt it wasn’t sufficient. King’s attorneys asked for all reports, records, communications, directives and other documents from the Idaho National Guard related to King. 
Di Toro agreed, and ordered the prosecutor to ensure the entities produce relevant documents. 
According to court documents and Nestler, the Idaho National Guard members who detained King on May 8 said they had “prior run-ins” with King and had been ordered to detain her. 
“We’re here now in the part of the law that requires the government to do more than just ask questions, so I’m going to direct you to actually spend a little more time trying to understand whether prior to May 6, the Idaho National Guard had what the defense is calling a run-in with Ms. King,” Di Toro told Assistant United States Attorney Vanessa Jacobsen Thursday. 
As of Nov. 6, there are 27 Idaho National Guard troops in Washington D.C. There are more than 3,000 National Guard members from other states and territories.
King is a former Army captain and Purple Heart and Bronze Star recipient, according to a press release announcing her tort claim.
“As a trained combat veteran, I never imagined that armed National Guard members would attack, injure, and traumatize me at my home,” King said in the press release. “We are not at war with Americans, and my porch is not a war zone.”
The trial in the case against King is scheduled to start July 27, 2027.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont stores feel ripple effect of strike at grocery distributor
description:
Some Vermont grocers say deliveries have been delayed since the strike by warehouse workers in New Hampshire began Monday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont stores feel ripple effect of strike at grocery distributor.
text:
An aisle in a grocery store with canned food items. Photo via Adobe Stock

Some Vermont grocery and convenience stores are seeing reduced stock and delayed deliveries as a New England labor union refuses to give up its pension plan.
“We certainly hope that this is resolved soon,” said Matt Cota, executive director for the Vermont Retail and Grocers Association, a trade group representing the state’s retail stores. 
Teamsters at the Associated Grocers Northeast warehouse in Pembroke, New Hampshire, have been on strike since Monday, said Teamsters Local 633 Business Agent Keith Judge. 
The strike’s impetus, he said, was a proposed contract by the grocery distributor that would remove employees from their pension plan, instead providing a 401(k) retirement plan with no matching contribution from the company. 
The contract had been officially in negotiation since June, Judge said, but union workers took to the picket lines this week after 98% of the union’s 255 members voted in favor of a strike.
Teamsters representatives met with officials from Associated Grocers on Friday, and the company “refused to come into the room and negotiate with us,” Judge said. A representative from Associated Grocers declined to comment on the strike Friday afternoon. 
Associated Grocers Northeast serves over 600 grocery and convenience stores between Pennsylvania and Maine, according to grocery industry media outlet The Shelby Report. The company is “a key supplier” for Vermont’s country markets, community stores and retail grocers, Cota said. 
Associated Grocers operates nine stores in Vermont communities: Essex Junction, Jericho, Londonderry, Newport, Richmond, Shelburne, Stowe, Waterbury and Woodstock. Representatives from those stores declined to comment on the strike and its impact on their business. 
The strike has affected some Vermont grocers more than others, Cota said, based on store owners’ choices of brand, type and quantity of goods to stock. Stores that rely on Associated Grocers, he said, are seeing delayed deliveries. 
“People can understandably be like, ‘Oh, this store used to have, you know, more variety or used to have more choices or whatever,’” Cota said. “These stores are still open, and if they have less stock, it’s really important that the community supports their local stores.”
The Teamsters plan to remain on strike until they reach a fair agreement, including the pension plan, Judge said.
“We can work through every other issue that’s on the table, whether it be health insurance, wages, languages that we’re trying to change in the contract,” Judge said. “Our nonstarter and pinch point is, and will always be, removal from the pension.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand emphasizes need for Iowa government to work together
description: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, emphasized Friday that his priorities, and those of Iowa lawmakers, will need to be the product of collaboration now that Republicans’ trifecta majority has been divided.  “We don’t elect a dictator, right? We don’t elect a king or a queen,” Sand said during the taping of “Iowa Press” on Iowa PBS. […]
text:
Gov.-elect Rob Sand spoke on Iowa Press Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Iowa PBS) Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, emphasized Friday that his priorities, and those of Iowa lawmakers, will need to be the product of collaboration now that Republicans’ trifecta majority has been divided. 
“We don’t elect a dictator, right? We don’t elect a king or a queen,” Sand said during the taping of “Iowa Press” on Iowa PBS. “We elect a governor, and what that governor does is dependent in part on what the Legislature does.” 
Sand, a Democrat who is currently serving as Iowa state auditor, won against Republican candidate Zach Lahn in the Tuesday election. While results haven’t been certified, Lahn conceded Tuesday night and Gov. Kim Reynolds and Sand are initiating the transition of the position. 
In his first interview since the election, Sand spoke about his priorities, including putting restrictions on data centers and cutting the state deficit in half. He also addressed the possibility of the Legislature calling a special session to try to restrict his powers before he takes office and the possibility of Iowa having the first Democratic caucus for the 2028 election cycle. 
He said his appointment to the position shows that Iowans want a government that works together.
“We’re going to have me as governor and a Republican-led Legislature,” Sand said. “We’re going to check and balance each other. That means everybody can settle down a little bit and breathe easy.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa House Republicans met for caucus Friday but did not announce plans to push for a special session. 
When asked about the possibility and what he’d say to folks considering that, Sand said, “Don’t do that.” 
“Are we here to serve the public or are we here to serve a private club?” Sand said. Voters “… knew what the laws were. We had conversations, and I answered questions about everything a governor can and can’t do. To come in now after the fact and change the meaning of what those voters said, that’s not public service, that’s politics.” 
Transition team
Sand announced the leaders of his transition team Thursday. Elisabeth Buck and Morgan Miller will serve as co-directors of the Sand Transition Committee. Buck, the former president of the United Way of Central Iowa, also worked on the transition teams — and as deputy chief of staff — for previous Iowa Democratic Govs. Chet Culver and Tom Vilsack. Miller, the political director of the Iowa State Education Association, has previously worked on several political campaigns and with AFSCME Council 61.
“I’m honored to have Elisabeth Buck and Morgan Miller on the team that will help me hit the ground running on day one,” Sand said in a statement. “Both Elisabeth and Morgan bring decades of experience, relationships, and public policy expertise that will help prepare me to serve the people of Iowa. I appreciate their commitment, guidance, and shared love for this state that will help me serve all Iowans as governor, and appreciate their service to our state.”
Sand has launched the website IowaForAll.com to share updates and information about the team’s work to prepare for office.
Reynolds pledged to support a smooth transition process as she ends her term as governor. In a statement, Reynolds said she spoke to Sand Thursday “to offer my congratulations and express my personal commitment to a strong transition.”
“Now that the election is over, it’s time to work together so Iowa remains the best state in the nation to live, work, and raise a family for generations to come,” Reynolds said in a statement. “My team and I will do our part to ensure the incoming administration is ready for their first day in office. Iowans deserve nothing less.”
Speaking on “Iowa Press” Friday, Sand said he is “not planning to ask for any resignations” of state officials, with two exceptions for the directors of Iowa Department of Education and the Iowa Department of Management.
Sand said he was concerned about the education department’s spending related to the state’s private school voucher program, which is something he has often criticized. He did not explain why the Department of Management was also a concern, but he said he wants to have conversations with these directors before making any decisions. 
“You want to make sure that you have public servants in these positions, and my assumption is going to be that I might have alignment with some of these people until I know that I don’t,” Sand said. “And I can’t do that unless I’ve got those doors open and I’m able to have those conversations with people.” 
Sand said he has not talked to his Lt. Gov.-elect Dave Mulhbauer about the responsibilities and projects he would take on in the role. 
“Whatever he says he’s interested in, it’ll be in that world of what he’s interested in,” Sand said. 
Sand says his budget will cut state’s $1B deficit in half
Sand said he doesn’t have a budget director yet but has been working with Randy Bauer, who served as state budget director under former Gov. Tom Vilsack, to put “pen to paper” on budget ideas like income limits on school vouchers, taxing marijuana, and making data centers pay “all of their taxes.” 
“Our budget deficit right now, $1 billion – $1.3 billion … I’m pretty sure I’ll have a proposal that’ll at least cut that in half,” the governor-elect said. 
He acknowledged that with any budget, however, it will have to be passed by the Legislature, which maintained a Republican majority after the election. 
“This is part of why I think that Iowans were moving my direction in this campaign,” Sand said. “They want us to be working together, and they just made a decision that forces us to do that, and I think that’s a good thing.” 
On Tuesday, Iowans also approved a constitutional amendment requiring a two-thirds vote of lawmakers to increase personal and corporate income taxes. 
When asked if the amendment would make it more difficult to fund state services, Sand, who opposed the constitutional amendment, emphasized the need for the state to improve its efficiency. He said the Public Innovations & Efficiencies, or PIE, strategy he implemented as state auditor, should be applied at the local and state level. 
Sand also said “we’ve got to fund” the Iowa Water and Land Legacy, or IWiLL, trust to support water and natural resources improvements. Sand said at minimum, the state should enact the three-eighths of a cent sales tax increase proposed in the 2010-passed constitutional amendment, but he said there are “several directions” to look at a sales tax increase. 
Iowa National Guard deployment
Washington D.C. Council Public Safety Committee Chair Brooke Pinto called Friday on newly elected Democratic governors to pull national guard troops from D.C. once they take office.
Sand was one of five states that flipped governor control Tuesday, according to unofficial results from the Associated Press. 
He said he would need to talk to National Guard leadership and Iowans on the ground about what their experience has been and what they are doing in D.C. before he would make a decision. 
“I want to make decisions that I know are based in reality,” Sand said. “And whether or not it’s somebody in one party or another party asking me to do it, I don’t really care about.” 
Iowa Democratic caucuses
In July, the Democratic National Committee panel denied Iowa’s waiver to hold an early caucus contest for 2028, despite the state’s long history of holding “first in the nation” contests to nominate presidential candidates on both sides of the aisle. The Iowa Democratic Party could decide to “go rogue” and hold a caucus without regard to the DNC calendar. 
Sand said that while he doesn’t “really care what a private club thinks,” it would be “smart to have us do historically what we’ve done.” 
“We’re going to follow Iowa law,” Sand said. 
Through the campaign process and speaking with members of national press outlets, Sand said he heard repeatedly that Iowans ask questions of candidates that are “head and shoulders above” what voters in other states ask. 
“Many folks have told me that we do a good job with this – we’ll see where we go from here,” Sand said. 
Going hunting
Since Tuesday, Sand said he has enjoyed spending some additional time with his family and said he hopes to take advantage of the cold front this weekend to go hunting. 
“I haven’t put that much time in the woods because I’m really excited about what comes ahead, and the responsibility, the opportunity, is a pretty incredible thing,” Sand said. “I want to do my best. I want to put everything into it.”
The “Iowa Press” episode airs on Iowa PBS Friday at 7:30 p.m. and Nov. 8 at noon. It is available to stream online.
Robin Opsahl contributed to this reporting.

text:
Rep. Mike Kennedy, R-Utah, and his wife Katrina Kennedy during the Utah GOP election night party on Tuesday, Nov 3, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)The expected composition of Utah’s congressional delegation is now confirmed as The Associated Press called victory for Republican incumbent Reps. Blake Moore and Mike Kennedy late this week.
Moore is expected to return to Congress to represent the state’s new 2nd District after securing 50.26% of votes, about 8 percentage points ahead of Democratic candidate Peter Crosby. Kennedy is also set to represent the state’s 4th District after claiming 53% of votes, leading over Democrat Jonny Larsen, who got nearly 40% of votes as of Friday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The races for the 1st and 3rd districts had already been called by the AP on election night for Democrat Ben McAdams, and incumbent Republican Rep. Celeste Maloy.
Republican incumbent Maloy wins as Moore, Kennedy lead in bids to return to U.S. House

Utah’s election results aren’t final until county and state canvasses are completed on Nov. 23.
Kennedy thanked Utah voters Thursday night on a social media post, saying he was humbled by their trust and grateful to be elected to his second term in Congress.
“I am determined to meet the challenges of the next two years head on. I will work with others when I can, stand firm when it counts, and never stop fighting for the people of Utah, and for our great country – the United States of America,” Kennedy wrote.
Larsen, who was vying for the 4th District seat, hasn’t conceded yet and said he remained optimistic. On a social media post, Larsen acknowledged AP’s call, but said that about 88,000 to 100,000 votes still need to be tallied and asked his followers to keep their eyes on the official Utah election results website. 
Candidates for Utah’s 2nd Congressional District, Democrat Peter Crosby, left, and Republican Blake Moore participate in a debate at Utah State University, Tuesday, Oct.13, 2026, in Logan, Utah. (Pool photo by Eli Lucero/The Herald Journal)
Moore’s campaign didn’t return a request for comment on Friday. However, he had already thanked voters for electing him on election night. 
“I’m incredibly grateful for the trust and support of the people of Utah’s 2nd Congressional District. It’s an honor to continue serving you in Congress,” he wrote on a social media post. “Americans want Washington to focus on making life more affordable and getting back to common sense governing. I’ll continue fighting for our community’s priorities.”
Crosby conceded on Thursday, also on social media, saying he wished Moore and his family “nothing but the best.”
“As his constituent, I hope he will take from this election a recognition that we, the people of Northern Utah, are not happy,” Crosby wrote. “We don’t need him pursuing leadership or committee assignments that advance his political career, we need him passing legislation that helps regular Utahns, and spending time here, in this district.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Some new faces among GOP leadership, though Stewart to remain at Senate helm
description: Legislative Republicans will have some new faces leading the party in Augusta next session after a bruising election left them with even less power in the Maine Senate and House of Representatives. Sen. Trey Stewart will continue to helm the Senate GOP caucus after he was selected by his peers during a closed-door meeting on […]
text:
Senate Minority Leader Trey Stewart reacts to Gov. Janet Mills State of the State address on Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Legislative Republicans will have some new faces leading the party in Augusta next session after a bruising election left them with even less power in the Maine Senate and House of Representatives.
Sen. Trey Stewart will continue to helm the Senate GOP caucus after he was selected by his peers during a closed-door meeting on Friday, though formal votes are held when the Legislature convenes to get sworn in on Dec. 2. 
In a statement Friday, Stewart said he was grateful to his fellow caucus members for their continued confidence. “The lessons we learned on Tuesday are clear,” he said, “Republicans have to focus on the issues important to Maine people, listen to what they are telling us, adjust our strategy to make it clear we have a plan to improve their lives and work together to ensure that plan is carried out.”
Stewart, who has served as minority leader since 2022, was re-elected to his fourth term representing Aroostook County. Prior to that, he served two terms in the House, where he was the assistant Republican leader.
As minority leader, Stewart is the principal speaker for the party during debates on the chamber floor and works to coordinate the party’s legislative agenda. Republicans will only hold 11 of 35 seats in the Senate, down from 14 this past session.
Sen. David Haggan of Hampden was selected to serve as assistant minority leader. Representing parts of Penobscot and Hancock counties, Haggan was just re-elected to his second Senate term after serving four terms in the House.
“Our caucus brings together new perspectives and proven experience, and I’m eager to put both to work for Maine families,” said Haggan in a statement. “We will pursue practical solutions to rising costs, demand discipline in state spending and work with colleagues across the aisle when it serves Mainers.” 
In the House, where Republicans will hold 61of 151 seats after losing a dozen this past Tuesday, Rep. Ken Fredette will lead the minority party, replacing Billy Bob Faulkingham, who was just elected to the Senate. The Newport representative, who held the leadership position from 2014 to 2018, was just elected to his sixth nonconsecutive term in the Legislature. 
In a statement, Fredette said that House Republicans look forward to working with Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree “and agree where we can agree, and where we disagree, fight for our values in all we do for the people of Maine.” 
Rep. Alicia Collins of Sidney was chosen to serve as assistant Republican leader after being elected to her second term in the House. Collins said in a statement that “the needs of everyday Mainers should be our top priority this session.”
With each of these leadership positions also comes a seat on the Legislative Council, which is responsible for the overall management of the legislative branch and has authority over whether to approve after deadline bills.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Voters defend gun law, and sponsor says it’s a model for other states
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: Since the 2024 gun law's passage, Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said the county has managed to prosecute 17 people who were making and using ghost guns, as well as nine people who fired into homes while residents were inside.
text:
TWO DAYS AFTER Bay State voters upheld the 2024 gun reform law, architect state Sen. Cindy Creem basked in the preservation of the statute and pitched it as a public safety framework for other states to follow.
“Wow, that was quite a vote the other day, right?” the Newton Democrat said at a press conference Thursday afternoon. “Thank you, thank you to all of you that voted, all of my constituents, all over the state. It was a great vote. Remember, ‘yes’ is a good word.”
Nearly 67 percent of Bay Staters cast a “yes” vote to keep the law that installed new oversight of untraceable ghost guns and 3D-printed guns, bolstered the state’s red flag law that allows courts to take guns away from people who are a threat to themselves or others, updated the assault weapons ban, expanded data collection and reporting requirements, and more.
Senate President Karen Spilka praised “the smart voters of Massachusetts” and offered a compliment for the House, with fellow bill architect Rep. Michael Day joining the Senate gathering.
“We couldn’t do this alone. The House is great to work with,” Spilka said.
The Ashland Democrat emphasized the gun laws are “not about choosing between public safety and individual rights.”
“They are about recognizing that rights and responsibilities must go hand in hand,” Spilka said. “They must go together.”
Sens. Brendan Crighton, Jamie Eldridge, Adam Gomez, Robyn Kennedy, Vanna Howard, John Keenan, Becca Rausch, Lydia Edwards, Michael Brady, Jake Oliveira and Pat Jehlen joined the presser, as did Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan.
Communities around Greater Boston and eastern Mass. overwhelmingly voted to keep the law, unofficial results show. 
“My hope is that the work we’ve done here will serve as a model for other states looking to strengthen their own gun safety laws and prevent senseless tragedies,” said Creem. “I’m thrilled that legislators in other states can look at these results on Tuesday’s vote and see there is overwhelming public support for commonsense gun safety laws.”
Since the law’s passage, Ryan said Middlesex County has managed to prosecute 17 people who were making and using ghost guns, as well as nine people who fired into homes while residents were inside.
Large swaths of southeastern, central and western Massachusetts voted to repeal the law, according to unofficial results. Municipalities where more than 65 percent of voters backed the repeal include Oakham, Russell, Phillipston, Granville, Savoy, Montgomery, Chester, Peru, Blandford, Monroe, and Florida.
Toby Leary, chair of the Civil Rights Coalition that pushed for repeal, said he was “not at all surprised” by the results but “disappointed that more Mass. residents aren’t concerned about assaults on their constitutional rights.”
“And frankly, maybe that was something we didn’t do a good job of spreading that message,” Leary told the News Service. “Like a lot of people don’t look at this as a constitutional issue — they look at it as just a, you know, a form of regulation.”
While the ballot campaign is over, Leary said there’s a handful of active legal challenges underway in Massachusetts and that others are being considered, including for data privacy issues related to a firearm registration portal online. He said gun rights advocates are also keeping tabs on oral arguments next month in the Supreme Court, which will hear consolidated challenges on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and other semiautomatic rifles.
“I think they’ve already tipped their hand that you cannot ban firearms that are in common and ordinary use,” Leary said of the Supreme Court. “So that’s a huge problem for Massachusetts with their handgun roster and the so-called assault weapon ban.”
Spilka, asked if she’s concerned how the Supreme Court case could impact state law, said, “We’ll have to see what happens, but there’s lots of time in between, and we’ll have to see what the oral arguments are.”
Ruth Zakarin, who chaired the Yes on 9 for a Safe Massachusetts campaign, told the News Service that she is not “hugely concerned” by the complaints working their way through state courts.
“So far, everything has been decided that this law is sound and it is constitutional,” Zakarin said. “And so we obviously pay attention to the litigation, but I don’t have a specific worry.”
Gov. Maura Healey signed an emergency preamble in October 2024 to make the gun reform law take effect immediately, thwarting gun activists’ attempt to suspend it while the repeal effort played out.
Healey has yet to flex that same authority with the abortion law she signed in August, even as the Compassionate Care Coalition claims it has filed enough signatures to suspend the law as it eyes a referendum on the 2028 ballot. A Healey spokesperson did not answer a News Service question Thursday about whether the governor will attach the emergency preamble ahead of Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s office starting to certify coalition signatures after Friday’s deadline. 
Under the constitution, the law is poised to take effect 90 days after Healey’s signature, or Sunday, November 8.
Day said Massachusetts must continue to implement the gun reform law “thoughtfully.”
“We have to make sure law enforcement has the tools and, more importantly, the training that it requests and needs,” the Stoneham Democrat said. “We have to support community-based violence prevention. We have to continue to evaluate what works and what we can do better across the spectrum.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Visualizing Montana’s midterm election

text:
Voting booths set up in Polson at the Lake County Elections Office on Nov. 3, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)More Montanans than ever registered to vote in Montana for this year’s midterm elections, and it was one of the largest midterm elections ever. 
The Secretary of State’s Office reported that 486,746 votes were cast in Tuesday’s election — the second highest number of any midterm election, surpassed by only 2018. 
That represents just more than 60% of the more than 808,000 registered voters in the state, the first time the number of registered voters has surpassed 800,000. 
Voter turnout in the state lags other midterms, but follows the federal trend that also saw lower numbers compared to 2022 and 2018, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. 
The major storyline from Tuesday’s election was the “blue tsunami’ that swept the nation as Democrats flipped dozens of U.S. House districts and seven Senate seats enroute to taking commanding control of both legislative chambers, with two Senate races and about 25 house races yet to be called as of Friday. 
The wave brushed against Montana’s shores and Democrats flipped the state’s western U.S. House district with smokejumper and union leader Sam Forstag winning over Republican Aaron Flint. 
But voters in every county and district in the state trended away from Republicans. 
Comparing both U.S. House races to 2024, nearly every single county swung left by an average of 5.8 points. Six counties, all in the east, saw the Republican-to-Democrat margin shift right. 
(The eastern district featured an independent candidate this year that further split the vote and may have shrouded shifts from Republicans. The GOP candidates’ share of the vote dropped in every single county.)
Shifts were more prominent in the west, where Forstag pulled off his victory. Democratic strongholds in Missoula, Gallatin, and Silver Bow counties swung left by more than 12 points, while Republican-leaning Madison County also saw a more than 12-point shift. 
The same leftward march played out in state house districts.
Between 2024 and 2026 — all state house districts are elected every two years —  all but two districts saw a move toward Democrats, by an average of 12 points. (Races with unopposed candidates in either election year were not considered in the analysis.)
Republican Brad Barker, a moderate who faced a conservative primary challenger in the district surrounding Red Lodge, picked up about 6% more votes than he did in 2024, while Republican Ty Linger picked up 3% more votes than his predecessor did in 2024. 
Those margins helped Democrats flip two seats in each chamber of the state house, according to unofficial tallies by the Secretary of State’s Office, and came within 15 votes of picking up a third house seat if current results stand. 
The shifts occurred in already heavily Democratic areas and those considered quite conservative — voters in the Bitterroot valley, for example, voted between 10 and 24 points more Democratic in 2026.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Pollsters, data centers and fraud risk: CT politics news
description: Plus: A Connecticut museum wins Award of Merit and CVS breakup raises questions for Hartford
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Not a bad night for pollsters
Quinnipiac was a winner Tuesday. Its last poll had Gov. Ned Lamont leading Ryan Fazio by 20 points, 58% to 38%. The latest unofficial results are Lamont by 19.1 points, 59.55% to 40.44%.
Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas led the Democratic ticket with 63.46% of the vote. Being cross-endorsed by both the Working Families and Independent parties didn’t hurt.
Every statewide Democrat except the governor exceeded 60%. Lamont’s showing was the best since M. Jodi Rell’s 63% in 2006.
By the way, Lamont and Rhode Island’s new governor-elect, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, have a common acquaintance. 
She is the niece of former U.S. Sen. Chris Dodd and daughter of Dodd’s late sister, Martha Dodd Buonanno.
— Mark Pazniokas, Capitol Bureau Chief
Connecticut’s Revolution exhibit wins Award of Merit
Connecticut’s Revolution, a new exhibit curated by the Museum of Connecticut History, won a 2026 Award of Merit from the Connecticut League of Museums. The installation weaves together a kaleidoscopic story of how Connecticut residents affected and were affected by the American Revolution. Commemorating the nation’s 250th anniversary, Connecticut’s Revolution is the largest exhibition the Museum of Connecticut History has installed in decades.
Connecticut’s Revolution will be on display at the Connecticut State Library through July 9, 2027.
— Kat Struhar, Manager of Audience Engagement
Audit finds SERC oversights raised risk of fraud
The State Education Resource Center, or SERC, did not comply with internal rules on bank reconciliations in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, increasing the risk of error and fraud, the Connecticut state auditor’s office revealed Thursday.
During the audited period, SERC completed 72 reconciliations for its operating, reserve and payroll accounts. Of those, 69 were not formally reviewed and approved.
SERC also underreported vendor expenditures by over $13 million during that same timeframe. It attributed the problems in part to chief financial officer turnover and told auditors it has implemented and will continue putting in place corrective actions.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
No settlement talks yet, Eversource CEO says
Eversource President Joe Nolan downplayed the prospect of reaching a near-term settlement with Connecticut regulators over the company’s request for an 18% rate increase.
“We’ve got a lot of wood to chop before we get to a position where we would be able to talk settlement,” Nolan said in a call with investors on Thursday.
Nolan’s comments came in response to a question about the midterm elections, in which Eversource faced criticism from both Republicans and Democrats over the rate request. Nolan had previously received flak for boasting in an earlier call that he had a friendly relationship with Gov. Ned Lamont, and the political rhetoric would die down after the election. Without a settlement, a decision on the rate case is expected in June. 
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter
Cromwell to consider data center moratorium
The town of Cromwell will consider a six-month moratorium on data center development following intense backlash to a project that was in the early stages of development, Mayor James Demetriades announced Thursday.
Plans for the project — a 550,000-square-foot data center powered by gas fuel cells — were published online by the developer, Global Commons. But city officials have said repeatedly that they have not received any applications for a building permit.
In September, the Planning and Zoning Commission considered and rejected a one-year moratorium on data centers. But Demetriades said Thursday that the commission would consider a shorter pause at a future meeting. Demetriades said a public hearing will be held on Dec. 3 at the middle school.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter
Pfizer announces $650M Groton manufacturing campus
Pharmaceutical company Pfizer is expanding its Connecticut footprint, with the company announcing this week that it plans to build a 220,000-square-foot facility to house a new manufacturing technology center at its Groton research and development campus.
The project, announced in a press release by economic development organization AdvanceCT on Thursday, will begin construction in 2027. The company hopes to open the manufacturing facility in 2031. Once operational, the center will produce pharmaceutical ingredients and drug products that will be used to support clinical trials.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CVS breakup raises questions for Hartford
CVS Health has announced plans to split its healthcare and drugstore operations, the latest shakeup in a series of organizational changes for the healthcare giant in recent years.
Under its released plans for the division, Hartford-based Aetna will become part of CVS Health, a new company that will also include CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health.
CVS’s 9,000 drugstores will become a separate company, called CVS Pharmacy, which will also oversee mail pharmacy, virtual care, and the company’s Health100 technology-services business. Shareholders will retain shares of both companies moving forward.
It’s still unclear what the restructuring will mean for CVS’s operations in Hartford, with the company saying that it expects to complete separation by early 2028.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
QuantumCT makes computing access deal
As its statewide quantum initiative comes online, Connecticut will partner with Maryland-based company IonQ to increase access to quantum computing power in the state.
In a deal announced this week, QuantumCT, the nonprofit leading the state’s efforts, will purchase, for an undisclosed amount, access to IonQ’s quantum computing technology, a move that supporters say will give local researchers and employers access to cloud computing and hardware that can help with product development, research, and workforce training.
It is possible that QuantumCT will enter into similar deals with other companies in the future, with the release noting that the initiative plans to promote access to a variety of quantum computing technologies in the state, giving companies and researchers the ability to choose which best fits their needs.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Strengthening health coverage during reentry
Federal rules have long prohibited Medicaid coverage for people who are incarcerated, but that will change in Connecticut beginning April 2027. State officials say the expanded coverage will help ensure healthcare isn’t interrupted when someone reenters the community post-incarceration.
On Friday, Gov. Ned Lamont announced that the federal government approved a Connecticut initiative to allow Medicaid coverage for eligible individuals 60 days before their release. In a statement, Lamont said the change will “help ensure folks continue receiving medical care, mental health services, and substance use treatment as they return to the community.” 
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Democrats set leadership teams for their expanded Indiana Statehouse caucuses
description: Democrats in the Indiana General Assembly this week selected leadership after major gains in the midterm election.
text:
House Minority Leader Phil GiaQuinta, D-Fort Wayne, and Senate Minority Leader Shelli Yoder, D-Bloomington, meet with reporters on Oct. 10, 2025. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democrats in the Indiana General Assembly have selected legislative leadership after enjoying big gains in Tuesday’s election.
Senate Democrats, who flipped five districts and retained control of their 10 seats, reaffirmed Sen. Shelli Yoder of Bloomington as leader, according to a Friday announcement.
Sen. Rodney Pol of Chesterton will move up to become assistant leader and Sen. La Keisha Jackson of Indianapolis will join leadership as caucus chair.
Indiana House Republicans pick new leader after big election losses

“This election is not the finish line. It is a responsibility,” Yoder said in a statement. “With new voices, new perspectives and a stronger caucus, we are ready to turn that momentum into action, and we will never stop fighting for the people and communities counting on us.”
Republicans will maintain a 35-15 supermajority for the upcoming legislative session.
The expanded Democratic caucus intends to focus on utility, grocery and housing costs, plus funding for public schools and childcare, among other priorities.
Across the Statehouse rotunda, Democrats were jubilant after gaining 16 seats in the House — far more than the four they needed to break the House GOP’s 14-year supermajority. Republicans appear set to have a 54-46 House majority.
House Democrats on Wednesday reelected their leadership team: Leader Phil GiaQuinta of Fort Wayne, Floor Leader Cherrish Pryor of Indianapolis and Caucus Chair Carey Hamilton of Indianapolis.
“We don’t take this moment lightly. Voters didn’t send us here to keep score,” GiaQuinta said. “They sent us with a clear message: They’re tired of what years of one-party rule have given them. They want groceries, rent and utility bills they can afford. They want public schools that are fully funded. And they want data centers and Big Tech to pay their fair share of taxes.”

“House Democrats are ready to get to work, and we extend a hand to our Republican colleagues to join us,” he said.
Republicans also made their picks Wednesday.
A narrower House GOP majority selected Rep. Ben Smaltz of Auburn as their next speaker. Smaltz will take the reins after House Speaker Todd Huston unexpectedly lost reelection.
Senate Republicans, meanwhile, executed a leadership change in the works for months.
Sen. Chris Garten of Charlestown will serve as the next Senate president pro tem, replacing Sen. Rodric Bray of Martinsville — a congressional redistricting foe targeted by President Donald Trump.
Indiana’s next legislative session will kick off in January, although new lawmakers will be sworn in on Organization Day — the ceremonial first day — later this month.

title: Colorado Connector officials look to finalize railroad agreements after voters approve tax hike
description: Officials with Colorado’s Front Range Passenger Rail District will return to the negotiating table with their railroad partner next week fresh off a major victory at the ballot box, where the district’s voters approved a sales tax hike to fund its plans for a long-awaited restoration of passenger service along the Interstate 25 corridor. Voters […]
text:
A next-generation Amtrak Airo train carries Colorado state and local officials for a ride on the test track at the federal Transportation Technology Center near Pueblo in August. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Officials with Colorado’s Front Range Passenger Rail District will return to the negotiating table with their railroad partner next week fresh off a major victory at the ballot box, where the district’s voters approved a sales tax hike to fund its plans for a long-awaited restoration of passenger service along the Interstate 25 corridor.
Voters in the 31 Front Range municipalities that make up the district approved Issue 7A, imposing a 0.333% district-wide sales tax to fund the Colorado Connector service, known as CoCo, by a margin of 55% to 45%.
Sal Pace, the rail district’s general manager, called the vote a “historic win” for a project that has been decades in the making.

“​​It shows that Colorado believes in itself, and believes in the ability to do great things,” Pace told reporters after the victory. “And we’ve decided that we want to be connected, instead of allowing I-25 to continue to divide us.”
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, who has championed CoCo as he prepares to leave office after two terms in January, celebrated with Issue 7A proponents on election night and said in a statement that the service “will connect Colorado communities, reduce traffic, protect our clean air, and save Coloradans time and money.”
Coloradans for CoCo, an issue committee that supported Issue 7A, raised about $1.3 million from donors including the Denver Broncos, Colorado Rockies, Conservation Colorado and liberal megadonor Pat Stryker.
The approved tax hike, equivalent to about 33 cents on a $100 purchase, will raise an estimated $295 million annually for “CoCo,” keeping it on track to launch along its full, 12-stop intercity route by 2032. Already, as part of a multi-phase plan finalized earlier this year, district officials said they had already secured enough funding to begin service between Denver and Fort Collins by 2029.
The northern segment is planned as a “joint service” in collaboration with the Colorado Department of Transportation and the Denver area’s Regional Transportation District, which has struggled for years to complete a Denver-to-Boulder commuter route, the B Line, first approved by voters in 2004.
The Front Range Passenger Rail District plans to launch the Colorado Connector in phases, including a “starter service” between Fort Collins and Denver by 2029. (FRPR)
“Because of the success of the ballot measure, we’ll be able to have service everywhere within five years,” said Pace.
12 stops planned
The  district’s full delivery plan calls for a gradual expansion to 10 daily round trips north of Denver and eight round trips on the southern segment. Permanent stations would be located in Fort Collins, Loveland, Longmont, Boulder, Louisville, Broomfield, Westminster, Denver, Littleton, Sterling Ranch, Colorado Springs and Pueblo. The plan also envisions special-event stops at the Broncos’ future home at Burnham Yards and the planned Denver Summit soccer stadium at I-25 and Broadway.
To follow through on that promise, the district will need to finalize access agreements with the CoCo service’s host railroads. An agreement is “close to wrapped up” for the northern segment, owned and operated by rail giant BNSF, Pace said, and those discussions will continue next week. BNSF and Union Pacific jointly own the southern segment between Denver and Pueblo, and those negotiations will likely begin in early 2027.
Along with station infrastructure and improved crossings, the track north of Denver needs to be upgraded with “positive train control,” a signaling and automated safety system that’s required under federal law for all rail lines with passenger traffic. The cost of such a system is the project’s “biggest single capital piece,” said John Putnam, chair of the rail district’s board.
After voters passed RTD’s FasTracks plan in 2004, the timely completion of the B Line was derailed in large part due to the unexpectedly high costs of leasing the tracks north of Denver from BNSF. But Pace and other state rail district officials have been adamant that their careful approach, which has included extensive engagement with the railroads about the service’s needs and design, will prevent history from repeating itself.
“We have laid all the groundwork,” Pace said. “We have a pretty good idea of what those railroads are going to be asking for, based on what we’ve already gone through with them over the last five years.”
