name: West Virginia Watch
title: In Berkeley County, third party candidates polled high
description: In six races, a single third party candidate represented the only alternative to Republicans and Democrats for voters in West Virginia House of Delegates and state Senate races. While most challenges were handily won by Democrat or Republican, two races in Berkeley County resulted in strong, competitive showings for the third party candidate.
text:
The West Virginia State Capitol. (Photo by Perry Bennett | West Virginia Legislative Photography)While much ink has been spilled on the Democrats’ victories both in West Virginia and nationally, a couple of third party candidates had strong showings in Tuesday’s midterm elections. 
In six races, a single third party candidate represented the only alternative to Republicans and Democrats for voters in West Virginia House of Delegates and state Senate races. While most challenges were handily won by Democrat or Republican, two races in Berkeley County resulted in strong, competitive showings for the third party candidate. 
State Sen. Jason Barrett, R-Berkeley, won 60% of the vote in his race against Libertarian candidate Travis Bost in the 16th Senate District, which covers Berkeley and Jefferson counties. And in Martinsburg, Constitution Party candidate Tara B. McCoy received 43% of the vote in her race against Republican incumbent Del. Mike Hornby, seven points higher than Hornby’s Democratic challenger in the 2022 election. 
Barrett said with the current political climate, he figured anyone running against a Republican would have a “floor of 35%” of the vote. 
“I think the results in my race, and what we saw in Jefferson County, speaks to the momentum Democrats had nationally and how some of that spilled over into West Virginia,” Barrett said. 
Barrett also noted that in the Eastern Panhandle, with its proximity to Washington, D.C., national trends tend to impact the area more than the rest of the state. 
“A lot of the news people are watching is Washington based,” Barrett said. “You also have a lot of people who work in D.C. but live in the panhandle. So national politics plays a role.” 
Bost, a resident of Gerrardstown in South Berkeley County, closed the gap on Barrett’s home county, winning 5,013 out of 12,973 votes cast in the county. In Barret’s first election, he beat incumbent Democrat Hannah Geffert by 4,200 votes. 
And Bost did it on virtually no money. State Senate seats are typically six-figure affairs – in the Northern Panhandle, the race between state Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio, and Del. Shawn Fluharty, D-Ohio, exceeded $500,000. 
Barrett raised $264,000 in the race, to Bost’s $1,000. 
Bost, whose first foray into politics was a failed campaign for Berkeley County School board in 2022, said the issues of swirling around local control of data centers and a proposed power line coming through Jefferson County led to the strong showing. 
“There were some avenues to pick up some of the disaffected voters that maybe didn’t have an option,” Bost said. 
Barrett said he believes that the pushback against data centers isn’t unique to his area, which is expected to have one soon. 
“We saw in this election a national pushback to data centers,”  he said. “Even though people use them everyday, they don’t want them in their backyards.”
Bost said by having no Democrat in the race, he was able to appeal to Libertarian-leaning voters who would otherwise be concerned about spoiling the vote for a Republican. 
“I also think the people that realized that, ‘hey, I can vote for Travis Bost. He shares a lot of the same ideas that Mr. Barrett has, but he’s better in some areas than maybe he is,’” Bost said. 
Bost said to make up for the cash differential – which opens the doors to peppering yards with signs and stuffing mailboxes with fliers – he turned out to any community event he could find. 
“Opportunities, like this, to earn media (attention) whenever I had the opportunity to go on the radio or go to a forum, I made sure I was out there talking to the people,” Bost said. 
Bost said he hopes the run will raise the profile of Libertarian Party policies in the state. 
“We like to say Republicans claim to be fiscally responsible, but you talk to just about any Libertarian, and they will say we’re really the real fiscally responsible people and economically literate group,” Bost said. “And there’s not a lot of legislative history with Libertarians, obviously, but we have a lot of legislative history of Republicans running as especially conservative, but not governing that way.” 
For Democrats in Berkeley County, the strong showings indicate that had they fielded candidates in the House 93rd or the Senate 16th, things could’ve been different, according to county party chair David Valente. 
“Yeah, we’re definitely going to target that,” Valente said. “We ( will) work with our friends in Jefferson next time to find a candidate to run against Patricia Rucker for that election, but in four years, we’re definitely going to be scouring Berkeley for a candidate that will run against Jason.

name: National
title: Democratic wins put Medicaid expansion back in play in holdout states
description: In a handful of holdout states, Democrats appear ready to use their newly won statehouse dominance to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In at least four states — Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin — the midterm election results have tilted the political calculus toward expansion, though lawmakers have yet to lay out details. […]
text:
Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms celebrates her victory on Nov. 3 in Atlanta. Bottoms made full Medicaid expansion central to her campaign and has called it “a day one priority.” Democratic victories could bring Medicaid expansion to a handful of other states. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)In a handful of holdout states, Democrats appear ready to use their newly won statehouse dominance to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
In at least four states — Georgia, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin — the midterm election results have tilted the political calculus toward expansion, though lawmakers have yet to lay out details. Medicaid is the joint federal-state insurance program for people with low incomes.
Georgia and Wisconsin have limited expansion programs, but neither has approved the broader expansion allowed under the Affordable Care Act.
“Before Tuesday, I wouldn’t have expected much activity in the 10 remaining states that have not expanded Medicaid” to more adults under the Affordable Care Act, said Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at the health research and policy nonprofit KFF, on a media call after the election.
“But I think that dynamic has changed.”
Under the Affordable Care Act, better known as Obamacare, states can expand Medicaid to cover adults earning up to 138% of the federal poverty line — about $22,000 a year for a single person — and the federal government will pick up 90% of the costs for those newly eligible enrollees.
Forty states took the deal, adding nearly 20 million people with low incomes to the rolls. In the remaining 10 states, which have been mostly controlled by Republicans, expansion has been blocked by GOP opponents who think it is too expensive or who are ideologically opposed to growing government programs.
Georgia Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms made full Medicaid expansion central to her campaign and has called it “a day one priority.”
“This is thrilling for me because this is the reason I ran for office in the first place,” said Dr. Michelle Au, a Democratic Georgia state representative and physician.
In Georgia, Democrats won every statewide office that was on the ballot and appear poised to take control of the state House, though Republicans will still control the state Senate. Democrats would need bipartisan support to get expansion passed.
“We are going to see a bill and it’s going to be an interesting process in the newly divided government,” said Au.
She said a 2024 Medicaid expansion bill had bipartisan support among state legislators, including from Republicans representing rural districts facing hospital closures and higher rates of uninsured residents. The bill eventually died in committee, she said, in large part because it didn’t have the backing of Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.
“What became apparent in that process was that there was nothing more important to the passage of this issue than having a strong governor who supports it,” Au said.
“If anything, this issue has only gotten more urgent and popular” among voters, she said.
Wisconsin’s new Democratic trifecta — the party will control both legislative chambers and the governor’s office — could make full Medicaid expansion much easier to pass. Wisconsin Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley has deferred to legislators when asked about expansion.
Democratic state Rep. Greta Neubauer, who is set to become House Speaker, stopped short of promising expansion in a call with reporters after the election. She said lawmakers will look at several options to address healthcare, reported the Wisconsin Examiner.
Neubauer said Medicaid expansion was complicated by the Trump administration’s new work requirements and other changes to the program.
“It’s a shame that Wisconsin has not done that up to this point,” she said. “We are going to be working very closely with the administration to figure out the best way to expand access to affordable healthcare for Wisconsinites, even given the Trump administration’s efforts to cut access and raise costs.”
In July 2025, Trump signed a broad tax and spending measure that is projected to cut federal Medicaid spending by an estimated $886.8 billion over the next decade, largely because new work requirements will push people off the rolls, according to estimates by the Congressional Budget Office. The new rules, which will take effect in January, will apply to people who became eligible for Medicaid as a result of expansion.
But the new Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to look at delaying or reversing the changes, which “may make it even more attractive for places like Texas and Georgia to try to expand,” Levitt said.
Texas voters also voted Democrats into every statewide office that was on the ballot, including electing Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor and flipping control of the state House. Republicans still control the state Senate.
Hinojosa told a Houston television station that she would push the state legislature to expand Medicaid.
Before the election, Kansas’ outgoing Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly called the Kansas’ Legislature’s refusal to expand Medicaid “the dumbest thing Kansas has ever done.”
She said the main roadblock was opposition by Kansas’ Republican House Speaker. But this week, Kansas Democrats flipped as many as 20 seats in the Kansas House, quashing the Republican supermajority.
Votes are still being tallied, but it appears that while Republicans will retain a majority in the state House and a supermajority in the state Senate, Democrat Cindy Holscher holds a narrow lead in the governor’s race.
Holscher campaigned on promises of expanding Medicaid, saying Medicaid expansion would help prevent hospital closures and improve access to mental health services. She noted that expansion is popular across the state.
“This is approved by, I believe, over 75% of the population,” she said. “This cuts across the political spectrum. Rural as well as urban areas say this is what we need to do.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Good wasn’t good enough: what Tennessee’s election results are trying to tell us
description: I started this election cycle saying that the moment demanded the highest level of spiritual, political and emotional maturity we could muster. Not enough of us summoned it. And it showed up in the vote count. Shelby County did good. We did significantly better than four years ago. Turnout increased. But good was not what […]
text:
MEMPHIS, TN -- Rep. Justin J. Pearson speaks during his Election Night Watch Party at the Power Center in Memphis.  (Photo by Brad Vest for Tennessee Lookout)I started this election cycle saying that the moment demanded the highest level of spiritual, political and emotional maturity we could muster.
Not enough of us summoned it. And it showed up in the vote count.
Shelby County did good. We did significantly better than four years ago. Turnout increased. But good was not what this moment required. We needed to be great. More than 300,000 registered voters in Shelby County still did not participate. Imagine just 100,000 more of them showing up. Not all 300,000. Just one-third.
That level of participation could have fundamentally altered the political landscape across all three congressional districts touching Memphis and, given the narrow statewide gubernatorial margin (approx. 53,000 votes), could have transformed that race as well.
That is why I agree with everyone who says this is not the season for finger-pointing. But we must understand the difference between blame and accountability. We spend so much time focused on the former that we often escape the latter altogether.
Accountability means asking who had the power, resources, platform, influence and responsibility to do something, then honestly assessing whether they did everything they reasonably could. The burden should not be distributed equally because capacity is not distributed equally. Somebody with 500 followers (or dollars) should not bear the same responsibility as somebody with 50,000 constituents, institutional resources, political machinery and an oath of public service.
Pearson accepts loss in U.S. District 9 race, but says ‘Tennessee politics will never be the same’

Every one of us should ask ourselves: Did I do my best?
And extraordinary circumstances require extraordinary standards. Conventional political etiquette designed to protect egos, personalities, relationships and future aspirations should have been subordinated to the urgency of this moment. Anything less represented a failure of political maturity, especially from people who have sworn to put the public interest ahead of their personal feelings.
That brings me to something else that irritates the hell out of me: describing Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District as simply a Republican “flip.” It was not the same district.
Republicans dismantled the old 9th, split Memphis among three congressional districts and constructed an entirely new district carrying the same number. The new district had voted for Donald Trump by roughly 21 points in 2024. Yet Brent Taylor defeated Justin Pearson by only 2,539 votes, roughly one percentage point. Calling that an ordinary “loss” misses the point.
If a boxer is forced into the ring with one hand tied behind his back and loses by one point on the judges’ cards, the story is not simply that he lost. The story is that somebody tied his damn hand behind his back and he still almost won.
Pearson is right to challenge the traditional parameters of victory and defeat. He should give them hell in the Tennessee House and then come back for that congressional seat. And the larger Tennessee numbers should shake loose some longstanding assumptions.
In 2022, Republican Bill Lee defeated Democrat Jason Martin by about 32 percentage points. This week, Marsha Blackburn defeated Jerri Green by less than 3 points. That is a nearly 30-point movement in the gubernatorial margin in four years. AP analysis also found that every Tennessee county moved toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election. Democrats flipped six Republican-held state House seats, their biggest multi-seat gain in decades.
And, perhaps most deliciously, Republicans’ congressional redistricting scheme did not accomplish its ultimate aspiration. They wanted nine Republican congressional seats. They got eight. 
While Republicans captured the newly reconstructed 9th, Democrat Victoria Broderick won the 4th District by roughly 280 votes. They essentially traded the traditional Democratic 9th for a new Democratic 4th.
All that happened with national Democratic investment that, relative to how competitive Tennessee ultimately proved to be, was nowhere near what this state warranted.
Sound familiar?
Before Georgia turned blue, organizers were told Georgia was red. Before Texas became genuinely competitive, people dismissed Beto O’Rourke’s statewide campaign as another noble Southern loss. Stacey Abrams did not transform Georgia in one election. Organizers contested supposedly unwinnable terrain until the terrain changed. Tennessee is on that continuum.
Some of us have been saying for years that this state is not “ruby red.” The data is finally making that argument harder to dismiss.
But there is another lesson, and it is less comfortable. Some people showed us who they are during this election. 
We. Must. Believe. Them.
Some stood on the sidelines because of bruised egos, personality conflicts, political calculations and immature impulses. Now that the results demonstrate how close these races were, some will suddenly rediscover the movement. Some are already emerging from the shadows. 
I cannot pretend I did not see who showed up and who did not. Receipts matter.
Going into 2027, we should know what organizations organized, what elected officials mobilized, what institutions invested, who communicated with their constituencies and who merely commented from the sidelines. Nobody should be too important, too established or too grandiose to show their work.
Because 2027 brings one of the most consequential municipal election cycles of our lifetime.
If Memphis learns to harness the political power sitting dormant inside hundreds of thousands of registered voters, we can shape our own destiny. If we do not, we may watch a blue, perhaps even Black, wave carry other cities and states forward while Memphis crashes out on the shore.
We did good. Next time, good cannot be good enough.

name: California
title: California’s new teen social media law challenged in court by Meta, TikTok and Google
description: California’s ban on addictive social media features for kids takes effect in January. Now Big Tech is trying to stop it in federal court.
text:
In summary

California’s ban on addictive social media features for kids takes effect in January. Now Big Tech is trying to stop it in federal court.



Tech giants Meta, Google, and TikTok are suing to block a landmark California law meant to protect kids’ mental health on social media platforms.
The law, one of a slate of bills signed by Gov. Newsom this year to protect kids online, would block social media companies from offering “addictive” features to teens under 16. 
Set to go into effect in January, the law defines addictive features as design choices like infinite scroll, autoplay, and recommendations. Those features are blamed in part for a teen mental health crisis, which the law seeks to curb.
The three suits, filed in multiple federal courts in California this week, argue that the law would infringe on the companies’ First Amendment rights. The Meta suit, for example, says that the law undermines the “fundamental principle” of free speech by making the state “the editor, curator, and controller of online speech.” 
Google, which owns YouTube, similarly argues in its lawsuit that the law would “frustrate YouTube’s efforts to provide under-16 users with safe, responsible, and enriching experiences on the platform.”
The companies want the courts to block the law before it takes effect. 
When the measure was before the California Legislature, some groups, like digital rights organization the Electronic Frontier Foundation, argued the law would amount to a full ban on social media for teenagers because it was so broad and the features it regulated so fundamental to the platforms. Teens would then miss out on precious online resources, the groups said. 
NetChoice, a tech industry-aligned group, also criticized the law. It released a statement supporting the lawsuits, saying “the state cannot restrict minors’ access to protected expression simply because it thinks the expression is bad for them.”
A supporter of the law, the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said in response to the lawsuits that courts have already been “rejecting the industry’s claims that the First Amendment shields them from accountability.”
The bill’s passage was just one in a recent series of damaging moments for the tech industry, which has faced intense scrutiny over its impact on teens’ mental health. Meta agreed in August to pay as much as $17 billion as part of a settlement with 47 states that argued the company had engineered its products to be addictive to children. 
A TikTok spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the suits. A Meta spokesperson declined to attach their name to a statement and CalMatters declined to publish it.
“We believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,” José Castañeda, a Google spokesperson, said in an email. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Preparing for transition, Mills and Pingree hope new Congress will reverse federal cuts
description: As Gov. Janet Mills and Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree partner to ensure a smooth transition of power, they said Friday they are also hoping the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress will reverse federal cuts that are expected to have severe consequences for the state. Many of the cuts to Medicaid that are expected to have […]
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree and Gov. Janet Mills at a press conference in Augusta on Nov. 6, 2028. (Photo courtesy of Office of Gov. Janet Mills)As Gov. Janet Mills and Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree partner to ensure a smooth transition of power, they said Friday they are also hoping the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress will reverse federal cuts that are expected to have severe consequences for the state.
Many of the cuts to Medicaid that are expected to have severe consequences for the state will take effect in January as the new Congress is sworn in and Pingree takes office. 
The handover marks the first time since the 1950s that Maine voters have elected consecutive chief executives from the same party.
“This is quite different than eight years ago, and we’re going to make sure that the state of Maine runs smoothly through a transition,” Mills said, referring to her experience following former Gov. Paul LePage in 2019.
“I’ve pledged my administration’s full cooperation in providing the smooth and effective transition that many people expect and deserve.”
The two Democrats have extensive experience working together, first in the Maine Legislature and more recently when Pingee served as head of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. The transition will include collaborating on details such as crafting the state budget and determining how many department leaders from the Mills administration will continue in their roles.
“I’m enormously proud of what we have accomplished over the past eight years, and I feel good about the state we will be handing over to the governor-elect in January,” Mills said.
“I believe Maine people selected Hannah Pingree for the very same reasons that I asked her to serve in my administration eight years ago: her deep experience, her sound judgment, leadership qualities, her relentless optimism for Maine’s future.”
Earlier this week, Pingree announced that her transition committee will be led by former Republican state Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot Ambassador Maulian Bryant. In coming weeks, she said her team will conduct interviews for all cabinet positions, although she acknowledged some Mills administration commissioners may want to be considered to continue their current roles. 
“We want the most talented team of people in the state government who are diverse, who are experienced, and ready to hit the ground running,” she said.
Cuts to healthcare and food assistance
Both Mills and Pingree on Friday celebrated the nationwide sweep of Democratic victories, saying it would help Congress undo some cuts that the Republican-led Congress approved, particularly to food assistance and healthcare. 
The state is preparing for cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Medicaid, Pingree said. But state funding is not enough to make up for the millions in lost federal funding, she said, nor can the state alter the new requirements that are expected to make thousands of low-income Mainers ineligible for Medicaid.
“I’m very deeply concerned about the Medicaid cuts, the SNAP cuts,” Pingree said. 
However, Pingree said she’s hopeful that members of Congress “come to their senses and realize just how devastating this will be for healthcare for people all across the country. But no matter what, we have to plan for where we’ll be in January, and that does mean planning for these cuts.”
In conversations with other governors, Pingree said she is aware of lobbying efforts urging Congress to postpone the Medicaid cuts, in particular, a majority of which take effect next year.
Mills added that postponing Medicaid cuts should be an “easy thing for them to do.” She also said she hopes the new Congress will  reverse changes made to the Affordable Care Act. After Congress allowed the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits, more than 60,000 Mainers who purchase health insurance through the marketplace saw steep increases in monthly premiums. Almost 10,000 canceled their health insurance plans, according to data from the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. Those costs are set to increase by some 20% again next year.
“They can reverse that with a stroke of pen,” Mills said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Senate Democrats stick with same leadership team
description: Maine Senate Democrats are sticking with the same leadership team heading into the next session, when they will have an even larger majority.  Sen. Mattie Daughtry of Brunswick will continue as president, Sen. Teresa Pierce of Falmouth as majority leader and Sen. Jill Duson of Portland as assistant majority leader. They became the first all-female […]
text:
Newly sworn-in Maine Senate President Mattie Daughtry addresses senators in the Senate chamber in Augusta on Dec. 4, 2024. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)Maine Senate Democrats are sticking with the same leadership team heading into the next session, when they will have an even larger majority. 
Sen. Mattie Daughtry of Brunswick will continue as president, Sen. Teresa Pierce of Falmouth as majority leader and Sen. Jill Duson of Portland as assistant majority leader. They became the first all-female leadership team in the upper chamber when first assuming those roles in 2024.
The caucus met behind closed doors on Friday to make its decisions, though formal votes are held when the Legislature convenes to get sworn in on Dec. 2. Democrats in the House of Representatives made their leadership picks on Thursday. 
“I’m so grateful to my colleagues for trusting me to lead this incredible team again,” Daughtry said in a press statement following the meeting. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and I’m as stubborn as ever about making sure Maine is a place where people can build a good life.”
Heading into the new session, Democrats now hold a 24-seat supermajority, the first since 1985, according to the release. A record number of Democratic women will also be serving in the Senate, the statement noted, making up two-thirds of the caucus .
A lifelong Brunswick resident and small business owner, Daughtry has served in the Maine Legislature since 2012, when she was first elected to the Maine House of Representatives at 25 years old. 
After serving in the lower chamber until 2020, Daughtry was elected to the Senate, becoming assistant majority leader two years later and president two years after that. At 37, she became the youngest woman to ever hold the role. Among Daughtry’s achievements are helping to craft Maine’s paid family and medical leave law.
As Senate president, Daughtry presides over floor proceedings, appoints all committee members and committee chairs in conjunction with the speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and oversees the flow of legislation, among other responsibilities.
As majority leader, Pierce represents the party on the chamber floor and helps direct legislative priorities and debate. She is wrapping her second term in the Senate. From 2014 to 2020, Pierce served in the House, including as chair of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee, which sets the state budget. 
Working alongside the majority leader, Duson also helps shape legislative priorities.  First elected to the senate in 2022, Duson was the first Black woman to serve in the upper chamber. During her first term, she served on the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee. Prior to her time in the Legislature, she spent more than 19 years on the Portland City Council.
With each of these leadership positions also comes a seat on the Legislative Council, which is responsible for the overall management of the legislative branch and has authority over whether to approve after deadline bills. 
On Tuesday, Daughtry won reelection with more than 70% of the vote, meanwhile both Pierce and Duson ran uncontested.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: LSU reinstates law professor suspended for political comments
description: LSU has reinstated a law professor that it removed from the classroom for making political comments critical of Gov. Jeff Landry in early 2025.  Ken Levy, a tenured professor of criminal and constitutional law, will make his return to the classroom in the spring semester, two years after he was suspended from teaching.  In an […]
text:
The LSU Law Center pictured on March 20, 2023, in Baton Rouge. (Photo by Matthew Perschall for Louisiana Illuminator)LSU has reinstated a law professor that it removed from the classroom for making political comments critical of Gov. Jeff Landry in early 2025. 
Ken Levy, a tenured professor of criminal and constitutional law, will make his return to the classroom in the spring semester, two years after he was suspended from teaching. 
In an interview, Levy said he is excited to return to LSU, but said his treatment by the university will have a chilling effect on him and other professors. 
“I’m going to do my job and my job is to discuss controversial topics and material,” Levy said. “But I will refrain from what I deem gratuitous commentary.” 
In a letter to Levy, LSU Provost Joseph Messina warned the professor to keep classroom discussion to the subject matter. 
“Expressing personal political views and extraneous political commentary in your classes do not serve a legitimate academic purpose related to the course and are inconsistent with law and LSU policy,” Messina wrote. 
In January 2025, Levy was removed from the classroom after he made a profane statement about the governor during a law school class that made its way to Landry. 
“If Governor Landry were to retaliate against me, then f*** the governor and f*** that,” Levy told students in his Administration of Criminal Justice class. 
After Levy’s comments went public, Landry shared a series of social media posts lambasting Levy and LSU. 
LSU suspended Levy pending an investigation into his behavior. Such an action is rare and usually only happens when a professor is accused of a serious infraction, such as sexual misconduct.
LSU’s letter to Levy, which was sent last month, does not detail why he has been reinstated after being removed from the classroom two years ago. LSU spokeswoman Meg Sunstrom declined to provide any additional details explaining Levy’s return to the school. Levy said he was not provided any explanation as to why he could resume teaching. 
Landry’s spokeswoman Kate Kelly has not responded to a request for comment.
Shortly after his suspension, Levy sued the university to be allowed to teach again. Levy was still employed by the university and was being paid while suspended. 
In his lawsuit, Levy said that his controversial statements about Landry had been a reaction to the governor’s previous attempts to remove fellow law professor Nick Bryner in 2024. 
Landry publicly asked LSU to discipline Bryner for his remarks he made about President Trump the day after the presidential election in 2024.  A video of Bryner’s comments were sent to the governor, who then circulated the video on social media. 
“I don’t know if anybody falls in that category, but if you voted for Trump on the idea that you don’t like him personally but that you like his policies, I just want you to think about the message that that sends to other people and how you can prove that, by treating other people in a way that matches that sentiment,” Bryner told his students Nov. 6, 2024.

While using salty language about Landry in 2025, Levy said he also asked his students not to record his lectures because he didn’t want to be targeted by the governor. 
Levy’s lawsuit was appealed to the state supreme court, which declined to hear the case, leaving in place an appeals court decision that permitted LSU to keep him out of the classroom, though it barred LSU from firing him outright.
While Levy’s lawsuit is still listed as active, it is not being actively pursued. 
Levy said in an interview this week he believes he would have been fired if he didn’t have tenure protections, which make it very difficult for LSU to fire him for his speech. 
While Landry did not publicly call on LSU to fire Levy, he did suggest that tenure should be abolished. 
Tenure provides an indefinite academic appointment to qualifying faculty members who have demonstrated excellence in their field. Academics with tenure can only be terminated for cause, but it typically only happens in extreme circumstances. College faculty view tenure as a key part of academic freedom at universities and a shield against political, corporate and religious intervention.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms announces transition team as ascendent Georgia Democrats prepare to run state government
description: Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms didn’t have long to celebrate Tuesday’s historic win.   The former Atlanta mayor became the first Georgia Democrat to be elected governor in decades, winning by more than 8 percentage points, and the first Black woman elected governor in the nation.  Less than three days after that victory, she was standing on […]
text:
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at the state Capitol about her transition into office on Nov. 6, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderGovernor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms didn’t have long to celebrate Tuesday’s historic win.  
The former Atlanta mayor became the first Georgia Democrat to be elected governor in decades, winning by more than 8 percentage points, and the first Black woman elected governor in the nation. 
Less than three days after that victory, she was standing on the steps inside the state Capitol unveiling her transition team as she prepares to lead the state starting in January. She rattled off a long list of transition team members, including Home Depot co-founder Arthur Blank and filmmaker Tyler Perry. 
“Now the work begins,” Bottoms said at a Friday press conference. 
“The decisions that we make over the next few weeks about who will lead our agencies will shape how we will deliver for all Georgians over the next four years,” she also said. “Our goal is simple: to be ready to govern on day one.” 
The incoming governor hasn’t released many details yet about her legislative agenda for the first year of her term. But she is calling her transition plan “Georgia’s Promise” as a nod to her intention to make her pledges on the campaign trail a reality. 
“We are going to continue to focus on those issues that we’ve heard loud and clear over the last year and a half of this campaign,” Bottoms said. “Those issues related to concerns surrounding the cost of living, all things related to affordability, expanding access to quality and affordable healthcare and investing in our public schools, our teachers and our students.”
Bottoms said that she had talked to outgoing GOP Gov. Brian Kemp and that he has offered to do what he can to help make a smooth transition. His office confirmed that they had talked but didn’t offer further comment about their discussion. 
Kemp announced Wednesday morning that he would not call a special session to curtail the governor’s powers or to redraw Georgia’s political maps. But he did leave open the possibility of calling a special session to address “budgetary issues” before lawmakers return to Atlanta in January. 
It’s not clear yet what Kemp is referring to, but the governor did make the unusual move in May to cut $300 million in new spending after the state’s budget director said that a new income tax cut package created a $1.3 billion hole in the budget. 
In addition to that, Bottoms will also inherit diminished reserves, which a recent report shows dropped from $14.6 billion as of January to $8.7 billion. 
Bottoms cited her experience overseeing Atlanta’s budget in the wake of the pandemic and said she’s “used to getting tough things done.”
“Show me your budget, and I’ll show you your priorities,” she said. “And the priorities that I believe will be consistent relate to all things related to the cost of living and how we can help relieve that burden for people, especially in the midst of the cuts that have come from the Trump administration.” 
But it was clear Bottoms was also still absorbing the historic significance of her electoral success. 
“My husband put it in context. He said there have been a lot of Black women in America over the course of history, and God has said, ‘You get to be the first,’” Bottoms said when asked to reflect on the accomplishment. 
“I don’t take that lightly. I believe that it is representative of just the best of who we all are, that in this place, the South, with our very rich history, that Georgia gets to break that barrier. So I’m grateful for it, and as I’ve said repeatedly, I look forward to representing all of Georgia, and I hope for young boys and girls across this state, no matter where they live, no matter their race, no matter their background, I hope they see some inspiration in this moment.”

name: VTDigger
title: ‘Where is your emergency?’: Hartford’s emergency communications specialists shortage echoes national trend
description:
The shortage is putting extra strain and pressure on Hartford’s current specialists.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘Where is your emergency?’: Hartford’s emergency communications specialists shortage echoes national trend.
text:
Christina Kramer, 47, answers a 911 phone call in the communications center of the Hartford Public Safety Building in White River Junction, Vt., on Thursday, October 29, 2026. An emergency communications specialist, Kramer takes phone calls and dispatches all over Vermont, often working between 65 and 70 hours a week. Photo by Sophie Levenson/Valley News

WHITE RIVER JUNCTION — In the bathroom at the Hartford Emergency Communications Center, there are two radios and a phone atop the toilet tank. There’s a notepad and a pencil, and some classic lavatory reading material: a handbook on how to take 911 calls.
Christina Kramer once took a call about a traffic accident from the bathroom at work. When there’s nobody else working the phones, she’s always on duty — even when duty calls.
Toilet calls don’t happen often in Hartford, as the police department tries to prevent one-person shifts in the communications center. Sometimes, though, it has no other option: Hartford has a shortage of emergency communications specialists, something that shifts undue pressure onto Kramer and her small team of coworkers. They know that if they don’t show up for work, people who need help will have a harder time finding it.
Hartford has four open positions in its communications center, which, if filled, would add to a current team of just six specialists, responsible for covering the phones 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year, preferably with more than one person working at a time.
Hartford’s short staffing problem is not unique. There are too few people answering and dispatching 911 calls nationally, according to a 2023 report from the International Academies of Emergency Dispatch. The survey conducted by IAED and the National Association of 911 Administrators indicated that the average vacancy rate in emergency communication centers across the country was about 25%. 
Being a communications specialist doesn’t pay much and often demands long hours punctuated by callers in distress. The background check process has a particularly high bar. The job requires a certain kind of compartmentalization as well as the ability to multitask and react fast. Social perception also likely plays a part, as public confidence in the police remains low, at 45% according to a Gallup poll from July.
“People don’t want to be cops,” Lt. William Furnari, a public information and police officer, said recently.
In the dispatch room
Very little light makes it into the dispatch room where Kramer spends so much of her week. She and Sarah Morse, the other specialist on her Thursday shift, prefer it that way. They each get plenty of bright light from the eight computer screens on each of their desks, home to maps, lists of officers, security cameras, connection interfaces and resources for the national suicide hotline. 
On this particular Thursday, Kramer pressed a button so that her desk rose to standing height, bringing her various monitors and phones with her. She has four landlines: One answers 911 calls, one is a backup for 911 calls, another answers calls straight to the department and the other is the backup for that. Kramer uses a thin microphone to dispatch police officers, fire fighters and EMTs.
She wore a gray hoodie branded with the communications center and a sparkly headband over close-cropped black hair. Her plastic water bottle read “KRAMER.”

READ MORE

A call came in and Kramer snapped into business mode. “Vermont 911, where is your emergency?” she asked the caller, who had witnessed an elderly woman faint outside a Dollar General. Kramer’s fingers flew over her keyboard, typing notes for herself so she didn’t forget any details when it came time for dispatch.
“Does anybody have any juice they can give her?” she asked, hearing that the woman was diabetic. On another screen, Kramer looked up the address of the Dollar General, then pressed a button to call in an ambulance.
As a communications specialist in Hartford, Kramer’s job is two-fold. She answers calls from the community and dispatches emergency services; at many communication centers, specialists only do one of those jobs. Vermont has six public safety answering points, each responsible for a geographic area so that when someone calls 911, their call goes to the closest available point. With understaffing an issue across the state, however, Kramer often answers calls from outside of Hartford’s catchment area, then has to dispatch to a different county’s emergency services force — not ideal, but effective enough.
“The best way this works is if the person answering the phone is also the person dispatching,” Furnari said.
A woman called 911 and told Kramer that her phone had been stolen. Kramer asked her a series of questions: “What is your name?” “Do you know what color the backpack was?”
After a few minutes of questions, Kramer put the phone down and turned to Furnari. “She said she’s had it with me,” she told him, a bemused expression on her face. 
‘Crime doesn’t have a schedule’
Once or twice, Kramer has burnt her lunch because she left it on the stove when a call came through. 
“Crime doesn’t have a schedule,” she said.
At 18, Kramer went to school for criminal justice at the New Hampshire Technical Institute in Concord. She thought she wanted to become a police officer but decided she would rather work “behind the scenes,” and found herself in a dispatch room. Fifteen years later, she’s still working in one; Kramer, 47, has been a communications specialist in Hartford for nearly five years.
These days, she works between 65 and 70 hours a week, earning overtime pay when she goes past 40 hours. Her shifts range from 10- to 14-hour stretches, sometimes from 5 a.m. to 3 p.m., other times from 7 p.m. to 5 a.m. Kramer has blackout shades and a sound machine in her bedroom in Claremont so she can sleep when she has the time, whether that’s day or night.
This year, Kramer is scheduled to work on Thanksgiving and Christmas Eve, but has Christmas Day off. The police department has invited her to their Thanksgiving potluck.
Kramer is popular at work; in 2024, she won employee of the year. She interacts with police officers often, not only to communicate professionally but also to seek peer support for the more difficult parts of the job. Kramer herself is getting certified as a peer counselor, learning to help her colleagues deal with grief or trauma associated with their jobs. Sometimes, communication specialists have to help people through calls that bring up something personal. Other times, they know the caller. That has happened to Kramer.
“I try to detach by just trying to help them so that they can get what kind of help they’re looking for,” she said. “There are certain calls that can be emotional, but I try not to let it get to me.”
For Furnari, one of the biggest components of peer support comes informally, when officers tell communication specialists what happened with the call they answered or dispatched. Not knowing how a difficult situation turned out can contribute to anxiety for the communications team, he said. 
“There’s an openness that comes from this kind of work,” Furnari said. “It can be stressful. It can be exciting. It can be a lot of different things, and that leads to stronger connections, as you’ve gone through things together, and makes communication easier and more direct.”
On her own, Kramer makes an effort to take care of herself by spending time with her son, going on walks around her neighborhood, working out at the gym. She tries to keep a busy personal life so that stress from work doesn’t affect her when she goes home.
This, of course, is one of the biggest reasons it has been hard for Hartford to hire communications specialists, even after posting open calls and offering walk-in tests in the Hartford Public Safety Building on VA Cutoff Road. For the 2027 Hartford budget, Police Chief Constance Kelley is requesting the funds for six more officers. The town currently employs 22, a number that has barely changed in the last decade, according to Furnari.
“We have not kept up with growth,” he said. 
“It’s an awful lot,” Ken Hawkins, deputy director at the Vermont Police Academy, said Monday. “More and more folks have placed more emphasis on family, and time off, and not necessarily the attitude of service before self.”
Kramer, however, has been putting service first since she decided to pursue a career in public safety as a teenager. Every time a line rang during this recent shift, she stopped her conversations with Furnari mid-sentence, cradled the phone against her shoulder, and typed furiously with one hand. In an instant, her tone turned serious, her questions came quick. When Vermonters panic, Kramer locks in.

name: VTDigger
title: Essex Junction cannabis and duck farmer poised to get his growing license back
description:
A judge ruled that Jason Struthers can resume his backyard cannabis growing on Taft Street because his operation predates the city’s new laws zoning cannabis cultivation. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Essex Junction cannabis and duck farmer poised to get his growing license back.
text:
Jason Struthers with some of the cannabis plants at his licensced growing operation at his home in Essex Junction on Tuesday, September 30, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Essex Junction man long mired in controversy for growing cannabis and raising ducks in his suburban backyard wants permission to keep cultivating. 
Vermont Superior Court Judge Thomas Walsh ruled late last month that Jason Struthers, who has farmed in his half-acre backyard since 2022, did not violate local zoning laws by cultivating cannabis. The Cannabis Control Board subsequently renewed his license to grow. Now he’s waiting on approval from the city. 
Struthers said in an interview that he had mixed emotions about the decision because he thinks it’s “highly likely (the town) will appeal to the Supreme Court again.” 
City officials denied requests for an interview with VTDigger. City Manager Regina Mahony said in an email that city councilors plan to review Struthers’s recent application for a growing license during an upcoming Nov. 12 meeting. 
Community Development Director Christopher Yuen recommends the city council renew Struthers’ license, according to a memo attached to the agenda for the upcoming city council meeting.
The controversy over Struthers’s growing operation — and his earlier duck farming — has played out across the past three years, sparking shouting matches between neighbors, letters to legislators, the passage of new state laws and now multiple lawsuits. 
The man used to raise ducks, farm veggies and grow cannabis in his residential backyard until his next door neighbors complained to the city about the smell of his crop and the noise from the ducks. The dispute between neighbors went through a series of appeals until it reached the state Supreme Court. 
Struthers argued that the city was acting outside of its authority by trying to regulate his farming practices, which he said are protected under state law from municipal regulation. In turn, his neighbors argued that it was illegal to farm ducks in their neighborhood, which is zoned as part of the city’s residential district — not the agricultural district. 

READ MORE

The state’s highest court eventually ruled against Struthers in June 2025, saying that municipalities can enforce local zoning laws regarding both farming and cannabis cultivation. 
After that ruling, Struthers gave up his ducks last year. Meanwhile, in July 2025, the city issued him a new zoning violation, saying he was out of compliance with the city’s new zoning laws from earlier that year. Those rules restricted where cannabis could be cultivated and required all plants be at least 50 feet from adjacent properties. 
Mahoney said in an email that the city issued Struthers the violation because it “has followed the directive from the Courts.” 
Struthers’s house on Taft Street, a small cul-de-sac close to Essex High School, was outside of the city’s new zoning boundaries, but he had received licenses to grow on his property from the local Cannabis Control Commission since 2022. 
Struthers first appealed the zoning violation on the local level, then brought the dispute to court, arguing that his growing operation was legal because it predated the city’s 2025 rules.
The case had a one-day trial in September, according to Struthers, who represented himself in court. Judge Walsh issued an Oct. 22 ruling that sided with Struthers, stating that his cannabis growing is a “preexisting nonconformity that may continue” on his property, court documents show. The ruling said that the ordinance violation he received was moot. 
Struthers said he thinks the city “acted in bad faith” by issuing him a zoning violation while knowing that his operation predated the new ordinance. He also said he thought the ordinances targeted his operation because his property was mentioned during local meetings when drafting the new rules. 
Struthers has been without a license to grow cannabis for the past year, he said, because the city’s local cannabis commission declined to renew his growing license until the dispute was sorted out in court. 
“It was a really stressful time for me,” Struthers said.

name: National
title: Democrats will hold most legislative trifectas since 1984
description: Along with a dramatic change in congressional majorities on Election Day, an analysis from the National Conference of State Legislatures showed large shifts in legislative majorities around the country, flipping from a majority of Republican legislatures to majority Democrat. Democrats also now hold a large number of trifectas, said the conference’s Katy Owe[...]
text:
Attendees cheer for Democrats as results roll in at a watch party during the midterm elections on Tuesday in St. Paul, Minn. Democrats will control both legislative chambers and the governorship in 22 states come January. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Along with a dramatic change in congressional majorities on Election Day, an analysis from the National Conference of State Legislatures showed large shifts in legislative majorities around the country, flipping from a majority of Republican legislatures to majority Democrat.
Democrats also now hold a large number of trifectas, said the conference’s Katy Owens Hubler, meaning they control both chambers of the state legislature alongside a Democratic governor. Heading into the elections, Republicans held 23 trifectas nationwide, and that was cut down to 17. Democrats now will have 22 trifectas beginning in January.
“This is a high point for Democratic trifectas going back to before 1984,” said Owens Hubler, director of the elections and redistricting program at the organization.
In blue wave, Democrats flipped legislatures, won trifectas and toppled GOP supermajorities

NCSL, the nonpartisan organization that represents and supports state legislatures nationwide, held a press event on Friday to discuss the election results. Prior to the election, Republicans controlled 28 state legislative chambers while Democrats controlled 18. Now, Democrats will control 24 chambers and Republicans will have 21. It’s the largest shift for Democrats since 2010, according to NCSL.
Votes are still being counted in some races, and results remain unofficial until certified in the coming weeks.
The legislative chambers that flipped or are expected to flip from Republican to Democrat include Houses in Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina and Texas, and the Senate in Pennsylvania. Both chambers flipped in Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. 
That leaves Alaska, Georgia, North Carolina and Texas as divided chambers that were previously both controlled by Republicans, although some races in Alaska and North Carolina remain too close to call.
“Going back to 2012, we have had both legislative chambers in all of the Southern states be red,” said Owens Hubler. “This new map … is pretty new and pretty different from the trend that we had been seeing for the last dozen years.”
At least five governor seats already officially turned from Republican to Democrat — Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada and Texas. Alaska is expected to elect a Democratic governor as well once all of the ballots are tabulated, the NCSL team said.
“If that is the case, we’re looking at 30 Democratic governors and 20 Republican governors,” Owens Hubler said. “Again, they haven’t had the majority of governors’ mansions since before 2010, and 30 is quite a large number for them.”
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Daily Montanan
title: A transplant lifeline is in jeopardy for Montana patients
description: Bigfork resident Todd Ware received the best gift of his life the day after Christmas 2020. Critically ill and in need of a double-lung transplant, Ware predicted he didn’t have more than two weeks of life left when the call came telling him there had been a match. Since that moment nearly six years ago, […]
text:
Todd Ware, a Bigfork resident, speaks during a LifeCenter Northwest event in 2025. (Courtesy LifeCenter Northwest)Bigfork resident Todd Ware received the best gift of his life the day after Christmas 2020.
Critically ill and in need of a double-lung transplant, Ware predicted he didn’t have more than two weeks of life left when the call came telling him there had been a match.
Since that moment nearly six years ago, his life has been transformed, as he’s taken to the skies and the slopes, doing two things that he was unable to do for years because of his failing lungs — fly as a glider pilot and go skiing.
For hundreds of Montanans who are on an organ transplant list, the wait for a life-saving donor comes with the added difficulty of being hundreds of miles away from the nearest medical transplant center. Guidelines proposed by the Trump administration could mean the only organization coordinating transplant services in Montana might lose certification, leaving already sick patients with even fewer options.
That’s why Montana’s congressional delegation — four Republicans — signed onto a letter with other western states lawmakers asking the Trump administration to reconsider its decision.
Federal delegations, medical providers and advocacy groups said a change in how the government regulates organ transplants could have massive downstream impacts, potentially closing as many as half of the organizations that provide those services across the country. 
The new rules, they add, are based on statistics they don’t control: for example, how many organ transplants an organization completes, which can vary by region and available medical expertise, and is a decision made by doctors, not transplant service providers.
Much of the West, particularly Montana, Alaska and Washington have few options for organ transplant care. Montana is one of four states without an organ transplant center and has just one provider of the service — LifeCenter Northwest, which is in Washington. It also serves Alaska and part of Idaho.
All four Montanans in Congress — Sens. Steve Daines and Tim Sheehy, and Reps. Troy Downing and Ryan Zinke — signed the letter, as did 13 others.
“The Trump administration proposed major oversight and accountability changes that will determine whether OPOs (organ procurement organizations) may continue operating during the 2026 recertification cycle,” Washington’s U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Democrat, said in a news release. “If these changes are finalized, it is estimated that approximately 75% of OPOs could be at risk of decertification.”
“Organ procurement organization” is a federal designation that allows organizations, like LifeCenter Northwest, to legally possess and transport human tissue and organs.
For Ware, the Bigfork man, getting a double lung transplant was a matter of life and death. 
He was diagnosed late in life with a genetic lung disease and then contracted pneumonia. Ware said his lungs were about 17% capacity when he got the call the day after Christmas that there was a match.
“I thought I had a matter of, you know, I’d be surprised if I could have lived two more weeks,” Ware said in an interview with the Daily Montanan. “That’s the number I gave myself.”
Ware made the trip to Seattle for the transplant, which went smoothly, he said. Montana hospitals generally do not do solid (e.g. heart, lung, kidney) transplants and instead these operations are done out-of-state.
LifeCenter Northwest is the organ transplant organization for Montana. (Courtesy LifeCenter Northwest)
 New rules, big problems

The rules frustrating the delegations and LifeCenter Northwest deal specifically with how organizations are evaluated annually.
Certification rules from federal Health and Human Services and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rely solely on “two closely related outcome measures,” which the letter argues does not properly account for the challenges associated with serving a wide geographic area.
The letter asks HHS and CMS to reconsider “automatic decertification based solely on the current outcome-only, single-year tiering methodology.”
LifeCenter Northwest, like all organ procurement organizations, is evaluated on the number of organ donors for whom at least one organ gets transplanted and the number of recovered organs that get transplanted.
“This second metric is particularly concerning because OPOs do not decide whether an organ is transplanted,” LifeCenter Northwest said in a statement to the Daily Montanan. “Those decisions are made by transplant doctors at transplant hospitals.”
Amendments to recent federal rule changes around organ donorship are set to go into effect before the end of the year, which has caused widespread industry concern it could lead to significant disruption in patient care, according to Bloomberg. 
“CMS’s methodology ignores recommendations by experts and instructions from Congress to apply performance, as well as outcome measures, to ensure a more accurate and objective evaluation of OPO performance,” LifeCenter Northwest said in a statement, adding “population health differences, process measures, risk-adjusted performance” are accounted for in other healthcare programs overseen by CMS.
It’s also unclear when, exactly those rules will go into effect.
“CMS has not yet issued those final amendments,” LifeCenter Northwest said in a statement. “While no specific timeline has been provided, they are expected to be released in late 2026.
According to the American Journal of Transplants, potentially half of all organ procurement organizations could be at risk of closing due to the new rules.
“In conclusion, our analysis … found that 64% of the 58 OPOs would have failed the standards if the metrics were applied to calendar year 2017,” the article states.
 Huge area with not many people.

More than 100,000 people nationwide are on organ donor lists. Last year, LifeCenter Northwest coordinated 1,318 organ transplants, which was 200 more than the previous year, according to the organization. That was a record.
LifeCenter Northwest services around 200 hospitals in its coverage area, and if it isn’t recertified, could leave Montana, Alaska and most of Washington without consistent organ transplant services.
The organization is the sole provider of the service in that area — which also includes 11 counties in Idaho — and spans more than 800,000 square miles and 10 million people.
There are only five transplant centers in the area covered by LifeCenter Northwest, all in Washington, and the organization relies heavily on aerial transportation and “narrow clinical timeframes,” according to the letter.
For Ware, LifeCenter Northwest opened his life back up again. He spent three months on the waiting list and said his experience with the organization was stellar.
“Life Center Northwest handled so much behind the scenes before I even got there. You know, I arrived and lungs were there,” Ware said. “Then later afterwards, you see the incredible process that it takes, and it’s not just miraculous that they can do the operation. It’s miraculous that they can synchronize me getting from Montana to Seattle and the organs coming in.”
CMS has increased oversight of the organ donor system under President Donald Trump. There’s been widespread organ shortages, which the Trump administration is also seeking to address.
But practical realities aren’t being taken into account, LifeCenter said, and CMS is treating their program differently than other healthcare providers.
“In other healthcare quality and performance programs, CMS accounts for factors that meaningfully impact outcomes, such as population health differences, process measures, risk-adjusted performance, and demonstrated year-over-year improvement,” LifeCenter said in a statement.
CMS says those changes deal with trust, and following a 2025 investigation into an organ procurement organization in Kentucky, federal Health and Human Services vowed to make changes.
CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz has claimed American’s trust in physicians decreased between 2020 and 2024 and said this was a way to “earn it back,” in a press release earlier this year.
The letter from members of Congress also asks for some consideration of the area’s unique circumstances and to provide LifeCenter Northwest a “clear pathway to demonstrate sustained, measurable improvement” before taking any decertification measures.
It goes on to say it supports evaluations grounded in “evidence based” measures, and that the current methodology doesn’t account for unique circumstances faced by rural healthcare providers.
“We are deeply concerned that their decertification would create unnecessary risk for our region – jeopardizing timely access to organ transplants and undermining support for donor families,” the letter says.
LifeCenter has said those circumstances and issues that come up while serving rural areas “disproportionately and negatively affect LifeCenter Northwest’s evaluation.”
 ‘A greater mission’

In 2025, 73 Montanans received transplants and another 211 donated organs. LifeCenter Northwest has also seen a 100% increase in lives saved over the last decade. Those interested in organ donation in Montana, can visit donatelifemt.org.
Todd Ware (Courtesy Todd Ware)
One of those recent recipients was Ware, who is thriving, he said. 
A highlight for him has been the ability to ski again — he hadn’t in nearly 20 years prior to the operation because of his lungs. He said that after he woke up from his surgery, it was about his third breath when he realized everything had changed.
“I was surprised at how well I could breathe.” Ware said. “It’s such an incredible amount of gratitude that one has when one’s suffocating, just trying to survive that suffocation for so many years, and then one can breathe, and it’s like a whole new life.
Ware has operated Air Therapy Aviation, an organization that offers powered glider flights with the intention of inspiring people through flight. Ware has also been a licensed massage therapist for 40 years and at one point also competed in flying competitions.
“Your life has a greater mission after surviving something like that,” Ware said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Wilson announces transition team
description: South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson announced his transition team Friday, a group that will include his wife and prominent business leaders, as he prepares to follow the state’s longest-serving governor.  Wilson, a Republican, won the highest number of votes ever for a gubernatorial candidate in state history but his race against Democrat Jermaine Johnson [...]
text:
Gov.-elect Alan Wilson announces his transition team on Friday Nov. 6, 2026, at Reeley's Body Shop in West Columbia, South Carolina. Beside Wilson is his wife, Jennifer Wilson, on the left and Lt. Gov.-elect Mike Reichenbach on the right. Behind them, from left to right, are Jim Brown, Robert Castellani, Randy Lowell, Thad Westbrook and Mikee Johnson. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)South Carolina Gov.-elect Alan Wilson announced his transition team Friday, a group that will include his wife and prominent business leaders, as he prepares to follow the state’s longest-serving governor. 
Wilson, a Republican, won the highest number of votes ever for a gubernatorial candidate in state history but his race against Democrat Jermaine Johnson was the narrowest win by percentage points in any governor’s race since 2010. Wilson faced major national momentum for Democrats, including a U.S. Senate race in the state that elected a Democrat for the first time in nearly 30 years. 
Wilson, who will be inaugurated in January, announced his transition team in a press conference Friday at Reeley’s Body Shop in West Columbia, where he had his first job at 15 years old washing cars. 
“A shop like this is where you come to fix a car, repair a car, improve a car, and that’s really what this transition is about. It’s about repairing those aspects of government, reforming those aspects of government, improving those aspects of government that are broken or damaged, and that we want to make work better for the people of South Carolina,” Wilson said. 
Wilson said the team is effectively the “board of trustees” for the transition, and additional roles such as transition staff members and senior advisers will be announced in the coming days. The nine-person team, including Wilson and Lt. Gov.-elect Mike Reichenbach, was kept “relatively small” to keep focused and to avoid turning it “into a mob,” Wilson said. 
The two co-chairs of the transition team are Thad Westbrook, of Lexington, and Randy Lowell, a prominent Charleston attorney for the law firm Burr & Forman. Westbrook, also a lawyer, was the chairman of the University of South Carolina Board of Trustees from 2022 through 2026, and still serves as the chair emeritus of the board. 
Wilson’s wife, Jennifer Wilson, is a member of the team. She currently works as a writer for the University of South Carolina and is a former broadcast journalist. The governor-elect said his wife had been a senior adviser to him during the campaign. Charisse Reichenbach, the wife of Mike Reichenbach who works with him at their car dealerships, is also on the transition committee.
“We said we were going to put families first, and I felt like I would start by leading by example, putting our families first on this transition team,” Wilson said. 
The three other members of the transition team are Mikee Johnson of Columbia, Robert Castellani of Greenville and Jim Brown of Florence. Johnson is the board chair and president of US Brick, a major brick and other materials manufacturing company. Castellani is the founder of North American Rescue Inc., which develops products to treat people after traumatic injuries. Brown is the CEO of BCN Management, a business that includes real estate and management consulting. 
“The men and women that are standing up here with me all come from varied backgrounds: business, law. They have even health backgrounds … So they have a full spectrum of experience that I will be relying on as we put this transition together,” Wilson said. 
The state hasn’t seen a major governor team transition since 2010, when Republican Nikki Haley was first elected. Gov. Henry McMaster, who was the lieutenant governor, became governor in 2017 after President Donald Trump appointed Haley to be the ambassador to the United Nations. McMaster was then elected to a full term in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. 
After he’s sworn in, Wilson said his administration will focus on their “families first audit initiative” to look into how state money is being spent, how money is tracked and how projects are implemented. The governor-elect also plans to advocate for the legislature to eliminate the state income tax,  lower property taxes and give the governor the authority to temporarily suspend the state gas tax when prices run high, an issue he raised on the campaign trail.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: State issues a warning to caregiver after nursing home resident dies
description: State licensing officials have issued a warning to an Iowa nurse for her role in the death of a nursing home resident. The board alleges that Elaine Allison, aka Elaine McCoy, of Beacon was working as a licensed practical nurse at the Oskaloosa Care Center on Sept. 6, 2025, when there was a serious medical […]
text:
The Oskaloosa Care Center in Mahaska County. (Photo via Google Earth)State licensing officials have issued a warning to an Iowa nurse for her role in the death of a nursing home resident.
The board alleges that Elaine Allison, aka Elaine McCoy, of Beacon was working as a licensed practical nurse at the Oskaloosa Care Center on Sept. 6, 2025, when there was a serious medical emergency and a resident of the home became unresponsive.
The board alleges a registered nurse asked Allison to call an ambulance and to verify the resident’s “code status” to determine whether lifesaving measures should be taken. Allison forgot to call the ambulance, according to the board, and also incorrectly identified the resident as “no code,” meaning no cardiopulmonary resuscitation or other lifesaving measures should be taken.
As a result, the board alleges, no CPR was performed and the man was subsequently pronounced dead.  A later review of the resident’s file indicated the man was a “full code” patient who had asked for lifesaving measures to be taken.
After charging Allison with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare, the board recently agreed to settle the matter by issuing Allison a warning and directing her to complete 30 hours of educational training. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Allison for comment.
Typically, a nursing home resident’s code status is marked on a sticker applied to the door of each resident’s room to prevent confusion and save time in the event of an emergency. According to a state inspectors’ report, the Oskaloosa Care Center’s director of nursing indicated the deceased resident’s door did not have the correct sticker due to recent changes in room assignments.
Inspectors reported that on the morning of the incident, employees entered the man’s room and saw him slumped over in his recliner and in distress – gasping, sweating profusely and stating he needed to sit. According to the inspectors’ reports, one of the workers left the room to obtain equipment to check the man’s vital signs, at which point the man’s eyes rolled back in his head as if he was having a seizure.
The director of nursing arrived in the room and instructed a licensed practical nurse – Allison, according to board records — to call an ambulance and verify the resident’s code status. After it was reported that the resident had a do-not-resuscitate order in place, the staff concluded the resident was dead and began to clean and clothe the body for the family’s viewing, according to inspectors.
The inspectors’ report of the incident indicates Allison told investigators she had been “flustered” during the incident had been “working on” calling 911 while also trying to locate the home’s crash cart, which had a defibrillator on board for restoring a patient’s heartbeat in cases of cardiac arrest.
According to inspectors, Allison said she “probably” would have initiated CPR had she known the resident was a full-code patient.
The Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing charged the facility with failing to carry out CPR in accordance with a resident’s wishes, and for workers’ inability to locate the facility’s crash cart in an emergency. According to the state agency, those failures placed residents of the home in immediate jeopardy.
The state proposed, but held in suspension, a $10,000 fine against the care facility. The federal Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services later fined the home $45,354.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Bears meet with Illinois leaders to ‘explore’ stadium legislation as Indiana site work continues
description: The Chicago Bears are completing due diligence for potential stadium sites in Indiana even as the franchise acknowledges meeting with Prairie State leaders ahead of a brief legislative session later this month.
text:
A giant flag for the Chicago Bears is seen during pregame festivities at Soldier Field in Chicago. (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images)The Chicago Bears are completing due diligence for potential stadium sites in Indiana even as the franchise acknowledges meeting with Illinois leaders ahead of state lawmakers returning to Springfield later this month.
In response to news media inquiries “about a meeting earlier this week in Chicago,” the Bears said Friday that team officials “appreciate the recent engagement from Illinois leadership to explore legislation which has allowed us to share our feedback.”
Indiana Toll Road cash delivered; Chicago Bears still deciding

That engagement comes with the Illinois Legislature scheduled to reconvene Nov. 17-19 and Dec. 1-3. Lawmakers there could take up a recast stadium bill they failed to push through over the spring.
Hoosier legislators, meanwhile, finalized a plan in March to lure the Bears to northwest Indiana. Senate Enrolled Act 27 would establish a stadium authority in Hammond to build and operate a new publicly owned stadium for the team, and allow increased county restaurant, hotel and admission taxes to pay for the project.
“We continue to work collaboratively with local and state leaders in Indiana to advance our stadium development plans in Hammond, where we are finalizing due diligence details across two sites in the Wolf Lake area,” the club said.
The Bears reaffirmed their commitment to “building a world-class stadium and mixed-use district” and said they “expect productive dialogue with both leadership teams in the coming weeks.”
“We have a responsibility and obligation to explore every option available to the club, and we look forward to developing a transformational project that will attract global events and deliver jobs and economic growth to all of Chicagoland,” the statement said.
The Bears hope to replace their current, aging home of Soldier Field along Chicago’s Lake Michigan shore.
