name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In CT towns affected heavily by Trump policies, voter turnout grew
description: Danbury, Bridgeport and New London all saw turnout increase by more than 10 percentage points compared to the 2022 midterm elections.
text:
Voter turnout held steady across most of Connecticut compared to the last midterm elections but jumped in towns more heavily affected by Trump administration policies.
In Tuesday’s election, 57.3% of eligible Connecticut voters cast a ballot, according to unofficial numbers from the Secretary of the State’s office, 0.3 percentage points lower than voter turnout in the 2022 midterms but above estimates for the nation as a whole, which currently sit around 49%.
Despite the small dip in Connecticut, Danbury, Bridgeport and New London all saw turnout increase by more than 10 percentage points. Danbury saw the highest increase, with turnout jumping 12.4 percentage points to 60.8%.
Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves said the increase is likely due to trust in local leaders combined with sentiments towards national issues — especially immigration.
“We saw, in Danbury, heavier ICE enforcement in the state. We had a hate group, a modern day KKK, marching through our streets,” said Alves, who is also chair of the Connecticut Democratic Party.
In August, Danbury was the target of ICE raids. In just five days, 118 people were arrested across the state, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security. The majority of these arrests were conducted in Danbury.
The days and months following the raids changed the way the community operated. Immediately following the arrests, streets that would have usually been lined with day laborers were empty. Children, some of whom had watched from their bus windows as a man was arrested at their bus stop, stopped going to school or playing outside. And ICE presence is still reported regularly in the community by advocates on Danbury Unites for Immigrants social media pages. 
“Now, what we’re hearing, what we’re seeing, is people were fed up. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve talked to Republicans who would say, ‘This isn’t what I voted for, and I can’t see myself voting for this administration again,'” Alves said. “We have a lot of cross-party support in Danbury right now.”
Along with bigger turnout in Danbury, there were also large swings to the Democrats across all races in the town. While this was a state and national trend, Danbury saw larger shifts towards Democrats compared to most other towns.
Just five years ago, Danbury had a Republican mayor, and until the 2018 midterms, the town was represented by a Republican state senator. Alves thinks the swing seen this election is the result of years of work from Democrats and “years of trust” gained in the community.
“We [have had] nearly a decade of Democrats organizing and working really hard in this city and giving people not just something to vote against but something to vote for,” Alves said.
Extreme immigration enforcement, like what Danbury residents experienced in August, may have driven voters to the polls elsewhere. Minnesota, for example, has been a hub for ICE arrests, activity and protests after two citizens were killed by agents last winter. The state is projected to have the highest voter turnout in the country this midterm election.
In Connecticut, Bridgeport and New London also saw high jumps in turnout and swings towards the Democrats. ICE has conducted arrests in both towns, although its activity has been less than in Danbury. In Bridgeport, which has the highest Hispanic population out of all Connecticut towns according to census data, a man was arrested at a bus stop earlier this year.
But these towns, like many urban areas, have also seen decreases in people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, as well as higher costs of living. In Danbury, Alves said the “affordability issue” along with “unnecessary wars” are driving forces in turnout and party shifts.
Many towns that saw an increase in turnout also have a majority-minority population, where more than 50% of residents are not white. The only majority-minority town to see a decrease in turnout from 2022 was New Haven.
But even though Danbury, Bridgeport and New London saw large increases in turnout since 2022, they did not have the highest voter turnout in the state. Less populated towns in the Northwestern corner and some towns along the shore saw some of the highest turnout. 
Some towns like Cornwall and Norfolk saw more than 75% of eligible voters cast a ballot.

name: VTDigger
title: Clear the grid backlog and lower Vermont’s power bills
description:
Congress has a chance to address climate change and lower energy costs. It should take it.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Clear the grid backlog and lower Vermont’s power bills.
text:
This commentary is by Alex Messinger, co-leader of the Vermont chapter of Citizens’ Climate Lobby.
There’s a new bipartisan bill in Congress that will significantly reduce emissions, speed up clean energy and lower energy costs for us here in Vermont. 
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a comprehensive package of permitting reforms that was recently introduced in the Senate. Climate champions Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., were at the forefront of bipartisan negotiations, ensuring the final product advances climate goals and supports clean energy while maintaining important environmental safeguards. 
The Senate is set to take up the bill in November, and I am urging Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Peter Welch, D-Vt., to support it with a “yes” vote. I encourage my fellow Vermonters to do the same.
This bill matters to Vermont residents like me because it will lead to significant emissions reductions, which are necessary to address climate change. The bill contains strong transmission provisions that can help unlock the enormous amount of clean energy waiting to connect to the grid.
And there’s lots of clean energy waiting to come online. Much of the energy capacity stuck in interconnection queues comes from clean energy projects. Several solar developers in Vermont have told me they’ve found it difficult to get clean energy projects connected to the grid. Reforming the process will help America build and connect clean energy much faster while preserving bedrock environmental laws.

READ MORE

More abundant, affordable electricity will help lower energy costs for households and businesses. According to analysis by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions, transmission and interconnection reforms like those before Congress would reduce Americans’ residential electricity bills by $19 billion through 2040.
We need these changes in Vermont. Since 2019, average monthly residential bills in the state have risen from $97.25 to $135 in 2026, a 39% increase. One reason for this increase is the need to bolster the electricity grid against stronger storms caused by climate change.
It may be helpful to compare this bill with the cost of doing nothing. Climate impacts are accelerating, and we can’t wait for the next Congress to put forth a better bill. Since the bill requires 60 votes in the Senate to advance, now is our best chance. Passing this bill will speed the clean energy transition, while reducing costs for all of us.
I’m proud that Sanders and Welch have been longstanding advocates for weatherization and energy retrofits, which have helped thousands of Vermonters reduce energy bills while addressing climate change.  
But Congress must go further. It needs to act now by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A new documentary looks not-too-far back at NC college student voting this election
description: Some ballots haven’t even been counted yet, but a documentary about the 2026 election from the perspective of North Carolina college students fighting for campus early voting sites has already had its debut. “Where Do I Vote Again?” screened Thursday night at The Rialto in Raleigh. It encapsulates the work of students who tried to […]
text:
Students at North Carolina A&T State University in Greensboro, North Carolina, begin a 40-minute walk to the nearest off-campus early polling site on Oct. 22, 2026. Election officials declined to put an early campus voting location at the school despite protests. (Photo by Elisha Brown/Stateline)Some ballots haven’t even been counted yet, but a documentary about the 2026 election from the perspective of North Carolina college students fighting for campus early voting sites has already had its debut.
“Where Do I Vote Again?” screened Thursday night at The Rialto in Raleigh. It encapsulates the work of students who tried to convince election officials to locate early voting sites on their campuses. It also highlights the work of Influence NC, the nonprofit that held voter information parties at a dozen campuses and offered students rides to the polls at three of them. 
The prelude: The Guilford County Board of Elections and the state Board of Elections didn’t give N.C. A&T State University students the campus early voting site they wanted. 
The N.C. State University site was moved from the centrally-located student center to a building at the edge of campus that students argued was inconvenient. 
A push from the state auditor’s office to prevent an early voting site at Western Carolina University failed.  
The documentary didn’t show all that resulted, but here’s part of the postscript:
A&T student marches to an early voting site made national news. 
The WCU early voting site Republicans fought was the second-most used in Jackson County. 
According to data from NC Election Live, voters ages 18-29 cast 11% of early ballots this year, compared to 5.4% in 2022. 
The documentary featured interviews with students; Jeff Carmon, a Democratic state elections board member; Dallas Woodhouse, a Republican political operative who worked at state Auditor Dave Boliek’s office advising counties on their early voting plans; voting rights advocate Bob Hall; and Gerry Cohen, a Democrat on the Wake County Board of Elections.
Boliek was recorded at an event sponsored by The Assembly and included his comments about locating an early voting site at Union Square Campus, a building used by A&T, UNC-Greensboro and Guilford Technical Community College. 
Ahead Media produced the documentary in collaboration with Influence NC. 
At the question-and-answer session following the screening, Hannah Preston, director of Influence NC, said organizing young people is easy.
Proposed ban on amplified music outside NC polling places draws criticism

“We had doughnuts, we had coffee, we had t-shirts,” she said. “You have to have something fun to motivate folks, and not just younger people.” About 3,000 students attended its campus events, she said. Influence NC is a nonprofit that was originally sponsored by the progressive group Carolina Forward. 
Does gerrymandering matter?
Democrats scored surprising victories on Tuesday to nearly win a supermajority in the state House, flip at least five congressional districts from Republican to Democrat with five more still too close to call, and to appear to fall just one seat short of a 25-25 tie in the state Senate.
During the Q&A, Western Carolina University political science professor Chris Cooper compared Democrats’ sweeping victories to a 100-year flood, one that breached the walls meant to protect Republicans in gerrymandered districts. 
It would be a mistake, however, to argue that gerrymandering doesn’t matter, he said. “It absolutely does.” 
Democrat Roy Cooper won the U.S. Senate race by nearly 20 percentage points, the largest US Senate win since 1974, he said. Yet, the state Senate still didn’t flip. “So why is that? The way the lines are drawn.” the WCU professor said. 

‘Vulgar music’
The documentary may have helped solve a mystery. 
One of the election rules the state Board of Elections approved along party lines this year bans amplified sound at polling sites. 
Students and voting rights advocates argued that the rule was aimed at Black and brown students and is meant to discourage activities that make voting a fun community event. 
Board members never said why they wanted the rule, but Woodhouse offered one explanation in the documentary.
“I don’t think we ought to have DJs blasting vulgar music outside of early voting,” Woodhouse said, because it intimidates people.
“If I went and played a bunch of Hank Williams, Jr. and a bunch of country artists outside of early voting sites in certain parts of the state, people would think that’s offensive or I’m trying to chase voters away. That’s inappropriate. These are not dance parties.”
Woodhouse’s comments prompted one student at the Q&A to ask if “vulgar music” was a racist dog whistle. 
Travis Fain, a former WRAL reporter who is an Influence NC board member, said he couldn’t say what Woodhouse meant because he wasn’t part of the conversation. 
Sometimes public relations professionals say things they don’t believe, Fain said. And for people who have been in that business for a long time, “the line starts to blur” between what they believe and what they say to win, Fain said. 
“I don’t want to judge based on a snippet of a conversation that I was not a part of, and you could be proven exactly right,” he told the student. “But we all just have to extend so much damn grace in this world these days to each other, whether people deserve it or not.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: In Mississippi, Black votes still count for less, advocates lament
description: An attendee holds a  sign at a rally for voting rights at the Jackson Convention Center, Wednesday, May 20, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Voters elected Johnny DuPree to the Mississippi Senate. His 2025 win marked the first time that Hattiesburg residents would have a Black senator representing them in Jackson, even though over half of the city’s population is Black. Now, because of machinations with the legislative map, that representation could be in jeopardy.
DuPree may be one of the first Black politicians to bear the brunt of the Supreme Court’s consequential April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais. But he won’t be the last. An NPR analysis predicts that post Callais redistricting could portend the largest drop in Black representation across the country since the collapse of Reconstruction.
Some politicians are already sharpening their knives. Gov. Tate Reeves has said it is a matter of when, not if, the tenure ends for Rep. Bennie Thompson, who is the sole Black member of the state’s congressional delegation holding one of Mississippi’s four House seats.
In Mississippi, like in many other states in he aftermath of the Callais U.S. Supreme Court ruling, a state-level Voting Rights Act has  been introduced in the Legislature. However, voter suppression policies aimed at Black voters, along with hostile  majorities in the state’s legislative chambers, make the legislation’s pathway for enactment incredibly narrow.
DuPree’s district only had a Black majority because a federal court found that parts of the state’s 2022 legislative maps violated the Voting Rights Act. The 2025 maps sought to correct a historic injustice. With that map likely gone because of Callais, the Black majority district it created could be wiped away too. For DuPree, the erasure is unsurprising given the state’s tradition of voter suppression.
In an October interview, he quipped, “here we go again.”
Black Mississippians have been saying some version of that since 1890. In an interview earlier this year, community organizers Oleta Fitzgerald and Phaedra Robinson told Human Rights Watch, “Courts are stacked, the Legislature is stacked. It’s always been a fight for us in Mississippi, and it feels like they want to go back to the good old days.”
Sens. Hillman Frazier, left, and Johnny L. DuPree are seen on the Senate floor at the Capitol in Jackson on Thursday, Feb. 12, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today

Until 1944, Mississippi, representative of the one-party rule that dominated Jim Crow states, held its November general elections after a Democratic Party primary in which only white people were allowed to participate.

The legislative maps are one front, but not the only one. Take a look at Section 241 of the state Constitution, which was drafted back in 1890 to codify Jim Crow era restrictions. That constitutional section imposes a lifetime bar on voting for crimes the delegates believed Black people were more likely to commit.
In 2022, the full U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals agreed the original provision was “steeped  in racism” but upheld it anyway.
The Sentencing Project estimates at least 43,700  Black Mississippians couldn’t vote in the 2024 elections because of that rule. Getting your vote back takes a governor’s pardon or a two-thirds vote of the Legislature. Between 2000 and  2015, only 335 people managed to claw back their right to vote.
That’s not all.
Mississippi ranks dead last nationally in the Cost of Voting Index, which measures how hard states make it to vote. The state requires photo identification at the polls, offers no early voting for most residents and no online registration.
Following the adoption of the 1890 Mississippi Constitution, near-universal registration among Black eligible voters dropped to around 7% and stayed that way until 1964. Within three years of the Voting Rights Act, nearly 60% of Black Mississippians were registered. Black Mississippians still register at rates among the highest in the country. That progress came from federal enforcement action and the Voting Rights Act. Those federal protections are exactly what Trump administration policies and Supreme Court rulings have been dismantling.
Within  hours of the 2013 Supreme Court decision in Shelby County v. Holder, which gutted parts of the Voting Rights Act, Mississippi announced it would move forward with restrictive voter ID rules. It also requires notarizing  both absentee ballot applications and ballot envelopes.
A new law Gov. Reeves signed in April called the SHIELD Act took effect July 1. It lets local officials demand a birth certificate, passport or naturalization papers from applicants and current voters whose citizenship they cannot confirm. Those documents cost money and time. Rural and low-income Mississippians, many of them Black women running households, often don’t have either to spare.
The U.S. has human rights obligations under international law that point the way back onto a better path. The United Nations Human Rights Committee has said that drawing electoral boundaries should not distort the distribution of voters or discriminate against any group.
 In 2014 it also said the US “should ensure that all states reinstate voting rights to felons who have fully served their sentences.” The Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination prohibit laws with racially discriminatory effects even when they look neutral.
Mississippi organizers have outlasted worse. Medgar Evers was shot in his own driveway in 1963 after a meeting about voter registration.
Today, Black women across this state are the ones knocking on doors and arranging childcare, so mothers and grandmothers can get to the polls.
As the winds at the federal level shift, it’s all the more important to pass the Mississippi Voting Rights Act, which would enshrine powerful and critical voting rights protections into state law. 

Henry Hicks is a consultant at Human Rights Watch.
Cassandra Welchlin is the executive director & co-convener of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable.

title: KY measles database revealed patient information, state officials say
description: Patient information for Kentuckians with confirmed cases of measles reported on the state’s disease dashboard was publicly accessible in September.  On Sept. 23, the “security vulnerability” was discovered, which “made some private patient information accessible to the public,” cabinet spokeswoman Beth Fisher said in a statement.  “Cabinet for Health and Fam[...]
text:
1972:  In this handout from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a histopathology of measles pneumonia is seen in this microscope image from 1972. Measles outbreaks have been reported throughout the U.S., with the latest reported February 5, 2015 at a daycare in suburban Chicago where as many as five children under the age of one have been infected. (Photo by CDC via Getty Images)Patient information for Kentuckians with confirmed cases of measles reported on the state’s disease dashboard was publicly accessible in September. 
On Sept. 23, the “security vulnerability” was discovered, which “made some private patient information accessible to the public,” cabinet spokeswoman Beth Fisher said in a statement. 
“Cabinet for Health and Family Services staff were quickly notified and took action to secure the information and prevent further public access,” Fisher said. 
It’s unclear how many people’s information may have been exposed. The cabinet is currently investigating the issue “to determine its scope,” she said, and “once the review is completed, the cabinet will make all notifications required by state and federal law.” 
At the time of the exposure, there were fewer than 100 measles cases confirmed. 
There are now more than 200 cases in Kentucky, the most since 1991. That year, Kentucky had 443 cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and they were mostly in children younger than five. 
Measles is extremely contagious and spread through the air from coughs or sneezes, according to the CDC. One infected person can infect nine in 10 unprotected people around them. 
Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash. The best protection against measles is the measles vaccination, which is generally available at pharmacies and through medical providers. 
The CDC recommends the measles vaccination series at 12-15 months and then at 4-6 years old.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Lee, Scruggs, Rothstein depart Moore’s Cabinet
description: Gov. Wes Moore announced the departures Friday of the secretary of state and the heads of the departments of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and Veterans and Military Affairs as his administration shuffles leadership in advance of his second term.
text:
Susan Lee, served more than two decades in the legislature before her appointment as Secretary of State in 2023. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)More changes are coming to Gov. Wes Moore’s Cabinet as the administration prepares to enter a second term in January.
Moore, a Democrat, announced the departures Friday, a day after announcing a new chief of staff and three days after winning election to a second term. Such staff changes are not unusual for two-term governors.
The list of changes announced Friday include Secretary of State Susan Lee, as well as Public Safety and Correctional Services Secretary Carolyn Scruggs and Veterans and Military Affairs Secretary Ed Rothstein. In all three cases, interim leaders took over immediately.
“Secretary Susan Lee, Secretary Carolyn Scruggs, and Secretary Ed Rothstein have devoted decades of faithful and exemplary service to the people of Maryland,” Moore said in a statement announcing the moves. “Our state has greatly benefited from their leadership, expertise, and service in the Cabinet, and I thank them for raising their hands to serve and leading these critical departments during these historically challenging times.”
Scruggs, appointed in January 2023, at the outset of the Moore administration, was the first Black woman to lead the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services. Her departure follows ongoing criticism about staffing issues within the state prison system as well as 22 deaths classified as homicides between 2024 and 2025.
Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services Secretary Carolyn Scruggs. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Scruggs’ departure was first reported Thursday by The Baltimore Banner. Union officials who have regularly sparred with Scruggs during her tenure said a change at the department “was long overdue.”
“We’re pleased to see the department moving in a different direction — as all facets of the agency (Parole and Probation, Home Detention Unit, Pretrial Detention, and the entirety of the Division of Corrections) need a change in leadership and a massive influx of resources,” said a statement from Jack Hughes, president of Maryland Council 3 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees.
“As has been documented at legislative hearings in the General Assembly and in our joint staffing analyses, DPSCS has nowhere near the number of staff and resources that are needed to fulfill its mission,” his statement said. “AFSCME looks forward to working with new department leadership to make our communities safer, protect those in the state’s care, and ensure that AFSCME members get home from work safely.”
Deputy Secretary of Operations David C. Greene, who has more than  20 years of service with DPSCS, took over as interim secretary Friday. He will remain in the position until a permanent replacement is named.
Lee, 72, was appointed by Moore soon after he was sworn in. Lee had been a state legislator from Montgomery County, serving in the House of Delegates from 2002 to 2015, when she moved to the Senate. She remained in the Senate until January 2023.
Two years ago, Lee took a leave of absence to “focus on a personal health matter.” A statement issued Friday by Moore’s office said Lee was departing “for personal matters.”
Moore named Deputy Secretary of State Michael Lore, an attorney, to serve until a permanent replacement is named.
Lore served as chief of staff to Lee when she was in the Senate. He also worked for Sen. Norman Stone (D-Baltimore County) and as a speech writer and researcher for Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-8th).
Fresh off reelection win, Moore names new chief of staff

Rothstein leaves the Moore administration after 15 months leading the veterans agency.
The Republican gave up his seat as a county commissioner in Carroll County to join the Moore administration. Prior to that, Rothstein served in the military for more than three decades, including a stint as an intelligence officer and garrison commander at Fort Meade.
Deputy Secretary James “Jimmy” Anderson will take over as acting Secretary of Veterans and Military Families effective Nov. 6, according to a statement from Moore’s office.
The moves come a day after Moore announced changes in his own office.
Lester Davis departed his role as Moore’s chief of staff, after just over a year on the job to become the interim CEO of the Maryland Technology Development Corp.
Succeeding Davis is Emmanuel “Manny” Welsh, who previously served as principal deputy chief of staff.
Both Davis and Welsh assumed their new roles on the day they were announced.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Chris Murphy discharged from hospital after stroke
description: Sen. Chris Murphy will spend a few weeks at a rehabilitation center after suffering a stroke. His doctor said he expects "a full recovery."
text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy is being discharged from the hospital on Friday after experiencing a stroke last weekend and will spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center before returning to work at the Capitol, according to a release from his office.
Murphy, the 53-year-old junior senator from Connecticut, was hospitalized last Saturday.
“I want to be direct with you, so here is my diagnosis,” Murphy said. “Last Saturday afternoon, I felt something was not right with my body and called 9-1-1 out of an abundance of caution, and I’m glad I did. I was diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of my brain,” Murphy said in a statement released on Friday afternoon.
“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” he continued.
Congress returns to Washington next week after a month-long recess. Murphy said he’ll miss votes as he recovers at a rehabilitation center and will work remotely.
“This has been a scary experience for me and my family, and I appreciate the continued respect for our privacy,” Murphy said. “As I’m working towards a full recovery, I am staying engaged with my team and colleagues remotely, and my staff continues to carry out our legislative priorities, serve constituents, and ensure the work of my office continues uninterrupted. I want to extend my deepest thanks to the excellent doctors and staff at Johns Hopkins who have treated me and cared for my family.”
His physician, Dr. Jose Suarez, the chief of neurosciences critical care at The Johns Hopkins Hospital, also released a statement on his prognosis and said he’s expected to make a full recovery.
“Sen. Murphy experienced a small hemorrhagic stroke,” Suarez said. “He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation.”
His office said Thursday that he’s making “remarkable progress,” but this is the first time since his hospitalization that they released details of his diagnosis.

name: VTDigger
title: Construction of the South Burlington Walk-Bike Bridge advances at Exit 14
description:
Phase one of construction is underway to connect Williston Road and University Mall.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Construction of the South Burlington Walk-Bike Bridge advances at Exit 14.
text:
Construction work continues on the South Burlington Walk-Bike Bridge near Interstate 89. Photo by Scarlett Glazebrook/Community News Service

Scarlett Glazebrook  is a reporter with the Community News Service, part of the University of Vermont’s Reporting & Documentary Storytelling program.
SOUTH BURLINGTON — For people traveling on foot, walking along Williston Road over Interstate 89 means navigating the traffic barreling on and off the ramps leading to the busy highway at Exit 14. And with the short, dark days of winter around the corner, reduced visibility adds to the challenges of crossing the stretch that helps connect Burlington and South Burlington.
Now, after decades of enduring the problem, walkers and bikers can see a solution taking shape in the big construction project just south of the overpass. Construction began in late July on the new South Burlington Walk-Bike Bridge over I-89, following a groundbreaking ceremony. When completed in 2028, the bridge will be maintained by the city year around and include nighttime illumination as one of numerous safety features.
“The whole point of the bridge is to pull pedestrians away from the road and cars. So if you’re asking if it will increase road safety, absolutely” said John Christman, South Burlington deputy fire chief of fire prevention and EMS.

READ MORE

The latest work on the project involves placing mechanically stabilized earth walls and working on placing pier footing, according to city construction updates.
The roughly $27 million project has been on the drawing board for years and came together with the help of federal transportation grants including the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity program and the Reconnecting Communities and Neighborhoods program.
The current phase of the project will connect Williston Road and the University Mall. The next phase of construction has not been awarded contracts yet. As the bulldozers and construction workers make progress, the long-discussed idea is translating to reality.
“Change comes gradually, and I think there will be some people who will immediately see the benefits. Especially the people living on one side of the bridge or the other,” said Havaleh Gagne, chair of the South Burlington Bicycle and Pedestrian Committee.
Both sides of the bridge will be located in South Burlington, but the west side is close to the Burlington line. People who go back and forth between the two cities are taking stock of the project. Oumar Haidara said he will definitely use the bridge when in the area or when going to shows at Higher Ground in South Burlington.
“I’m pretty positive about something like that. It reminds me of my cities back home. In Connecticut, there’s a lot of overpass bridges where people can walk. It’s pretty cool,” said Haidara, a resident of the Burlington area for almost seven years.
Gagne said the bridge could help address the affordability struggle surrounding rising gas prices, giving people an alternative to motor vehicle based-transportation.
“South Burlington has a fragmented path system right now. That is one of the biggest areas where we are missing a link, but we have a lot of other links that are going to be built in the next few years,” Gagne said.
The city is in the process of envisioning new sections of path where residents could walk or bike more easily from South Burlington’s growing city center to downtown Burlington and points in between.
Residents can subscribe to project updates through the South Burlington government website.

She will be the first Black woman to hold the position. 
Bacon will lead a Democratic supermajority in the 76th General Assembly, which will convene on Jan. 11. She will succeed Speaker Julie McCluskie, a Dillon Democrat who is term-limited and won’t return to the chamber in January.

“I know that my job is to help lift you up, lift up your communities, share successes, share insights and fight for you,” Bacon said to House Democrats.

Voters made clear in the June primaries and on Tuesday that they want change, not the status quo, Bacon said. She said she will prioritize the agenda constituents have asked for.

name: Delaware
title: $56 million Kingswood Center opens with promise of new opportunities for Riverside
description: Image Courtesy of the Kingswood Center New Wilmington community center combines education, health care and recreation in a major public-private investment. Its long-term success will be measured by opportunities created for families and lasting neighborhood improvements. By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE WILMINGTON, Del. — A new chapter in Wilmington’s Riversi[...]
text:
Image Courtesy of the Kingswood Center

New Wilmington community center combines education, health care and recreation in a major public-private investment. Its long-term success will be measured by opportunities created for families and lasting neighborhood improvements.
By George Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — A new chapter in Wilmington’s Riverside neighborhood began Friday, Nov. 6, with the opening of the $56 million Kingswood Community Center, an investment designed to expand educational opportunities, improve access to health care and help families build more prosperous futures.
The two-story, 81,000-square-foot facility is nearly five times the size of its predecessor, which served Riverside residents for generations. The new center brings together services for children, families and seniors while serving as a cornerstone of a broader effort to revitalize one of Wilmington’s historically underserved neighborhoods.
For residents, the new building represents an opportunity for greater neighborhood stability and access to services. For taxpayers, donors and community leaders, it also raises an important long-term question: Will the investment deliver measurable improvements in education, employment, family well-being and economic independence?
The answer will ultimately be determined not by the size of the building but by the opportunities it creates for the people who use it.
U.S. Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, Gov. Matt Meyer, Attorney General Kathleen Jennings, Wilmington Mayor John Carney and City Council Member Zanthia Oliver joined community leaders for Friday’s opening ceremony.
Building opportunities for families
The expanded Kingswood Community Center brings several important services together under one roof, making it easier for residents to access programs that support education, health, recreation and family stability.
Among its features are:




A gymnasium accommodating more than 600 basketball spectators or up to 1,500 people for community gatherings.






A Nemours pediatric care center providing access to children’s health services.






The Ernest L. Webster Montessori Academy, expanding early childhood educational opportunities.






An expanded Jimmy Jenkins Senior Center in a separate building, serving older residents.






A commercial kitchen and dining room supporting food programs and community activities.






Flexible meeting and event spaces for neighborhood organizations and families.




The services could have practical economic benefits beyond their immediate purposes.
Reliable early childhood education can help working parents maintain employment. Accessible health care can reduce the time and transportation challenges families face when seeking treatment. Recreational and educational programs can provide young people with constructive activities and opportunities to develop skills.
Together, these services are intended to help address barriers that have limited economic opportunity for some Riverside families.
Public and private partners share the investment
The Kingswood project illustrates how government agencies, nonprofit organizations, financial institutions and private partners can combine resources to address longstanding community needs.
The project received substantial government support, including state funding and federal resources. The state described Kingswood as a $56 million development when construction began in August 2024.
Its financing also involved New Markets Tax Credits, private financial institutions and philanthropic support, demonstrating an approach that extends beyond traditional government-funded community programs.
One notable partner is Nemours Children’s Health, which provided an eight-figure, low-interest community impact loan to help advance the project’s construction.
In a September 2026 account of the partnership, Nemours President and CEO R. Lawrence Moss said the loan helped unlock additional financing and was repaid in full ahead of schedule.
Nemours is also establishing a pediatric care center at Kingswood and working with community partners to connect neighborhood residents with skilled employment opportunities at its hospital.
The arrangement demonstrates how private institutional investment can support neighborhood development while connecting residents to health care and potential careers.
It also highlights the importance of financial planning and responsible stewardship in projects involving both public and private resources.
An 80-year commitment to Riverside
The opening comes as Kingswood celebrates 80 years of serving Wilmington residents.
Founded in 1946, the original community center became a gathering place and support system for generations of Riverside families, offering youth development, educational programs and services for older adults.
“The Kingswood Community Center had an amazing 80-year run rooted in humble beginnings,” said Logan Herring, CEO of the WRK Group, which includes Kingswood Community Center, REACH Riverside and The Warehouse.
Herring credited generations of community leaders and volunteers for adapting Kingswood’s programs to meet changing neighborhood needs.
“The new Kingswood Community Center builds on all of this. It will continue that same legacy of rising to meet the needs of Riverside by providing the community with more resources, support and opportunity,” he said.
The new building provides significantly more space, but the organization’s challenge remains much the same: helping residents strengthen families, develop skills and build better lives.
Connecting education, employment and economic mobility
The new center is part of the WRK Group’s larger effort to transform Riverside through a coordinated approach involving housing, education, health care and economic opportunity.
Other investments include Imani Village, a mixed-income residential development that began opening in 2022; The Warehouse, which provides programs for Wilmington teenagers; and expanded STEM educational opportunities at EastSide Charter School.
The strategy recognizes that improvements in one area often depend on progress in others.
Children are better positioned to succeed academically when they have stable housing, access to medical care and strong educational support. Parents are better able to pursue employment when reliable child care and other family resources are available.
The new Kingswood Center is intended to bring many of those resources within easier reach of Riverside residents.
Of particular importance is the potential to connect young people and adults to workforce development programs, employers and career opportunities.
The WRK Group has described economic mobility and self-sufficiency as central goals of its Riverside redevelopment effort.
Success in those areas could help create a stronger local economy, greater household financial stability and an environment more attractive to private investment.
Measuring the return on investment
The opening of Kingswood marks a significant construction and fundraising achievement. The larger challenge will be sustaining the facility and demonstrating its impact over time.
The building will require ongoing expenditures for staffing, maintenance, utilities, security and programming. Long-term financial planning will be essential to maintaining services without placing unsustainable demands on government or philanthropic resources.
Equally important will be demonstrating whether the programs achieve their intended results.
Potential measures of success include the number of children benefiting from early education, improvements in school readiness, participation in job training, employment outcomes, health care access and residents’ progress toward greater economic independence.
The redevelopment also presents an important question for longtime Riverside residents: Will neighborhood improvements create opportunities for existing families to remain, prosper and participate in the area’s changing economy?
New housing, improved community facilities and expanded services are important signs of progress. But lasting revitalization also depends on stable neighborhoods, family advancement, employment and a growing base of private economic activity.
Public reporting on program outcomes, operating expenses and funding sources would help residents, donors and taxpayers evaluate the results.
Those measures will become increasingly important as the Riverside transformation moves from major construction projects to the long-term operation of its facilities and programs.
A new chapter, with work still ahead
For Herring, the opening is both a tribute to Kingswood’s history and a commitment to future generations.
“We are opening a new chapter, opening new doors to space built to serve generations to come,” he said.
The grand opening also reflects years of collaboration among Riverside residents, nonprofit leaders, government officials, businesses and philanthropic organizations.
With the center completed, the focus now turns to making the most of its expanded capabilities.
For Riverside families, the opportunity is immediate: improved access to education, health care, recreation and community support.
For Wilmington, the larger opportunity is to demonstrate that a combination of public investment, private participation and strong community institutions can help produce lasting neighborhood improvements.
The new Kingswood Community Center provides the facilities and resources to pursue that goal.
The next chapter will be measured by what Riverside residents accomplish with them.
Community invited to celebrate Saturday
The WRK Group will continue its grand-opening weekend Saturday, Nov. 7, with Kingswood Community Day, a free celebration offering residents and visitors an opportunity to explore the new center.
Activities will include building tours, family entertainment, youth activities and opportunities to learn more about the educational, recreational and community programs available.
The celebration also recognizes Kingswood’s 80-year history and the generations of residents, volunteers and community leaders who helped make the institution an important part of Riverside.
TO GO: Kingswood Community Day

What: Grand-opening community celebration and open house.
When: Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Where: Kingswood Community Center, 2500 Rosemont Ave., Wilmington.
Admission: Free; advance registration requested.
Activities: Building tours, family entertainment, educational activities and information about community services.
Register: CelebrateKingswood.org
Learn more: Kingswood Community Center

Budget director Adam Proffitt and Kansas Legislative Research Department director Shirley Morrow talk to reporters during an April 20, 2026, briefing on the state budget. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The new governor and lawmakers will enjoy an improved budget forecast when they take office in January, based on a revised estimate of state tax collections and expenditures.
Forecasters revealed the latest “consensus revenue estimate” on Thursday, based on input from the Kansas Legislative Research Department, state agencies and economists from the University of Kansas, Kansas State University and Wichita State University. The estimate is revised each April and November.
For the current fiscal year, which began July 1, the state is now expected to collect $426 million more than the same forecasters predicted in April. The change is based mostly on robust corporate and individual income tax collections, as well as sales taxes on goods that have seen higher-than-expected inflation.
The five-year budget outlook also underwent a transformation from when the Legislature finished its work seven months ago. At the time, it looked like a new governor and Legislature would have to deal with budget-busting deficits that would rapidly deplete reserves, starting in 2028. Now, the forecast shows surpluses will increase from $489.1 million in fiscal year 2028 to $813.8 million by fiscal year 2031.
And instead of eating into reserves, the rainy day fund is expected to grow from $2 billion now to more than $2.3 billion in five years.
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher, who was leading Republican Senate President Ty Masterson by about 7,000 votes in the governor’s race, will benefit from the state’s financial stability as she launches her administration. Her predecessors were less fortunate: Republican Gov. Sam Brownback took office in 2011 following an economic downturn, and Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly inherited Brownback’s failed tax experiment.
Budget director Adam Proffitt, who also serves as secretary of the Department of Administration, attributed the state’s strong financial standing to Kelly’s “steadfast stewardship.”
“We were facing a budget crisis eight years ago, and there’s been a lot of work that’s gone into stabilizing the budget, undoing all the budget maneuvers, the accounting gimmicks, making sure that we get back to crystal clear budgeting,” Proffitt said.
“There’s been a restoration of real budgeting in the state of Kansas,” he added.
House Speaker Dan Hawkins, a Republican from Wichita who just won the race for insurance commissioner, also took credit for the economic recovery.
For the past two years, the GOP-dominated Legislature ignored the governor’s budget proposals and built its own spending plan. State spending continued to increase, and Republicans clashed with Kelly over her numerous line-item vetoes.
“House Republicans took the reins of the budget process because Kansans deserve responsible stewardship of their hard-earned money,” Hawkins said. “We’re seeing strong revenues, and we’re committed to making sure those dollars are managed wisely. Strong revenues don’t mean a blank check for bigger government. It means we have an obligation to stay disciplined, protect taxpayers, and keep Kansas on solid financial footing. That’s why Republicans took charge of the budget, and our state is stronger for it.”
In terms of the revised revenue estimate, Kansas Legislative Research Department director Shirley Morrow said “the most noteworthy and the biggest factor” was the reemergence of inflation during this calendar year.
Morrow said agriculture producers “are especially exposed to the inflation and price pressures that are prevalent in the economy.”
She also pointed to a stable unemployment rate of just below 4% in Kansas, and a strong job market, especially in construction, leisure and hospitality, and health services.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuits challenge Money Out of Politics ballot measure on First Amendment grounds
description: Two lawsuits have been filed against Proposal 2, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Tuesday with over 80% of the vote, arguing it violates the First Amendment.  The proposal is scheduled to take effect by Dec. 3, 2026, under Michigan election law, unless a court blocks its implementation. The […]
text:
Getty ImagesTwo lawsuits have been filed against Proposal 2, the “Michiganders for Money Out of Politics” ballot measure that passed on Tuesday with over 80% of the vote, arguing it violates the First Amendment. 
The proposal is scheduled to take effect by Dec. 3, 2026, under Michigan election law, unless a court blocks its implementation. The measure bans campaign spending from “regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to those utilities or contractors.”
Both lawsuits — one filed by the Mackinac Center for Public Policy and the other filed by CMS Energy, Consumers Energy and DTE — were filed in federal court in the Western District of Michigan. 
Both lawsuits question whether the state can restrict political spending by utilities and their employees based on their contributions to the elected officials who regulate them.
The Mackinac Center, a free-market policy think tank, writes in its lawsuit, “It is an alarming and far-reaching law. It also violates the First Amendment.”
Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians and a co-chair of the ballot effort, speaks to supporters in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026 after The Associated Press called the race for the “yes” vote. (Screenshot)
Specifically, that suit challenges the portions of the law related to “Electioneering Communications” and “Campaign Expenditures,” arguing that the text of the law that Proposal 2 enacted is too broad in defining which organizations would be subject to significant reporting requirements of their donors and contributions under the new law. 
“Mackinac has no way of determining which of its public communications will qualify as supporting, promoting, attacking, or opposing a candidate or ballot question under Proposal 2, as this broad phrase could include virtually every statement made about those subjects,” the lawsuit writes. “Mackinac likewise has no way of determining which communications will qualify as being made ‘for the purpose of influencing or attempting to influence the action of the voters.’ Mackinac will thus be required to either refrain from speech that could fit these vague standards or face the burdensome reporting requirements that apply to political committees.”
They argue that this is a First Amendment violation in limiting the free speech rights of the Mackinac Center because, “The reporting requirements burden Mackinac’s ability to engage in constitutionally protected speech by imposing onerous costs on Mackinac and exposing it and its supporters to harassment. This creates an impermissible chilling effect on Mackinac’s speech and association.”
“Michiganders shouldn’t face fines or jail just so that they can discuss politicians, policy, or elections,” said Patrick J. Wright, vice president of the Mackinac Center Legal Foundation, in a press release announcing the lawsuit. “These rules threaten access to information voters rely on and violate the privacy of people who support organizations they believe in. We’re bringing this lawsuit to protect free speech and open debate and to prevent giving partisans a nasty tool that can be used to criminally punish their opponents for daring to speak their minds.”
The lawsuit from CMS, Consumers and DTE, on the other hand, argues that the First Amendment is violated by Proposal 2 through “speaker-based viewpoint discrimination” in specifically targeting utility companies and their employees. Even if treated as content-neutral, the lawsuit continues on, the law fails to meet the threshold needed to limit campaign contributions, which would be “preventing quid pro quo corruption or its appearance.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There is no evidence of such corruption by Michigan’s utilities—no scandal, no exchange of official acts for money, no examples whatsoever,” lawyers for the utility companies wrote, adding that the coalition of organizations behind the MMOP ballot measure have “regularly opposed Michigan’s utilities” on policy issues.
Samuel Bagenstos, a University of Michigan law professor and lawyer for the ballot measure, however, was confident that the defense in court of the new law would be strong, adding that new campaign finance laws regularly trigger lawsuits, but that the proposal was drafted with existing judicial decisions in mind.
Maura Cowley, the campaign manager for the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics campaign, said the lawsuit was “no surprise.”
“The corporations bankrolling our opposition have been gearing up for this lawsuit since Proposal 2 first qualified for the ballot, if not before,” Cowley wrote. “On Tuesday, Michiganders spoke loud and clear, voting to pass Proposal 2 with an overwhelming majority and delivering a resounding mandate to end pay-to-play politics and put power back where it belongs – with the people. The bottom line is that we are confident Proposal 2 will withstand legal scrutiny, and we were fully expecting and are prepared to take on this and any challenge.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico launches $9M at-home reading initiative for students in grades K-3
description: New Mexico this week starts sending what will be more than 750,000 books to thousands of students in grades K-3 as part of a new at-home reading initiative to help with the state’s literacy goals.
text:
The New Mexico Public Education Department launched a new at-home reading initiative on Oct. 28, 2026, that will provide literacy packs for K-3 students statewide. Over 750,000 books will begin to arrive at schools this week. Pictured above: students at Valley View Elementary School in Las Cruces. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)New Mexico this week starts sending what will be more than 750,000 books to thousands of students in grades K-3 as part of a new at-home reading initiative to help with the state’s literacy goals. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed Senate Bill 37, also known as the High Quality Literacy Instruction Act, into law in March. SB37 aims to improve literacy outcomes by requiring schools to adopt a pedagogy known as “structured literacy,” a method that uses phonics, vocabulary and comprehension. The bill specifically requires instructional materials to align with structured literacy standards; assessing K-3 students for reading difficulties; and supporting students with such difficulties at home and in school.
The book distribution, announced last week by the New Mexico Public Education Department, will provide “Take-Everywhere Literacy” packs for an estimated 80,000 K-3 students statewide for the 2026-2027 school year. 
Education officials say the books in the literacy packs, developed by the company Just Right Reader, are tailored to match students’ developing reading skills, as well as writing activities and a QR code on the back for video phonics lessons —  available in English, Spanish and more than a dozen additional languages — that families can use for at-home teaching. The state paid Just Right Reader nearly $9 million for the packs, PED spokesperson Janelle Taylor García told Source NM, approximately $119 per student.  
“Teachers identify the skills that are working for students and where they need support and then the books are packed specifically for each kiddo,” Amanda DeBell, PED deputy secretary of teaching, learning and innovation, told Source NM. The literacy packs, “look like a present almost, but it is the gift of books and the gift of reading.” Teachers will develop an individualized family literacy plan for each K-3 student, PED added in a news release, and will update the plan four times during the school year to adjust for student reading progression, along with another literacy pack. 
PED wanted to “ensure that students are practicing reading at home and that their families also have a way to support,” DeBell said. “This opportunity with the reading plans will allow them to work side by side with their classroom teacher.” 
Though New Mexico students improved by 10 percentage points in literacy proficiency between 2022 and 2026, “we know that we still have a long way to go,” DeBell said. She added that there is “a lot of excitement from classroom teachers” about the initiative, and with books set to arrive this week, she expects to hear positive impacts from families soon.
“I’m sure that we will hear from our families that their students are practicing, that they are becoming better readers and that will translate into us developing better scholars as the kids grow up and into the next grade,” DeBell said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Pillen eyes 2028 ballot if Nebraska lawmakers again stall on property tax reform
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years. But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: […]
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hasn’t budged on his approach to cap local spending and cover K-12 education costs to alleviate property taxes he’s called for in the past four years.
But in 2027, Pillen’s second term begins with a more skeptical, divided Legislature to his ideas than before. Though he is adding a backstop: If the Legislature fails, he’ll go to the 2028 ballot.
“All of us, from the river to Harrison, from Falls City to Chadron, from South Sioux City to Benkelman, we’re all ticked off. It’s got to be fixed,” Pillen said at a 30-minute news conference.
Gov. Jim Pillen is joined by two dozen lawmakers for a news conference at the end of the Legislature’s special session to address property taxes that began almost one month prior. Aug. 20, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Many of Pillen’s proposals are familiar — capping local property taxes and valuations, having the state take on the operational costs of K-12 schools and encouraging local governments to cut spending to lower property taxes. The governor said Nebraskans “spoke loud and clear” and gave him and other state leaders a “mandate” to “solve the property tax crisis.” 
He said his ideas should receive bipartisan legislative support and that a broadened sales tax base remains a solution, which is “such a no-brainer, it’s unbelievable, such common sense.”
“I believe in it so much that if we don’t get things accomplished in ‘27, our team will be working on taking it to the ballot for ‘28, and we’ll let the people speak,” Pillen said.
Going to the 2028 ballot
As for what going to the 2028 ballot would look like if needed — petitions, a legislative constitutional amendment (which requires 30 votes) or wading into legislative races — Pillen said he could not say. Some Republican lawmakers are proactively raising funds for reelection should they face primary challengers for opposing Pillen’s ideas.
“I don’t have all those specifics worked out in our head, but all I’m telling you is that we’re dead serious about fighting for Nebraskans to solve this property tax crisis,” Pillen said.
Data that Gov. Jim Pillen’s team compiled showing how state property tax relief has affected effective property tax collections over time is projected during a news conference Nov. 6, 2026, in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The governor also could not say exactly what deadline he’s imposing, such as whether it’s early on in the 2027 session, when the session ends in late May or a special session in the summer
Said Pillen, “We’ll just see what the attitude of the new Legislature is.”
“If the Legislature doesn’t want to solve the problem, we’ll get started sooner than later,” Pillen continued. “If they’re open to the conversation, if they’re going to make it a red-blue conversation, we’ll figure that out pretty quickly. It doesn’t take a rocket scientist to know that.”
The governor presented data his team compiled indicating that ongoing property tax relief efforts, including state credits to offset local costs, have turned the tide on property taxes. For property taxes on agricultural land, for instance, Pillen said collections are effectively the same as 2013 levels. For residential property, it’s back to 2021 levels, and for commercial property, taxpayers are paying what they did in 2019.
Eric Underwood of Lincoln, former chair of the Nebraska Republican Party, has outlined a 15-petition effort aimed at the 2028 election, including many on property taxes. 
It’s not yet clear whether Pillen might lend support to Underwood’s proposals.
A changing Legislature
Multiple lawmakers who usually supported Pillen’s ideas, such as broadening sales tax revenue, include term-limited state Sens. Rob Clements of Elmwood, Speaker John Arch of La Vista and Ben Hansen of Blair. Those three Republicans will be succeeded by more skeptical conservatives who have expressed some concern about a tax “shift” or more taxation.
The 2026 candidates for the Nebraska Legislature arranged by district. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The Legislature’s 33-Republican legislative supermajority — the minimum votes needed to overcome a filibuster — is also set to end. State Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston, a Republican, lost reelection, and two other Omaha-area races could flip blue or purple. State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, Revenue Committee chair, is another Republican who could lose reelection if results hold. He was seen as a frontrunner to succeed Arch as speaker.
Pillen has called for lowering the threshold to end filibusters from 33 to 30. However, a majority of lawmakers, across geography and ideology, have said they’re opposed to the idea.
As he’s done in the past, Pillen said his solution is talking more with lawmakers. He said he and his team will “communicate nonstop.”
“When we can all agree on what a definition of a tax shift is, what the definition of a tax cut is, it starts becoming crystal clear that we’ve been duped by special-interest lobbying groups for 50 years,” Pillen said.
He views sales taxes as the right solution because taxpayers can choose whether to make those purchases, as opposed to mandatory income or property taxes. He noted laundry services and ironing of clothes, for instance, which he said he’s done a few times. He joked that first lady Suzanne Pillen might argue with his ironing a little bit.
“I’ll iron my shirt. I’ll mow my own lawn. I’ll wash my car. I’ll do all the normal things that we used to do,” Pillen said. “That’s not people that are in tough shape. They have that opportunity.”
Yet for multiple years, Pillen has tried to rally lawmakers behind his cause. The needle hasn’t moved to push it over the edge of narrow defeats multiple times over.
2026 special session?
Multiple returning lawmakers and lobbyists have questioned whether Pillen might pursue a special session in the next two months, possibly with a more favorable Legislature. Some have wondered whether Pillen might try to cut spending, and some lawmakers have speculated whether legislators could pause lowering income tax rates before it lowers to 3.99% in January.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference talking about his approach for property taxes ahead of the 2027 legislative session on Nov. 6, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska, days after securing reelection for four more years. At right is a map the governor said shows the “mandate” he and other state leaders have to act based on unofficial election results and margins between Republicans and Democrats. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“Anything could be possible” in a special session, Pillen said, though he said he has not talked to any lawmakers as he’s “worked my brains out” running the state and running for reelection.
“I gave up speculation a long time ago because it almost broke me trying to speculate markets,” Pillen said.
Pillen called a special session in the summer of 2024 solely on property taxes.
However, multiple state senators and lobbyists the Nebraska Examiner has spoken to for months have said few ideas might have 33 votes to pass in 2026, let alone before a new Legislature with more than a dozen fresh faces coming in at voters’ wishes on Jan. 6.
Balancing Nebraska’s budget
Largely absent from Friday’s news conference was talk about Nebraska’s budget, likely in part because Pillen denies that Nebraska is in a “budget crisis.” Some Republicans, such as former state Sen. Julie Slama of Dunbar, have broken from Pillen and called it a “crisis.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen talks with reporters after declaring victory in his reelection bid to lead the Cornhusker State on Nov. 4, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Through mid-2029, Nebraska faces a budget deficit that could grow as high as $1.2 billion.
“Those numbers over three years are not near as complicated,” Pillen told reporters.
Pillen said he held a cabinet meeting Friday and spent a couple of minutes celebrating cultural improvements and the work that’s already been done. He said the expectation across the Executive Branch is that agency heads will be in the office, rolling up their sleeves and finding efficiencies, such as cutting out “silly things” happening in government.
“Really, really crystal clear: Pleased but sure as heck not satisfied,” Pillen said of his cabinet.
The Legislature convenes Jan. 6. Pillen’s next four-year term begins the next day.

title: Auditor: Former retirement director had pattern of absences before resignation
description: LINCOLN — New research from State Auditor Mike Foley into the short-lived executive director of Nebraska’s Public Employees Retirement System showed the director had a tumultuous experience in the agency before he walked off the job. Thomas Pfeifle submitted his resignation to the state retirement board Sept. 21 after roughly three months leading the agency,[...]
text:
Nebraska Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley testifies before the Legislature's Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee. Feb. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — New research from State Auditor Mike Foley into the short-lived executive director of Nebraska’s Public Employees Retirement System showed the director had a tumultuous experience in the agency before he walked off the job.
Thomas Pfeifle submitted his resignation to the state retirement board Sept. 21 after roughly three months leading the agency, saying he wanted to be closer to his children in Colorado. His resignation letter set his last day as Oct. 31, which the board approved at a special meeting Sept. 30.
NPERS staff said Pfeifle did not work in the NPERS office after Sept. 21. Foley estimated he would receive roughly $28,000 in salary and benefits for six weeks of unperformed work over three payroll periods — two of which have already been issued.
“You can’t make this stuff up,” Foley said in a press release. “The (retirement board) is hell-bent on lavishing tens of thousands of dollars on a spectral former administrator who, besides having an incredibly short, but evidently troubled, tenure of under four months with NPERS, was no longer working at the agency during the period for which he is being paid.”
Nebraska auditor presses state retirement agency for answers on outgoing director’s pay

Foley’s office sent a letter to NPERS last week outlining the improprieties associated with Pfeifle’s continued payment and disclosing new details about the director’s time with the agency.
After the retirement board approved the terms of Pfeifle’s employment on June 15 — including approval of an annual base salary of $205,000 — Foley’s letter said Pfeifle sent an inquiry from his personal email on July 8 to a major financial services company and retirement plan provider to solicit possible employment.
The letter claims that Pfeifle also drafted multiple resignation letters in early September that were eventually deleted, and that Pfeifle was given a “personal improvement plan” that he was to follow from Sept. 8 through Nov. 13. The personal improvement plan listed several areas of improvement, including proper use of work time, according to Foley.
The letter lists several emails sent from Pfeifle to NPERS staff in July and August stating that he had left the office midday and that he would remain out of the office for a day or more. Foley alleged NPERS paid Pfeifle for eight hours of work, despite his putting in a partial day or not being present at all.
“I think they wanted to get that guy out of there so bad that they (said), ‘Let’s just pay him and get him out of here,’” Foley told the Examiner.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Through the research, Foley’s office “became aware” that multiple employee complaints had been submitted involving Pfeifle, which Foley said required administrative action under NPERS’ policy. The letter does not specify what the complaints were and notes that Foley’s office did not determine the validity of the allegations.
However, Foley criticized the agency for not sending the complaints to the required offices until “well over a month” after the initial complaints were filed. The letter said the complaints were distributed the same day Foley’s office reached out to confirm that this policy was followed.
In NPERS’ response to this criticism, officials said the agency would provide board members and staff with education and training on its internal policies to ensure that reportable incidents are reported in a timely manner.
Foley recommended the board cease all future payments to Pfeifle and take steps to recoup the two prior payments he said were issued illegally. NPERS response said the board intends to develop reporting procedures to address oversight of the executive director’s working hours and in-office work, and will consider policies that directly address leadership employment and end-of-employment matters.
Foley said he was not satisfied by the agency’s response and expressed frustration that his office lacks enforcement authority to demand corrective action. He said there was little his office could do beyond what it already has done.
“Everyone knows exactly what is going on — from the (retirement board) members themselves to the director of Administrative Services, who processed this outrageous payout, to the highest state officials,” Foley said. “But nobody will lift a finger to stop it.”

name: WyoFile
title: How to grade the next Congress on Wyoming’s cost of living
description:
Affordability touches multiple policy spheres from energy to housing to national security, writes columnist David Giralt.
The post How to grade the next Congress on Wyoming’s cost of living appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
I ran for Wyoming’s U.S. House as a Republican in this year’s primary. Now my wife and I have a newborn son, and we’re adjusting to a new rhythm: sleepless nights, dirty diapers and the usual worry about keeping up with the bills. Naturally, that has changed how I see these midterm results. I’m looking at them as a father who wants the next two years to be steadier for Wyoming families than the last few.

Opinion

On Tuesday, Democrats won both chambers in convincing fashion. They will hold at least 54 Senate seats with two races still uncalled, and the House majority will land somewhere in the neighborhood of 260 seats. A massive loss for the Grand Old Party. Predictably, national coverage tied the sweep partly to voter frustration over rising costs, the same worry Wyoming voters put first in a recent survey.
Unified control of Congress is not unified control of Washington. President Donald Trump still holds the veto, and most bills still need 60 Senate votes unless Democrats change the filibuster. What Democrats can do on their own is run committees, write spending bills, hold hearings and confirm or block nominees, and each of those touch Wyoming’s energy permits, public lands and housing. So, for Wyoming, expect more oversight than new law, and expect it to show up as delay and uncertainty rather than a single marquee vote. For a Wyoming family, the question is what that does to the cost of living. Here’s how I’ll be watching it.
The University of Wyoming’s 2026 Election Year Survey asked 660 residents to name the single most important problem facing the state. Forty percent chose the economy and cost of living as their top issue, a category that includes inflation, jobs, wages and taxes. That is nearly three times the share for any other issue, and it led among Republicans, Democrats and independents alike. Fifty-two percent said the state economy got worse over the past year. 
The first place that pressure will show up is the energy sector. Oil, gas and coal underwrite a large share of state revenue, local jobs and the tax base that funds schools and roads, from the Powder River Basin to Sweetwater County. Over the past decade these industries have generated nearly $18 billion in state revenue. Democratic chairs will now lead the committees that oversee energy, appropriations and federal lands, so expect more aggressive hearings and scrutiny of leasing and permitting. The veto and the filibuster will limit what becomes law, but there will still be delay and uncertainty, and the new majority will have leverage in spending bills and on federal nominees. Watch whether federal lease sales, drilling permits and mine approvals in Wyoming keep moving on schedule or slow. Any delay from Washington will show up as slower investment and tighter local budgets.
Housing is the second place families will notice Congress’ impact. In the same UW survey, 28% of renters spend more than 40% of their income on housing. A Democratic Congress is more likely to pass new housing spending, but relief that reaches young families in a state with tight inventory is not guaranteed. One bipartisan idea is waiting: Since 1997, homeowners have been able to exclude $250,000 in profit from a home sale from capital gains tax ($500,000 for couples), and Congress has never adjusted that for inflation. That cap keeps longtime owners from selling and locks away inventory. Watch Wyoming rents, home prices and mortgage rates, and whether Congress can move a bill that meaningfully addresses housing costs.
The war with Iran was another key issue for voters across the state and has already hit Wyoming’s fuel pumps. Wyomingites drive long distances to work, shop and see doctors, so higher gasoline and diesel prices, and the groceries trucked in on diesel, hit hard here. Watch how Congress tries to reassert itself in national security decisions.
Then there is the long-term game: the rules themselves. A Democratic Senate can slow or block President Trump’s judicial picks, and that matters for Wyoming, whose federal cases go to the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals. If a Supreme Court seat opens during the lame duck, expect a standoff rather than an easy confirmation. Since Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo ended deference to federal agencies, BLM, EPA and Interior rules on leasing, permitting and public lands face closer court scrutiny. That won’t change this winter’s heating bill, but it shapes the regulatory climate for years, and the costs families ultimately absorb.
The real test for both parties is whether members show the independent judgment John F. Kennedy praised in “Profiles in Courage” (a book that I’m reading in between diaper changes). Can Congress put families’ cost of living above the easier and flashier politics of confrontation?
The real test is this: Are Wyoming permits and lease sales moving? Are housing costs easing? Do prices at the pump and the store come down? The mandate of Nov. 3 is simple: Get the cost of living under control.
