title: Commentary: Bigotry against Somali Minnesota voters was a losing strategy
description: President Donald Trump has called Somali Americans “garbage.” He’s said they are “low IQ” but somehow also the “number one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs.”  This was not surprising, if you know Trump’s history. The Nixon administration successfully sued Trump and his father — Trump is a nepo baby, bigly — for systematically discriminating against Black and[...]
text:
Voters in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood cast their ballots during the midterm elections Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Minneapolis. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)President Donald Trump has called Somali Americans “garbage.” He’s said they are “low IQ” but somehow also the “number one buyers of Mercedes-Benz and BMWs.” 
This was not surprising, if you know Trump’s history. The Nixon administration successfully sued Trump and his father — Trump is a nepo baby, bigly — for systematically discriminating against Black and Puerto Rican renters as part of their vast outer borough real estate operations. 
Now, he is the government, and he sent 3,000 armed, masked, ill-trained immigration agents here with an unclear objective, so they roamed the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood, routinely racially profiling people, demanding their papers. Nearly 84% of Somali Minnesotans are citizens as of 2023, and they responded this election season with stoicism — and power — by going to the polls in huge numbers.
According to data compiled by retired journalist David Brauer, the heart of Cedar-Riverside in Ward 6 saw turnout that surpassed 2024, an unusual outcome given the typically greater intensity of presidential elections. In precinct 3, turnout was 135% of 2024, yielding an extra 548 votes. In precinct 9, turnout was 125% of 2024, yielding an additional 336 votes.  
And based on Reformer interviews with voters conducted by our contributor Atra Mohamed, we can be certain what motivated these voters. 
Halima Elmi, 53, a healthcare worker and mother of four, said during Operation Metro Surge she and her daughter went to a rental car company and encountered ICE agents in the parking lot. Masked men jumped out of a black van, grabbed them and pushed them in. She said they didn’t even give them a chance to produce their documents. “We screamed, and the rental car staff who were expecting us came and told them this was private property and that they were not allowed to pick up people here. In the meantime, we produced our passports, and they finally left us alone.” 
Elmi spent a lot of time volunteering this fall, taking people to the polls, she said.
Najma Tohu, 28, an entrepreneur and Whittier neighborhood resident, called Trump’s comments “a disgrace.” 
“Somali people have jobs and businesses and pay taxes like anyone else, and for him to say that we don’t work and live off government resources is a lie and disrespectful,” she said.
Faduma Abdi, 40, a mother of three who lives in the Cedar-Riverside neighborhood and works at a nursing home, said she previously voted to fulfill her civic duty, but Tuesday she voted to fight back against Trump by voting for every Democratic candidate on the ballot.
“Trump targeted us, and now we have the opportunity to fight back. He called us ‘garbage.’ And that’s not acceptable,” Abdi said.
Hibo Muse, 28, is a healthcare worker and Cedar-Riverside resident who voted for Trump in 2024. This year, she voted all Democratic-Farmer-Labor.
“I regretted voting for him. I feel as though I’m part of all the pain and suffering that Trump caused,” Muse said.
She said she wants candidates in office who respect and treat all Americans equally.
Trump’s hateful rhetoric, which his followers parroted, didn’t help Minnesota Republicans break their two-decade losing streak in statewide races. And every Minnesota House district voted more blue than in 2024. 
I’m sure it was mostly driven by the cost of food and fuel, and the naked corruption of the Trump administration and their cronies, but forgive my idealism if I also believe that Minnesotans also sought to send a message against his bigotry. 
The looting of the pandemic-era food relief program known as Feeding Our Future and some of our Medicaid programs is a big deal, which is why the Reformer has reported on it, and it’s why I editorialized on the issue beginning in 2023, when I could sense the Democratic establishment was negligent in confronting it. We were the first outlet I’m aware of, in 2024, to publish a piece by a Somali Minnesotan about the uncomfortable fact that nearly all of the people convicted in the Feeding Our Future scandal were of East African descent. If the Walz administration and the Legislature had fixed the problem sooner, that may have prevented it from becoming fodder for racist demagoguery. 
But that doesn’t change the fact that you don’t judge an entire community on the actions of a few, as most of us learned in elementary school. 
And, it was a little hard to take MAGA’s concerns about fraud seriously when KARE 11 reported last month that the Trump administration paid private prison operator CoreCivic $495 million for the Appleton prison — after the company offered to sell it to the state just a year prior for $75 million. CoreCivic gave $500,000 to Trump’s inaugural committee. 
The word “garbage” is an apt descriptor, but not of my Somali neighbors.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi GEAR UP programs help students navigate paths to college
description: Shannon Tatum, media manager for student publications at Jackson State University, asks students questions about storytelling during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Like some middle schoolers, La’David Hall never thought about going to college. Back then, anything beyond high school wasn’t part of his plan. 
That changed when Hall, a seventh grader at the time, heard a career coach speak at an assembly about careers in nursing, engineering, teaching, law and medicine. 
“We never really had people talk to us about our futures or careers,” said Hall, now a junior at  O’Bannon High School in Greenville. “I remember leaving school that day curious and thinking like, “‘Yeah, I can see myself doing any of those things.’” 
The 2021 event marked the start of Delta State’s participation in Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs, or GEAR UP, a federal, grant-funded program that aims to help students attending high-poverty schools prepare for education and careers after high school. 
Students participate in the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The program is one example of efforts across Mississippi to help disadvantaged students in rural areas navigate higher education and careers after high school.
The U.S. Department of Education awarded Delta State a $15 million grant to prepare students across the Mississippi Delta for college through programs and resources including summer camps, mentoring, academic support and trips to the Cleveland campus. 
In 2019, before Delta State earned a federal GEAR UP grant, Mississippi State University was awarded a $28 million GEAR UP state grant to work with Greenville, McComb and Meridian school districts. Two years later, completed applications for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as FAFSA, increased by about 4% among the participating high schools.
Only about 73.4% of Mississippi’s graduating high school seniors completed FAFSA applications in 2025, according to estimates from the National College Attainment Network, a national organization that advocates for federal and state policy issues around college affordability and support services. Completing the federal application is considered a key indicator that a student will enroll in college. 
Now, Jackson Public Schools is also participating in GEAR UP. In August, JPS officials announced the district secured a $10.67 million GEAR UP federal grant. The grant will go toward serving 2,000 middle schoolers across six schools — Blackburn, Brinkley, Cardozo, Kirksey, Lanier and Peeples — over seven years. JPS is partnering with local colleges and universities, museums and education-based organizations to provide mentoring, summer camps, career exploration programs and parental college financial guidance workshops. 
Instructors guide students through a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
About 52% of JPS graduating senior class of 2025 enrolled in college, said Jana Williams, the district’s college and career readiness manager. Supporting the participating middle schools with graduation-based career coaches will help students envision opportunities beyond high school and provide guidance on the academic and financial steps needed to pursue them, she said. 
“It’s about exposure,” Williams said, “seeing their eyes open up and providing them the  opportunity to learn more about college.” 
Helping students see higher education as a viable option
When the Delta State program began, about 43% of students surveyed in Delta communities believed they could attend college, said Sha’Ketta Davis Drungole, executive director of the university’s Mississippi Delta GEAR UP Partnership. Now, program data indicate that 64% of students plan to attend. 
“I have seen growth and development in the way they present themselves, the way they talk about college or careers in their thought processes, the way they engage with each other as students,” Drungole said, “and it’s just really heartwarming to see.”
Delta State’s GEAR UP program has served more than 4,600 students and provided 88,500 hours of services including parent workshops, teacher training and college visits to students, Drungole said. 
The program also provides staff and advisers to offer training for teachers in Delta-area school districts and to help students understand how to apply for college and how to transition to college after high school. 
Laura Miller, English instructor and coordinator of First-Year Writing, right, and Ebony Lumumba, department chair and associate professor of English, speak to students during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents participates in a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents participates in a writing activity during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Glenda Lollis-Hawkins said her daughter Laroya, a senior at Cleveland Central High, has gained money management skills such as budgeting through attending GEAR UP summer camps. The program also offers parents access to resources that help with financial aid applications and understanding college admissions. 
“GEAR UP not only educates the child but [also] the parent about the importance of advancing your career past high school,” Lollis-Hawkins said.
“GEAR UP’s workshops help me parse through the important information,” she said. “They let us know about the ACT, the deadlines and finances when it comes to college.” 
Uncertain federal funding for GEAR UP may put such programs at risk. The Trump administration has proposed budgets that would eliminate funding for GEAR UP, but Congress has pushed back and rejected the request. 
Funding for the program is not guaranteed even if states or school districts were previously awarded grants, said Brandi Lyndall, director of college access strategy and statewide outreach at Get2College, a college access program of Woodward Hines Education Foundation.
For now, the program is helping Mississippi students and their families prepare for higher education. 
Craig Meyer, associate professor of English and director of Jackson State University’s writing program, speaks to students during the GEAR UP writing workshop at the university on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Hall, the O’Bannon High School student, said his curiosity led him to ask his parents questions about college. He wanted to know how to apply. He also asked his mother how she got her nursing degree and her master’s degree in social work. Hall’s father, who did not attend college, encouraged him to keep up with his studies.  
Hall has attended science and entrepreneur summer camps at Mississippi Valley State University over the past few summers. He has toured Mississippi State University’s campus in Starkville. He has also talked with his high school advisers about applying to college. He is now looking beyond his hometown for potential careers such as becoming a teacher, mortician or funeral director. 
“It’s just a new world out there for me,” Hall said.

title: Delaware 5Ks turn fitness into a force for good this weekend
description: From helping children play sports to supporting families facing illness and hardship, Delaware’s weekend races give walkers and runners a chance to improve their health while helping their neighbors. WILMINGTON, Del. — Getting healthy and giving back to the community can go hand in hand this weekend as Delaware hosts a series of 5K races and walks benefiting[...]
text:
Image was created on 11/6 using AI
From helping children play sports to supporting families facing illness and hardship, Delaware’s weekend races give walkers and runners a chance to improve their health while helping their neighbors.
WILMINGTON, Del. — Getting healthy and giving back to the community can go hand in hand this weekend as Delaware hosts a series of 5K races and walks benefiting charitable organizations across the state.
From Wilmington to Lewes, events scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, and Sunday, Nov. 8, will bring together runners, casual walkers, families and volunteers to raise money for causes ranging from childhood epilepsy and rare diseases to youth athletics and support for first responders.
And participants don’t have to be experienced runners to make a difference.
A 5K covers 3.1 miles, a manageable distance for many recreational walkers. At a comfortable walking pace, most people can complete the course in about 45 minutes to an hour.
For those looking to become more physically active, a community 5K can provide extra motivation. It offers a specific goal, an opportunity to exercise with friends and family, and the satisfaction of knowing that participation helps support a worthwhile cause.
The benefits extend well beyond the finish line.
Many Delaware charity races help nonprofit organizations raise money, introduce their missions to new supporters and recruit volunteers. For participants, they offer an opportunity to turn a healthy weekend activity into a contribution to the community.
Here are several opportunities to get moving for a good cause this weekend, along with a preview of the annual Bishop’s 5K, now called the Igniting Hope 5K, later this month.
Saturday, Nov. 7: Four ways to get moving
Nicola Pizza 5K Run/Walk — Lewes
The fourth annual Nicola Pizza 5K Run/Walk begins at 8 a.m. at Nicola Pizza in Lewes.
The event benefits the Warrior Weekend Program, which supports military veterans. Participants will follow a course through the Five Points area and onto the Georgetown-Lewes Trail before gathering for a post-race celebration.
Organizers welcome both runners and walkers, making it an opportunity for families and friends to enjoy exercise while supporting veterans.
Seashore Striders
Delaware Dash for Rare — Wilmington
The second annual Delaware Dash for Rare begins at 9 a.m. at Kelly’s Logan House in Trolley Square.
Organized in support of the National MPS Society, the event raises awareness and money for individuals and families affected by rare diseases.
Participants can choose a 5K race, a 1-mile walk or a virtual option. The shorter distance provides an accessible way for people who may not be ready for a full 5K to participate in the fundraising effort.
Make Today Count 5K — Newark
The Make Today Count 5K begins at 9 a.m. at Canal Little League on Glasgow Avenue.
The race supports the JB12 Foundation, established in memory of Jack Birch to help children participate in sports regardless of their families’ financial circumstances.
Proceeds help cover registration fees, uniforms, equipment, camps and other athletic expenses.
The event’s message connects two aspects of physical fitness: encouraging adults to exercise while making it possible for more children to enjoy organized sports. Casual walkers are welcome.
Harvest Hustle 5K — Camden-Wyoming
One of Delaware’s longtime fall races returns for its 20th anniversary at 10 a.m. at Fifer Orchards.
The Harvest Hustle benefits the American Cancer Society of Delaware and is held in memory of Patricia Vincent and Shelly Eckert.
The course takes runners and walkers through the countryside surrounding the farm, including a stretch through the apple orchard.
Participants and their families also receive admission to Fifer’s U-Play and corn maze, making the fundraiser an opportunity for a family outing.
Sunday, Nov. 8: Walking together for others
Walking Beside Kaden 5K Run/Walk — Newark
The Walking Beside Kaden 5K begins at 10 a.m. at Autumn Arch Beer Project on Pencader Drive.
The event supports Kaden Dennis, a young child whose experience with epilepsy inspired his family to create a fundraiser benefiting the Epilepsy Foundation of Delaware.
The organization provides awareness, advocacy and resources for individuals and families affected by epilepsy.
The race includes a dedicated competitive walking division, giving walkers an opportunity to participate without running. Teams and individual participants also can raise additional money for the cause.
Jack o’ Lantern Revenge 5K — Wilmington
The Jack o’ Lantern Revenge 5K begins at 10 a.m. at Kelly’s Logan House in Wilmington.
The race benefits the Trauma Survivors Foundation, which supports people affected by traumatic experiences, including first responders and health care workers.
The organization also uses proceeds to support its annual Thanksgiving meal for police officers and other first responders working on the holiday.
The event welcomes runners and walkers of different ages and abilities and concludes with a community celebration in Trolley Square.
Looking ahead: Bishop’s 5K returns with a new name Nov. 21
The charitable running season continues Saturday, Nov. 21, when the Diocese of Wilmington hosts its annual Bishop’s 5K, now renamed the Igniting Hope 5K.
The event will take place from 9 to 11 a.m. at Saint Mark’s High School in Pike Creek, with registration beginning at 8 a.m.
Organized to benefit Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Wilmington, the race supports programs that provide food, emergency shelter, housing assistance, counseling and other services to individuals and families experiencing hardship.
The organization serves communities across Delaware and Maryland’s Eastern Shore.
Last year’s Bishop’s 5K attracted 260 participants, raised nearly $30,000 and collected 75 pounds of donated food for people in need.
This year’s organizers are encouraging families, businesses, churches, schools and community groups to form teams. The event includes activities for children, food and refreshments.
Registration is $40 for adults and $25 for participants 18 and younger, with adult pricing scheduled to increase after Nov. 10. Walkers are welcome.
Participants are also encouraged to bring nonperishable food donations to support Catholic Charities’ hunger relief programs.
The race offers another example of how a community fitness event can help an organization provide assistance long after participants cross the finish line.
A small commitment can make a difference
For Delaware residents who have been thinking about becoming more active, participating in a charitable 5K can be a practical first step.
Walking regularly can improve cardiovascular fitness, support healthy weight management and help reduce stress. Participating with friends or family members can also provide encouragement to maintain an active lifestyle.
And unlike some competitive sporting events, many community 5Ks emphasize participation and charitable support as much as finishing times.
Whether someone runs the entire course, walks with friends or volunteers along the route, the weekend offers opportunities to improve personal well-being while helping others.
For Delaware’s nonprofit organizations, that combination of exercise, generosity and community involvement is what makes a charity 5K about much more than a race.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Former WV US Sen. Rockefeller, ‘a compassionate, decent, and true leader,’ dies at 89
description: Jay Rockefeller, a former West Virginia governor and a five-term U.S. senator representing the state, died Friday at the age of 89.
text:
Sen. Jay Rockefeller (D-WV) speaks during a news conference about preserving Medicaid funding during the "fiscal cliff" negotiations at the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill December 11, 2012 in Washington, DC. The legislators were joined by representatives from major unions and policy organizations in calling on the White House and Congressional negotiators to protect funding for Medicaid, a health program for people and families with low incomes and resources.  (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)Jay Rockefeller, a former West Virginia governor and a five-term U.S. senator representing the state, died Friday at the age of 89. 
A native of New York and heir to the Rockefeller family fortune, Rockefeller first came to West Virginia as an anti-poverty worker in 1964. He was elected to the House of Delegates in 1966 and to secretary of state in 1968, according to his biography with the National Governors Association.
Rockefeller was first elected governor in 1976 and served until 1984. He went on to serve in the U. S. Senate from 1985 until 2015, spending most of his tenure as junior senator under the longserving Robert C. Byrd. 
As a senator, Rockefeller was a lead author of the Children’s Health Insurance Program, a joint state and federal program that provides healthcare to low-income children. He championed the 2010 Affordable Care Act, which expanded healthcare to millions of low-income people. 
Former U.S. Rep. Nick Joe Rahall, a Democrat, served in Congress alongside Rockefeller. He said Rockefeller was a leader in expanding access to healthcare and helping West Virginians affected by violent floods. 
“I just cannot thank him enough for his decades and decades of service to our people in West Virginia, to our nation, and indeed to all of humankind,” Rahall said. “Jay was a compassionate, decent and true leader of this nation, and his works, his many deeds, will stand on the top of our highest mountains in West Virginia forever.” 
Wes Holden worked for Rockefeller in the Senate as his director of constituent services, where he helped West Virginians with a litany of problems, from shoring up a creekbank behind someone’s house to pulling strings to get people on organ transplant lists. 
“The thing that I loved about him, he gave me free rein and allowed me to do things he was unaware of, and he trusted me that much, and I didn’t have a leash on me,” Holden said. “And he only found out about it after it made the press or some sort of thank you letter. So I will always appreciate that.” 
In a statement Friday, West Virginians for Affordable Health Care called Rockefeller a “steadfast champion of accessible, affordable health care.”
“Sen. Rockefeller understood that access to quality, affordable health care is fundamental to the strength and well-being of our families and communities,” Executive Director Ellen Allen said in the statement. “He devoted much of his life to making sure that children, working families, seniors, and some of our most vulnerable neighbors were not left behind. His commitment to West Virginia was evident in the way he listened to people, understood their struggles, and carried their concerns into the halls of government. 
“His legacy will live on in the countless lives made better by his service and his unwavering belief that every West Virginian deserves the opportunity to live a healthy life,” she said. 
Andy Richardson, a former Charleston city councilman, was a liaison for Rockefeller’s campaign at the West Virginia University campus during his successful gubernatorial run in 1976. Richardson was a freshman at the university at the time. Volunteering for Rockefeller’s campaign was his first foray into politics, he said. 
“He was a younger candidate, and I think that it is natural for young people to connect with young people,” Richardson said. “So I think that that was an important part of it. And I think that in West Virginia became less of a factor as time went on. 
“The luster of that Rockefeller name was attractive to a lot of people as I think back on it,” he said. “But for a person that had such affluence, being a northeastern blue blood, he honestly could also be very down to earth, and people like that.”
Richardson remembered Rockefeller as a friend and a “tremendous advocate” for the state. 
Several of West Virginia’s elected officials shared tributes to Rockefeller Friday morning. Gov. Patrick Morrisey said Rockefeller’s legacy will live on in West Virginia history. 
“From his early work in some of our state’s most disadvantaged communities to his efforts to strengthen healthcare, protect coal miners and their families, and support our veterans, Sen. Rockefeller demonstrated a deep commitment to the people of West Virginia,” Morrisey said. “His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians.” 
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-West Virginia, shared her condolences on social media. 
“He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” she said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.” 
Sen. Jim Justice, R-West Virginia, also remembered Rockefeller’s contributions. 
“His years of dedicated service as Governor and Senator truly reflect the love he had for his great state,” he said. “Sen. Rockefeller worked hard for West Virginians and made a difference in countless lives.” 
Del. Mike Pushkin, chair of the West Virginia Democratic Party, noted that Rockefeller didn’t have to devote his life to public service. 
“Jay Rockefeller was born into one of the wealthiest and most privileged families in American history. He could have spent his entire life enjoying every comfort and opportunity that wealth could provide,” Pushkin said in a statement. “Instead, he chose a different path. He came to the hills of West Virginia as a young VISTA volunteer, saw the struggles of working families firsthand, and made it his life’s mission to do something about them.”
Rockefeller was more than a statesman. He also had a bit of a jokester side to him, as Rahall and Holden recalled. 
Holden said he remembered in the later part of his career being texted a photo of a tree by Rockefeller, who was riding in a car with staff. The senator wanted to know what type of tree it was. 
“Who am I going to call for what’s what?” Holden recalled saying to himself.   
So he called a garden and found out. When he replied to Rockefeller 10 minutes later, Holden said the boss wasn’t surprised at all. 
“He was just wanting to show this other person that I was the go-to guy to get things done,” Holden said. 
During campaign season, Rahall said Rockefeller would stay at his house from time-to-time. In the mornings, the two candidates would stop at a gas station to get a cup of coffee. 
“He didn’t have any money,” Rahall said, with a laugh. “He never carried money around with him. It was always up to me to pay the bill.” 
Rockefeller leaves behind his wife Sharon, four children and nine grandchildren.

Cash and Target gift cards collected through Dec. 7 will help local children shop for gifts, clothing and other necessities
DOVER, Del. — The Dover Police Department is asking residents and businesses to help make the holidays brighter for local children by supporting its 14th annual Holiday Heroes program.
The department is accepting cash and Target gift cards through Monday, Dec. 7, for the annual shopping event, which pairs Dover police officers and department staff with children selected with the help of Capital School District teachers and counselors.
The children are taken on a shopping trip to the Dover Target, where they can choose gifts for family members and themselves while also purchasing everyday necessities such as winter coats, shoes and hygiene products.
The amount raised will help determine how many children are able to participate.
Community support drives program
Holiday Heroes is supported by donations from residents, local businesses and Target, a longtime partner in the program.
The goal is to give children from families facing financial challenges an opportunity to enjoy the experience of holiday shopping while also helping meet practical needs.
Dover Police said the program has become an annual tradition connecting officers and department employees with children and families in the community.
Donation rules changed this year
People who have donated by check in previous years should note that updated purchasing policies mean the department can accept only cash or Target gift cards for the 2026 program.
Target eGiftCards also may be purchased online and emailed directly to the department.

Hunters in parts of Sussex County face mandatory check stations as state responds to first confirmed cases of chronic wasting disease
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s most popular deer hunting season opens Friday, Nov. 13, but this year hunters will head into the woods under new rules designed to contain chronic wasting disease after the fatal wildlife disease was detected in the state for the first time.
The 10-day general firearm deer season runs through Sunday, Nov. 22, and typically accounts for about 40% of Delaware’s annual deer harvest, according to the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control.
The biggest change affects hunters in Wildlife Management Zones 11, 14 and 16 in Sussex County, which DNREC has designated as Delaware’s Chronic Wasting Disease Management Zone.
Any deer harvested in those zones during the general firearm season must be brought to a DNREC check station, where wildlife officials will collect samples for CWD testing.
Delaware has confirmed three cases of chronic wasting disease in wild white-tailed deer this year. The first, announced in April, was also the first confirmed case on the Delmarva Peninsula. A third case announced in September prompted DNREC to expand its management zone to include Wildlife Management Zone 11.
Why CWD matters
Chronic wasting disease is a fatal neurological disease affecting deer, elk, moose and other members of the deer family.
It is caused by abnormal proteins known as prions that can spread through saliva, blood, urine, feces and contaminated soil, food or water. There is no treatment or vaccine, and infected deer ultimately die from the disease.
No transmission of CWD to humans has been documented. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that hunters in areas where CWD is present have deer tested before eating the meat and not consume meat from animals that test positive.
Delaware had tested deer for CWD for more than two decades before detecting its first case this year. DNREC says it has tested nearly 13,000 samples since surveillance began in 2003.
Mandatory check stations
Hunters who take deer in Wildlife Management Zones 11, 14 or 16 during the Nov. 13-22 firearm season must report to one of three check stations:

Delaware Solid Waste Authority Jones Crossroads Landfill, 28560 Landfill Lane, Georgetown
Gumboro Community Center, 36849 Millsboro Highway, Millsboro

Redden State Forest Jester Tract parking lot, Redden Road, Kings Crossroads
The stations will operate from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. each day of the firearm season.
Hunters should bring their deer registration information, including the new QR code generated during registration. Hunters without the QR code can still have their deer sampled.
Deer harvested outside the management zone may also be voluntarily submitted for testing. Hunters can drop deer heads at designated Delaware Hunters Against Hunger locations, and DNREC staff also plan to collect samples at selected deer processors in Middletown, Camden and Milton.
Movement and bait restrictions
DNREC has also imposed restrictions intended to reduce opportunities for CWD to spread.
Baiting and feeding deer are prohibited within the management zone, and natural urine-based deer attractants are prohibited statewide. Hunters moving deer harvested inside the management zone to other parts of Delaware also face special transportation and disposal requirements.
DNREC adopted emergency regulations after the first CWD cases were discovered and expanded the management area following the third confirmed case in September.
Other hunting rules changed this year
CWD is not the only change hunters will notice during the 2026-27 season.
Delaware expanded Sunday hunting to all game species, broadened the types of straight-walled pistol-caliber rifles and muzzleloaders that can be used and eliminated the minimum-age requirement for DNREC special youth hunts.
State law also now allows 16- and 17-year-olds who have completed basic hunter education to hunt and practice shooting without direct adult supervision if they have permission from a parent or guardian.
DNREC has published an addendum to its 2026-27 Hunting and Trapping Guide outlining the CWD rules and other regulatory changes.
Hunters part of the response
Wildlife officials say the concentrated firearm season gives Delaware an opportunity to collect a large number of samples in a short period and better determine how widely the disease has spread.
DNREC Wildlife Section Administrator Joe Rogerson said information gathered during the season will help officials assess the disease’s distribution and prevalence and shape Delaware’s approach for the 2027-28 hunting season.
That makes this year’s deer harvest about more than recreation.
Thousands of hunters heading into Delaware’s woods this month will also provide wildlife managers with information that could influence how the state manages its deer population for years to come.
To Go

What: Delaware general firearm deer season
When: Friday, Nov. 13, through Sunday, Nov. 22
CWD requirement: Deer harvested in Wildlife Management Zones 11, 14 and 16 must be brought to a DNREC check station during the firearm season.
Check station hours: 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily
Learn more: DNREC’s Chronic Wasting Disease page and the 2026-27 Delaware Hunting and Trapping Guide contain regulations, maps, testing information and updates.

title: Commentary: I study polling failures – this time, pollsters were mostly right, if not precise
description: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. The crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. text:
Voters exercise their right to vote at Greenbush Elementary School in West Warwick on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
The crucial test for preelection polls is whether they broadly indicate how voters are likely to decide. By that fundamental measure, the 2026 midterm polls largely succeeded in anticipating outcomes on Election Day.
If somewhat tentatively, the polls overall had been signaling important gains for Democrats. And that is what voting produced.
It was, perhaps, polling’s most reassuring performance since accurately anticipating Barack Obama’s presidential election in 2008, an outcome cited in my book, Lost in a Gallup: Polling Failure in US Presidential Elections.
This is not to say the 2026 preelection polls offered precision estimates before returns poured in. They appear to have underestimated support for Democratic candidates in some Senate races.
But spot-on precision, while enviable, is not what polls can be expected to produce, considering the many ways error can infiltrate opinion surveys. Given their checkered record in recent national elections, pollsters and media analysts tended to couch their end-of-campaign assessments in measured tentativeness.
For example, Nate Cohn, chief political analyst for The New York Times, wrote just before the election that “it’s reasonable to wonder whether the polls might be overestimating Democratic strength yet again. This is a real possibility. President Trump’s supporters are relatively unlikely to respond to polls, which introduces the ever-present risk of a polling misfire.”
That risk was mostly unrealized, as Republican candidates were swept in a red wipeout.
The 2026 polls tended to confirm the truism in American politics that midterms typically are rough on candidates of the party that holds the presidency.
Another truism, again reaffirmed, is that a president’s approval ratings often are useful in gauging the country’s mood before midterm elections. President Donald Trump’s preelection approval ratings hovered at or below 40 percent, according to survey data compiled by RealClearPolitics.
The US war with Iran, launched by Trump, was a major factor propelling the unenviable ratings. The conflict went unresolved while fuel prices surged, bringing pain to consumers.
Those and other problems prompted polling analyst Nate Silver to write that Trump “almost seems to have a death wish in these midterms. And the one superpower he has – turning out low-propensity voters in presidential years, the sorts of voters who apparently are often missed by pollsters – has never really worked when Trump himself wasn’t on the ballot.”
And it didn’t work this time, either, even though throughout the campaign Trump encouraged supporters to pretend his name was on the ballot and turn out to vote.
 Few polling misses

When examined closely, the polls delivered some disagreement in the days before the election. Pollsters offered ranges that, in some races, were sizable.
For example, was Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton up by 1 percentage point in Texas late in the campaign, or was he down 7 points? Paxton lost by double digits to Democrat James Talarico, a margin that no pollster anticipated.
Similarly, was long-serving Republican Sen. Susan Collins ahead by 2 points in Maine or was she losing by 9 points? The outcome was closer to the latter reading, with Democrat Troy Jackson winning by more than six points.
In Minnesota, was Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan up by 14 points, or by just 2 points? With most votes counted by the day after the election, Flanagan’s margin of victory was about 10 points.
Such polling gaps in high-profile races offer a reminder to not focus on any single survey but, instead, to consider overall polling averages, which tend to remove or reduce the effects of outliers.
None of this necessarily is to declare that pollsters have resolved their persistent problems in sampling, especially in interviewing hard-to-reach voters. But big polling misses like that in the Texas governor’s race – where Democrat Gina Hinojosa won by double digits, although polls had shown Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ahead by a few points – were few this election cycle.
Meanwhile, the electorate’s broad inclinations were plainly if not precisely depicted.
That outcome has to be heartening for pollsters, an often-beleaguered and much-criticized cohort.
W. Joseph Campbell, is professor emeritus of communication at American University School of Communication.

title: New Mexico Gov.-elect Haaland names state labor secretary as chief of staff
description: On Nov. 6, 2026, New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland named current Department of Workforce Solutions Secretary Sarita Nair as her chief of staff.
text:
On Nov. 6, 2026, New Mexico Gov.-elect Haaland named Secretary of Workforce Solutions Sarita Nair (pictured at the podium during a Feb. 24, 2025 news conference at the state Capitol) as her new chief of staff. (Photo by Eddie Moore / Albuquerque Journal)New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland on Friday morning announced that the state’s current secretary of the Department of Workforce Solutions would be her chief of staff.
The New Mexico State Senate confirmed Sarita Nair as DWS secretary in February of 2023. She worked previously as chief administrative officer for the City of Albuquerque
“I am confident that Sarita will serve as a trusted partner and tireless advocate for all New Mexicans,” Haaland said in a statement. “She is a distinguished leader with over 20 years of experience in public service and the law. Her expertise will be essential as we build a state government that is accountable to New Mexicans and is focused on cutting costs for working families.”
A news release says Nair’s responsibilities as chief of staff will include guiding the transition to Haaland’s administration, and coordinating her staffing, cabinet appointments and policy priorities. It was not immediately clear if Sair would also continue as DWS secretary. Haaland on Thursday named several members of her campaign staff to her transition team as well.
“It is an honor to serve the people of New Mexico as the Chief of Staff for Governor-elect Haaland. I am committed to supporting her and the incoming Cabinet to lower costs, expand access to healthcare, and strengthen public safety,” Nair said.
This is a developing story.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Podcast: What South Dakota’s blue ‘ripple’ means for the state Democratic Party
description: Though they didn’t win any statewide seats, South Dakota Democrats gained ground in the Legislature after Tuesday’s election for the first time since 2008, bringing their numbers from eight to 12 out of 105 total legislators. Shane Merrill, the state party’s chair, joined the Searchlight Report podcast to talk about what the legislative wins mean […]
text:
Shane Merrill, chair of the South Dakota Democratic Party, speaks at the party's election night watch party in downtown Sioux Falls on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




Though they didn’t win any statewide seats, South Dakota Democrats gained ground in the Legislature after Tuesday’s election for the first time since 2008, bringing their numbers from eight to 12 out of 105 total legislators.
Shane Merrill, the state party’s chair, joined the Searchlight Report podcast to talk about what the legislative wins mean for the state party and how it can use the momentum it’s getting from the blue “ripple” in South Dakota, as compared to the “tsunami” that swept Democrats into power in Congress.
Plus, hear from longtime South Dakota journalist Kevin Woster, who spent decades covering the Legislature. He breaks down how the Democratic numbers got so low and where the party could go after Tuesday’s wins.

title: Violent, property crime victimization rates fell in 2025, federal data shows
description: A new federal report released the week before Tuesday’s midterm elections found that Americans experienced declines in several categories of violent and property crime victimization in 2025, including aggravated assaults, burglaries and motor vehicle thefts. The preliminary survey findings from the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics offers a fresh look at cri[...]
text:
Crime scene tape surrounds an entry to the Barus & Holley engineering building at Brown University. The rate of violent crime victimization declined 25% between 2024 and 2025, while the rate of property crime victimization fell 19%, according to the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics’ preliminary National Crime Victimization Survey. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)A new federal report released the week before Tuesday’s midterm elections found that Americans experienced declines in several categories of violent and property crime victimization in 2025, including aggravated assaults, burglaries and motor vehicle thefts.
The preliminary survey findings from the U.S. Bureau of Justice Statistics offers a fresh look at crime trends as the country emerges from another election cycle, providing new data on Americans’ experiences with crime, including incidents never reported to police.
The rate of violent crime, excluding simple assault, declined 25% between 2024 and 2025, while the rate of property crime victimization fell 19%, according to the agency’s National Crime Victimization Survey.
Unlike crime statistics based solely on offenses reported to law enforcement, the National Crime Victimization Survey captures both reported and unreported crimes. The nationally representative survey interviews people aged 12 or older about their experiences with violent crime, excluding homicide, and household property crime. It also collects information about the frequency, characteristics and consequences of those incidents.
Researchers point to community violence programs, pandemic recovery in historic homicide decline

The preliminary survey results are consistent with other national crime data, including the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting program, which tracks crimes reported to law enforcement and has documented several years of declining crime rates nationwide. Preliminary FBI data suggests those declines have continued into 2026.
Independent analyses, including crime trends reports from the nonpartisan Council on Criminal Justice, have identified similar patterns, with declines reported in some of the nation’s largest cities. However, crime trends vary across communities, with some experiencing different patterns.
“To see that those things really align, it gives me much more confidence that I’ve had over these past several years that what we’re seeing is a real decline in crimes beyond homicides,” said Thaddeus Johnson, a senior fellow at the council. Johnson also is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at Georgia State University.
Violent crime declines
Americans aged 12 or older experienced an estimated 7.5 million violent victimizations in 2025, a rate of 25.7 victimizations per 1,000 people, according to the report.
The rate of violent crime excluding simple assault fell from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025, a 25% decline. 
Aggravated assault rates dropped from 4.5 victimizations per 1,000 people in 2024 to 3.1 per 1,000 in 2025 –– a 31% decrease. The rate of simple assault victimization decreased slightly from 18.8 per 1,000 people in 2024 to 18.3 in 2025.
The robbery victimization rate declined 27% from 2024 to 2025, while the rate of rape and sexual assault victimization fell 11%.
Property crime also falls
U.S. households experienced an estimated 14.9 million property victimizations in 2025, according to the report.
The rate of property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 victimizations per 1,000 households in 2024 to 111.2 per 1,000 in 2025.
Motor vehicle theft recorded one of the largest decreases, with its victimization rate falling 30% over the year.
The rate of burglary or trespassing declined 25%, while other types of household theft fell 19% and vandalism decreased by nearly 11%.
Survey redesign and limitations
The Bureau of Justice Statistics fully transitioned to a redesigned National Crime Victimization Survey in January 2025, changing how the agency collects information about Americans’ experiences with crime.
The agency redesigned the survey to improve how it identifies and measures crime victimization. The updated questionnaire uses shorter, more specific questions intended to help respondents recall incidents they may have experienced, including crimes that were never reported to police.
The redesign also expands questions about sexual assault, victims’ experiences with law enforcement and the consequences of crime. The agency cautioned that estimates from the redesigned survey cannot be directly compared with those produced using the previous version.
The preliminary 2025 estimates may change when the agency publishes its final report, which is expected to be released next year.
Stateline reporter Amanda Watford can be reached at awatford@stateline.org.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missourians rejected another abortion ban. Republicans say they’re not giving up yet.
description: Missouri Republicans spent two years trying to reinstate an abortion ban. They emerged from Tuesday’s election with fewer ways to do it — and no plans to stop trying. About 55% of voters rejected Amendment 3, preserving the constitutional right to abortion approved in 2024. Voters also approved Amendment 6, which sharply limits lawmakers’ power […]
text:
Dr. Margaret Baum, chief medical officer of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, embraces Margot Riphagen, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Rivers, during an Amendment 3 watch party in St. Louis. The crowd celebrated after the ballot measure aimed at banning abortion was voted down by Missourians on Tuesday (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).Missouri Republicans spent two years trying to reinstate an abortion ban. They emerged from Tuesday’s election with fewer ways to do it — and no plans to stop trying.
About 55% of voters rejected Amendment 3, preserving the constitutional right to abortion approved in 2024. Voters also approved Amendment 6, which sharply limits lawmakers’ power to overturn citizen-approved measures, while Democrats won enough legislative seats to end the GOP’s supermajority in the Missouri House.
The results dealt a significant setback to anti-abortion activists who had hoped Missouri could provide a national model for reversing abortion rights victories at the ballot box.
Missouri voters reject Amendment 3, preserving abortion rights approved in 2024

But state Sen. Nick Schroer, a St. Charles County Republican who will become Senate majority leader in January, said abortion will remain a priority for his caucus, even as lawmakers grapple with the new restrictions imposed by Amendment 6.
Schroer said the issue will be a “hot topic” at upcoming Republican caucus meetings, though lawmakers have yet to settle on a strategy. Several attorneys, including himself, are examining what options remain.
“But are we handcuffed by Amendment Six?” Schroer asked, adding that Republicans will “have to be strategic in what we do.”
Republican lawmakers placed Amendment 3 on the ballot last year, arguing that voters hadn’t understood the reproductive rights amendment they approved in 2024. But Tuesday’s results were more decisive: Roughly 55% rejected the proposed ban, compared with the 51.6% who approved abortion rights two years earlier.
“It’s hard to say this time that they were tricked,” said Matt Harris, a political scientist at Park University. “ … it’s maybe close, but Missourians have demonstrated that they want abortion rights.”
The vote preserves abortion rights before fetal viability. Abortion is available at five Planned Parenthood clinics across Missouri, including in Springfield, where procedural abortions resumed this year for the first time in 21 years.
Mallory Schwarz, executive Director of Abortion Action Missouri, celebrates the defeat of Amendment 3 on Tuesday (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
“Throughout this campaign I’ve been asked a lot about how it feels on the ground,” Mallory Schwarz, executive director of Abortion Action Missouri, said during a victory speech Tuesday evening. “The best answer I could give was people are mad, just plain pissed off that we had to do this again. Mad that our votes, our rights, our values were being undermined by Missouri politicians who thought they could just overturn any vote they didn’t like.” 
 Republicans look for another path

Amendment 6 creates a formidable new obstacle for lawmakers hoping to revisit abortion rights through another constitutional amendment.
Under the measure, any legislative attempt to change or undermine a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment must receive support from at least 80% of both legislative chambers before going to voters for approval. That includes the reproductive rights amendment approved in 2024.
With Republicans losing their legislative supermajorities, reaching that threshold would require substantial Democratic support. The new restrictions could face legal challenges, however, leaving some uncertainty about their ultimate reach.
State Rep. Brian Seitz, a Branson Republican who helped lead the push to put an abortion ban on the ballot, said Wednesday that abortion will always be on the agenda in Jefferson City. 
Rather than pursuing another constitutional amendment, Seitz said he intends to focus on new abortion regulations.
“Incrementalism is key, especially in this political environment,” he said, pointing at the new makeup of the legislature, which is no longer controlled by a Republican supermajority.
That approach has a long history in Missouri. Over several decades, Republican lawmakers enacted dozens of abortion regulations that steadily eroded access to the procedure, even before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
After the 2024 reproductive rights amendment passed, Planned Parenthood and the ACLU of Missouri challenged about 40 of these regulations as unconstitutional. A Jackson County judge struck down most of them, but left in place a requirement that patients see a doctor in-person before being prescribed medication abortion. 
Under federal law, medication abortion can legally be mailed into any state from providers in states where abortion is legal. This telehealth access remains one of the main obstacles to Republicans limiting abortion access in any state. 
Between 2023 and 2025, the number of Missourians getting abortion pills by mail from out of state providers tripled. An estimated 3,220 Missourians obtained medication abortions through telehealth last year.
Seitz said he plans to again introduce legislation aimed at stopping medication abortion from coming into Missouri through the mail. 
Other GOP lawmakers have floated legislation establishing legal personhood for fetuses, potentially setting up another court fight over abortion rights. This includes State Sen. Mike Moon, a Republican from Ash Grove who voiced loud opposition to Amendment 3 because he disagreed with the inclusion of any abortion exceptions.
A personhood law could not itself override the state constitution, and any attempt to pass new abortion restrictions would face additional political and legal obstacles after Tuesday’s election.
State Sen. Adam Schnelting, a Republican from St. Charles who carried the failed abortion ban proposal in the Senate in 2025, didn’t share specifics Thursday on what legislation he might put forward.
“I’m never gonna stop fighting for life,” he said. “What form that takes is yet to be seen.”
State Rep. Ed Lewis, a Republican from Moberly who lost his run for state Senate in the August primary, said outside personhood bills, he foresees reluctance to attempt to legislate abortion after what he characterized as a “strong repudiation” Tuesday. 
“I don’t think there’s gonna be anything done in two years,” Lewis said. “I think that it’s just too raw, too much money spent, too much effort. We’re probably gonna have to wait and let things play out a little bit.”
But he does guess there will still be a large focus by Republicans on initiative petition reform, including attempts to limit out-of-state funding to initiative petitions efforts and raise the threshold for passage.
“I think you’re going to see this continued fight over IP,” he said. “And forcing the other side to just spend their money over and over again.” 
The campaign to pass the 2024 abortion rights amendment spent about $30 million. This year, they again raised more than $30 million.
Sam Lee, a longtime anti-abortion lobbyist, said one of his top priorities next year will be asking for more funding for Missouri’s Alternatives to Abortion program, as well as expanding tax credits for pregnancy resource centers, maternity homes, domestic violence shelters and food pantries.
Sam Lee, a deacon and longtime anti-abortion lobbyist, joined Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe on a statewide tour in support of Amendment 3, a proposed abortion ban, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at the Spirit of St. Louis Airport in Chesterfield (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
“I know it’s a tough budget year, but if lawmakers are serious about protecting pregnant mothers and their unborn and born children, then we should do that,” he said.
Outside the statehouse, Lee said the initiative petition process is still on the table for anti-abortion activists, and remains the only option for putting another ban before voters if Amendment 6 stands.
“It is what it is,” Lee said. “We’ve dealt with disappointments in the past, and we’ll continue to do so in the future, and we’ll just keep trying.”
State Sen. Tracy McCreery, a Kirkwood Democrat, doesn’t see much of a reasonable path forward for Republicans hoping to further legislate around abortion.
“I feel like the issue is now settled,” she said. 
Instead she hopes to see bipartisan support addressing issues like quality childcare and public school access. As she knocked on doors this fall, she heard from countless families lamenting how unaffordable childcare was, and how long waitlists were. 
She also hopes more lawmakers will support her ongoing efforts to increase accessibility to IVF and a full range of birth control options. 
“One of the best things we can do is help make sure people have access to what they need to avoid unintended pregnancy,” she said.
 Did pairing abortion and transgender care backfire?

Supporters of Amendment 3 had hoped that combining an abortion ban with restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors would broaden the measure’s appeal. Tuesday’s results raise questions about whether that strategy worked.
Ahead of the election, David Bereit, executive director of Life Leadership Conference, gathered in Washington, D.C., with anti-abortion advocates from numerous states to talk election strategy. That day, he said, they all galvanized around Missouri.
“We have to win this one because this will set the precedent for the rest of the nation,” he recalled. “ This will send a chilling effect to the abortion industry to say, ‘you are not going to impose this onto us, and if you try to, we will reverse it.’”
The drafters of Amendment 3 tied the proposed abortion ban to a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors. Missouri’s statutory ban on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones is scheduled to expire in 2027, while the prohibition on gender-affirming surgeries for minors is permanent. 
Bereit emphasized during an October virtual fundraiser that if Amendment 3 passed, other conservative states where voters had approved abortion rights could follow suit, proposing similar amendments linked to restrictions on gender-affirming care.
An August poll by SLU/YouGov Poll showed 44% opposed the abortion ban and 43% supported it. The remaining 13% were unsure.
A February SLU/YouGov survey found a majority of Missourians opposed access to gender-affirming healthcare for minors, with 66% of those surveyed opposing hormone therapy or medications for minors and 72% opposing gender transition surgeries. 
But Ken Warren, a professor emeritus of political science at Saint Louis University and co-director of the poll, said he predicted Amendment 3 would ultimately fail, despite the February and August poll numbers, because polling consistently showed support for abortion rights in Missouri and nationally.
“I thought that as soon as the advertisements came out against Amendment 3, that Amendment 3 would be exposed for what it was,” he said. “It was pretty much a trick by the legislature to try to revisit abortion rights, throwing in an unrelated issue on transgender rights on the ballot to try to confuse voters.”
He said the measure’s defeat was also likely influenced by lower Republican turnout amid a national wave of Democratic victories.
State Rep. Elizabeth Fuchs, a St. Louis Democrat, said she hopes Republicans throw out their playbook to link abortion and transgender healthcare on the ballot.
“Using trans people as a political pawn did not work, and it will not work,” she said. “Missourians saw right through that.” 
TJ Billard, a Northwestern University communications professor who studies media and transgender politics, said it’s easy to interpret these results as a story of who turned out to vote.
“It is very likely that the mobilization in the midterms against the kind of disastrous overall Trump administration meant that more Democratic voters were turning out,” Billard said. “But even beyond more Democratic voters, Independents and Republicans who have found themselves dissatisfied with the current administration.”
Billard also noted that numerous anti-trans ballot initiatives passed in other states while failing in Missouri. But none were linked to an abortion measure. 
“Part of me also wonders,” Billard said. “If — counter to what right wing strategists thought in bundling abortion and gender-affirming care — if instead maybe the abortion component buoyed opposition to this ballot initiative.”
Billard spoke to The Independent a few hours before KFF, a health policy nonprofit, released an election poll analysis that found about six in 10 Missouri voters polled opposed repealing abortion rights and about six in 10 also supported restricting access to gender-affirming care for minors. 
When asked to prioritize their vote, about 45% of respondents said the issues held equal weight for them. But among those who picked an issue, poll respondents were five times more likely to prioritize abortion as an issue over gender-affirming care for minors.
The Independent’s Rudi Keller and Jason Hancock contributed to this story.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Judge rules that feds erred in greenlighting controversial mine project near Nome
description: Federal regulators acted improperly when they granted a permit in 2024 for a controversial gold mining project near Nome, a federal judge has ruled. U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason, in a Nov. 2 ruling, said the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers violated both the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act when […]
text:
Seabirds rest on a sandbar on in Safety Sound east of Nome on Sept. 30, 2020. A Nevada-based company called IPOP LLC is seeking to conduct a dredging operation to mine for gold in an area of Safety Sound called Bonanza Channel, but there is widespread opposition in the Nome area to the project. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Federal regulators acted improperly when they granted a permit in 2024 for a controversial gold mining project near Nome, a federal judge has ruled.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason, in a Nov. 2 ruling, said the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers violated both the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act when it granted a permit to a company proposing to extract gold by dredging a wildlife-rich channel east of Nome.
Gleason’s ruling stopped short of overturning the Clean Water Act permit granted to IPOP LLC, the company behind the project. She gave the parties 21 days to submit new information that will be used to decide the fate of the permit.
The ruling was the result of a lawsuit filed in 2025 by five tribal governments whose members hold an interest in the region for traditional harvests and activities. The lawsuit faulted the Corps for reversing its 2022 decision that denied the IPOP permit on environmental grounds.
IPOP LLC, based in Las Vegas, Nevada, has proposed mining for gold by dredging a nearly 3-mile section of Bonanza Channel, an ecologically important part of Safety Sound, a sheltered body of water that flows into Norton Sound.
The project was originally pitched as the basis for a new Alaska-themed reality show that was to be called Rivers of Gold. IPOP has since said the TV show aspect of the project has been dropped.
The plan has been widely opposed by residents in Nome and the Bering Strait region. Organizations weighing in against, in addition to the plaintiff tribal governments, include Kawerak Inc., a regional tribal consortium; the regional Native-owned Bering Straits Native Corp.; the local Native-owned the Norton Sound Economic Development Corp.
In her ruling, Gleason said the Corps’ Hawaii-based Pacific Division, which approved the permit in 2024, failed to properly explain why it came to a different conclusion than the Alaska district office, which denied the permit application in 2022.
Gleason listed several areas of divergence, including analysis of impacts to migratory birds, Bonanza Channel’s floor and turbidity in the water column. She also noted that the regional Pacific division office used a study that had been discredited by the Alaska district.
The Pacific division office “failed to explain its rationale for reaching a different conclusion from the District; indeed, it did not even acknowledge the District’s different conclusions. Not only are the Pacific Division’s findings ‘in apparent conflict’ with the Alaska District’s findings; the Division’s findings are also unsupported by ‘a rationale to explain the disparate findings,’” Gleason said in her ruling.
In its defense against the case, the Corps argued that the tribal plaintiffs’ allegations were “vague and ambiguous” in the way they defined key terms. 
Those terms included such phrases as “pristine, ecological valuable estuary,” “haven for subsistence users” and “first such suction dredge mine project,” the Corps said in its July 16, 2025 answer to the complaint.
Tribal plaintiffs in the case welcomed the federal court’s ruling as protecting an area critically important to their food security and cultures.
 

The village of Solomon is seen from the air in 2009. The village is no longer inhabited year-round, but the area is used seasonally for traditional food gathering and other cultural practices. (Photo provided by the Alaska Division of Community and Regional Affairs)
 

	Among the five plaintiffs, the Village of Solomon has the closest geographic ties to the Bonanza Channel area that IPOP proposes to dredge.
Solomon is no longer a year-round village, but it serves as a “seasonal village” for tribal members and used for annual youth and elder camps, said Deilah Johnson, treasurer and tribal resources director for the Village of Solomon.
Tribal members return regularly to fish, pick berries and connect with their heritage, Johnson said.
The area is especially important to tribal members because year-round Solomon residents were displaced from the site decades ago, forced to move away in the 1950s when the Bureau of Indian Affairs closed the school, she said.
“When we’re there, we feel whole,” she said. “We always say, you know, ‘Our heart is in Solomon.’”
The other plaintiffs are the King Island Native Community, the Village of Council, the Chinik Eskimo Community and the Native Village of White Mountain.
Separately from Gleason’s ruling, IPOP has been unable to perform development work at the proposed mining site. The project lacks another important permit: a land-use permit from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources.
DNR’s Division of Mining, Land and Water rejected the permit application twice – initially last year and again in March, when it rejected IPOP’s appeal.
In its 34-page decision signed by DNR Commissioner John Crowther, the department described IPOP’s proposal as riddled with flaws and omitting required information that would justify the proposed land disturbance.
IPOP has failed to demonstrate that surface use of the land is necessary to dredge what it says would be up to 900,000 cubic yards of material a year, the rejection decision said. And that failure clashes with requirements in Alaska’s constitution, laws and regulations that require proof that surface use of state land is necessary and development will be done in ways to minimize adverse effects and environmental resources.
“While DNR seeks to encourage the development of state resources by making them available for maximum use, that use must be consistent with the public interest,” the appeal rejection said. A large-scale dredging project not supported by exploration data “would result in unnecessary and undue degradation,” as defined in state law, the rejection said.
Johnson, of the Village of Solomon, said she expects IPOP to keep trying to get permits. And the groups that have been fighting against the project for years will keep doing so into the future, she said.
“I feel like we’ve really bonded over some of this, because it’s kind of like trauma bonding,” she said.

title: Archmere Volleyball advances to the second round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament along with other higher seeds
description: The first round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament is complete with all the higher seeds moving on to the second round.   CLAYMONT, Del. — The Archmere Auks defeated the Charter School of Wilmington Forces, 3-0, in the first round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament on November 5. The Auks took control of the ... Read More
text:
Archmere senior Grace Mahoney rises up for a kill in the Auks first round game against Charter School of Wilmington in the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
The first round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament is complete with all the higher seeds moving on to the second round.
 
CLAYMONT, Del. — The Archmere Auks defeated the Charter School of Wilmington Forces, 3-0, in the first round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament on November 5.
The Auks took control of the match early in set one scoring six straight points to take a 8-3 lead at the start of the set. The Forces fought back to cut the Auk lead to three near the middle of the frame, but the Auks rattled off another run of five straight points to spring ahead by six. The final point of that run came on a Caroline Hahn kill after a couple diving efforts from Archmere’s back line players — including senior Madeline Frampton — kept the possession alive garnering cheers from the Archmere contingent of fans. The Auks won the first set, 25-16.
“Most importantly what I saw tonight was the ability to keep the ball in play,” Archmere head coach Jerry McCarthy said postgame. “Our back row with Michaela [Iacono] and Maddie and Olivia [Borsello] and then the setters in and out, you know, what do you say? They kept the ball in play and they gave us the ability to terminate and get the point.”
Archmere held Charter School of Wilmington to 13 points in the second set and won the frame, 25-13. Six different Auks recorded a kill in the set and the team was paced by senior Grace Mahoney and junior Brooke Maddox who each had four kills in the set. 
The Auks won the final set getting significant contributions from their serving unit. The Auks recorded seven aces in the set from Frampton and fellow senior Michaela Iacono. 
“Tonight they were 100 percent focused and they wanted to move on,” McCarthy said. “I think the serving can make us dangerous throughout the tournament.”
Archmere junior Vivienne Govatos sets the ball for a teammate during the Auks first round game against the Forces. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
Mahoney led the team with four kills in the frame and freshman Elise Shahan earned the game winning kill with a hit to the back left corner of the court.  
Shahan’s score secured the Auks’ their fifth straight second round appearance in the DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament and an upcoming battle with No. 8 Sussex Central. Archmere and Sussex Central will play their second round game on Saturday, November 7, at 6:00 p.m.    
More First Round Games:
No. 10 Lake Forest defeated No. 23 Sussex Academy, 3-0: Spartan junior, Coryn Louder, led the team with 13 kills, helping Lake Forest defeat Sussex Academy for the second time this season. The Spartans will play No. 7 Dover on Friday, November 6.
No. 11 St. Georges defeated No. 22 Delmarva Christian Academy, 3-0: Sophomores Jocelyn Ball and Lena Garland combined for 29 kills in the Hawks first round win. The Hawks are advancing to the second round for the second time in the last three seasons. St. Georges will play No. 6 Saint Mark’s on Friday, November 6.
No. 12 Appoquinimink defeated No. 21 Wilmington Friends, 3-0: Four Jaguar players recorded five or more kills in their win over the Quakers, Thursday night. Appoquinimink senior Julia Sobczynski led the team with ten kills and juniors Riley Robino and Bridget Archer contributed to the win with 22 assists and 16 digs, respectively. The Jaguars face No. 5 Tower Hill in the second round.
No. 13 Caravel defeated No. 20 Concord, 3-0: The Buccaneers earned their first win against the Raiders this season and held Concord to 15 points or less in each set. Caravel will face No. 4 Newark Charter on Friday, November 6.
No. 14 Cape Henlopen defeated No. 19 Sanford, 3-0: Six different Vikings recorded a kill in Cape Henlopen’s opening round victory. The Vikings are moving on to the second round of the DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament for the third season in a row and will face No. 3 Padua in the next round. Senior Camilla Willis led the Vikings with eight kills in the game.
No. 14 Smyrna defeated No. 18 Mount Pleasant, 3-1: The Eagles continued their strong run of play earning their fifth straight victory and a ticket to the second round of the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament. Smyrna has made it to the second round in every season since 2020 and won the state championship in 2023. Smyrna will move on to play No. 2 Middletown on Saturday.   
Smyrna senior Emma Mayew keeps a ball in play during one of Smyrna’s regular season games. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
No. 16 Conrad defeated No. 17 Delaware Military Academy, 3-1: Similarly to these two teams’ first game in early October, this matchup was close throughout. Conrad sophomore Delani Camilli led the way for the Red Wolves with 19 kills and one ace. Junior setter Payton Singleton contributed 24 assists and three Red Wolves each had three aces, helping Conrad reach the second round of the DIAA Girls Volleyball State Tournament for the first time since 2019.

title: Veterans Day in Delaware: Where to honor those who served and how to give back
description: Parades, ceremonies, free meals and opportunities to volunteer offer Delawareans ways to recognize military service and the freedoms veterans have helped preserve. text:
