Generations of Americans have served to defend the nation, protect its constitutional system and preserve the freedoms that shape everyday life — from voting and speaking freely to building businesses, raising families and pursuing individual dreams. Created with AI on 11/6
Parades, ceremonies, free meals and opportunities to volunteer offer Delawareans ways to recognize military service and the freedoms veterans have helped preserve.
DOVER, Del. — Delawareans will honor the men and women who served in the U.S. Armed Forces with parades, ceremonies, community events and special offers as the state prepares to observe Veterans Day on Wednesday, Nov. 11.
Events begin Saturday with a parade in Dover and a veterans luncheon in Georgetown. Additional observances are scheduled in Wilmington, New Castle and Milford.
Businesses and public agencies will also offer free meals, transportation and other benefits to veterans. For residents looking to participate, organizations throughout Delaware provide opportunities to volunteer and support veterans year-round.
Why Veterans Day matters
Veterans Day began as Armistice Day, marking the end of fighting in World War I on Nov. 11, 1918. In 1954, the holiday was renamed Veterans Day to recognize Americans who served in the military during war and peacetime.
Unlike Memorial Day, which specifically honors those who died while serving, Veterans Day recognizes all who have worn the nation’s uniform, living and deceased.
The contributions of veterans extend far beyond the battlefield. Generations of Americans have served to defend the nation, protect its constitutional system and preserve the freedoms that shape everyday life — from voting and speaking freely to building businesses, raising families and pursuing individual dreams.
That service often comes with considerable personal sacrifice, including time away from families, physical injuries and challenges that can continue long after military service ends.
Many veterans also continue contributing to their communities as teachers, business owners, first responders, volunteers and civic leaders.
Veterans Day is an opportunity to remember that the security, freedoms and opportunities Americans enjoy have been protected through generations of military service.
Attend: Veterans Day events in Delaware
Saturday, Nov. 7 — Dover Veterans Day Parade and Festival
Dover’s Veterans Day parade begins at 11 a.m., celebrating military service and America’s 250th anniversary.
The parade starts at Jerusalem Way and Forrest Street, travels through downtown and concludes at Water Street. A community celebration featuring speakers and veterans organizations will take place near Legislative Hall. Admission is free.
Saturday, Nov. 7 — Veterans Luncheon in Georgetown
A free luncheon and ceremony honoring veterans will be held from 10 a.m. to noon at 40 Ingramtown Road in Georgetown.
Veterans and guests are invited. RSVP by calling 302-856-4551.
Nov. 7-10 — Free Admission at Hagley Museum
Hagley Museum and Library in Wilmington will offer veterans free general admission Saturday through Tuesday.
Beginning Nov. 7, the museum will also conduct daily signal cannon demonstrations at 1 p.m., weather permitting.
Wednesday, Nov. 11 — Veterans Breakfast in Wilmington
Delaware Technical Community College will host a Veterans Day breakfast from 8 to 9:15 a.m. at its Wilmington campus, 300 N. Orange St.
A continental breakfast will be served. Information: 302-571-5305.
Wednesday, Nov. 11 — Delaware Memorial Bridge Ceremony
The Delaware Commission of Veterans Affairs will hold its annual ceremony from 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. at War Memorial Plaza, 163 Cherry Lane, New Castle.
The event is hosted by the Delaware River and Bay Authority.
Wednesday, Nov. 11 — Veterans Ceremony in Dover
Kent County Veterans Memorial Park will host a ceremony from 2 to 4 p.m. recognizing 250 years of American military service.
Retired Brig. Gen. Karen A. Berry, Delaware’s first secretary of Veterans Affairs, is scheduled to deliver the keynote address.
The park is located at 760-816 S. Little Creek Road in Dover.
Saturday, Nov. 14 — Special Forces Veteran Speaks in Milford
Christopher VanSant, a retired Delta Force soldier and Caesar Rodney High School graduate, will speak at 1 p.m. at the Milford Public Library, 11 S.E. Front St.
VanSant served in 11 combat deployments and will discuss his military experiences, the challenges of injury and recovery, and his transition to civilian life.
The program is sponsored by the Milford Museum and Milford Public Library.
Veterans offers: Free meals, transportation and discounts
Veterans and active-duty military personnel can take advantage of special promotions on Nov. 11. Most require proof of service, and participation varies by location.
DART Offers Free Rides Statewide
DART First State will provide free rides on its statewide bus services to veterans presenting qualifying military identification or a DD Form 214. Certain spouses and partners with qualifying identification are also eligible.
Information: DART First State.
Restaurants Offer Free Meals
Several national restaurant chains are advertising Veterans Day promotions:

Applebee’s: Free entrée from a special Veterans Day menu.
Chili’s: Free meal from a select menu.
Denny’s: Free Original Grand Slam breakfast, 5 a.m. to noon.
Red Lobster: Free Shrimp & Chips.
Red Robin: Free Red’s Big Tavern Burger and bottomless fries.
Golden Corral: Free buffet during its Military Appreciation Night.
Wendy’s: Free Dave’s Single at participating Flynn Group-operated restaurants.
Starbucks: Free 12-ounce brewed coffee for eligible veterans, service members and military spouses.

Great Clips and Sport Clips are also advertising haircut promotions, while participating national parks will waive entrance fees Nov. 11.
Veterans should confirm offers before visiting. Promotions may be limited to participating locations, and identification, dine-in or other conditions may apply.
For additional offers, visit the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs Veterans Day offers guide.
Give back: Supporting Delaware veterans year-round
Veterans Day is an opportunity to express appreciation, but the needs of veterans and their families continue long after the ceremonies end.
Volunteer at the Delaware Veterans Home
The Delaware Veterans Home in Milford welcomes community support through donations and volunteer activities, including reading, music, arts, gardening and special events.
Learn more: Delaware Veterans Home.
Support the Wilmington VA
The Wilmington VA Medical Center offers volunteer opportunities assisting patients, providing transportation support and helping with hospital programs.
Learn more: Wilmington VA Volunteer Services.
Recognize Veterans in Your Community
Residents can honor veterans by inviting them to speak at schools or civic organizations, writing letters of appreciation, supporting local veterans groups or helping preserve veterans’ personal histories.
Churches, Scout units, businesses and neighborhood organizations can organize activities that continue throughout the year.
Remembering those who served
The Wilmington VA recently recognized World War II Marine Corps veteran Robert Leroy James Quinn with its 2026 Wall of Honor award.
Quinn, a Purple Heart recipient who fought in the Pacific campaign, died in 2025 shortly before his 101st birthday.
His daughter, Karen Quinn, encouraged veterans to share their stories with their children and families.
Her message reflects the broader meaning of Veterans Day: preserving the experiences of those who served while recognizing the sacrifices made by veterans and their families.
For Delawareans, Veterans Day is more than a single day of remembrance. It is an opportunity to recognize that the freedoms, security and opportunities of American life have been preserved through generations of military service.
Attending a ceremony, listening to a veteran’s story or offering meaningful support are ways to ensure that service is never taken for granted.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Democrats won big on Election Day. Here’s how they did
description: New Jersey Democrats had a big Election Day, winning all but one of New Jersey’s House seats as U.S. Sen. Cory Booker handily won reelection.
text:
People react as results come in on election night during the Rebecca Bennett election night watch party at the Bridgewater Manor on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/ New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey Democrats had a great Election Day, in case you haven’t already heard.
They won two GOP-held House seats and won all nine of their own, leaving just one Republican representing New Jersey in the House of Representatives when Congress begins its new term in January.
Almost all of the votes have been counted in every race, and here’s where they all stand:
 U.S. Senate
U.S. Sen. Cory Booker (D) won a full third term on Tuesday, winning 62% of the vote. Republican challenger Justin Murphy won 35%.
Booker’s winning percentage is a bit higher than his last two victories. In 2020, he won 57% and in 2014, 56%. This year was the first time Booker has won Hunterdon and Monmouth counties.
Sen. Cory Booker speaks at an election eve rally on Nov. 2, 2026, in Springfield. (Photo by Dana DiFIlippo/New Jersey Monitor)
 U.S. House
1st District
Rep. Donald Norcross (D) won 70% of the vote against Republican challenger Damon Galdo’s 30%.
2nd District
Democrat Zack Mullock, the Cape May mayor, won in a close race against incumbent Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R). Mullock won 51% of the vote to Van Drew’s 48%.
When Van Drew won reelection in 2024, he won 58% of the vote.
Zack Mullock appears at a campaign event in Vineland on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
3rd District
Rep. Herb Conaway (D) won 63% of the vote in his first bid for reelection. GOP challenger Michael McGuire won 36%.
4th District
The night’s sole Republican winner, Rep. Chris Smith, defeated Democrat Rachel Peace 59%-41%. Two years ago, Smith won 67% of the vote.
5th District
Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D) won 62% of the vote against Republican Sean Kirrane, who won 35%.
6th District
Rep. Frank Pallone (D) defeated Republican Hillary Herzig 69%-31%.
7th District
In the most closely watched race of this cycle, Democrat Rebecca Bennett won 57% to 41% for Rep. Tom Kean Jr. Kean (R) won about 51% the last two times he won in this district.
Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D) speaks during her victory party in Bridgewater on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
8th District
Rep. Rob Menendez (D) had no GOP challenger this year. He won 89% of the vote against three independent candidates.
9th District
Rep. Nellie Pou (D) won her first reelection campaign with 67% of the vote. GOP challenger Rosie Pino won 32%. Two years ago, Pou won 51%.
10th District
Rep. LaMonica McIver (D) won reelection with 85% of the vote. Her Republican challenger, Carmen Bucco, won 16%. When McIver faced Bucco in 2024, she won 74%.
11th District
Rep. Analilia Meji (D) won her first full term against Republican Joe Hathaway 61%-39%. When now-Gov. Mikie Sherrill won this seat in 2024, Sherrill captured 57%.
12th District
First-time candidate Adam Hamawy (D) won 70% of the vote to 28% for Republican opponent Gregg Mele. Hamawy will succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, who won 61% of the vote in 2024.
Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, who won New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District on Tuesday, speaks outside the federal courthouse in Newark on Nov. 4, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Tom Emmer sold himself as the 6th District’s seat at the table. The restaurant’s been shuttered.
description: For four years, Rep. Tom Emmer’s pitch to Minnesota’s 6th District has been access. He is the current House majority whip, the No. 3 Republican in the chamber and the only Minnesotan in House leadership. “We continue delivering for Minnesota,” he told St. Cloud LIVE in August, pointing to more than $40 million for district […]
text:
U.S. House Majority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., left, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., center, and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., take part in a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 17, 2024 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)For four years, Rep. Tom Emmer’s pitch to Minnesota’s 6th District has been access. He is the current House majority whip, the No. 3 Republican in the chamber and the only Minnesotan in House leadership. “We continue delivering for Minnesota,” he told St. Cloud LIVE in August, pointing to more than $40 million for district infrastructure. St. Cloud LIVE was one of only two local outlets he answered this fall, out of at least eight that asked, by MN-06 Watch’s count. His office says he secured about $43 million for the 2026 fiscal year. That’s real money, though he shares the credit: $18.1 million came from his requests alone, and Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith also requested the other six projects.
On Tuesday, voters in the 6th District gave him a seventh term, by the narrowest margin of his career: 55.7% to DFLer Doug Chapin’s 44.2% in a solid R district. Nationally, voters took the “majority” out of his title. President Trump had asked them to “pretend please that I’m on the ballot.” They did. In the NBC News exit poll, 43% of voters said one reason for their House vote was to oppose Trump; just 16% said it was to support him.
Republicans lost a Kentucky district Trump won with 57% and an Indiana seat he carried by 17 points. In North Carolina, four Republican incumbents lost districts Trump won by 15 to 17 points, on a map the legislature redrew last year at Trump’s urging. One was Rep. Richard Hudson, chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the job Emmer held before him. NBC projects Republicans will end up with about 177 House seats, down from 218. They lost the Senate too.
Emmer may not even keep his leadership job in the minority. On Wednesday, Rep. August Pfluger of Texas, outgoing chair of the Republican Study Committee, announced he was running for the minority whip job. Republicans “need fresh ideas and a leadership team committed to rebuilding a culture with a clear game plan to win in 2028,” Pfluger wrote to colleagues, according to CBS News. “We started 2025 with a clear mandate, and although there were successes, I believe we left a lot on the table,” he wrote.
Emmer wrote his own letter. “There is no sugarcoating the failure we just experienced,” he told colleagues. “We lost, and I take that loss personally.” He is calling colleagues to line up votes, campaigning for this job more than he did in the 6th District, where I found no public campaign event by Emmer this fall. House Republicans vote by secret ballot on Nov. 10.
Where he went
Emmer rose to leadership by fundraising for other members. He spent two cycles running the NRCC, and his letter leans on that: Republicans were expected to lose up to 24 seats in 2020, he wrote, and gained 15. In 2022, Republicans expected a red wave and instead won a 222-213 majority. “We delivered,” Emmer told reporters. His colleagues, many of whom he had helped with campaign funds, made him whip, 115 to 106.
This time the election results were not good for the Republicans he campaigned with. I logged 53 stops where Emmer campaigned for House Republicans this fall. His committees gave those candidates $4.5 million, according to Federal Election Commission records. By NBC News calls as of Thursday afternoon (full results):

20 won, all in safe Republican seats. They received $124,000.
28 lost. They received $3.8 million, including a safe Republican (Rep. Addison McDowell of North Carolina).
were still being counted.

Given these results, if he sat down next to you at the blackjack table, you’d call him a “cooler” for cursing you with bad cards. 
Leadership money flows to close races, and none of the candidates he visited in races that election forecasters rated “lean Republican” or tighter have been declared winners. 
The 28 who lost won’t be in the conference that picks the next whip. In other words, Emmer spent the fall helping build a majority that didn’t materialize. Now he has to persuade the smaller conference that remains to vote for him.
Emmer’s defenders have a fair case. The president’s party almost always loses House seats in a midterm. The whip’s job is to count votes and pass his party’s agenda, not to set it, and by that measure Emmer delivered. 
But his pitch to the 6th District was something else: That his position in Congress delivers local results. Doing the whip’s job well and representing Minnesota well are not necessarily the same. At least twice in the past two years, they were at odds, and both times he sided with his party.
The first test: Operation Metro Surge
In December, Homeland Security launched Operation Metro Surge, which brought some 3,000 federal immigration agents to the Twin Cities. In a February KARE 11/Star Tribune/NBC News poll, 66% of Minnesotans said the tactics of ICE and Border Patrol agents had gone too far. That poll was statewide, not just the 6th District, but disapproval ran high in the suburbs as well as the cities.
On Jan. 6, Emmer posted “God bless our brave ICE agents. Go out there and get ’em,” over a DHS post that read “GOOD MORNING MINNEAPOLIS!”
The next morning, an ICE agent shot and killed Renée Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, in south Minneapolis. About two hours later, Emmer shared DHS’s account, which called her driving “an act of domestic terrorism.” Witnesses disputed that account. Emmer added: “Shame on the elected officials who endanger these agents by spewing lies and hateful rhetoric.”
On Jan. 24, federal agents killed Alex Pretti, also a U.S. citizen. Emmer again shared DHS’s account, blamed “the governor and local leaders’ rhetoric” and wrote that he would “not jump to asinine conclusions” even though bystander video contradicted the account he amplified. Nine months later, Minnesota is suing the federal government for the evidence, and Pretti’s parents say the government has given them no answers.
Another Republican with access to the White House used her influence differently. On Jan. 27, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine asked Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to pause the operations in Maine and in Minnesota. Two days later, she announced that ICE’s surge in Maine had ended. Maine Democrats called it a political move, and Collins lost her seat on Tuesday anyway. But she asked, publicly, on behalf of both states.
I found no evidence of Emmer asking the administration to pause or change the operation. In February, Star Tribune columnist Rochelle Olson asked his office about rumors that he had worked behind the scenes to get Trump to relent on Minnesota. His spokeswoman called those rumors “completely false.”
Emmer and his supporters may not agree that opposing the surge was in his constituents’ interest. But the episode raises the question his campaign never answered: What is a seat at the table worth to Minnesota if it isn’t used when Minnesota and the administration disagree?
The second test: the tax-and-spending law
Emmer’s signature achievement as whip is H.R. 1, the 2025 tax-and-spending law Trump called the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” It passed the House 218 to 214. Trump singled him out at the signing. Emmer has called its tax provisions “the single-greatest victory for working families in history,” and this spring he blamed Gov. Tim Walz and the DFL for keeping no-tax-on-tips and no-tax-on-overtime out of the state code. The federal law doesn’t change state income taxes. To match those deductions, Minnesota would have had to pass its own and pay for them in a budget the state must balance. The state Revenue Department estimated the overtime and tips deductions would cost the general fund about $366 million and $126 million, respectively, in fiscal 2027.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Emmer has said much less about what the law cut. In trying to win public support for it, MinnPost reported, Emmer focused on the tax breaks and said little about the cuts to Medicaid and other programs. When he did address them, in a joint op-ed with Minnesota’s three other House Republicans, the four wrote: “Nothing in our bill takes away health care from the very people Medicaid was intended to help.”
Minnesota’s own agencies rebutted that assertion. The Department of Human Services projects that as many as 140,000 Minnesotans could eventually lose Medicaid coverage. State Auditor Julie Blaha said in July that at least 18,000 Minnesotans had lost SNAP benefits since the law was signed.
As whip, Emmer did his job: He delivered on the agenda that was set by his party. Whether the result was good for Minnesota is a separate question. It just so happens it’s the one he asked voters to judge him on.
The law also cuts against what Emmer once said brought him to Washington. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in July 2025 that it adds $3.4 trillion to federal deficits over a decade. In 2015, Emmer wrote that his seven children “are the reason I am in public office, yet every day I watch as their financial obligations to this country grow larger and larger.” This October, he told the St. Cloud Times the law’s spending cuts were only a start on the debt: “It doesn’t even scratch the surface.”
Bending the knee
In 2023, Trump sank Emmer’s bid for speaker with one post. “RINO Tom Emmer, who I do not know well,” he wrote, and asked: “Has he only changed because that’s what it takes to win?”
Emmer spent the next three years answering Trump’s question by acquiescing to his agenda. In 2024 he chaired Trump’s Minnesota campaign. When Trump took the country to war with Iran this year, Emmer defended it the morning the strikes began. When gas prices rose, he parroted the line that the pain would be brief. “This is a short-duration event,” he told WCCO in March. Gas is  about $4.00 a gallon, and diesel remains over $6. In May, he told the 6th District GOP convention that affordability was “the biggest BS word I’ve ever seen.” In September, he told Fox Business that “beef is at less than $2 a pound for ground beef.” Federal data put the average at about $7. Two days before the election, Trump posted that Emmer “will never let you down!” Emmer replied: “Thank you, President Trump!”
On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance explained the loss in six words: “The reason we lost is the war.”
Will he remain whip?
In his letter, Emmer made his case as the member who holds the conference together. “My role is to support every Member of this conference and help you succeed,” he wrote, according to The Hill. “We have never made false promises or tried to buy your votes.” Success in the minority, he wrote, “will require no less support and unity in our conference.”
He has described how he gets that unity. When a member balks at a vote, he told NBC News, his answer is: “OK, that’s great, but talk to the president.” A White House official told NBC that Emmer is the “tougher cop” to outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson. “Donald Trump is the Republican Party right now,” Emmer said. He tells reluctant members they’re with Trump “because your constituents support what Donald Trump is trying to do.” Voters overwhelmingly rejected that claim on Tuesday.
Tom Emmer talks tough, reveals weakness

Emmer’s method and culture ran through the White House. In January, the president Emmer sent holdouts to will face a Democratic House and Senate for his final two years in office, barred by the Constitution from running again.
Back home
Chapin, who says he’ll run again in 2028, held 23 town halls, by his campaign’s count. Emmer hasn’t held an in-person town hall in the district since Aug. 21, 2023. He told St. Cloud LIVE this fall that threats against him, his family and his staff have “exponentially increased” and that security concerns have changed how his office holds public events. The threats are real: Capitol Police investigated a record 14,938 cases against members of Congress in 2025. But outside the district, Emmer’s appearances were advertised in advance. A North Carolina campaign posted his Oct. 2 rally in Rocky Mount with a public RSVP form, and Florida Republicans promoted a Nov. 1 “Meet & Greet Rally and BBQ” for Rep. Aaron Bean with Emmer as the featured guest.
What did he succeed at?
As whip, Emmer delivered. H.R. 1 passed by four votes, and Trump singled him out at the signing.
Most of his campaigning time went to Republicans who lost, and they won’t be in the room when the conference picks its next whip. When Minnesota and the White House split over Metro Surge, I found no evidence of him using that access to seek changes. The law he whipped is projected to cost as many as 140,000 Minnesotans their Medicaid coverage while adding trillions to the debt he once said his children would inherit. And the president he tied the conference to asked voters to judge him. They did.
Two electorates judge Emmer this month. The 6th District already has, returning him by the narrowest margin of his career. His colleagues vote Tuesday. Even if he wins, he’ll be the whip of a minority. 
That access he sold the district on? For at least the next two years, it will be worth about as much as an Emmer campaign visit to those 28 Republicans.

name: California
title: Will Newsom’s death penalty commutations stick?
description: Gavin Newsom reminded everyone that he’s still the governor on Thursday when he handed down a historic commutation of every California death sentence. We have more on that below.  It was a big day in Los Angeles, too, where the city ousted Mayor Karen Bass and elected democratic socialist Nithya Raman.  Come along with us […]
text:
The courtyard at San Quentin State Prison on July 26, 2023. Photo by Semantha Norris, CalMatters




Gavin Newsom reminded everyone that he’s still the governor on Thursday when he handed down a historic commutation of every California death sentence. We have more on that below. 
It was a big day in Los Angeles, too, where the city ousted Mayor Karen Bass and elected democratic socialist Nithya Raman. 
Come along with us today and learn more about those stories, as well as meeting our new education reporter and checking in on voting access challenges for Native Americans. 
As one of his final acts before his term ends, Gov. Gavin Newsom on Thursday commuted the sentences of all 548 condemned California prisoners and denounced what he called “state-sanctioned killing.” In an open letter to the public, Newsom said he firmly believes the death penalty “is incompatible with California’s values.”

Newsom: “The people sentenced to death in California caused indescribable suffering to victims, their families, communities, and our state as a whole. … Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”

The California Supreme Court has to sign off on more than 400 of Newsom’s commutations, meaning most of the prisoners are not quite off of death row yet. An advocacy group from crime victims also plans to challenge Newsom’s order, report CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang and Nigel Duara.
In an October letter to the governor, San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow said a blanket clemency order “would be a slap in the face” to murder victims and their loved ones.

Dow: “A governor who uses clemency to overrule the voters in every capital case at once is no longer acting as the People’s elected representative. He is acting as a sovereign king.”

Newsom has long opposed the death penalty. Shortly after taking office in 2019, he issued a moratorium on executions. Three years later, he announced a plan to dismantle death row at San Quentin State Prison, which has since been rebranded as the San Quentin Rehabilitation Center.
Jess Nichol, the sister of Polly Klaas who was murdered in 1993 at age 12, supports Newsom’s decision. Klaas’ murderer, Richard Allen Davis, is one of the prisoners included in Newsom’s clemency, though his case will need further court approval. In a statement, Nichol said she used to believe Davis deserved to be executed, but later changed her view.

Nichol: “The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.” 

Read more.
An unprecedented move: Pending further approval from the state’s high court, Newsom would be responsible for the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history. His actions underscore how governors can be more proactive in stopping executions, during a time when federal courts appear less likely to do so. Read more from our partners at the Marshall Project.



Get CalMatters text alerts: We can send you our latest investigations, political coverage and more, and you can send us story tips, comments and feedback. Sign up here.

Other Stories You Should Know


Barriers to Native American voting


A voting sign outside the Bob Glass Gym in Perris on Nov. 5, 2024. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters




Voting access remains out of reach for some California Native American communities, despite the state adopting universal mail-in ballots in 2021 to make voting easier, writes CalMatters’ Melanie Henshaw.
Unreliable mail services, a lack of nearby polling places and the rejection of certain types of identification are some of the obstacles Native Americans face when voting, according to advocates from the California Native Vote Project. 
The issues persist even after California passed a law in 2020 to increase access. The legislation calls for the creation of the Native American Voting Accessibility Advisory Committee, which is supposed to set guidelines to reach Native American voters, suggest ways to boost poll worker recruitment and issue advice on language assistance. 
But the committee, whose members are appointed by the secretary of state, still hasn’t been formed. A spokesperson for the office said it plans to begin recruiting members “after the November election.”

Calvin Hedrick, director of policy for the California Native Vote Project: “We can’t allow them to promise us it’s something they’re going to do next year, we need to hold their feet to the fire and make sure it gets done.” 

Read more.



Our new education reporter coaches youth ballet


Rebecca Pelvin joins CalMatters as the new education reporter. 




We’re excited to welcome Rebecca Plevin to CalMatters as an education reporter. 
She brings two decades of journalism experience, most recently as a reporter for Proof News, where she investigated how artificial intelligence is changing people’s jobs. She previously reported on equity for the Los Angeles Times and led the bilingual Central Valley News Collaborative as an editor for The Fresno Bee. Before that, she covered immigration for The Desert Sun in Palm Springs and reported on health for KPCC in Los Angeles. Rebecca graduated with a journalism degree from Northwestern University and reports in English and Spanish.
When she’s not reporting, you’ll find Rebecca taking modern dance classes and performing in community productions. She is currently choreographing two youth pieces for The Desert Nutcracker, a version of the traditional holiday ballet with a California desert twist.
Plevin is based in the Inland Empire. She joins an expanding education team at CalMatters that is now one of the largest in the state. Have a tip? Email her at rebecca@calmatters.org.



And lastly: Setback for carbon capture project


Oil pumps around the Elk Hills Power Station, the site of a planned carbon capture project, along Elk Hills Road on March 29, 2024. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local




A Kern County judge handed environmental groups a win this week, ruling that the state’s first operating carbon capture and storage project violated state environmental law. 
County supervisors approved the project in 2024, which would entail injecting carbon underground to keep it from warming the atmosphere. But advocate groups, including the Sierra Club, sued to stop the project, arguing that it did not adequately review its full environmental impact. Read more from Emma Foehringer Merchant for CalMatters.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: If California’s redistricting reverts to the independent commission, Democrats will likely lose members — so will the party’s leaders decide whether to allow the commission to do its work or abolish it via another ballot measure?
CalMatters contributor Jim Newton: Mayor-elect Nithya Raman ushers in a new era for L.A., and while the democratic socialist inherits a city full of promise, it’s also burdened by challenges such as homelessness and public safety.
