text:
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announces the state's lawsuit against American Shaman in a press conference outside her office March 31, 2026 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri’s crackdown on intoxicating hemp products is already underway, a week before a new state law threatens to push thousands of businesses out of the market.
Attorney General Catherine Hanaway announced four new lawsuits Wednesday against retailers accused of illegally selling marijuana disguised as hemp. That same day, a federal judge dismissed a hemp industry challenge to the law, clearing another obstacle to its Nov. 12 implementation.
Now, some hemp business owners hoped to burn their products on the steps of the Missouri Capitol on Veterans Day, one day before the new restrictions take effect. But they were denied a permit because “open flames” are prohibited on Capitol grounds.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hanaway told The Independent in an interview Wednesday that she didn’t need to wait for the new law to go after stores selling what’s known as “THCA flower,” a product that becomes intoxicating when smoked just like marijuana. She said laboratory test results posted on the stores’ own websites show they are selling marijuana without the required state licenses.
“The bottom line is: marijuana is legal in Missouri,” Hanaway said. “Great, just comply with the law. We have so many of these shops that are selling it, and some of them very openly and notoriously claiming that they’re selling marijuana.”
Hanaway said her concern is that products sold outside Missouri’s licensed marijuana system aren’t subject to the same state testing and safety requirements, potentially exposing consumers to harmful metals or other contaminants.
 The new law tasks Hanaway’s office – along with the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, the state’s cannabis regulatory agency – with enforcement. The department previously estimated that 40,000 food establishments and smoke shops and 1,800 food manufacturers could potentially be affected by a state ban on intoxicating hemp products, “but the majority of these facilities are at low-risk of requiring investigation.”
After Nov. 12, Hanaway’s office will have “more tools at our disposal” to go after law breakers. 
“You’re going to see more lawsuits,” she said. “The law is stronger and easier for us to enforce.”
Under the new law, products containing more than 0.3% total THC, including THCA, generally fall outside the state’s definition of hemp. Finished hemp-derived cannabinoid products also face a limit of 0.4 milligrams of THC per container. Intoxicating products that fall under the new restrictions can be sold only through Missouri’s licensed marijuana system.
The law establishes Missouri’s first comprehensive restrictions on intoxicating hemp products. Similar bills had been debated since 2023 but failed to pass. In the absence of comparable state oversight, smoke shops have been able to sell intoxicating hemp products containing as much as 1,000 milligrams of THC outside Missouri’s licensed marijuana dispensaries.
Under existing federal law, hemp is defined largely by its concentration of delta-9 THC. Missouri’s new law, like pending federal restrictions, takes a broader approach by counting other forms of THC, including THCA.
John Grady, a hemp business owner and industry advocate, stands on the Missouri Capitol steps as part of a group asking Gov. Mike Kehoe to veto a bill they say would harm Missouri hemp producers (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
John Grady, a veteran who owns Slaphappy Hemporium in Rosebud, got into hemp farming and retail, he said, because his disabled veterans payments would be put in jeopardy if he was part of the federally illegal marijuana market. 
Grady and others are planning on protesting Missouri’s law on Veterans Day, Nov. 11, because the federal ban has been delayed until Dec. 11. 
Congress could end up passing regulations that are less restrictive than Missouri’s law that goes into effect on Nov. 12. His business produces intoxicating hemp beverages, which will remain on the shelves until Dec. 11 under Missouri’s law. 
“They’ve now taken all of our time and investment and everything away from us,” Grady said, “and we find that untenable. It’s not about safety because they’ve denied regulations for four years straight, and instead they pursued bans. It’s about market protection for campaign contributors.” 
 Case dismissed

The muddled definition of hemp and marijuana is at the center of the hemp industry’s lawsuit, filed in July in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Missouri. 
The plaintiffs, led by the Missouri Hemp Trade Association, argued the state has created overlapping definitions, under which a product could be classified as legal “hemp” in one part of state law and illegal “marijuana” in another. It leaves businesses unsure what they can legally sell when the law goes into effect and argued the case over House Bill 2641 deserves to be heard in court. 
Judge M. Douglas Harpool disagreed in his order to dismiss the case Wednesday, concluding the new law has not yet taken effect and its application to the plaintiffs remains uncertain. 
The plaintiffs included St. Louis-based MNG 2005 Inc., which is the parent company for 55 CBD Kratom stores nationwide; the Missouri Hemp Trade Association; and a Wisconsin-based hemp business, Lifted Liquids Inc.
“So much of that order was based on the fact that no enforcement had taken place,” said Craig Katz, government relations and compliance manager for MNG. “Based on that, we’ll have to see what happens on Nov. 12, and what they do in terms of enforcement.”
The plaintiffs are assessing their next steps, he said, and whether they want to appeal.
(Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent)
One of the four lawsuits Hanaway announced Wednesday targets a CBD Kratom store in St. Louis County, accusing the business of violating Missouri’s consumer protection law by selling marijuana products labeled as hemp.
On Oct. 8, the attorney general’s investigators made undercover purchases of two “hemp flower” products from the CBD Kratom Cannabis Dispensary in Des Peres and sent them to a state-licensed lab for testing. The results showed both products exceeded the federal THC limit for hemp, according to the lawsuit.
One package stated the delta-9 THC concentration was 0.28% on a dry weight basis, but lab results included in the lawsuit showed the concentration was 4% — or more than 10 times the legal maximum for hemp products.
Katz said the timing of Hanaway’s lawsuit was “curious” because it came a week after the plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction in the federal case on Oct. 9. 
The other three stores Hanaway sued are Puffers Choice LLC in Aurora, Herb Depot in Independence and Token THC Dispensary in Rock Port. 
All four of the petitions begin with a bold statement: “The days of ‘hemp shops’ masquerading as legal marijuana dispensaries are over in Missouri.”
Hanaway alleges the stores used “deceptive and unfair tactics” designed to make it difficult for consumers to tell whether they are walking into an unregulated hemp business or a state-licensed marijuana business. 
“These shops offer intoxicating products that look and smell like marijuana; they refer to those products as cannabis; and they set up their stores to mimic—and even call them—dispensaries,” the lawsuits state. “Just because these drug pushers have a storefront and an LLC does not mean that their activity is legal.”

name: Nevada Current
title: ‘Nevadans deserve better’: Long Election Day lines in Clark County raise concerns
description: A new in-person voting process, voter enthusiasm, and a lengthy four-page ballot created a “perfect storm” of conditions that led to hourslong waits for many voters in Clark County and the delayed release of election results Tuesday night. Nevada state law prohibits the release of any election results until after every voter in line at […]
text:
A staff member holds up  a cell phone with the message "Last voter voting" for U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford as he speaks at the Nevada Democratic Party's election results watch party at MEET Las Vegas on November 03, 2026. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images)A new in-person voting process, voter enthusiasm, and a lengthy four-page ballot created a “perfect storm” of conditions that led to hourslong waits for many voters in Clark County and the delayed release of election results Tuesday night.
Nevada state law prohibits the release of any election results until after every voter in line at a polling place on Election Day has cast their ballot. Voting sites are considered “closed” at 7 p.m. but anyone in line at that time is permitted to cast their ballot.
Dozens of the more than 100 polling places across Clark County reported having voters waiting in line at 7 p.m., and the final ballot was not cast until shortly before midnight at Brinley Middle School in Las Vegas.
That means some voters waited upwards of 4 or 5 hours to cast their ballots. And it meant an eager public watched Election Day turn into election night and threaten to become the next day without any results being released.
Election officials and advocates in Nevada agreed that delaying results until the last voter votes is sound policy because every voter should feel like their vote matters and not be influenced by early results. But they agreed that long wait times are unacceptable and can be viewed as a form of voter suppression.
“Voters in Nevada deserve credit for their dedication during this General Election,” Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar said in a statement. “They showed up despite the chaos the federal administration tried to incite in the months leading up to the election, and they overcame serious challenges on Election Day. That dedication is worthy of commendation, but no voter should have to wait in line for five hours.”
Aguilar’s statement continued: “Nevadans deserve better, and my team is ready to support Clark County officials and officials from any county willing to take ownership and confront these issues head on.”
In 2022, the final Nevada voter cast their ballot in Washoe County sometime around 9:18 p.m., according to media reports, and election results began to trickle in within the hour. In 2024, the final voter cast their ballot in Nye County around 9:23 p.m.
This year, 16 of Nevada’s 17 counties wrapped up voting by 9:30 p.m. Clark was the exception.
In a brief press conference Wednesday, Clark County Registrar of Voters Lorena Portillo defended county operations, saying polling places had “sufficient” equipment and personnel based on prior-election analysis. She suggested Brinley MS might have been more popular this Election Day than in prior ones.
“The popularity of that site was determined by voters,” she said, “and now we have heard the voters. They do like that site, and we will be adjusting accordingly.”
Voters flocking to the same high-profile polling places, like the Galleria Mall or Desert Breeze Community Center, and overlooking sites with shorter wait times has been a reoccurring issue for the counties.
“Every election cycle teaches us so much,” said Portillo, “about not only how to improve the process but how to improve the voter experience. It is extremely important to us.”
In her comments she noted that other counties experienced long lines and that some large voting sites in Clark had no wait. She did not acknowledge that Clark wrapped up voting more than two hours later than Washoe, which was the second-to-last county in the state to close.
Battle Born Progress Executive Director Shelbie Swartz described the long lines on Election Day in Clark County as “a perfect storm of a very excited electorate, a new voting system, and a very long ballot.”
She continued, “The blame is not on one person. I know Cisco (Aguilar) and Lorena (Portillo) worked incredibly hard to make sure we had an efficient election.”
Kelly Durmick of All Voting Is Local said there needs to be more voter outreach about the state’s two-week early voting period, universal mail ballots, and the ability to find the best place to vote on Election Day. She noted that even after voters at sites with long lines were told by volunteers that other nearby polling places had significantly shorter lines they were reluctant to leave and opted to wait in line.
The process of voting in person also changed this year, with counties moving to a new system. Voters made their selection on a tablet screen and then a paper ballot showing their selections was printed out. Then, voters walked that physical ballot over to a tabulation machine to be counted.
Clark County used this new process in the primary earlier this year, but for many voters Tuesday was their first interaction with it.
Durmick said she noticed the process took longer when she attended a mock election held by Clark County earlier this year. Still, she said the new machines are good for the state, with many voters seeing the print ballot component as more transparent.
Another factor may have been the sheer length of Clark County’s ballot. It spanned four pages and included nearly 60 judicial races, although most were uncontested. Clark County officials noted that the ballot included “142 contests and 254 candidates.”
Election observers also believe a flurry of new voters utilizing same-day registration may have contributed to wait times. The University of Nevada Reno and the College of Southern Nevada were among the vote sites across the state that saw long wait times throughout Election Day.
Durmick is optimistic that election officials and state legislators will look at the issues and avoid a repeat of Tuesday two years from now.
“Besides the long line issue, which everyone takes very seriously, the (election) process went smoothly — during early voting and the vote by mail system.”
SOS Aguilar expressed a similar sentiment in his statement, saying a newly modernized election system adopted by the state provides “more insight into county processes and voter activity than we have ever had before.”
He added, “We’ve been pouring over the data since last night to better understand what happened and will readily share what we learn with counties to help them ensure it doesn’t happen again.”
Nevada is set to host the nation’s second presidential primary in 2028, and it will have a much bigger spotlight on its general election as a swing state.
The Nevada State Democratic Party, which has pushed hard for that spotlight, did not respond to the Current’s questions about whether the extreme wait times for voters, which delays the release of results, undermines those efforts.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: They fell in love through dance. Then they built a ballet company together.
description: Claire Mazza and Alejandro Ulloa will be performing with their ballet company at the Quick Center in Fairfield on Nov. 7.
text:
Stepping into a pool of mid-afternoon light, Claire Mazza raised her left arm above her head, eyes fixed on the whisper-thin space between her thumb and second finger. Behind her, Alejandro Ulloa stepped forward in slow motion, his arms slack at his sides. He looked forward, lips parted, his whole face wide open. Even in the stillness, a person could see the gentle rise and fall of his chest. 
Around them, a violin from Valentin Silvestrov’s “Dedication: IV Andantino” drifted up into the sun-dappled corners and high ceiling of the studio. The dancers spun around each other, planets in orbit, hands nearly touching. Then their arms dropped, and they stepped in opposite directions. Even in an empty studio, electricity buzzed and crackled through the room. 
The affecting duet, entitled “Through You,” is the heartbeat of “Dancescapes,” coming to the Regina A. Quick Center for the Arts at Fairfield University on November 7. For Ulloa and Mazza, co-founders of the East Coast Contemporary Ballet who are partners in both life and work, the duet is a story of their love told in three parts, with a care for the form that has bloomed into 45 choreographed pieces, a 10-member company, and eight years of work. 
“It’s our story of existing separately in the dance world, then finding each other, and falling madly in love,” Mazza said during a rehearsal at the Darien Arts Center, where she directs the organization’s 350-student dance program. “We’ve really trusted each other because we’ve had to. It’s allowed us to be so vulnerable with each other.”
That story, and the company it has birthed, is almost a decade in the making. Before Mazza and Ulloa ever collaborated, both were dancing, just a world apart. Mazza grew up in the School of American Ballet in New York, after starting lessons in a Brooklyn neighborhood studio as a small child. Ulloa came to it as a teenager from his native Nicaragua, where he danced traditional folklore, then transferred to the Escuela Nacional de Ballet. 


Close to a decade ago, the two crossed paths at the Connecticut Ballet, often overlapping on the company’s pieces. While the state’s dance landscape is diffuse, both agreed it can also feel small, especially within a specific form. So when they began collaborating on a project with a small company in Westport, it made sense that they clicked almost instantly. 
In part, their chemistry came from a belief that the project was beautiful, but left its artists chronically overworked and undercompensated. The longer they worked on it, the more they realized that they wanted to create their own model, in which artists — who often cobble together a living over multiple part-time jobs and punishing rehearsal schedules — could earn a salary that reflected the labor they were putting in. The idea behind East Coast Contemporary Ballet was born. 
“It sounds so cheesy now, but we wanted to have a place where dancers are being treated correctly,” Ulloa said. “Let’s take care of people.”
From the jump, Mazza and Ulloa have tried to practice what they preach: their most significant expense in the organization’s $300,000 budget is its people. As artists themselves, they also remain keenly interested in exploring and sharing the difference between contemporary ballet and its classical foundation, with a focus on the form’s fluidity and lyricism. 
“I love that it [ballet] gives you all the tools to explore and be proficient in other styles of dance,” Mazza said. “In contemporary ballet, you can use classicism as a base, but the vocabulary of dance becomes more abstract and more diversified.” 


As they began to build the company in 2018 and 2019, the two knew they wanted full seasons, with performances in both Connecticut, where they teach and work (Ulloa was an educator at the New Haven Ballet for years), and New York, where they live together in Harlem and perform with multiple companies. After an unwelcome pandemic-enforced hiatus in 2020, the company debuted in 2021, with hours of masked rehearsals and original work set to the music of the late Cuban composer Ernesto Lecuona. 
“We never wanted the company to be a project” that had a finite lifespan, Ulloa said. So it was perhaps not a surprise that the company continued to grow beyond 2021, with Mazza and Ulloa launching the Fairfield County Dance Festival alongside the New Canaan-based company Thomas/Ortiz Dance that same year. By 2022, Mazza was leading the dance program at the Darien Arts Center, where Ulloa is also a dance educator. With 12 faculty members, the program serves roughly 350 students from ages three to over 70. 
Since 2021, the ensemble has created nearly 50 pieces for its repertoire, with artistic collaborators ranging from New York-based, Argentine-born bassist and composer Pedro Giraudo to Stamford’s own Orchestra Lumos to Italian sculptor Luca Serasini. Last year, for the first time, the company also rolled out its “Salon Series,” a kind of open rehearsal that travels to different museums, galleries, studios, and arts spaces to make the work ECCB is doing more accessible. 
Across all of the company’s iterations, “Through You,” which Mazza and Ulloa choreographed as they fell in love with each other, has been a creative through-line. While it did not start as a narrative about partnership, Mazza said, the two quickly realized that’s what they were building. At one point, she remembered sitting in an Airbnb, listening to the music scoring the piece, with tears streaming down her face. The duet has three movements, set to works by Silvestrov, Dustin O’Halloran, and Lecuona, respectively.
As the two ran through it in a large, light-drenched studio last week, that journey felt palpable. Mazza began alone on the floor, her arms extended to their full wavelength. She began to cross the floor, toes nearly melting into the ground as they slid back, then rose again, lifting with the swan-like motion of her leg. She twirled, unhurried, and then bent forward, arms out as if in supplication. Her left leg became a pendulum, swinging back and forth as she looked on, winding one arm around the other as if it were a clock. 
Credit: Nico Malvaldi / East Coast Contemporary Ballet
Only then, as she turned again, did Ulloa seem to come alive at the back of the room, his reflection springing forward in a wall-length mirror. He spun, one hand pressed to his heart, then extended it toward where the audience would be. Silvestrov’s melancholic strings soared around him, enveloping the duo in their sense of pining. Only after a few beats, perhaps, did a viewer catch on that he and Mazza were mirroring each other in passing.
Suddenly, one could see the storyline. The two danced in parallel, sometimes echoing each other’s movements, sometimes moving around each other like atoms that had lost their way. When at last they touched, backs pressed to each other, it felt as though the whole room shared a collective exhale.  
Mazza seemed to know; she leaned back, her hand creeping along the floor. Her fingers pressed into the surface, curious, urgent. At last, they found Ulloa’s and held them for a moment, certain without needing any words at all. The two turned around, as if seeing each other for the first time. 
“It has come to a different place since we first performed it,” Ulloa said of the duet. “They tell you that you keep falling in love, and it’s true. It’s a way more mature love [that we have now]. It’s an appreciation, as well. I feel privileged to be able to live with this love in my life, but to experience it with dancing, with no words at all …” he trailed off. 
“It’s like falling in love all over again,” Mazza finished. 
In addition to “Through You,” Saturday’s seven-piece program will include original work spanning the company’s eight years, from “Vessels,” an ensemble work with which ECCB debuted in 2021 to Mazza’s new piece “Power Play,” which she devised to the music of Cristina Spinei, to the Impressionism-inspired work “Brushstrokes,” set to the “Lautrec Suite” by the late composer Nicolas Flagello. Flagello’s surviving widow Dianne, a former director of the Manhattan School of Music, arranged the suite in his honor.  
Elizabeth Hall, a longtime dance teacher at the Darien Arts Center who now serves as a substitute teacher and dedicated volunteer for the Center’s annual performance of the “Nutcracker,” said she’s thrilled to watch the two evolve and especially excited for the performance. Not only do the students love them; other faculty members do, too.   
“Claire and Alejandro bring the best out in every dancer,” Hall said. “I’m just so excited for them. It’s a huge, huge deal, and they’ve worked so hard to get there. I’m super super proud of them, and I just feel lucky that the Darien Arts Center gets to have them as professional dancers who bring their knowledge and their expertise to everything they do.”

name: California
title: California’s congressional gerrymander worked. What happens after the next census?
description: The next census will prompt a redrawing of districts. Democrats will want to keep as many seats as they can, likely by using gerrymandered maps.
text:
Last year, after Texas Republicans reconfigured their congressional districts to grab five more seats, California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, and its Legislature countered with a gerrymander to shift five seats their way.
Both partisan maneuvers, and those in a few other states, were designed to either bolster or erase the paper-thin GOP majority in the House.
On Tuesday the Texas two-step failed spectacularly. Democrats won four of the five targeted districts there, while California’s counterplay succeeded even more spectacularly as five Republican congress members from here were wiped out.
The GOP held just eight of the state’s 52 congressional seats going into the election, plus one Republican-turned-independent. Their ranks now shrink to a miniscule four, even though a quarter of the state’s voters are Republicans.
It’s a testament not only to the determination of Newsom and Democratic legislators to affect the national power struggle over Congress, but also to the professional competence of Paul Mitchell, the Sacramento-based political guru Democrats recruited to draw the new, gerrymandered redistricting maps.
The plan, which was pushed through the Legislature and onto a special election ballot as Proposition 50 last year, didn’t go exactly as envisioned, but the result was exactly what Newsom and Co. intended. And it burnishes Newsom’s status as a partisan warrior for his almost certain bid for the Democratic Party’s presidential candidacy in 2028.
As it turns out neither the failed Texas gerrymander nor California’s successful one played decisive roles in the “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into solid majorities in both houses of Congress.
California now has five new members of Congress, most likely for at least six years. But what then?
The gerrymandered maps of 52 congressional districts will legally be in effect through the 2030 election, after which the state, under current law, will revert to the prior districts drawn by an independent commission for the 2032 elections and beyond.
However, it’s not that simple. Political ambition and demography will likely combine to create a dilemma for the state’s dominant Democrats.
The five new members will presumably want to keep their seats after 2030. But that year’s census will confirm that California has had scant population growth since the 2020 census, or even a slight decline.
The size of each state’s congressional delegation hinges on its population trend over the previous decade. California’s stagnant population will almost certainly result in a loss of  three to five of the nation’s 435 congressional seats.
If redistricting reverts to the independent commission, as current law says it will, it probably would pare down — or even erase — the extra five gerrymandered seats, even if there is no overall decline in the delegation.
With a likely decline, a fair commission plan would probably end the careers of more than five Democratic members and return a few to the GOP.
Democrats will still dominate levers of control after 2030. And their leaders must decide whether to allow the commission to do its work or abolish it via another ballot measure in the 2028 or 2030 election.
Party leaders have never liked commission redistricting, a process forced upon them by a pair of initiative ballot measures in 2008 and 2010 championed by former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Abolishing the commission system would return the drafting of new maps to the Legislature, thus allowing Democratic leaders (and possibly Paul Mitchell again) to redraw districts that maximize their party’s share of seats.
That’s what they did, or at last tried to do, after the 1980, 1990 and 2000 censuses, and what they probably would prefer to do after the 2030 count. 
We shouldn’t be surprised if gerrymandering becomes permanent.

name: California
title: Distant polls, spotty mail obstruct Native American voting 6 years after law meant to help them
description: Advocates say distant polling places and unreliable mail still keep Native Americans in California from voting, and the state panel meant to help has never met.
text:
Six years after California passed a law requiring the secretary of state to form an advisory committee to help improve voting access for Native Americans, the committee still has not been formed, the secretary of state’s office confirmed to CalMatters/ICT. 
Advocates from the California Native Vote Project said they received some reports of problems at polling sites on Election Day, and say the underlying barriers the committee was meant to address, including distant polling places and unreliable mail service, remain.
A spokesperson for Secretary of State Shirley Weber who declined to provide their name said in an email that the office plans to begin recruiting members “after the November election.”
“It’s really frustrating,” said Calvin Hedrick, director of policy for the project, an advocacy group promoting voting rights for Native American peoples in California. “It’s a bummer to have to fight for something again after it was already promised by statute.”
A promise on paper
The law, Assembly Bill 2314, which called for a Native American Voting Accessibility Advisory Committee, was authored by Assemblymember James Ramos and sponsored by then-Secretary of State Alex Padilla. 
“California’s nearly three-quarters of a million Native Americans deserve to have their voices heard in our democracy,” Padilla said in an August 2020 statement released by Ramos’ office.
Anthony Roberts, Chairman of the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, which supports the law, said in 2020 that a lack of polling places and the rejection of certain types of identification remained obstacles. “Until those obstacles are addressed, California’s Native Americans remain at risk of being excluded, with no voice in government, the education of their children and other vital services.”
A voter places their ballot into the box June 2, 2026 at the vote center at Sol Mexican Grill in Chico. Photo by Salvador Ochoa for CalMatters
The law required the committee to set guidelines for reaching Native American voters, recommend public service announcements at least 45 days before elections, suggest ways to improve Native American poll worker recruitment, and advise on language assistance and plain-language materials. But the committee’s recommendations would be nonbinding. The secretary of state was required only to consider them.
The law set no deadline for forming the committee, provided no funding and did not require input from tribal governments or groups. 
Members, who are to be chosen by the secretary of state, would have to have experience with voting rights or be county elections officials. The law also set no meeting schedule. By contrast, the state’s separate Language Accessibility Advisory Committee, which is supposed to ensure voters can understand the voting process, must meet at least four times a year. 
“Lacking those things, it’s pretty clear it’s just going to end up in the dustbin,” said Allison Neswood, senior staff attorney for the Native American Rights Fund, an advocacy group promoting the interests of Indigenous communities. Neswood is Diné.
Ramos, who is Serrano/Cahuilla and a lifelong resident of the San Manuel Indian Reservation, was not available after multiple requests from CalMatters/ICT. “It’s been difficult finding a time, but still working on it,” wrote a spokeswoman in his office, in October. A Democrat from San Bernardino, he is the first and only Native American from a California tribe elected to the Legislature. 
The state’s response
A spokesperson for Weber acknowledged the committee does not exist, in response to questions from CalMatters/ICT in October. The office said it has been “working closely with Native American advocates to review our committee-related documents” and is planning to recruit members. 
The secretary of state’s office did not respond to additional questions about why it had not done anything for six years, who it had contacted for recruitment, whether it had requested any funding and whether it had any documents available for review. 
Hedrick said his organization, which promotes voter registration and provides nonpartisan voting information in California Native communities across the state, has been doing its own voter outreach without support from the secretary of state’s office. With only two employees to cover all of Northern California, he said, his team is “stretched really thin.” 
Resources from a committee would be an important boost to his group’s efforts, Hedrick said.
“It’s something we need to really be pushing for over the next few years — and we can’t allow them to rest and forget about it,” said Hedrick. “We can’t allow them to promise us it’s something they’re going to do next year, we need to hold their feet to the fire and make sure it gets done.” 
In California, the state’s broader responsibilities for ensuring voter access sit mostly with the secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer and must make reasonable efforts to promote voter registration and encourage eligible voters to cast ballots. But when it comes to where people vote, the state points to the counties.
The state sets guidelines for drop boxes, including the minimum number per county. But county election officials decide where they go, whether to add any beyond the minimum and when they’re open. Unlike some states, California, which shares geography with 109 federally recognized tribal nations, does not mandate that there be polling locations on tribal lands.
Barriers that remain
In Shasta County, a monitor for the Native Vote Project saw a citizen of the Redding Rancheria turned away from the polls on election day. He later  reported he was able to vote. 
On the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation, the largest reservation in the state, advocates coordinated a vehicle caravan to transport elders from rural areas of the tribe’s lands to reach the only polling site on the reservation. 
The Native American Rights Fund produced reports in 2020 and 2026 that found significant barriers to political participation for Native Americans and Alaska Natives. The 2020 report drew on testimony at nine hearings, including two in California. The 2026 report analyzed federal election data from 2020 to 2024, but did not study any California counties specifically. Hedrick said that he continues to hear complaints from Native Americans, especially those in rural communities, about the time and resource costs of voting.
“For people who live in a city where their ballot box is often a 10-minute drive or less, it’s unfathomable to think someone would have to drive an hour or more to vote — but that’s the reality in many of our communities,” said Hedrick, who is Mountain Maidu.Since 2021, California has mailed a ballot to every active registered voter. Advocates say that doesn’t fully address the gaps, because tribal communities, particularly in rural areas, often lack reliable, timely mail service. Some reservations lack even a single polling place or ballot box, forcing tribal citizens to take time off work and drive miles out of their way to cast their ballots. 
A 2024 article in the Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review found that voting by mail in Indian Country was “plagued” by overlapping barriers, including a lack of post offices.
“The inadequate postal infrastructure in Indian Country immediately impacts the ability of voters to receive and cast a ballot via mail,” wrote Torey Dolan, a Choctaw citizen and associate law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.  
Native Americans were not granted automatic U.S. citizenship until 1924 and were not able to vote in all states until 1962. According to Ramos, they often live long distances from post offices: About 89% of current post offices were established before 1920, research has found. 
Registering is also difficult. Many Native people who live on tribal lands in California have no permanent address, which makes it hard to place them in a voting precinct. Tribal communities in California have also historically had less access to internet and broadband services.
At least one California tribe successfully brought voter services closer to its citizens in recent years. In September 2023, the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians accepted a designation from the secretary of state making its tribally run health center a voter registration agency under the National Voter Registration Act. Weber said at the time it was the first such designation of a tribal medical facility in the country. 
What the committee could do
Hedrick and his colleagues at the California Native Vote Project travel to tribal communities across the state, engaging with voters and educating them about the electoral process. He also meets with people who haven’t registered to vote and works to better understand what’s keeping them from doing so.
If the committee were established it could not require counties to open voting sites. But Hedrick said if the committee existed, it could do similar work and could play an important role in building trust between the state and communities that have long felt ignored.
That trust is thin, Neswood said, in part because Native peoples rarely see themselves reflected in government. 
“If Native people consistently see that their voices and their priorities and their people aren’t represented in these institutions, it just reinforces the lack of trust,” Neswood said. “We’re fighting an uphill battle.”
Hedrick said rebuilding that trust starts with showing up in tribal communities.
“We need people out in tribal communities listening to voters and talking to people who aren’t registered — I think that’s something this committee could be doing,” Hedrick said. “It became statute in 2020, we’re talking in 2026, and (the committee) still hasn’t happened yet and it’s not happening now.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Ford vows no new taxes, will ‘fight like hell’ to tackle high cost of living
description: In his first speech since winning election, Nevada Democratic Attorney General and Governor-elect Aaron Ford on Wednesday reiterated he wouldn’t raise taxes and promised to declare the affordability crisis a state emergency saying he would “fight like hell” to fix it as the next governor. Ford defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo amid a seismic […[...]
text:
Governoe-elect Aaron Ford addressing supporters Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026 in Las Vegas. (Photo: Michael Lyle/Nevada Current)In his first speech since winning election, Nevada Democratic Attorney General and Governor-elect Aaron Ford on Wednesday reiterated he wouldn’t raise taxes and promised to declare the affordability crisis a state emergency saying he would “fight like hell” to fix it as the next governor.
Ford defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo amid a seismic wave of Democratic victories in Nevada and the nation. 
The election was a stunning rebuke to the Trump administration, which failed to address the cost of living increases hitting American households while also reneging a campaign promise not to start a new war, which in turn exacerbated the affordability crisis.
In his speech highlighting his legislative priorities, in which Ford switched between speaking in English and Spanish, he identified expensive health care, unaffordable child care, rising utility prices, and the affordable housing crisis among the list of pressing issues. 
Speaking briefly to the reporters following the event, Ford said he didn’t believe state lawmakers needed to address the state’s existing tax structure to enact legislative priorities targeting the affordability crisis.
Instead, he said “we don’t have to raise taxes in order to invest in our people” but rather it was “a matter of budgeting.”
“It’s a matter of priorities,” he said, adding that “on day one we’re going to issue an affordability emergency.” The emergency, he said, would enable state agencies to look at ways to “put money back in people’s pockets.”
Ford, who was one of five Black governors elected nationwide on Tuesday, also made history as the first Black governor elected in Nevada.
The Associated Press called the victory for Ford shortly before 2 a.m. Wednesday. Lombardo conceded later that day, writing in a statement he “hoped Nevadans would move forward with a renewed sense of purpose united by our love for the state.”  
Ford said he spoke with Lombardo, but wouldn’t detail the specifics of the conversation, saying only that Lombardo “was gracious.”
Lombardo vetoed record-setting numbers of bills after both legislative sessions while was governor.  Many of those vetoes were tied to affordability, killing legislation that regulated corporate landlords purchasing homes, bolstered tenant protections, provided paid family and medical leave, and prevented collection agencies from threatening to arrest people for medical debt.
Without citing the vetoes specifically, Ford referenced some of the bills Lombardo killed including the efforts to rein in corporate homeownership. 
“We’re going to make sure that people who live and work in Nevada have a fair shot at owning a piece of it,” Ford said. “I firmly believe that a home should be where our family builds the future, not an investment vehicle for Wall Street firms and out-of-state corporations.” 
Though the cost of living played a significant role among voters this election cycle, Ford said it was also his lived experience that included surviving on Medicaid and food stamps while in college and couch surfing during times he couldn’t pay rent that also influenced his policy proposals.
“I understand the struggles you’re facing, and I will fight like hell to lower your costs and to make Nevada affordable,” he said. 
In addition to tackling high costs, Ford pledged to be the most pro-union governor and end “that farce that’s called ‘right to work.’”
“We’re going to tackle perhaps the most fundamental issue of all: lifting up working-class Nevadans,” he said. “These people who build our roads, who care for our patients, who teach our children, who mine our minerals, and who keep the lights on up and down the Strip. They deserve a fair day’s pay for a fair day’s work.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: How Nevada can help stop stop L’Arc de Trump before it rises
description: On Thursday, the stacked National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), where Trump appointees, agency heads and Republican members of Congress hold 8 of 12 seats, met to vote on L’Arc de Trump. Surprising no one, it passed.  Hours later, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, in whose courtroom the suits against the arch by veterans and Public […]
text:
A protestor holds up a sign during a demonstration against President Trump's proposed triumphal arch at Memorial Circle on November 5, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Tom Brenner/Getty Images)On Thursday, the stacked National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), where Trump appointees, agency heads and Republican members of Congress hold 8 of 12 seats, met to vote on L’Arc de Trump. Surprising no one, it passed. 
Hours later, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, in whose courtroom the suits against the arch by veterans and Public Citizen as well as Virginia and the District of Columbia have merged, issued an order prohibiting any construction for 14 days.
Fiery testimony in opposition from civic organizers, architects and residents lasted hours during the hearing, including dead time when the stream crashed and had to be moved to the NCPC YouTube channel. A disgusted Rep. Jared Huffman told the commissioners in support of the arch, “You can try that argument in court. I don’t think it’s going to fly. … You’re going to lose. You’re going to lose. … This is an illegal project.” It had no effect. In a scene worthy of Kafka, the commission approved the arch with military plans it was not allowed to see.
While legal battling over the arch continues, we should not resign ourselves to a rogue, voluminous mass on Memorial Circle that would wedge itself in the sightline between Lincoln’s memorial and the Union dead he mourned buried at Arlington. In May, Nevada’s own Democratic Rep. Dina Titus, with Democratic Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, introduced the Arlington National Cemetery Viewshed Protection Act (H.R. 9047). In three short provisions, it would bar any plans to build this arch. It would also permanently cut off federal funding for the project and require Congress to approve any arch taller than 50 feet anywhere on capital-region parkland.
That last provision is the arch killer. The 1986 Commemorative Works Act gives Congress, not the president, the final say over memorials in the capital. But the administration argued that a plan authorized 101 years ago for two never-built 166-foot columns at Memorial Circle somehow stretches to a 250-foot arch, which per Trump would now be a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” with drones and snipers. That enhancement appears nowhere in the submitted plans and the Park Service denies knowledge of such transformer-like capabilities. Titus’ H.R. 9047 still sits unheard in committee with 46 co-sponsors and not one Republican.
Bills die when a Congress ends, so in January, with Democratic majorities in both chambers, Titus and Beyer should reintroduce H.R. 9047 on the first day. That same month, the two congressional seats on the NCPC will pass to the new Democratic committee chairs, and its split will become 6 to 6. Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson should commit now to co-sponsoring. Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto should immediately introduce an identical bill in the Senate. The president can veto it, and I don’t expect 13 Republicans to break ranks for an override. That’s why I think this should be Plan B. I have a Plan A.
Congress’ strongest check is money. Titus and Rep. Chellie Pingree wrote to the president that spending on “a project that has no legal basis to proceed is an abuse of taxpayer dollars.” Taxpayers are already expected to foot the bill. The White House’s spending plan for the National Endowment for the Humanities set aside $15 million for the arch: $2 million directly and $13 million in matching grants. Chutkan said in court that she still didn’t know where the rest of the money was supposed to come from.
But Titus’ leverage actually starts in December, not January. Funding for permits, work crews and grants comes from congressional appropriations. Under the current stopgap bill, the government runs out of money Dec. 11, three weeks before the new Congress is sworn in. Sixty Senate votes would be needed to avert another painful shutdown. Democrats should block any essential spending bill unless it includes a single-sentence rider barring the National Park Service, the Interior Department and the National Endowment for the Humanities from any arch spending. Trump would have to sign the bill or trigger a shutdown over what most voters see as a vainglorious monument to himself. Republican senators up for reelection in 2028 would need to choose whether to vote with Democrats or align themselves with a decidedly unpopular president and another contentious decoration project while voters struggle with bills. Who knows? Disowned by Washoe County Republicans for refusing to back the scandal-plagued Flippo, Rep. Mark Amodei, who sits until Jan. 3 on the Appropriations subcommittee that funds Interior, might come along.
To be sure, Democrats could wait for their new majorities in January. But depending on when the construction begins, a spring bill would hit a project already months underway. With work planned 20 hours a day, a spring rider would come too late to stop the expense and the disruption in the corridor, and taxpayers would pay again to restore the site. In August, the Supreme Court let Trump keep building his ballroom while its legality is still in court. Trump’s “Build first; let the courts catch up” maneuver has already worked. We must try to stop him this time. Every month it rises, the specious argument for completion hardens like concrete.
Despite and even because of this week’s decisive rebuke of Trump and the Republican Party, I remain deeply anxious about Trump’s compulsive willingness to destroy anything to avoid being branded a loser. Thus, I also have a Plan C. In January, the House should hold hearings and subpoena the funding and approval records and refer any illegal spending to the Government Accountability Office. The House can also make warranted criminal referrals to the Justice Department, which, even if Trump’s attorneys ignore them, would, barring pardons, set up the case for a later prosecutor. Most federal crimes can be charged up to five years later.
In Trump’s closing speech before the midterms vote, he expounded on his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool. On Nov. 4, the day after voters repudiated his agenda, he spoke to reporters inside his unfinished ballroom, calling it “one of the biggest” and “the most beautiful ballroom I think anywhere in the world,” and hailed his new nearby helipad as “a thing of beauty.” This arch, which he markets as a symbolic commemoration of the 250th anniversary of our Union, is transparently not about America at all. It is a triumphal arch for one 80-year-old modern-day Ozymandias, a self-styled “great” president desperate to shape how he’s remembered. Like his signature properties, whatever stands at the end of that bridge must be enormous, gilded and recognizably Trumpian. Our representatives must not let it rise.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fairfield Dems credit election wins to national politics, NY transplants
description: Fairfield, a former Republican stronghold, flipped completely into a town fully represented by Democrats at the federal and state level.
text:
Democrats in Fairfield had a very good Election Day, having completely flipped a former Republican stronghold, into a town fully represented by Democrats at the federal and state level.
Fairfield Democratic Town Committee Chair, Erin Lopez, said it was years in the making, to cheers at a restaurant in Fairfield on Election Night.
“We started with Cristin McCarthy-Vahey as our only Democratic representative,” Lopez said. “Nevertheless, the last 10 years, we’ve chipped away, and now we have full Democratic representation at every level in Fairfield.”
Lopez soon stepped aside as Rob Blanchard, who previously ran and lost against popular Republican State Sen. Tony Hwang in 2024, spoke in front of the crowd to more cheers as he flipped the 28th district state senate seat to Democratic control for the first time since 1974.
Blanchard wasn’t the only Democrat to have a good night. Michelle Embree Ku in nearby Newtown, flipped a Republican state representative seat.
Lopez is among those who say President Donald Trump’s unpopularity with Connecticut residents, a focus on local issues and even moving patterns from New York to Fairfield County, have helped the Democratic Party.
But Jonathan Wharton, who is a political science professor at Southern Connecticut State University, is skeptical of some of those claims.
Wharton said many residents moved to and from Connecticut over the last few years, and said it takes a while for transplants to integrate within their communities. Wharton said he’s not certain the numbers actually back that up throughout the state.
“It was a bump, but it wasn’t anything significant per se,” Wharton said. “Maybe in some districts more than others, but I don’t think it was such a wide ranging number that we saw this overall impact for the entire state.”
Wharton also mentioned unaffiliated voters have seen the most growth throughout the state, and according to registration statistics from the Secretary of the State’s office, the numbers back up Wharton’s assertions.
Fairfield Democrats and supporters look on as live election results come in for candidates representing Fairfield, at the Boca Grill and Raw Bar in Fairfield, on Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eddy Martinez / Connecticut Public
The number of active unaffiliated voters in Fairfield was over 700 in 2020. By 2026, the numbers had sharply risen to more than 17,000, compared to decreases for both registered Republicans and Democrats, with similar findings for Stamford and Newtown.
Blanchard said he won because he focused on affordability and hyper local issues such as the controversial UI monopole project.
“You can’t just be a Democrat that says I’m not Trump; elect me,” Blanchard said. “You have to be a Democrat that says in Fairfield, for example, I’m going to stand up to the utilities and fight things like the monopole project.”
Blanchard also said voters in the 28th district were energized by national politics, and President Donald Trump’s unpopularity.
Democratic State Rep. Cristin McCarthy Vahey,who succeeded Democrat Kim Fawcett, in 2014, who also flipped the seat during the 2006 midterms, said a focus on kitchen table politics helped many Democrats.
McCarthy Vahey said those local issues were impacted by federal policies, including cuts for social safety net programs.
“Here in Connecticut, we’ve seen $2 billion in cuts,” McCarthy Vahey said. “People understand that these impacts are having an effect on their day-to-day lives, on being able to fill their tanks, being able to heat their houses, being able to pay for food and medicine.”
Lopez also credits the Blue Wave across Connecticut in this election to the influx of liberal New Yorkers who moved to Fairfield and other parts of the county , especially during the COVID-19 pandemic.
“A lot of them came up to Fairfield, and I think that has made a difference with younger Democrats who maybe weren’t as aware of the local politics, but were Democrats in Brooklyn, and became Democrats in Fairfield,” Lopez said.
According to Lopez many voters in the district are moderate and would probably vote for a moderate Republican, but she said that’s not what voters saw in this election.
“I think that this extreme version of MAGA has driven away a lot of people who are small c conservative, in a way, but are turned off by a lot of the social issue stuff or the cruelty coming out of the Donald Trump MAGA part of the party, ” Lopez said.
This story was first published Nov. 5, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Advocates bring new food security network to rural Utah communities
description: West of the Great Salt Lake and the Bonneville Salt Flats, in Wendover, a small city at Utah’s border with Nevada, high schoolers spent their morning packing and giving away food boxes to people facing food insecurity.  It was the first event of a new “community-based food security network” launched on Thursday by Chicanos por […]
text:
Wendover High School students pack food boxes as part of a new food security network for rural communities in Utah. (Courtesy of Chicanos por la Causa)West of the Great Salt Lake and the Bonneville Salt Flats, in Wendover, a small city at Utah’s border with Nevada, high schoolers spent their morning packing and giving away food boxes to people facing food insecurity. 
It was the first event of a new “community-based food security network” launched on Thursday by Chicanos por la Causa, a community development nonprofit, and Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, as the number of people facing food insecurity in the state grows. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to data collected by Chicanos por la Causa, food security is one of the top needs among Utahns — alongside housing and healthcare, said Leo Gonzalez, program manager at the organization.
“We knew that we needed to do something,” Gonzalez said. “We came together, and the plan now is to be able to take food to every single county in the state of Utah. It’s a huge undertaking, of course, but it’s also a huge gap that we understand that needs to be taken care of.”
A box of food donated as part of a new food security network for rural communities in Utah. (Courtesy of Chicanos por la Causa)
The number of people experiencing food insecurity in the state rose by nearly 100,000 people in a year, reaching 445,000 Utahns in January of this year, according to the Utah Food Bank. That includes 1 in 5 children. 
After changes implemented in Congress’ spending package known as the “Big, Beautiful bill,” over 5 million people throughout the country have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, including almost 29,000 Utahns, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
Wendover, which has a population of about 1,130 people, is the type of community the new resource is targeting, organizers said, since it is an area that can be difficult to reach through traditional food assistance programs. 
“Many times Wendover gets left behind,” Gonzalez said. “And we wanted to make sure that that wasn’t the case with our food network.” 
Other areas organizers will prioritize include areas like the west side of Salt Lake, as well as rural areas in Tooele, Summit, Carbon and Sanpete counties, where they have identified the biggest gaps in resources.
During the launch on Thursday, students at Wendover High School packed 90 boxes containing meats, fruits and vegetables, among other food items, Gonzalez said. The initiative is being funded by the private sector, with donors like the Larry H. Miller Foundation, Mountain America Credit Union, Marathon Petroleum and the Brent and Kathryn Wood Foundation.
Local producers, including Utah Natural Meat, International Rescue Committee New Roots, OakDell Egg Farms and Utah Refugee Goats are providing the food for the network, organizers said in a news release, and other organizations are helping out with distribution.
Utah Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla speaks during launch event for a new food security network for rural communities in Utah. (Alixel Cabrera/Utah News Dispatch)
Escamilla, who has sponsored food security legislation for several years, has been keeping tabs on the needs through data the nonprofit has collected. 
“What we do know is children are going hungry to bed. I mean, in Utah, 1 out of 5, and those numbers continue to grow,” Escamilla said during the launch. “And as we are prepping for more cuts into the programs that are providing a safety net to our children in our community, we know that number is going to increase.”
Now that Democrats are projected to flip some seats in the Utah Legislature, Escamilla is more hopeful about the odds of passing her future bills tackling the issue, she said.  
Apart from a request for appropriations to better support the state’s Food Security Council, housed at Utah State University, Escamilla is also looking to make statute modifications to allow the body to take direct action to connect people with services.
And, for the third year in a row, Escamilla is expected to propose a bill to provide free lunch to more K-12 students in the state. 
“This is going to be a little bit different,” she said. “But we’re trying to work with children under 200% of poverty level. It’s the first group that we will guarantee the free lunch.” 
More information on the program can be found at Chicanos por la Causa’s Utah website.
Wendover High School students attend an event to pack food boxes as part of a new food security network for rural communities in Utah. (Courtesy of Chicanos por la Causa)

name: Washington State Standard
title: The Nature Conservancy opens new community forest in Cle Elum
description: The Nature Conservancy, an international environmental nonprofit, just acquired 2,600 acres of timberland in central Washington. Historically owned by industrial timber companies, the lands within the Cle Elum Ridge Community Forest are now protected from development and accessible to the public. “This moment reflects what happens when people come together a[...]
text:
The Cle Elum Ridge is Washington's newest community forest. (Photo by Benjamin Drummond)The Nature Conservancy, an international environmental nonprofit, just acquired 2,600 acres of timberland in central Washington.
Historically owned by industrial timber companies, the lands within the Cle Elum Ridge Community Forest are now protected from development and accessible to the public.
“This moment reflects what happens when people come together around a shared idea for the forest,” said Darcy Batura, forest partnerships director for the Nature Conservancy in Washington. “It’s a moment to transition toward looking forward and thinking about the generations of children that are going to enjoy these forests and will inherit the responsibility of caring for it.”
While the purpose of the acquisition is to protect the land from development, the organization’s priorities extend well beyond that. The community forest will support recreation, wildlife migration paths, watershed function and wildfire resiliency work. 
The nonprofit also plans to transfer the land to the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation, whose ancestral homelands encompass the forest’s boundaries. 
The forest, which lies adjacent to the Teanaway Community Forest near Cle Elum and Roslyn, is home to a variety of woodland animals: elk, mule deer, cougars, black bears, foxes, grouse, turkeys and the occasional wolf.
“Having this as a managed forest means that they don’t need to come down into our communities and hopefully we avoid a lot of those conflicts,” said Nicky Pasi, a senior manager at Mountains to Sound Greenway Trust, a longtime stewardship partner for the Cle Elem Ridge Community Forest. 
In 2014, the Nature Conservancy partnered with Central Cascades Forest to acquire nearly 50,000 acres of forestland between Snoqualmie Pass and Ellensburg. Today, much of that land has been protected by the U.S. Forest Service and the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, according to the Nature Conservancy.
“We hit the pause button on housing development pressures more than 10 years ago so we could better understand what these lands needed most,” said Batura.
Since the initial acquisition, the Nature Conservancy wasn’t a “passive landowner,” she said. It reintroduced prescribed fire, thinning and other climate and wildfire resiliency work with local crews. 
The forest also became a “living laboratory” for Emily Howe, aquatic ecologist at the nonprofit, who conducted a study on how forest management could maximize snowpack retention.  Washington’s snowpack has decreased 25% since 1950, and it’s projected to decrease up to 50% more by the end of the century, according to state climatologist Guillaume Mauger.
On Oct. 28, the Nature Conservancy purchased 2,600 acres from Central Cascades Forests, making it the sole owner of the land. The Cle Elum Ridge is now one of 17 community forests in the state. 
The Nature Conservancy also partnered with Mountains to Sound Greenway Trust, a local nonprofit that stewards 1.5 million acres of land along I-90. The organization, which largely helped with community outreach and engagement, also built a 13-mile “sustainable” trail system within the forest. It was designed by trail construction experts, a landscape architect and with input from local mountain biking and trails groups, Pasi said. 
“We maintain [the trails] with local volunteers,” Pasi said. “They are non-motorized, multi-directional, multi-use trails.”
Though a timeline isn’t yet decided, the nonprofit plans to transfer the forestland to the Yakama Nation. 
“I think it’s really important that we take the time to build some norms, to build trust, and to work with the Nation at a pace that’s comfortable for them,” Batura said, noting that the transfer could occur in one year or in several. 
“And that’s absolutely fine to us,” she added.
For now, the Nature Conservancy is inviting the public to review and comment on a draft community forest management plan at a meeting in Cle Elum on Nov. 17.

name: Mississippi Today
title: SpaceXAI started Southaven data center construction without water permits, state alleges. Fines could exceed $6M
description: The xAI power plant in Southaven on Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s environmental regulators released details this week on a set of penalties against SpaceXAI for violating state water pollution laws by starting construction on its Southaven data center facilities without needed permits. 
The company first announced the potential fines to investors two weeks ago, speculating the amount could reach as much as $6.1 million. 
To limit pollution from construction reaching public bodies of water, state law requires companies to first obtain a permit. Without proper protections, rain, for instance, can carry debris and chemicals off construction sites and pollute natural habitats, drinking water systems and recreational areas, federal regulators warn. 
Earlier this year, SpaceXAI  – through its subsidiary, MZX Tech LLC – asked the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality for permits allowing construction within its growing Southaven footprint, which includes a power plant as well as land to build a $20 billion data center facility called MACROHARDRR. 
The Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice are threatening to sue Elon Musk’s xAI over the company’s use of temporary turbines to power its operation in Southaven. Credit: City of Southaven
But during a July meeting between MDEQ and MZX Tech, “it became apparent” the company had already begun construction on the land in question, impacting about 30 acres, MDEQ records show. 
On July 16, a day after the meeting, MDEQ staff visited Southaven and confirmed the infractions. The agency sent two notices of violation to MZX Tech on Aug. 10, both of which “will be subject to the maximum statutory penalty” of $25,000 for each day construction continues without the needed permits, MDEQ wrote. 
“The Company is cooperating with MDEQ and is in discussions to resolve the matters through a single agreed order,” SpaceXAI wrote in its Oct. 22 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. 
It’s unclear where the $6.1 million figure came from. Based on the $25,000-per-day figure, it could suggest the violations lasted for several months. But MDEQ declined to say if the amount was accurate, citing its policy not to comment on pending enforcement matters.
A screenshot of MDEQ’s report from its July 16 inspection of SpaceXAI’s facilities in Southaven.
At one of the MZX Tech properties, a former Southaven training facility that neighbors Horn Lake Creek, MDEQ staff found that “no steps have been taken to protect stormwater infrastructure at the site,” and that there was a lack of protection against “fugitive dust emissions.” 
At the 2400 Stateline Road property, the site for MACROHARDERR, the staff found “no controls around storm inlets.” The MDEQ inspectors noted that, while construction appeared to have started around the beginning of 2026, the property’s last construction storm water permit expired in 2023. 
MDEQ responds to federal judge about its turbine exemptions
Last week, a federal judge found that MDEQ had misinterpreted federal clean air statutes when allowing SpaceXAI to run 69 temporary natural gas turbines without a permit. U.S. District Court Judge Debra Brown included the opinion in her ruling against a motion to dismiss the NAACP’s April lawsuit against the data center company. 
MDEQ relied on a federal Clean Air Act exemption intended for mobile generators, and SpaceXAI’s turbines clearly did not meet that criteria, Brown reasoned. That distinction is a key focus of the NAACP’s argument against the company. 
The agency responded to the order in a statement to Mississippi Today on Wednesday. 
Jaricus Whitlock, left, and Jeffrey Bland prepare for a Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality public hearing on an xAI permit application at Northwest Mississippi Community College in Southaven on Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“MDEQ is aware of the Court’s order and takes seriously all opinions by a federal court,” agency spokesperson Jan Schaefer said. “Nonetheless, MDEQ is not a party to that case and the order is not binding upon the agency.  Furthermore, that litigation is ongoing and subject to appeal so it is not final at this point.  
“MDEQ always seeks to make sure our policies are in compliance with state and federal law and will do the same here once that litigation concludes.”
The agency first told the Elon Musk-owned company last year that it could run the generators without a permit because the units are “affixed to a portable unit (i.e., a flatbed trailer)” and are therefore considered mobile. 
Brown, though, disagreed. She argued that, given the size of the generators and the fact they aren’t “self-propelled or intended to be propelled” while operating, the federal exemption for mobile sources can’t apply.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: A look at how SC voters’ support shifted to flip the US Senate seat
description: COLUMBIA — Senator-elect Annie Andrews made history with a voting shift for the Democrat across every South Carolina county, as Republicans and independents split their ticket, an analysis of election data shows. Andrews flipped South Carolina’s U.S. Senate seat with 51% of the vote, 4.5 percentage points more than GOP Sen. Darline Graham, according to […]
text:
Dr. Annie Andrews celebrates with supporters in downtown Charleston Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, as the Associated Press declared her the winner of South Carolina's U.S. Senate Race. To her left is Jaime Harrison, former chairman of the Democratic National Committee, who lost his own bid for Senate against the late Sen. Lindsey Graham in 2020. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Senator-elect Annie Andrews made history with a voting shift for the Democrat across every South Carolina county, as Republicans and independents split their ticket, an analysis of election data shows.
Andrews flipped South Carolina’s U.S. Senate seat with 51% of the vote, 4.5 percentage points more than GOP Sen. Darline Graham, according to unofficial results.
Record-breaking turnout and a surge in Democrats’ enthusiasm help explain her win in an election that brought a blue tsunami nationwide. Other states where Democrats flipped U.S. Senate seats long held by a Republican included Maine, North Carolina, and Texas.
Broken down by county, Andrews won more votes than the three-month incumbent in 25 of South Carolina’s 46 counties, including traditionally ruby red Greenville and York counties.

Democrats are also celebrating a flip in the coastal 1st Congressional District and a shockingly close finish in the 2nd District held by U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson since 2001.
In both races, the margin seems to fall just outside the 1-point-or-less spread that would trigger an automatic recount, according to unofficial results. As of early Friday, The Associated Press had yet to call either contest.
State Democratic Party officials point to shoe-leather campaigning in driving turnout across the state. Since the June primaries, the party’s outreach efforts included 6 million attempts to contact voters by phone or in person; 750 volunteers for the party knocked on doors in the last two weeks, Jay Parmley, state director, told reporters Wednesday.
“We are absolutely convinced that through the volunteer efforts, through the paid efforts, that this made a big difference here to capture this sort of national frustration, national mood,” he said.
“We made sure we had folks on the doors, just this constant door turn happening in the background,” added state party Chair Christale Spain.
That also helps explain 10 flips in the state House that erased the chamber’s GOP supermajority.
But Democratic enthusiasm didn’t flip any other statewide office in South Carolina.
Republican Attorney General Alan Wilson, Joe Wilson’s son, won the governor’s office with the same, 4.5-point margin as Andrews.
While that’s the smallest winning spread for a GOP gubernatorial nominee since 2010, when Rep. Nikki Haley defeated Sen. Vincent Sheheen by 4.5 points, it shows Andrews’ win can’t be fully attributed to more Democrats showing up and unenthused Republicans staying home.
Wilson received a greater share of votes than Graham in every county.
In a state where voters don’t register by party, that’s clear evidence of Republicans crossing over to vote for Andrews over Graham.
Comparing 2024 to 2026
President Donald Trump, whose encouragement and endorsement of Graham prompted her to run, came to South Carolina twice in 10 days to rally support for the younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, who Trump called his best friend. To bolster turnout, Trump told supporters repeatedly to pretend that he was on the ballot.
What SC voters had to say about the midterm election

The results Tuesday show Trump’s popularity waning even in a state he won by nearly 18 percentage points two years ago.
Compared to his 2024 numbers, Darline Graham received a smaller percentage of votes in every county.
The most dramatic shift came in conservative Spartanburg County. Graham won the county, but with a winning margin 15.3 percentage points smaller than Trump’s.
Statewide, 30 counties saw Graham’s share of support at least 10 points below Trump’s winning percentage over Vice President Kamala Harris.
Beyond Spartanburg County, the biggest drops were in Kershaw County (14.3 points), Graham’s home county of Lexington (13.5 points), and Berkeley County (13.3 points).
Split tickets
The crossover vote was most evident in the seven counties won by Wilson in the governor’s race that went blue for Andrews in the U.S. Senate race: York, Greenville, Clarendon, Calhoun, Colleton, Barnwell, and Jasper.
The split tickets are at least partly due to GOP infighting over Graham’s nomination. Trump’s backing angered many Republicans, who saw it as interference in South Carolina’s decision, particularly supporters of U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman of Rock Hill, who lost to her in the runoff, days after Trump rallied for her in Myrtle Beach.
In that Aug. 25 contest, Norman won 12 conservative counties in the state’s northwest corner, including Anderson and York counties, the two places where Trump rallied ahead of the election to try to help her.

While Norman said he would personally vote for Graham, honoring a pledge to support the GOP nominee, he refused to campaign with her and made clear his entire family didn’t support her. His son, Warren Norman, endorsed Andrews. Some of Norman’s supporters launched a social media campaign asking conservatives to write in his name.
But ultimately, the “write in Ralph” effort didn’t make a difference.
Fewer than 4,900 people statewide wrote in someone’s name, according to the state Election Commission’s uncertified numbers.
How many voters specifically wrote Norman’s name is unknown. Counties aren’t required to separately count write-ins unless there’s enough to impact an election, according to the state agency.
The total write-ins surpassed tallies in U.S. Sen. Tim Scott’s 2022 re-election and Lindsey Graham’s 2020 re-election but not remotely enough to sway the outcome.
More than 91,000 votes separated Andrews from Graham.
The Libertarian and Constitution candidates also weren’t spoilers. The two, minor-party candidates received a combined total of less than 40,400.
Turnout and takeaways
The election broke the state’s record for the highest voter turnout in a non-presidential year by both percentage and total numbers.
According to the state Election Commission, 2 million voters cast ballots out of 3.4 million registered voters — a turnout of 60%. That breaks the previous record, set 24 years ago, by 5 percentage points. And it surpassed the 2018 record of 1.7 million total votes.
Those numbers were propelled by early voting, which also set a new record for a gubernatorial year.
More than 1 million people voted during the 12 days of early voting. That approaches a doubling of the 562,000 early votes cast in 2022, which is both the last time races for governor and a U.S. senator were on the ballot and the first election under the then-new early voting law.
According to political science professors across the state, Andrews’ win came down to a combination of Democratic enthusiasm, the Iran war and high prices angering voters across the political spectrum, Andrews’ focus on affordability and ability to deflect Republican arguments, and voters disliking the idea that Graham inherited her spot on the ballot, particularly conservatives upset at Trump over meddling in the primary.
“It was the perfect storm to kind of boost Annie Andrews and sink Darline Graham,” said Scott Huffmon, a Winthrop University professor and director of the Winthrop Poll.
In his post-election analysis for the Winthrop Poll newsletter, he summed up Andrews’ recipe for a win this way: “Take one lackluster candidate, one great candidate, one terrible economy, one big GOP family fight and mix well. Fold in angry independents. Bake at 2026.”
Whether this election means South Carolina will be seen as a “purple state” depends on whether Democrats can repeat their momentum, said Shannon Bridgmon, a political science professor at the University of South Carolina.
For now, she said, the state is more “pale red” than purple.
