name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Rabies vaccine hesitancy a recurring topic for NH veterinarians, legislators
description: Last month, the House Environment and Agriculture Committee recommended reconsidering the contents of a sidelined bill from last session: House Bill 1488, which sought to increase rabies vaccine exemptions for New Hampshire pets.  The bill was sent for interim study by the full New Hampshire House in March and, with the 2026 session closed and […]
text:
For household dogs, cats and ferrets, rabies is the only vaccine required by New Hampshire state law. (Photo by Sebastian Condrea/Getty Images)Last month, the House Environment and Agriculture Committee recommended reconsidering the contents of a sidelined bill from last session: House Bill 1488, which sought to increase rabies vaccine exemptions for New Hampshire pets. 
The bill was sent for interim study by the full New Hampshire House in March and, with the 2026 session closed and the biennium winding down, was no longer eligible for passage. Instead, the committee voted, 10-1, to recommend the topic be addressed in future legislation.
That move came as a surprise to some.
“Truthfully, we didn’t think it was going to go as far,” said Dr. Jane Barlow Roy, who chairs the legislative committee of the New Hampshire Veterinary Medical Association.
That’s because there is broad consensus among veterinarians that the rabies vaccine — which protects against a disease both transmissible to humans and universally fatal — is safe and life-saving. Yet the bill was driven forward by pet owners concerned about the rare but non-zero occurrence of adverse reactions to the vaccine, reflecting the increasing prevalence of hesitancy around both human and pet shots that is driving the resurgence of some infectious diseases in the U.S.
Committee members said at an October work session they wanted to keep the door open to potential future changes to rabies vaccine guidance and ensure the topic is revisited if more information becomes available. But answering some of the questions raised by pet owners and legislators, veterinarians said, will require research that is complicated and ethically fraught. 
A lethal disease
For household dogs, cats and ferrets, rabies is the only vaccine required by New Hampshire state law.
The viral illness is transmitted when saliva from an infected animal touches broken skin or mucous membranes like those inside the mouth, nose and eyes. The virus moves slowly through nervous tissue, incubating for weeks or more before symptoms like fever, headache, confusion, vomiting, and, later, aggression, difficulty swallowing or paralysis begin to manifest. While post-exposure treatment can prevent the disease from progressing if it is administered soon enough, once symptoms appear, the disease is considered incurable.
Wildlife are the most common transmitters of rabies in the U.S., where the prevalence of vaccines has reduced both the disease’s incidence in domestic animals and the rabies death rate in humans and pets. But globally, about 70,000 people die of rabies each year, and more than 99% of people who get the disease outside the U.S. are infected by a dog, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In the U.S., there was an unusually high number of human exposures documented this year, according to the CDC. And recent research suggests that the disease is responsible for more human deaths nationwide than scientists once believed.
Hesitancy
Kelly Arsenault, a Sandown Realtor, is skeptical about some vaccines. But rabies, she said, is not one that she skips when she brings her small dogs to the vet.
“I believe in the ability of the body to heal,” she said. “However, rabies is not one of them — and I know that — it is not one of those that the body is going to heal from.”
Yet Arsenault, who has for years worked to help rehome and rescue small dogs, also has  questions about the rabies vaccine.
More than 150 dogs, most of them fluffy and weighing under 15 pounds, have passed through Arsenault’s care over the years, she said. To date, one that she is aware of has had a significant negative reaction to a vaccine, she said, becoming severely ill after injection. Treating the dog with allergy medication managed the reaction, she said, but it was unsettling. She wonders why it happened and whether the incident could have been prevented.
Negative reactions to vaccines in pets are uncommon, but most often appear similar to what many people experience after a flu shot, like injection site soreness and mild discomfort, said Dr. Lisa Boyer, a Seacoast area veterinarian, in an online seminar this October. Less commonly, severe reactions can involve facial swelling, vomiting or difficulty breathing.
These reactions are managed with veterinary care, said Barlow Roy. And in New Hampshire, as in some other states, a pathway exists in state law to allow owners of pets susceptible to reactions to seek an exemption from the requirement. 
“The process is there for those dogs and cats that truly should not be getting the rabies vaccine,” said Barlow Roy. 
That exemption must be approved by the New Hampshire state veterinarian; after it is granted, exempt animals must be kept away from other animals or muzzled. Owners also assume more liability for their unvaccinated animals.
For these reasons and the lethal nature of the rabies virus, the veterinarians consider the vaccine more than worthwhile for almost all pets.
Yet the online proliferation of information and misinformation about vaccines has raised more curiosity among pet owners, who are asking more questions and starting conversations the veterinarians said they welcomed. However, in some cases, they said, pet owners have also become more likely to push back against professionals’ recommendations.
Titer testing
HB 1488 sought to broaden the allowed cases for rabies vaccine exemptions in New Hampshire under one condition: A pet has received a series of tests attempting to demonstrate that their immune system has responded to the vaccine.
Those tests, known as antibody titers, can measure the level of rabies-specific antibodies, or immune system proteins, in a pet’s blood. The pet’s own white blood cells produce antibodies after they are exposed to the inactivated virus molecules in a vaccine; then the antibodies remain in the pet’s blood, ready to raise the alarm if they ever encounter the rabies virus again, such as if the pet is exposed to rabies from a wild animal.
The idea of a titer testing protocol appeals to Arsenault, she said, because if a test could demonstrate that her pet is protected against rabies, she could skip additional “booster” shots.
But the problem, according to veterinarians, is that there is currently no test that can prove definitively whether or not a pet has enough antibodies to be protected against rabies.
If a titer comes back showing rabies antibodies in a pet’s blood, that confirms that the animal has some degree of immunity against rabies from a previous vaccination, Barlow Roy said. But it takes a certain threshold amount of antibodies to actually combat the virus in the case of a real exposure.
That makes the rabies titer test unhelpful for two reasons. One limitation, according to American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jennifer Quammen, is that the test is a snapshot in time of a dynamic situation. The amount of antibodies in a pet’s blood changes as time goes on; this is part of the reason booster shots are called for.
Second, scientists don’t have a reliable way of knowing what threshold amount of antibodies a pet’s blood must contain in order for them to be fully protected against the rabies virus. Therefore, in the face of a deadly disease like rabies, veterinarians recommend pets get boosters on schedule to ensure they are protected.
An ethical dilemma
The limitation of the rabies titer test doesn’t apply to some other diseases for which scientists have developed titer testing protocol. Pet owners may opt to use an antibody titer test to guide decisions about booster shots for some other illnesses, like canine distemper and parvovirus, veterinarians said.
With rabies, the factor that has limited the development of a titer testing protocol is the disease’s lethality. 
Reaching a conclusion about what level of blood antibodies is enough to protect a dog requires testing on living animals. Dogs with different levels of antibodies in their blood, for example, would be intentionally exposed to the disease; some are expected to contract the illness. That result helps scientists determine how much antibody is actually protective.
Animals that contract diseases for which treatments exist can be supported after that experiment with medical intervention, Barlow Roy said, making these studies less problematic for investigators. But an animal that begins showing signs of rabies is effectively facing a death sentence, making the protocol more fraught.
“We’re not comparing apples to apples, you know? We’re in the same realm,” she said, describing the differences in rabies titer research versus that on other diseases. “It’s more challenging from an ethical point of view … and that’s why we hesitate,” she said. 
Arsenault said she was conflicted: While she wants the results of the experiment, she also feels moral qualms about what it would necessitate.
“That’s probably where this whole thing gets difficult,” she said. “Would I be willing to be part of that study and watch a dog die from rabies? No … I don’t know if I could live with myself.”
However, some advocates of reducing rabies vaccine frequency have pushed for that research to move ahead, and some studies of limited scope have been completed. That included a 2020 study funded by the Rabies Challenge Fund Charitable Trust that involved the euthanasia of at least 45 beagles, some of which were infected with rabies, raising objections from animal rights groups like People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. 
But research has not yielded enough data to draw conclusions, veterinarians told legislators at hearings on HB 1488.
Most rabies policy and vaccine guidance is based on a document called the “rabies compendium,” compiled by the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians. The document is due for revision this year, said Dr. Nathan Harvey, New Hampshire assistant state veterinarian, at an October work session on the bill.
Veterinarians expect that the compendium will include updated guidance on the vaccine, possibly — but not certainly — to include guidance around the use of titer testing. 
“They are looking at whether or not we can start making those correlations to (titer levels) being protective, and that information may come out in the compendium. But we can’t assume that information is going to be published, or not,” Barlow Roy said.
The reality at present continues to be that titer tests cannot replace vaccine programs, for the sake of animal and human health, Quammen said. 
Body size
Some pet owners have also raised concerns about particularly small animals, like the dogs that Arsenault rescues.
Some negative reactions seem to occur with more frequency in small animals, Barlow Roy said, though she stressed that they are still uncommon. 
But while pet owners like Arsenault have asked whether a smaller “dose” of vaccine could be administered to smaller animals, that is misleading, Boyer said. Confusion can arise, she said, because many medications are dosed by body weight. But the way that vaccines work — by triggering an immune response — is not as sensitive to body size, meaning that the amount of a vaccine’s active ingredient that an animal must receive for the vaccine to work is not necessarily different for, say, a Pomeranian and a Lab.
“If you cut the dose in half and assume you have an appropriate dose, you will not be fully vaccinated or fully protected,” she said.
But there are other components besides dead viral molecules in a vaccine, and some formulations exist that deliver the same amount of active ingredient in a smaller volume, Boyer said.
A matter of public health
Veterinarians continue to recommend the rabies booster schedule that is widely accepted as the safest and best option for people and pets.
South Acworth Republican Rep. Judy Aron, who chaired the House Committee on Environment and Agriculture last session but did not seek reelection this fall, said during the Oct. 6 work session that the topic could be revisited by the Legislature if more guidance is released in the revised compendium.
Barlow Roy urged pet owners to discuss any concerns with their veterinarian, including by reporting any incidences of suspected vaccine side effects, which she said clinics routinely share with vaccine manufacturers. 
For Barlow Roy, the urgency of keeping pets protected from the virus is augmented by her compassion for the animals that visit her exam table — and the humans who love them.
“If I ever, God forbid, have an animal in my care that has rabies and it is given to, you know, a child in the household, or another family member, a human, that we could have prevented, that would definitely crush me,” she said. “That’s always the thing in the back of my head: Rabies is 100% fatal. It results in death 100% of the time. I think that’s why we are so adamant about rabies and this whole titer discussion.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Two major Election Day developments can help improve government in Indiana
description: There are countless threads to pull after a sweeping Democratic victory up and down the ballot Tuesday night. But one must start with Beau Bayh — the heir apparent to the state party. To be clear, many of the votes were more anti-Republican than pro-Democrat. But Democrats put themselves in a position to take advantage […]
text:
(Cartoon by Daniel Ackley for Indiana Capital Chronicle)There are countless threads to pull after a sweeping Democratic victory up and down the ballot Tuesday night. But one must start with Beau Bayh — the heir apparent to the state party.
To be clear, many of the votes were more anti-Republican than pro-Democrat. But Democrats put themselves in a position to take advantage of that frustration. And it showed all over the state.
Countless reliably Republican areas turned blue, led by Bayh.
He raised and spent millions, stuck to a disciplined message and his coattails no doubt helped take the state comptroller office and flip at least 21 legislative seats in the Indiana General Assembly. Oh, and the party also picked up a congressional seat.	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



To put this into perspective, the last Democratic secretary of state was Joe Hogsett from 1989 to 1994. Before that it was Beau Bayh’s dad, Evan Bayh. And the last Democratic comptroller — aka auditor — was Otis E. Cox from 1982 to 1986.
Straight-ticket voting was likely a factor for Bayh, but not the reason he won.
Nearly 127,000 Marion County voters cast straight-ticket Democratic ballots, compared to 40,000 for Republicans, according to unofficial Indianapolis election results.
Interestingly, Bayh wants to get rid of straight-ticket voting. And there have been bills to do so led unsuccessfully in the past by Republicans. While it would no doubt help Democrats in many parts of the state, he acknowledged it could hurt his party in Marion County.
“I don’t support policies because they benefit my political party,” he told the Capital Chronicle last week. “I support them because they’re the right thing to do for the people of our state.”
Allen County — which in 2022 had nearly double the straight-ticket Republican ballots than Democratic — saw Republican straight-ticket ballots only slightly leading Democrats.
In the end, it’s clear Hoosier Republican voters crossed over to support Bayh. He reached 1 million votes — well above the 742,000 the Democratic nominee received in 2022.
Supermajority’s end could temper extreme legislation
Hoosiers voted for change and now Democrats have to deliver. I suggest they don’t get caught up in payback for the last two years and pick their battles strategically. It would be a mistake to wear out their welcome just in time for a 2028 presidential race.
Democrats need to focus like a laser on what voters are saying: they can’t afford their groceries, gas, medicine, property taxes. They don’t like all the self-dealing and insider perks in government.
They’ll need to leverage their influx of new members to tackle those topics under a legislative process that will look drastically different in the House.
House Republicans saw their majority drop from 70 to 54, which will fundamentally change what bills are heard, what amendments are offered.
Under the supermajority, Republicans often didn’t even listen or consider Democratic thoughts on a topic. They could easily lose 10 to 15 of their own members and still pass a bill that was objectionable to many. Now, input will be necessary to forge compromise and agreements. That makes for a better process and outcome.
“I think we’re certainly going to be taken more seriously as the session goes forward,” House Democratic Leader Phil GiaQuinta said. “… We pride ourselves on being pragmatic problem-solvers, but we’re going to work and reach across the aisle where we can, and we try to take on serious issues and find solutions to those problems.”
Even Gov. Mike Braun agrees, saying, “I think, actually, supermajorities may have hurt us there.”
Democrats also flipped some seats in the Senate, slimming the Republican supermajority there.
Both of these major developments point to a more balanced government for Indiana — one that considers more Hoosiers.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blue wave in CT legislature may test Lamont on taxing the rich
description: Legislators have talked about taxing Connecticut’s wealthy to finance relief for the poor and middle class, but it’s only been talk — so far.
text:
State legislators have talked about taxing Connecticut’s wealthy to finance relief for the poor and middle class, but for most of the past eight years, it’s only been talk.
Because doing otherwise meant crossing one of Gov. Ned Lamont’s deepest lines in the political sand.
But after winning historic majorities Tuesday in the state House and Senate, Democratic legislators — who campaigned on pledges to reverse Connecticut’s affordability crisis — are poised to redefine their relationship with the governor, just in time for a watershed debate over state finances.
The numbers “position us more strongly than in years past to be more assertive,” said House Majority Leader Jason Rojas of East Hartford. He leads a Democratic caucus that will hold 116 out of 151 House seats, numbers not seen since immediately post-Watergate.
“We’ve been duly elected, and we have a mandate to improve affordability,” said Norwalk Democrat Bob Duff, majority leader in the Senate, where his party’s 33-3 advantage will be the widest in state history.
And while Rojas says he’s confident his colleagues will work “constructively and in partnership with the Democratic governor,” the two sides bring different perspectives to the regular 2027 session, which convenes Jan. 6. Duff says the same.
Lamont, who easily won a third term Tuesday over Greenwich Republican Ryan Fazio, also has stressed affordability.
But the governor repeatedly insists Connecticut needs “more taxpayers, not more taxes” and says raising state income tax rates on the rich only would drive them from the state. Lamont, a former cable TV entrepreneur, and his wife Annie, a co-founder of a venture capital firm, also live in Greenwich.
And when asked Wednesday what mandate he believes voters delivered, Lamont said people like the status quo, “how we’re managing through these very complicated times.”
But can Connecticut invest in programs, pay down its hefty debt and deliver noticeable relief, all at the same time?
Tax compromise was easy when CT was awash in federal grants
For most of Lamont’s tenure, it was relatively easy to find common ground with more liberal Democrats on budget issues.
Between 2020 and 2025, state government was awash in more than $4 billion in federal COVID grants. So even as budget caps pulled more than $1 billion in traditional state funds yearly off the budget, pandemic grants, exempt from such restrictions, could be spent in their place.
By 2026, though, those funds were exhausted, and Connecticut’s happy budget picture began to darken.
Suring Medicaid costs ate into funds earmarked to expand affordable childcare. To keep the latter program on schedule, state officials tapped a cap-protected surplus that normally would have reduced pension debt.
They went to the same well to find another $280 million in extra municipal aid last summer, just as their reelection campaigns launched.
It’s unclear whether Lamont will keep bending budget rules next year.
Meanwhile, advocates say hundreds of millions are needed to properly compensate doctors who treat Medicaid patients, a problem largely ignored for two decades. And a citizens’ assembly reported last month that local schools are being buried under billions in annual special education costs the state needs to assume.
Lamont insisted during the campaign and again Wednesday that he would “maintain the momentum to speed up transportation in this state.” His administration already announced plans to reduce borrowing for highway, bridge and rail upgrades.
Connecticut’s list of problems only gets longer unless the new Democratic-controlled Congress can convince President Donald Trump to reverse some of the deep cuts ordered last year to federal human services programs.
More than 60,000 residents, including almost 19,000 children, have lost eligibility for federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits since July 2025, and anti-hunger advocates want a state-funded program to assist the neediest of that group.
Many legislators and Lamont also say they want to use state funds to replace some of the nearly $300 million in healthcare tax credits Trump and Congress took away. Connecticut used $115 million last winter to assist more than 100,000 low- and moderate-income residents.
Candelora: There’s ‘enormous pressure’ on Dems to cut taxes
State House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, said Thursday, “We can have pretty good confidence they [federal officials] are going to act” and reverse some cuts, though it’s unclear how long that may take.
Meanwhile, can Connecticut maintain pre-election investments in childcare and town aid, spend more on other programs, and take big chunks out of its debt — all while delivering new tax cuts to working households and sparing the rich from any hikes?
Democratic legislative leaders declined to speculate.
“I think it’s too early for me to say where the caucus is going to be on that,” Ritter said.
“They’re going to bring [those objectives] to the caucus, and they’re going to get things done,” Duff said.
But House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said the writing is on the wall.
“There definitely was a progressive element that got elected,” said Candelora, who, like most Republicans, opposes raising taxes on one group to finance relief for another. “There is going to be enormous pressure on these people who ran on ‘affordability’” to deliver big state tax cuts.
GOP lawmakers say Democrats repeatedly ignore opportunities to cut state spending, doling out excessive raises to state workers, ignoring huge reserves at public colleges and universities and refusing to eliminate unnecessary jobs in dozens of state agencies.
Carol Platt Liebau, president of the Yankee Institute, a conservative fiscal think-tank, also fears Democratic agenda includes tax hikes when they could curb spending instead.
“One of the biggest temptations after a sweeping election victory is to assume you’ve been given a blank check,” she said. “But winning an election doesn’t repeal economic reality. Connecticut families and businesses are already struggling with high taxes, expensive energy and burdensome regulations. The last thing they need is more of the same.”
But tax reform advocates say it’s time to be realistic. Education, human services and municipal aid all need additional funds, and low- and middle-income families need relief. Addressing all of those problems could well require asking more from the state’s top earners, who faced an income tax hike in 2015.
“I don’t think voters are going to welcome a honeymoon period,” said Meghan Holden, spokeswoman for The Connecticut Project, a policy group pressing for a new state income tax credit to assist renters. “They really expect government to be ready to serve them from Day One.”
“One of the takeaways from the midterm elections should be that economic justice strengthens democracy,” said Emily Byrne, executive director of Connecticut Voices for Children. “Now we need democracy to strengthen economic justice.”
The Connecticut Project recently released a Wesleyan University poll showing more than 70% of voters back both tax-cutting options and 76% favor “increasing taxes on millionaires and billionaires.”
And Byrne notes that state government has been releasing tax fairness studies since 2014 that show low- and middle-income households pay far higher effective tax rates than do Connecticut’s top earners.
The citizens’ assembly seeking more aid for local schools and municipal budgets also recommended what many call a “millionaires’ tax.”
Rojas said he doesn’t believe Democratic legislators are predisposed to such a tax hike.
But he echoed an argument raised last month by Salisbury Democrat Maria Horn, who co-chairs the tax-writing Finance, Revenue and Bonding Committee. Simply put, that option no longer can be dismissed out of hand, Rojas said.
“It deserves its time before the legislature,” he added. “In order to arrive at a thoughtful end result, it needs to be part of the conversation.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin’s election was held without a hitch, but Dems have plans for reform
description: After months of Democratic anxiety and planning by election officials in case the Trump administration interfered with voters casting their ballots or officials counting them, Tuesday’s election in Wisconsin went off without a hitch.  The state’s prominent election deniers, including former state Rep. Janel Brandtjen, left Milwaukee’s central count facility [...]
text:
Election workers count absentee ballots at Milwaukee's central count for the 2026 midterm election. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)After months of Democratic anxiety and planning by election officials in case the Trump administration interfered with voters casting their ballots or officials counting them, Tuesday’s election in Wisconsin went off without a hitch. 
The state’s prominent election deniers, including former state Rep. Janel Brandtjen, left Milwaukee’s central count facility on Tuesday long before the city was finished counting as it became clear that Democrats had swept into trifecta control of state government, even before Milwaukee made its final vote tally. The Wisconsin Elections Commission announced Wednesday that the election was held with only minor glitches at the more than 3,600 polling sites across the state. 
“This election is a testament to months of preparation and the professionalism of Wisconsin’s election officials,” Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin Elections Commission, said in a statement. “Election officials stepped up to serve their communities and came together to run a fair, safe, and transparent election. Their hard work was evident every step of the way.”
A Trump administration official told CNN that Tuesday’s results were “too big to rig,” implying that a closer result could have led to 2020-style interference. Ahead of the election, the Trump administration had sued Wisconsin for access to the private information included in the state’s voter registration database. In other states over the past few years, federal agents had seized ballots and arrested people accused of registering to vote as non-citizens. 
Jeff Mandell, general counsel of the voting rights focused firm Law Forward, said that lawyers and advocates spent two years preparing and planning for the threat of election meddling by Trump. 
“I think that it shows how well and thoroughly the pro-democracy community had thought through all of the possibilities and prepared,” he told the Examiner. “You know, some of it might be that we thought of things, and just by thinking about them and talking about them and preparing, we foreclosed the administration doing those things. The other reality is that it looks like the will of the voters was so strong that those kinds of shenanigans were not going to move the needle, and it’s possible that the administration recognized that.” 
Trump has often questioned the results of elections and the fact that his administration did not undertake any “shenanigans” doesn’t mean that the risk of them doing so was zero. 
“The fact that it didn’t happen is something that we should all be celebrating as a democracy matter,” Mandell said. “This is good, but that doesn’t mean that there was no possibility it would happen, and it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be taking it seriously, and it doesn’t mean that it’s not to the benefit, long-term, for our democracy that we prepared.” 
Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the elections commission, said that pro-democracy organizations did a good job communicating their plans and discussions and the possible risks while not discouraging turnout. 
“While people talked about the fears that they had about something like that happening, I think there was a lot of thoughtfulness about how to talk to people about it,” Jacobs told the Wisconsin Examiner. “So it didn’t depress turnout. It didn’t convince people not to go vote, and that was a conversation I was having with lots of people at the time, and I think is a good reminder of the importance of being level-headed and keeping in mind that while there are risks of bad things happening, the important part about it is planning and reassurance.” 
Proposed democracy and voting reforms 
With the election now in the rearview mirror and Democrats in Wisconsin preparing for the start of the legislative session in January, among the issues competing for priority attention are reforms to Wisconsin’s democracy and voting system after 15 years of GOP control in which campaign finance laws were eased, restrictions on voting were advanced and the maps were skewed to benefit Republicans. 
In a statement celebrating Democrats winning control of Wisconsin’s government, former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder said it’s important they use that power to undertake some structural reforms. 
“In the face of grave, ongoing threats to our democracy, now is not the time for Democrats to sit on the sidelines. Voters are demanding that their leaders take bold action to meet the moment, and now is the time to use the power entrusted to elected leaders to level the playing field and protect the voting power of the American people,” Holder said. 
Jacobs said she’s “so excited about the idea of being able to have those discussions with the Legislature,” and that she has a list of “straightforward” proposals for making voting easier. 
First on the list,  she said, is finally passing a bill that would allow election officials to begin processing absentee ballots on the Monday before an election. She also said that she understands a large majority of Democratic voters support some level of voter ID requirements, but that Wisconsin does not have to have the strictest ID law in the nation. To make voting less burdensome, she suggested helping college students get IDs for voting without so much “rigmarole.” Current law requires that student IDs used to vote have a signature, an expiration date and an issuance date, which many do not.
Also on Jacobs’ list are expanding the period for early in-person absentee voting again. Republicans limited it to just two weeks under former Gov. Scott Walker. She added that WEC should be able to provide grants to smaller communities without the manpower or money to pay to hold in-person early voting.
“There’s a lot of things we can do that would make voting better, that isn’t a huge lift, that we could do right away. I would love to see some of these things happen promptly,” she said. 
Mandell named some of the same priorities as Jacobs while also suggesting Democrats could take bolder action to make the state’s democracy stronger. 
“I think there’s a lot of room in this state and a lot of need in this state to strengthen our democracy and make it more robust, and some of that is about addressing limits and constraints that were improperly put on our democracy during the gerrymander period, and some of that is just updating and bringing new thinking and new ideas, and I think there’s room for both of those things,” he said. 
He said Democrats should advance a nonpartisan, independent system for drawing congressional and legislative maps — a proposal that is likely going to put elected Democrats squarely between their voters, who spent years fighting for fair maps against the Republican gerrymander, and the national Democratic party, which has been in a federal tit-for-tat with Republicans on a series of mid-decade redistricting efforts. 
Ahead of the election, Wisconsin Democrats’ potential trifecta control of both houses of the Legislature and the governor’s office was often brought up in national discussions of states where Democrats could draw new maps to eke out a few more seats in the U.S. House of Representatives. 
Mandell noted that Law Forward’s lawsuit against the congressional maps is still pending at the state Supreme Court. He also suggested that the best way to enact a new map-drawing process is through a constitutional amendment, which would have to pass in two legislative sessions before going to voters. That means in order to be enacted by the time the current maps expire in 2030, that process needs to start now. 
“I do understand that there may well be pressure from D.C. and from others that maybe we should be careful to lock Wisconsin in on congressional maps,” Mandell said. “We’ve seen states around the country that have tried to walk away from some of their independent redistricting commitments in response to the White House’s unprecedented effort at mid-decade opportunistic redistricting in red states, and that’s something that’s at least worth considering.” 
 “But,” he added, “fundamentally gerrymandering is bad for voters, and that’s sort of the original sin of gerrymandering. It’s bad for voters. It undermines the value of the right to vote. So I’m not a political campaign consultant, and it’s harder for me to get into the details because I’m not as well steeped in them about the tit-for-tat of state here and state there. But you know we’re in this for voters, and gerrymandering is bad for voters. So I think we should stop gerrymandering.”
On Thursday, Sens. Kelda Roys (D-Madison) and Mark Spreitzer (D-Beloit) expressed a commitment to a fair maps process. 
“​​Having fair maps that make sure that the party that gets the most votes gets control is of the utmost importance to me, and I think to Wisconsinites, because we never want to be in a situation again where right-wing politicians essentially silence the voters and insulate themselves from any political consequence,” Roys told the Examiner. “Because we have seen how devastating that is for Wisconsin: The real harm that has been caused to our public education system, the way it’s caused our property taxes to skyrocket, the harm to farmers and small businesses. You know, it has been really devastating to have a Legislature that felt like it could do whatever it wanted, no matter how extreme and how opposed the majority of Wisconsinites were to what they were doing.”
Spreitzer echoed Mandell’s call for the maps to be handled through the constitutional amendment process and added that he hoped Tuesday’s landslide win for Democrats would discourage more mid-decade redistricting.
“The only way to get ourselves fully out of the equation is to amend the constitution, and the only way to keep a future Legislature of either party from changing it when they happen to find themselves in power after the census is to put it in the constitution,” he told the Examiner. “And we are in a position now where if we initiate a constitutional amendment this session and then hold our majorities in 2028, we could actually get a constitutional amendment on the ballot ahead of the 2030 census, and so that is going to be my goal to figure out how to do that.”
Mandell also said campaign finance reform should be a priority, pointing to the massive amounts of money that flowed into this year’s race for governor and recent campaigns for the state Supreme Court.
“When we have a governor’s race that just shattered all records, it feels like ordinary Wisconsinites are left out of this process, or left out in the sense of influence, but then sort of bear the consequences under the deluge of negative ads and mail that we all experience every election cycle,” he said. “And so I think it would be a good thing for the Legislature to take a really careful look and think about what kinds of campaign finance do we want in this state.”
Spreitzer and Roys said that voting and structural reforms are important, but with campaign promises on affordability to answer to and a state budget that will need to be passed, the timeline is up in the air. 
“Obviously, our first priority as Democrats is to restore faith in democracy by delivering for people on affordability and the economy,” Roys said. “I think that voters delivered a clear rejection of the Trump agenda, both the high costs, but also the corruption and assaults on democracy and authoritarianism. So I feel confident that my colleagues and I are going to be able to deliver for people on affordability and make a tangible difference in people’s lives and pocketbooks, and that’s going to be our very first priority to tackle in January.”
“At the same time,” she added. “I think voters are really hungry for a government that is actually responsive — and, I would say, puts what people need rather than special interests and big corporations first. So pro-democracy reforms are absolutely on the agenda. Everything from getting rid of the Walker and Vos era voter suppression laws, tackling corruption with campaign finance reform and good government measures, things that enhance the ability of people to influence their government, like national popular vote and voting rights measures, and things like fair maps.” 
Roys was the co-author of a 2023 bill that would add Wisconsin to the national popular vote interstate compact, an agreement among a number of states that have pledged to assign their Electoral College votes to the winner of the national popular vote. Since 2006, 19 states have signed on to the agreement, totaling 222 of the 270 Electoral College votes a candidate needs to win the presidency. 
On Tuesday, Democrats took trifecta control of state governments in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin, and Nevada. If all five states vote to join, that pushes the agreement to 283 Electoral College votes. 
Roys said that on Wednesday she posted online asking constituents what they want her to start working on in the new session and “hundreds” of comments and direct messages were pushing for Wisconsin to join the agreement.  
Spreitzer, who has been one of the leading Democrats on voting issues during his time in both the Assembly and Senate, said that he thinks the Legislature can tackle “low-hanging fruit” such as the Monday processing bill early in the session and then return to the broader reforms next fall after the budget is signed.
“The two years goes very quick, and we’re going to have to do a lot,” Spreitzer said. “Obviously, that’s why we’ve been trying to prepare and get bills ready and have caucus conversations on a lot of these topics”
With so many new members, he added, it takes time to get everyone on the same page.  
“But I think if I had to guess,” he said, “some of the easier things that are already fully drafted, like Monday processing, we could probably do in the first 100 days …  and then some of the more complicated, more system change kinds of things probably get more attention in the fall, post budget.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Trump will leave Kansas more progressive than he found it
description: Take yourself back to 2017, the first year of President Donald Trump’s first term.  Kansas was represented in Washington by two Republican senators and four Republican representatives. Sam Brownback served as governor, flanked by Kris Kobach as secretary of state and Attorney General Derek Schmidt — all Republicans. In the wake of Tuesday’s midterms, the […]
text:
A rally attendee watches as President Donald Trump speaks on Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Take yourself back to 2017, the first year of President Donald Trump’s first term. 
Kansas was represented in Washington by two Republican senators and four Republican representatives. Sam Brownback served as governor, flanked by Kris Kobach as secretary of state and Attorney General Derek Schmidt — all Republicans.
In the wake of Tuesday’s midterms, the Trump coalition in Kansas has buckled and tumbled.
It’s likely (if not certain) that Republicans have lost both the offices of governor and attorney general. Democratic U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids earned her fifth term. In the most historic swing in the nation, Adam Hamilton became the Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate in Kansas since 1932.
Election night brings out the hot takes, and I’ve got mine: Over two terms and 10 years, Trump made Kansas more progressive.
Trump has improbably turned a feverish red Kansas into a complicated, if momentary, purple, especially for the state’s high-profile offices.
 
On election day
Consider the Senate vote shares of Republican U.S. Sens. Roger Marshall and Jerry Moran since 2016. Moran’s electoral victories marginally tightened, from 62% of the vote in 2016 to 60% in 2022. A Trump acolyte, Marshall saw his share of the vote decline more steeply, evaporating from a comfortable win in 2020 with 53.2% of the votes to a decisive loss with 46% this year.
To gauge Trump’s effect on U.S. House races in Kansas, examine the vote shares of Republican candidates since 2016. On average, Republican candidates in Kansas earned a steady 56.6% of the vote from 2018 through 2024. This week’s election saw that average drop to 50.5% across the four House districts. 
Davids, the Democrat, enjoyed her largest margin of victory this week in eastern Kansas: 21 percentage points.
If you are tempted to pin this U.S. House performance on poor candidates, slow down. The cast of candidates hasn’t changed that much. Republican U.S. Rep. Ron Estes has been on the ballot in District 4 since 2018, gathering 62.5% of votes on average before this midterm. However, in this election, his vote share dropped 8.5 percentage points.
This midterm clearly signals that Kansans are punishing Trump and his allies.
However, it also reveals increasing comfort with Democratic candidates whom Trump opposed. 
Since Trump’s inauguration, Kansans have elected a Democratic female governor twice decisively — and perhaps once more with Cindy Holscher’s likely narrow win this week. That threepeat reads like a repudiation of Trump’s hostility toward women in government. 
Holscher in particular seems a pointed jab at Trump’s ruthless brand of name-calling politics. Genial and cheery on social media, Holscher reads like an anti-Trump personality — not just in  policy positions.
Trump’s smear campaign against Hamilton, with an additional final Kansas event two days before the election, didn’t damage the pastor-turned-senator. Maybe it helped his victory.
At campaign rallies throughout election season, Trump called Hamilton a “bad person” and “a disgrace,” before posting on Truth Social that he is a “Radical Left LUNATIC Dumocrat.” And yet, Hamilton won.
As Trump backed flawed Kansas candidates in statewide elections (between them, Marshall and Kobach have lost three general election races during Trump’s presidential era), his vitriolic presidency has recruited talented moderates to run as Democrats. Opposing MAGA seemed like a de facto campaign mission statement.
Each time Hamilton invoked his motivation as being “sick and tired of the hyperpolarization in Washington,” he was gesturing toward the president.
Kansas Democrats will benefit strategically from having the subtle hand of Hamilton in the Senate. If you think Hamilton’s campaign garnered national media attention during the campaign, just wait. An eloquent, genial senator with both folksy charm and Bible verses? Reporters and television cameras in Washington, D.C., will make him Kansas’s most visible senator. (So much for your three-term seniority, Moran.)
 
On the issues
After Trump’s loss to Joe Biden in 2020, Kansas counties did indeed swing for Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Kansas election maps showed nearly every county as a net gain in his race against Democrat Kamala Harris in Kansas that November. The only counties that shifted toward Harris were electorally insignificant.
Since then, Trump’s policies have nudged — no, shoved — Kansans away from the GOP and to the left. Prices for consumer, agricultural and industrial goods have risen, the result of Trump’s insistent tariff policies and clumsy ongoing war with Iran. (Not coincidentally, Vice President JD Vance seems suddenly allergic to that war following this week’s election.) 
Immigration raids in Kansas received critical press coverage as schools and businesses reacted to instability in communities such as Garden City. According to polling, likely Kansas voters came to trust Democrats on immigration over the past few months.
A New York Times poll during the past few weeks noted that Democrats and Republicans were essentially a toss-up among Kansans for “which candidate do you think would do a better job on immigration.” In a policy area that Republicans have traditionally dominated, polling showed Democrats with a 1 point polling advantage.
More proof? In September, Kansans who were likely voters said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of immigration more than they approved — by a margin of 7 percentage points.
With these policies, Trump activated progressive pockets of grassroots Kansas. Drive past a Tesla dealership or a No Kings rally and behold the Baby Boomers who found purpose in rebelling against Trump. Their aging hands held signs that read “Trump is a Traitor” or “Pro-America Anti-Trump.” Eight percent of Kansas voters over the age of 65 swung to Democrats in the U.S. Senate race this week as compared to 2024. 
While a small part of the Kansas electorate, Hispanic voters also broke for the Democrats by 49 percentage points over Republicans, a swing of more than 38 percentage points from 2024.
The shift among young Kansans was similarly drastic. When compared with 2024, young Kansas voters (18-29 years old) shifted their vote to the Democrat in 2026 by 35 percentage points. Among young men, the shift was almost ludicrous: 43 percentage points. 
While progressives shouldn’t count on the continued allegiance of these voting blocs (after all, they just changed their minds from 2024), their party change signals that their attachment to Trump’s Republican Party didn’t stick. 
 
Trump remains
Every hot take — even mine — demands caveats. 
Kansas has surely moved to the left thanks to Trump, but the president’s influence on Kansas politics and national elections isn’t over. 
Along with many other political writers and pundits, I long ago erroneously and repeatedly forecast (and perhaps begged) for Trump’s political demise. We have seen him as toxic, irrelevant, radioactive and guilty — but never retreating. 
The residue of Trump’s nasty and racist politics will remain in our culture and in the minds of many ardent MAGA voters in Kansas. The president synthesized the well-funded Republican political machine with a ferocious rhetoric of grievance. Voters who danced to his dog whistles are still listening.  
Many Kansans also have a loyalty to the GOP that predates Trump. Their conservatism will remain a signature of the state’s politics. (Perhaps you noted that Hamilton, the Democratic victor, invoked the name of legendary Republican U.S. Sen. Bob Dole to wild cheers during his victory speech on election night.)
Yes, Kansas rewarded some marginally liberal candidates with office this week, but that does not make it a blue state. 
During a late-night interview with the New York Times on election night, Trump sounded gutted and bedraggled. 
“I think the results were fine. … I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump said after months of alleging widespread election cheating.
He continued: “We’ll work with the Democrats. We’ll look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”
One thing is for sure: There are now many more elected Democrats for the president to cooperate with in Kansas.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Infant dies from measles as Wisconsin outbreak grows
description: A Wisconsin infant has died of measles — the first death from the viral illness since 1990, the state health department reported Thursday. The death comes as Wisconsin has experienced the largest number of measles cases in more than 35 years, Dr. Ryan Westergaard, chief medical officer for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, told […]
text:
A University of Utah health clinic sign warns visitors about the spread of measles. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services reported Thursday that an infant has died from measles in Wisconsin as the number of cases in the state has reached a level not reported in decades. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)A Wisconsin infant has died of measles — the first death from the viral illness since 1990, the state health department reported Thursday.
The death comes as Wisconsin has experienced the largest number of measles cases in more than 35 years, Dr. Ryan Westergaard, chief medical officer for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, told reporters at a media briefing Thursday afternoon.
DHS officials have not released other information about the death, citing the privacy of the family involved.
In 2026, nine people have been hospitalized with measles, and the state has recorded 431 measles cases in 13 counties. That is “almost certainly an underestimate,” Westergaard said. “Not everyone who becomes infected gets tested or comes to the attention of public health.”
The cases reported in 2026 are more than 10 times the number reported in 2025.
Ryan Westergaard, M.D., Wisconsin Dept. of Health Services
“Just last year, we reported 36 cases, and in the decade before that, most years we had either zero or one measles case per year,” Westergaard said.
“Measles was once a common childhood infection in the United States,” he said. “What brought it under control was vaccination to the point that many physicians practicing today have never seen a case. That was an extraordinary public health achievement. But it wasn’t permanent and it wasn’t inevitable that we would have that success.”
The MMR vaccine, which protects against mumps, measles and rubella, is the principal line of defense from the virus, but vaccination rates have been falling.
“Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% protective against measles,” Westergaard said. “This is a vaccine we’ve used for decades. We have extensive experience about its safety and its effectiveness.”
For maximum effect, about 95% of the population needs to be vaccinated to prevent measles from spreading easily through a community. In Wisconsin, about 85% of kindergarten-age children are vaccinated, and nationally the rate is 92%.
“And that’s really the central issue here,” Westergaard said. “Measles is now spreading because there are enough people who are susceptible to infection for the virus to continue finding new hosts.”
Vaccination rates also vary widely across the state, falling well below the 85% average in some areas.
Stephanie Schauer, Ph.D., Wisconsin Dept. of Health Services
“We have many pockets in communities throughout Wisconsin that have these lower levels, that we are concerned if measles is introduced, we could see community spread,” said Dr. Stephanie Schauer, the Wisconsin immunization program manager. “You have to really be aware of what are the rates at your school and in your community and in your county.”
Westergaard said DHS is recommending that people get the MMR vaccine if they haven’t had it. Statewide, healthcare providers have given about 42,000 doses of the shot since August, he said.  
DHS also has issued new guidance recommending that infants who are 6 to 11 months old and who are considered at increased risk of exposure to measles get an early dose of the vaccine. Westergaard said DHS has sent healthcare providers a notice about the early shot and that providers can recommend it to those patients with infants whose risk level warrants it.
Schauer said between 500 and 600 infants in Wisconsin have received the early shot in the last three months.  
Measles typically begins with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, with its telltale symptom, a red rash over the body, showing up several days later. It is not simply a childhood illness, Westergaard said. It can cause pneumonia, inflammation of the brain, permanent disability and death.
Measles is also extraordinarily contagious. The airborne virus can remain in a room for as long as two hours after an infected person leaves. When a person who’s not immune is exposed, “there’s a very high likelihood they’ll become infected,” Westergaard said.
For that reason, “we need people to recognize measles infections when they do occur and do everything we can to avoid exposing others,” he said.
Schauer said the state needs to ensure all children have access to vaccines, and that more can be done to make families aware of the Vaccines for Children program, which enables families with no insurance or  inadequate insurance to get vaccines at no cost.
Wisconsin Policy Forum graphic. Republished by permission.
Falling vaccination rates aren’t limited to the MMR vaccine.
A report the Wisconsin Policy Forum released Thursday finds that the percentage of students in grades K-12 who have met all of Wisconsin’s minimum immunization requirements for schoolchildren is at a near-record low, 87.4% for the 2025-26 school year.
That rate is up slightly from the previous year, but it’s still “much lower than the level that would provide population-wide protection against outbreaks of disease,” the report states.
The report identifies several reasons for the declining rates. They include an increased number of shots added to the list of required vaccines, the “disruption and controversy” surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent vaccines for that illness, and an increase in the number of waivers from school vaccine requirements sought by families.
The report suggests that public health officials work to target students behind schedule in their vaccines, reduce the number of “personal conviction waivers,” which parents can file if they are opposed to vaccination in order to exempt their children from school requirements, and rebuild trust with the public.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Lewiston becomes latest Maine city to restrict syringe service programs
description: Lewiston will become the state’s largest municipality to restrict syringe service programs, after a majority of voters on Tuesday opted to pass a referendum to bring back needle exchange limits. The successful citizen initiative reinstitutes a one-for-one needle exchange, mandating that syringe service providers can’t distribute more than 20 sterile syringes[...]
text:
A sharps disposal box sits beside Needlepoint Sancutary's set up at Camp Hope, an unhoused encampment in Bangor. The syringe service program hands out provisions and clean syringes along with kits containing fentanyl testing strips and the overdose reversal drug Naloxone. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Lewiston will become the state’s largest municipality to restrict syringe service programs, after a majority of voters on Tuesday opted to pass a referendum to bring back needle exchange limits.
The successful citizen initiative reinstitutes a one-for-one needle exchange, mandating that syringe service providers can’t distribute more than 20 sterile syringes per person each day. It also prohibits mobile exchange units and requires exchange programs to operate from one location.
More than 8,200 voters supported the restrictions and 5,700 opposed them, despite a coalition of public health experts, doctors and advocates campaigning against them. Research has shown that syringe service programs help in harm reduction and curb the spread of infectious diseases. The restrictions come as Penobscot County to the north has an active HIV outbreak — primarily among people who are unhoused or who use intravenous drugs — that reached 50 cases, as of Thursday.
Eryn Soule, a former city councilor who led the effort to limit syringe service programs, told Maine Morning Star, “it’s a win for Lewiston and all involved.”
“It’s a fair balance for public health,” added Soule, who on Tuesday lost an independent bid for Maine Senate. “All services (and) programs are still available just as before.”
Earlier this year, the Maine Legislature rejected proposals to limit these programs statewide. Maine removed one-for-one limits on needle exchanges in 2022, adopting new rules that allowed participants to bring in one used syringe in exchange for 100 clean ones. The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has backed the expanded program, saying limits on clean needles are not “supported by evidenced based practice, would limit access, and increase infectious disease transmission risk including HIV and Hepatitis C,” according to legislative testimony by Maine CDC Director Dr. Puthiery Va.
But some local officials — citing concerns about discarded syringes littering streets, parks and sidewalks — have pushed for stricter limits on these programs. 
Sanford passed similar limits, last December opting to temporarily halt needle distribution for a year. Portland city councilors rejected a proposal attempting to bring back a one-for-one limit in 2024, later introducing a needle buyback program to address syringe litter. Portland Public Health Director Bridget Rauscher said last year the initiative has helped reduce syringe litter by 76% and also resulted in a 58% increase in used syringe return.
